# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## AND MOST REVEREND SISTO VISDOMINI, BISHOP OF MODENA:

->Giovanni Paolo Gallucci of Salò<-
->Sends warmest greetings.<- <note>The original Latin "S. P. D." stands for "Salutem Plurimam Dicit," a standard formal greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

<image-desc>A large woodcut historiated initial letter 'O'. Inside the circular frame of the letter, a figure is seated in a landscape with trees and birds, playing a stringed instrument similar to a viola da braccio.</image-desc>

**O**F every kind of living creature, *Most Illustrious and Reverend <term>Prelate<note>Original Latin: "Antistes." A high-ranking religious official, used here as a respectful title for the Bishop.</note></term>, and not least to man, it is naturally innate to protect oneself and one's body, and to utterly avoid and escape, if possible, whatever one thinks might be harmful. That law of nature is pointed out by that famous Paulus in the writings of <term>Cicero<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE) was a Roman statesman and philosopher. This refers to the "Dream of Scipio" (*Somnium Scipionis*), where the spirit of Aemilius Paullus speaks to his son, Scipio Africanus the Younger.</note></term>, when he commands his son Africanus that he must keep his soul in the custody of the body; he must not depart from this life without the command of Him by whom the soul was given, lest he should seem to evade the human duty assigned to him by God. Nor did God wish men to know they were born under this law for this reason alone, but He also declared to us through Moses: 'Thou shalt not kill.' <note>Original Latin: "Non occides."</note> If we interpret this correctly, we will easily understand that men are forbidden not only from killing others, but even from killing themselves*

<summary>In this dedication to Bishop Sisto Visdomini, Giovanni Paolo Gallucci argues that self-preservation is a natural and divine law, citing both Cicero’s philosophy and the Ten Commandments.</summary>
<keywords>Sisto Visdomini, Giovanni Paolo Gallucci, Modena, Cicero, Dream of Scipio, self-preservation, Ten Commandments, natural law</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Sisto Visdomini, Bishop of Modena. It completes the thought from the previous page regarding the prohibition of suicide and self-harm, transitioning into a discussion on how poor health habits are a form of neglecting God's mandate, and praising the Bishop's use of both medicine and astrology to maintain his health.</meta>

...should kill [themselves]. Among the many reasons by which men flee the duty imposed on them by God through their own death, one is widely evident: that many are so enticed and dragged by the allurements of pleasure that they very frequently fall into diseases. Being thus afflicted by diseases, they do not apply the diligence they should to thoroughly drive away the body's evil ailments from themselves. From this it follows that they depart from human life before the <term>head of the household<note>Original Latin: "paterfamilias." In this context, it refers to God as the master of the world and the human "house."</note></term>, by whom they were sent into this <term>vineyard<note>Original Latin: "vineam." A biblical metaphor for the world or the field of human labor and spiritual duty.</note></term>, has released them after the day is done.

Therefore, for those who adopt this way of living, such that they neglect the precepts of Nature and of God, how can the entrance to heaven be open, and to the company of those who—having been holy while on earth—enjoy eternal life in the heavens? Rightly, therefore, you, Most Illustrious and Most Reverend <term>Prelate<note>Original Latin: "Antistes." A high-ranking religious official, here referring to the Bishop.</note></term>, so that you might recover your former health—lost through the study of sacred letters, long and most troublesome journeys undertaken for just causes, and the heavy burden of the greatest affairs—assembled the most excellent doctors in Venice. 

But also, since you know (being learned in the studies of both philosophy and sacred Theology) that Astrology claims for itself no small part in this matter, you by no means allowed what astrologers have written on this subject to remain hidden from you. For this reason, since there has come into your hands this book concerning the recognition <note>The sentence continues onto the next page with "and healing of the human body's ailments."</note>

<meta>catchword: and hea-</meta>

<summary>Gallucci argues that neglecting one's health is a failure of divine duty and praises the Bishop for consulting both elite Venetian physicians and astrological wisdom to restore his health.</summary>
<keywords>Sisto Visdomini, Venice, health and divinity, medical astrology, theology, duty to God, physicians</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Sisto Visdomini, Bishop of Modena. It concludes the translator's explanation of why he compiled these specific medical and astrological texts at the Bishop's request, framing the preservation of health as a spiritual duty.</meta>

...and for curing diseases based on the position of the celestial bodies by the most excellent doctor and <term>astrologer<note>In the Renaissance, astrology was a standard part of medical training, used to determine the best times for treatments like bloodletting or administering herbs.</note></term> Johannes Hasfurt, you wished to employ me as his interpreter (because many things are somewhat obscure and seem to require interpretation). Once these things were understood, because they seemed great and pleasant to you, you strove with urgent requests that I should not only write down the interpretation, but also deliver it to the press for the common benefit of all. Therefore, since you were the cause for these things being written and brought into the light, you ought to acknowledge, embrace, and protect them with a cheerful countenance as your own; especially because to this work, we have joined a small book by that <term>thrice-greatest Hermes<note>Original Latin: "Hermetis illius ter maximi." Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical, alchemical, and astrological texts were attributed.</note></term> on the same subject, along with another by <term>Galen<note>Original Latin: "Galeni." A 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over 1,500 years.</note></term>, the prince of doctors, together with the books of the divine <term>Marsilio Ficino<note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was an influential Italian scholar and priest who led the revival of Neoplatonism in the Renaissance.</note></term> on the <term>Triple Life<note>Original Latin: "de triplici vita." This refers to Ficino's famous work *De vita libri tres*, which offered advice to scholars on how to maintain their health through diet, lifestyle, and astral magic.</note></term>. All of these authors hand down the method of enjoying health and of curing the sick as doctors and astrologers in such a way that I think nothing more useful can happen to men for living well (if they give diligent attention to these things). For thus they are arranged, <note>Original Latin: "Sic enim positæ, quoniam suaues miscetis odores." A quotation from Virgil's second *Eclogue*, metaphorically comparing the collection of books to a bouquet of sweet-smelling flowers.</note> since you mix sweet scents. Therefore, if you do not neglect their doctrine (as you are currently doing), I have no doubt that you will not only recover your former health, but preserve it once recovered; so that you may not only fulfill the human duty imposed on you by God, but also easily sustain the greater burdens which will be imposed upon you. That

<summary>The translator explains that he published this collection of medical-astrological texts by Hasfurt, Hermes, Galen, and Ficino at the Bishop's request to aid in his recovery and benefit the public. He argues that health is essential for fulfilling God-given duties and frames the compilation as a "sweet-smelling" bouquet of wisdom.</summary>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Sisto Visdomini, Bishop of Modena. The translator is moving from the scientific and astrological justifications for the work to a more personal and political eulogy of the Bishop’s career and character, transitioning from "mathematical" (astrological) predictions to the visible evidence of his virtues.</meta>

*For I seem to see this not only from <term>mathematical reasoning<note>In the Renaissance, "mathematics" was a broad term that included astronomy and astrology. The author is likely referring to the Bishop's horoscope or the favorable alignment of stars mentioned on the previous page.</note></term>, but from those things which seem to have greater force to many. For it is quite impossible that the choir of all the virtues—which is most certain to everyone to reside in you—should perish (if virtue can ever perish) before it has fully completed its duty. And that cannot happen before you have the greatest opportunities for action. Therefore, you ought to expect the highest honors owed to your virtue. How great this upright habit of your mind truly is was recognized long ago through many proofs by the most Illustrious and Reverend Cardinal <term>Giovanni Morone<note>Giovanni Morone (1509–1580) was one of the most influential cardinals of the 16th century, a presiding officer at the Council of Trent, and a mentor to Visdomini.</note></term>, who desired you to be chosen as Bishop of <term>Modena<note>Original Latin: "Mutinensem."</note></term> and often employed you in the most important affairs for the Christian commonwealth. The entire Republic of Genoa is a witness to this, and for that reason, it holds you in memory with the greatest goodwill. Rome has known your singular learning; more than once has that city heard you debating and disputing on the most difficult matters, and it looked upon you with admiration. The most Serene <term>Alfonso, Duke of Ferrara<note>Alfonso II d'Este (1533–1597), a major patron of the arts and sciences in Italy.</note></term>, knew both your scholarship and your practical experience, and he wished for you to go as an ambassador to the King of Spain, where you displayed a specimen of your virtue to everyone. What shall I say of the whole city of Modena, which you have often taught Christian <term>piety<note>Original Latin: "pietatem." This encompasses both religious devotion and social duty.</note></term>, both through your example and your most learned and holy sermons—and which you continue to teach whenever there is need?*

<summary>The author praises Bishop Sisto Visdomini by recounting his distinguished career as a diplomat and orator under Cardinal Morone and the Duke of Ferrara, arguing that his past successes and inherent virtues guarantee future honors.</summary>
<keywords>Sisto Visdomini, Giovanni Morone, Modena, Genoa, Alfonso II d'Este, diplomacy, Renaissance virtue, preaching</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the dedicatory epistle to Sisto Visdomini, Bishop of Modena. The author finishes his eulogy of the Bishop’s character by referencing his high standing with the Duke of Ferrara (mentioned on the previous page) and transitions into a formal closing typical of 16th-century scholarly correspondence.</meta>

For [the Duke] so esteems, loves, honors, and venerates you, that it seems nothing more could be added. Finally, this is recognized by anyone who is familiarly acquainted with you—and by me especially, who respects and honors you in a marvelous way. I am rightfully silent here regarding your praises, since they are far more numerous than could be recounted by anyone in a <term>letter<note>Original Latin: *epistola*. In the Renaissance, these formal dedicatory letters were public documents meant to secure patronage and display the subject's virtues to the world.</note></term>, let alone properly extolled. 

I wish that you would continue to care for your health diligently, as you are doing; and I most earnestly desire that you count me among those who regard you with the highest veneration. 

Farewell. Venice, on the <term>Nones of September<note>The "Nones" was a marker in the Roman calendar. In September, the Nones falls on the 5th day of the month.</note></term>, 1584.

# A POEM BY XENOPHON BINDASSIUS
## FOR GIOVANNI PAOLO
## GALLUCCI.

<image-desc>A small decorative woodcut ornament featuring a central face/mask within a cartouche, flanked by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' set within a square frame with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

*Apollo, moved once by relentless prayers,*
*Wishing to aid the fields by his own art:*
*Approached his brother as a suppliant, entreating*
*That he might teach the heavenly signs to those who honor the healing power of medicine.*
*He <note>Mercury, Apollo's brother in this mythological allegory.</note> agreed, and gave to the lands one who, knowing the stars,*
*Might also know how to drive away diseases by means of those stars.*
*And he even commanded that those things received from heaven,*
*He should entrust to paper, and consult new writings.*
*He <note>Referring to an ancient author, likely the one Gallucci is editing or reviving.</note> carried out the God’s commands, but when he was taken by death,*
*His writings became obscure to others and grew stiff with neglect.*
*Phoebus <note>Another name for Apollo, god of the sun and wisdom.</note> grieved at this; "Eloquent minister of heaven,"*
*He said, "I ask that those writings of old at last be opened up."*
*Mercury, embracing his brother, said, "I shall certainly not*
*Allow your vows to be in vain; cease your prayers."*
*Then from heaven (so they say) he directed the one who sees*
*All lands and cities to the home of Neptune <note>A poetic reference to Venice, the city rising from the sea where Gallucci lived and worked.</note>.*
*And from among many known for their fame above the heavens,*
*He then chose one to whom he might give his commands.*
*Receive them then, reader; it is GALLUCCI who, by the high*
*Council of the gods, makes these things plain for you.*
*Great glory indeed belongs to the first author; yet no small amount to the second:*
*But certainly, equal glory is granted to them both.*

<note>original: "Xenophon Bindassius, Ioannes Paulus Gallucius, Apollo, Mercurius, carmen, astronomia, medicina"</note>
**Vocabulary:** Xenophon Bindassius (the poet), Giovanni Paolo Gallucci (the author), Apollo (god of healing), Mercury (god of eloquence and science), poem, astronomy, medicine.

<summary>A commendatory poem using classical mythology to frame Giovanni Paolo Gallucci as a divinely chosen scholar tasked with reviving ancient astronomical and medical knowledge in Venice.</summary>
<keywords>Xenophon Bindassius, Giovanni Paolo Gallucci, Venice, Apollo, Mercury, medical astrology, Renaissance poetry, celestial signs</keywords>

# ON
## RECOGNIZING,
### AND TREATING
### DISEASES
### From the position of the celestial bodies,
#### BOOK ONE.
#### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER I.

*It teaches what Astronomy and Astrology are, and explains that Astronomy is a science that can exist without Astrology, but Astrology cannot exist without Astronomy; it carefully enumerates the matters with which each is concerned.*

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'P' featuring two figures in a classical setting. On the left, a figure (likely an astronomer or scholar) sits by a globe, while a standing figure appears on the right. The scene is enclosed in a decorative frame with architectural elements.</image-desc>PTOLEMY, in the first book of the *Tetrabiblos* <note>original: "quadripartiti"; Ptolemy’s four-part foundational work on astrology written in the 2nd century AD.</note>, states that there are two great and principal things by which the prognostications of the stars are perfected. The first of these is the science of the Sun, the Moon, and the five wandering stars <note>The "wandering stars" refer to the planets known to the ancient world: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, demonstrating their configurations, which are made manifest through their own motions and their relationship to one another and to the earth. This subject is called <term>Astronomy</term> <note>From the Greek 'Astron' (star) and 'nomos' (law/rule).</note>, named from *Astron*, which signifies a star, and *nomos*, a rule—as if it were the science of the rules and motions of the stars. For it treats the circles and orbits of the planets and their movements. It reveals the eclipses <note>original: "deliquium"</note> of the Sun and Moon, investigates the roundness of the earth, and assigns the cause for the length or brevity of the day and night. Finally, it distinguishes the world into seven <term>climates</term> <note>In ancient geography, 'climates' were zones of latitude determined by the length of the longest day of the year.</note>. It examines the rising and setting of the zodiac signs, as well as the stars...

<summary>This page introduces the first book of the treatise, defining Astronomy as the scientific study of the laws and physical motions of celestial bodies, including planets, eclipses, and geographic climates. It establishes the work's theoretical foundation by citing Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos.</summary>
<keywords>Ptolemy, Astronomy, Astrology, Tetrabiblos, planetary motion, eclipses, celestial spheres, seven climates</keywords>

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page continues the definitions of astronomy and astrology, moving from the movement of the stars to the specific effects they have on the earthly realm. It establishes the hierarchy between the two fields, arguing that while astronomy is a complete science of "causes," astrology is the science of "effects" and depends entirely on astronomical calculation.</meta>

### BOOK
<meta>catchword: Knowledge</meta>

of the wandering <note>the planets</note> and fixed stars, and teaches the applications of one to another. And this science is complete in itself without **Astrology**, which is why one can learn **Astronomy** without involving oneself in **Astrology**.

The second matter of which Ptolemy spoke is the science by which the changes and works are explained, which happen and are fulfilled because of their natural circular configurations, within those things which the heaven surrounds. This second matter is called <term>Astrology</term> <note>From the Greek 'Astron' (star) and 'logos' (discourse or reason).</note>, from the words *Astron* and *Logos*: a discourse: as if it were a science or discourse concerning the stars. For it teaches how to predict effects: changes and works: which occur through various configurations or aspects of the planets and stars in lower things <note>The "lower things" refers to the sublunary world—the Earth and its atmosphere.</note>, such as wars, deaths, high prices <note>original: "Charistia"; referring to periods of scarcity or famine when goods become dear.</note>, rain, thunder, wind, and other accidents of this world. And **Astrology** is not by itself <gloss>1.</gloss> a complete science, but it presupposes **Astronomy**; nor can a man know **Astrology** without **Astronomy**. For **Astronomy** concerns causes, while **Astrology** concerns effects; for effects cannot be known except through knowledge of the cause. It is a certain fact that the celestial bodies are the causes of lower things; indeed, according to the diverse relationship of the stars to one another, diverse effects are prefigured in this world. Ptolemy says <gloss>2.</gloss> in the book *The Hundred Sayings* <note>Known as the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>, in the ninth saying: <gloss>3</gloss> "The faces of this world are subject to the faces of the sky." And the influence of heaven receives mutability and variability from things: first, by reason of the elements, through which it is directed to these lower things. For the air, through which the influence of the heavens passes to these lower things, does not always behave uniformly, but is unstable and changeable; whence Ptolemy said in the first book of the *Tetrabiblos*: "The element of air, in which the operation of this science occurs, is not stable nor does it remain in one state, and because of this it is difficult to understand the arrangement that occurs in the air." Second, the influence of the heavens is changed by reason of the matter in which it is received; for it is said in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s work.</note>: "Matter is the root of contingency and variation." Therefore Ptolemy rightly says in the *Hundred Sayings*, in the fifth saying: "The best astronomer will be able to prevent much evil that is to come from the stars when he has determined their nature beforehand: for thus he will forewarn the one to whom the evil is coming, so that he may be able to endure it." Third, the influence of heaven can be changed by the **Divine Will**, as is read concerning Isaiah and Elijah in the fourth book of Kings <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings, chapter 20.</note>, the twentieth chapter. One of them obtained from God through prayers the lengthening of the day, while the other obtained that it should not rain upon the earth. Hezekiah also finally obtained a lengthening of his life by fifteen years. Whence the author of *Judges* said: "The pious Creator himself, willing it, gave nature its character; that same pious one, when He wishes, makes nature limp." <note>This refers to the theological concept that while God established the "laws of nature," He remains the master over them and can cause them to deviate.</note>

## EXPLANATIONS.

1 **Complete science.** In this place, as in others where Astrology is called a science, although it relies on the principles of Astronomy, the name "science" is not to be understood in its strictest sense. The author himself seems to agree, as he teaches that events do not always correspond to the predictions of astrologers.
2 **Ptolemy in the *Book of a Hundred Words*.** <note>original: "lib. centum verborum"; a work traditionally known as the *Centiloquium*.</note> Experts do not believe this is Ptolemy’s work, but rather the work of **Hermes** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure to whom many foundational texts on alchemy and astrology were attributed.</note>.
3 **Faces.** <note>original: "Vultus"; here referring to the appearance or aspects of things.</note> Whatever happens on earth happens because of those causes that are in the heavens, except for those things which happen by the free will of either God or man; alternatively, since these earthly things are the effects of those celestial causes, they are similar to their causes. On this matter, however, see **Marsilio Ficino** <note>A famous Italian physician and philosopher of the 15th century.</note>, chapter 13, in his book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "de uita cælitus comparanda"; a seminal work on how the stars influence human health and spirit.</note>, which is included in this volume.

## EXPLANATIONS.

*That part of the heaven which the sun and the rest of the planets traverse in their own motion and course toward the East is called the Zodiac, named after the images and forms of animals that the men of old devised. To Aristotle, it is the "oblique circle" <note>original: "Aristoteli circulus obliquus"</note>. However, this differs from the other circles of the sphere because it has a width of twelve degrees.*

--- Page 39 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical classification of the Zodiac signs, transitioning from the specific medical effects of Pisces to the general mathematical and physical properties of the celestial circle. It concludes with an introduction to the planets in Chapter 3.</meta>

<header>BOOK ONE</header>

It possesses <note>This completes the description of Pisces from the previous page.</note>. First, it is divided into four parts, and each of these contains three signs. The first of these is **Aries (♈)**, which is called "mobile" <term>mobile: or 'moveable', referring to the signs that mark the start of a season</term> by reason of the change of the season of the year: for from winter, it becomes spring. The second sign is **Taurus (♉)**, and it is called "fixed," because at that time spring has its stable state. The third sign is **Gemini (♊)**, which is "common" <term>commune: also known as 'mutable', signs that bridge two seasons</term>, because the time of year then shares in both spring and summer. The same is to be said of the remaining three parts. This is what the author means by saying some signs are mobile, others fixed, and others common. Furthermore, any sign is usually divided into thirty parts; these are called degrees from the "stepping" <note>original: "gressu", meaning the progress or pace</note> of the sun. For the sun daily traverses one degree and a little more. Indeed, the sun in its annual revolution runs through the whole Zodiac, which is divided into 360 degrees, and the days of the year are nearly 365 1/4.

A "right" sign, or one of right ascension, is that with which a larger part of the equinoctial circle <term>equinoctialis circuli: the celestial equator</term> rises. An example is **Cancer (♋)**; since this is divided, as was said, into thirty degrees, thirty-six degrees rise along with it in our regions. However, signs of oblique ascension are those with which a smaller part of the equinoctial circle rises, such as **Aries (♈)**, with which only 17 degrees rise. The signs that ascend rightly are **Cancer (♋), Leo (♌), Virgo (♍), Libra (♎), Scorpio (♏), and Sagittarius (♐)**. Those that ascend obliquely are **Capricorn (♑), Aquarius (♒), Pisces (♓), Aries (♈), Taurus (♉), and Gemini (♊)**.

Masculine signs are the odd-numbered ones if you begin counting from Aries (♈); feminine signs are the even ones. They are called such by a certain similarity. For just as a man excels a woman in strength <note>This reflects the Aristotelian and medieval view of gender hierarchy commonly used in historical science to describe "active" versus "passive" forces.</note>, so also masculine signs excel feminine ones in a certain power of acting or signifying. The masculine signs are **♈, ♊, ♌, ♎, ♐, ♒**. The feminine are **♉, ♋, ♍, ♏, ♑, ♓**. The "equinoctial" signs are **Aries** and **Libra**, because when the sun enters them, the days become equal to the nights; this happens twice a year, in the months of March and September. Likewise, there are two "solstitial" signs, **Cancer (♋)** and **Capricorn (♑)**; this is because for some days before the sun enters them, and after it has entered, it seems to "stand still" <note>original: "stare"</note> by reason of its path—that is, it does not seem to progress [north or south]. When the sun enters Cancer, it is the longest day for us; when it enters Capricorn, it is the shortest.

The "nocturnal" sign and the "diurnal" sign refer to the same thing as masculine and feminine, but for a different reason. For masculine is called diurnal (belonging to the day), and feminine is called nocturnal (belonging to the night), because the day excels by far in the performance of actions, just as men excel women; so too the days excel the nights. Regarding the eastern and western nature of the signs, we shall see in Chapter 6.

## EXPLANATIONS.

<margin>Saturn</margin> is called the "greater misfortune" <term>Infortuna maior: a term for a planet that brings difficult or "malefic" challenges</term>. It is questioned whether a Christian can call any planet a "misfortune" when Moses left it written in the Bible that "everything He had made was very good." This question, if I am not mistaken, can be solved in two ways. First, they were very good when compared to the order of the whole universe, but "bad" in relation to this or that specific man who is harmed by these misfortunes. Second, they were very good then <note>At the moment of Creation.</note>, but are now bad for men because of the fault of our first parent <note>Adam, referring to the Fall of Man.</note>.

Regarding the terms diurnal <term>diurnal: belonging to the day</term>, masculine, nocturnal <term>nocturnal: belonging to the night</term>, and feminine: what was said about the Zodiac signs can be applied here as well. For where there is the most moisture, there the nature is feminine; therefore the Moon (☾) and Venus (♀) are feminine; Saturn (♄), Jupiter (♃), Mars (♂), and the Sun (☉) are masculine; however, Mercury (☿) is considered to have a shared or "common" nature.

The nocturnal planets are said to be the Moon (☾), Venus (♀), and Mars (♂); the diurnal ones are the Sun (☉), Jupiter (♃), and Saturn (♄). Mercury is common to both. Thus, it seems the same rule applies to all—diurnal, nocturnal, and feminine—except for Mars (♂). Although Mars is masculine, he is nocturnal because the moisture of the night tempers his heat, making him behave better at night than during the day.

Regarding those things in which the nature of the planets resides, not only are many listed here, but you will find more in the book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* by Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century Italian scholar and priest who revived Neoplatonism.</note>. We have taken great care to print this current booklet alongside his work for that very reason.

Mercury is "common" and takes on the nature of the planet he is joined with; if he is joined to none, he takes the nature of the house <note>The segment of the sky or Zodiac sign.</note> or the "exaltation" <note>The specific degree of a sign where a planet's influence is strongest.</note> in which he dwells.

It seems worthwhile to add what Ptolemy <note>An influential 2nd-century astronomer and geographer.</note> thinks of this matter, and what Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano, a 16th-century polymath and astrologer.</note>, a most prolific author, says, so that the reader, by observing both, may see which approaches closer to the truth and become more skilled. Thus says Valentin Naboth <note>original: "Noibodin"; a 16th-century German mathematician and astrologer.</note> on Al-Qabisi <note>original: "Alcabitium"; a 10th-century Arab astrologer.</note>.

*It is also worthwhile to understand which diseases the individual planets produce when we are dealing with illnesses here; these we have gathered from the most excellent authors, in addition to what the author himself teaches.*

From **Saturn** <note>original: "♄"</note> *arise all cold diseases that come from a downward flow of humors, such as gout <note>original: "podagra"</note>, leprosy, skin eruptions <note>original: "scabies"</note>, cancer, paralysis, wasting of the body <note>original: "tabes"</note>, black jaundice <note>original: "ictera nigra"; associated with an excess of black bile</note>, quartan fever <note>a fever that returns every fourth day, typical of malaria</note>, bowel obstruction <note>original: "illiaca passio"</note>, dropsy <note>original: "hydrops"; swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, phlegmatic catarrhs of the lungs and chest, coughing, and similar melancholic and Saturnine infirmities.*

From **Jupiter** <note>original: "♃"</note> *arise inflammation of the lungs <note>original: "Peripneumonia"</note>, stroke <note>original: "Apoplexia"</note>, cardiac pleurisy, quinsy <note>original: "Angina"; severe sore throat or throat blockage</note>, spasms or convulsions, stupor, inflammation of the liver, headaches, ailments of the spine, as well as gas in the body, fevers of the blood, and diseases that arise from wind, foul odors, or putrefactions.*

From **Mars** <note>original: "♂"</note> *arise burning abscesses <note>original: "Apostemata"</note>, acute fevers, wounds (especially to the face), sharp diseases, tertian fevers <note>fevers occurring every third day</note>, both continuous and intermittent, yellow jaundice, erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>, carbuncles, fistulas, epilepsy, dysentery, and similar hot and dry ailments.*

From **the Sun** <note>original: "☉"</note> *arise fainting <note>original: "syncope"</note>, heart palpitations <note>original: "παλμὸς" (palmos)</note>, heart distress <note>original: "καρδιακὴ" (kardiakē)</note>, spasms, red cholera <note>an excess of yellow bile</note>, ophthalmia <note>eye inflammation</note>, discharge from the eyes, catarrh, coldness of the liver and stomach, and pustules of the womb and lower parts.*

From **Venus** <note>original: "♀"</note> *arise ailments of the womb, suffocations <note>often referring to "suffocation of the womb," a historical diagnosis for various female distresses</note>, gonorrhea <note>in this period, any involuntary loss of seminal fluid</note>, diabetes, weaknesses of the liver and stomach from cold and humid causes, the "French Itch" <note>original: "scabies gallica"; a common euphemism for syphilis</note>, lientery <note>a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note>, and coldness of the stomach, etc.*

From **Mercury** <note>original: "☿"</note> *arise mania, loss of the common sense, lethargy, delusions of all kinds, stammering and speech impediments, hoarseness, the falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, coughing, excessive spitting, blockage of the gallbladder, vomiting, catarrhs from an abundance of humors in the head, and all melancholic diseases.*

From **the Moon** <note>original: "☾"</note> *arise epilepsy, paralysis, colic, catarrhs, menstrual issues, lientery, dropsy, phlegmatic abscesses, and ailments proceeding from the blockage of the veins.*

*It must be noted, however, that the planets do not produce all these diseases in every zodiac sign; rather, they produce now this one, now 그that one, according to the nature of the sign, the location in the heavens, and their aspect to the luminaries* <note>The Sun and Moon</note>.

### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 5.

> This chapter teaches which parts of the body and which diseases are subject to each of the houses of heaven; for this reason, these parts are affected for better or worse depending on the condition of the house.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' featuring a decorative floral and foliate background within a square border.</image-desc>**Experts** in the stars have divided the entire globe of the heavens into twelve parts, which they have called the "houses of heaven." Six of these are always visible above the horizon, while the other six remain hidden below the horizon; these will be treated more extensively in the following sections. Specific members of the human body are attributed to these houses individually. For instance, the first house governs the head, eyes, face, ears, <term>polyps</term> <note>original: "polipum"; growths in the nasal passage</note>, and bad breath <note>original: "oris'que fœtorem"</note>. The second house governs the neck, throat, and <term>glands</term> <note>likely referring to the tonsils or lymph nodes</note>, and so on for each, as shown below.

THE FIRST HOUSE governs the head, eyes, face, ears, polyps, and bad breath.
THE SECOND house governs the neck, throat, and glands.
THE THIRD House governs the shoulders, arms, and hands.
THE FOURTH governs the chest, lungs, <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "Isophagum"</note>, and spleen.
THE FIFTH governs the stomach, liver, heart, nerves, sides, and back.
THE SIXTH governs the lower belly with the intestines, and the colon down to the <note>original: "podicē"</note> anus.
THE SEVENTH governs the area from the navel to the buttocks, including the flanks, thighs, kidneys, and loins.
THE EIGHTH governs the bladder, the pubic area <note>original: "pectinen"</note>, the genitals, the spine, <term>tenesmus</term> <note>original: "tenasmon"; the painful sensation of needing to pass stool</note> of the ileum, <term>strangury</term> <note>original: "stranguriam"; painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>, kidney stones <note>original: "calculum"</note>, and hemorrhoids.
THE NINTH governs the <term>vena cava</term> <note>original: "caua hepatis"</note> of the liver, and the middle of the hips along with the buttock.
THE TENTH governs the lower part of the hips and the knees.
THE ELEVENTH governs the legs down to the ankles.
THE TWELFTH governs the feet along with <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagra"</note>.

BOOK I. SUMMARY CHAPTER VI.

## *It enumerates the dignities which the individual planets have in the signs—which are house, exaltation, triplicity, term, and face—and teaches which parts of the sign the individual planets rule.*

Observers of the stars attribute two types of powers or dignities to the <term>erratic stars</term> <note>original: "stellis erraticis"; the planets, so called because they appear to wander across the sky compared to the fixed stars</note>: essential and accidental. An **essential dignity** is attributed to a star by reason of its own nature, as well as the signs and fixed stars that share its nature and essence. For example, when the Sun revolves within Leo, it is said to be in its essential dignity and power, because in Leo there are many fixed stars of the Sun’s nature which strengthen its nature fivefold. The same may be said of the Moon when it is found in Cancer: for every like thing, when joined to its like, strengthens it. 

**Accidental dignity**, however, does not belong to the planets by their own nature, but comes to them either by reason of the <term>houses of heaven</term> <note>the twelve divisions of the sky relative to the horizon</note> or in comparison of one planet to another. These include the "joys" of the planets, as well as being <term>Oriental</term> <note>rising before the sun</note>, <term>Occidental</term> <note>setting after the sun</note>, Northern, Southern, <term>Almugea</term> <note>an Arabic term for a specific relationship between a planet's position and the Sun or Moon</note>, <term>Leadership</term> <note>original: "Ductoria"</note>, <term>Combustion</term> <note>original: "Combustio"; being weakened by being too close to the Sun</note>, and others which are discussed below. 

There are five essential dignities of the planets: namely, **House**, **Exaltation**, **Triplicity**, **Term**, and **Face**. When a planet is found in its own house, its influence is strengthened fivefold. But if it is found in its exaltation, its strength is quadrupled. If in its triplicity, it is tripled. If it is in its term, it is doubled. But if it possesses its face, then one power is added to its natural power.

### OF THE FIRST DIGNITY, which is called the house.

From the ancient observations of the ancestors and unique experience regarding the strength of the planets across the twelve signs of the zodiac, Capricorn and Aquarius are assigned as the dwellings of Saturn. Aries and Scorpio are the dwellings of Mars, and so on for the others, as shown in the following figure.

# THE SECOND essential DIGNITY is exaltation,
<note>original: "exaltatio"</note>
Planets have certain specific degrees within the signs in which, when they are found, they are said to be in their "exaltations." The Creator and greatest Maker (according to the <term>teachings of Hermes</term> <note>original: "Hermetis doctrinam"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of astrology and alchemy</note>) made and created these planets at the very beginning of creation in the degrees of their exaltation. <term>Ptolemy</term> <note>Claudius Ptolemy, an influential 2nd-century astronomer</note> says that the exaltation of a planet applies to the entire sign. Others, however, say they are only exalted in certain specific degrees of the sign, as shown in the following figure. The sign opposite to the sign of exaltation is called its **fall** <note>original: "casus"</note>, or the descent of the planet, or its disgrace. A planet in its exaltation is like a man in his glory, residing within his own kingdom.

# BOOK ONE. 11

### TERMS: THE FOURTH ESSENTIAL DIGNITY
The <term>TERM</term> <note>From the Latin *terminus*, meaning a boundary or limit. In astrology, these are specific subsections of a zodiac sign that grant a planet a specific type of strength.</note> is the fourth essential dignity. There are certain degrees within the signs in which, when a planet is found, it is said to be in its own term, and there its power is tripled. For example: when Jupiter is found in the first six degrees of the sign of Aries, it is said to be in its term. From there, Venus holds the term from the sixth degree of Aries up to the twelfth degree. Afterward, Mercury will possess its term from the twelfth degree up to the twentieth. Then Mars is said to be in its term from the twentieth degree up to the twenty-fifth. Finally, Saturn is said to be in its term from the twenty-fifth degree of Aries up to the thirtieth. The same applies to the other signs and planets, as the following table shows you. Note that "term" and "end" <note>original: "terminus, & finis"</note> of a planet mean the same thing. A planet located in its own term is compared to a man living among his parents, his relatives, and his own people.

The **TERM** <note>original: "Terminus"</note> is the fourth <term>essential dignity</term> <note>A system used by ancient astrologers to determine the strength of a planet based on its specific position within a zodiac sign.</note>. There are certain degrees of the signs in which, when a planet is found, it is said to be in its "term," where its power is tripled. ## EXPLANATIONS.

**1** **The Heart of the East and West.** The <term>Heart of the East</term> <note>original: "Cor orientis"</note> is that part of the heavens from which the sun rises at the time of the <term>equinox</term> <note>The two days of the year when day and night are of equal length.</note>. The **Heart of the West**, however, is where it sets at that same time. The **Heart of the South** is the place where the <term>meridian line</term> <note>A line running from north to south that marks the sun's highest point at noon.</note> divides our horizon toward the southern part. The **Heart of the North** is where that same line of the south divides the horizon in the northern part. If you turn your eyes toward those directions, you will immediately recognize which is the right side and which is the left.

In his first book on astrological judgments, Ptolemy describes the <term>terms</term> <note>Specific degree-ranges within a zodiac sign that belong to a particular planet.</note> distributed in that way; however, he more strongly approves of the division of the Chaldeans, and explains with many reasons why he was so persuaded. Therefore, I will describe these terms here, so that anyone may follow whichever system pleases them more.

No mention is made of <term>faces</term> <note>Also called decans; these are 10-degree segments of a zodiac sign, with three faces per sign.</note> in Ptolemy. However, Alchabitius <note>A 10th-century Arab astrologer whose work served as a primary textbook for medieval and Renaissance students.</note>, who concisely transmitted the doctrine of the Arabs and seems to follow Ptolemy in other matters, counts "faces" among the <term>essential dignities</term> <note>The inherent strength or "rank" a planet holds based purely on its position in the zodiac.</note> of the planets. Almost the entire crowd of recent astrologers follows his lead.

### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER VII.

*It reviews the **accidental dignities** of the planets, as they are called, omitting several that seem least necessary for his purpose. These are: **Joy**, **Friendship** and **Enmity**, **Orientality** and **Occidentality** in relation to the sun, **Hayz**, **Almugea**, **Combustion**, **oppression**, **void of course**, **being in the light**, **besiegement**, **conjunction**, **application**, **separation**, **prohibition**, **translation of light**, **return of light**, **pulsation** (or **mission of nature**), **reception**, **return of virtue**, and the **aspects** of the planets.*

But if Joy is considered in relation to the twelve <term>houses</term> <note>The twelve divisions of the sky based on the time and location of birth/event, rather than the zodiac signs themselves.</note> of the heavens, then it is an **accidental dignity**; for instance, Saturn rejoices in the twelfth house, and Jupiter in the eleventh, as shown in the following figure.

## ON THE FRIENDSHIP OF THE PLANETS.
There are also planets that love one another and those that hate one another, as the experience of the ancients has taught. And if enemy planets are joined together, they bring about contrary effects, yet according to the nature of the stronger one, as will be more clearly elucidated in what follows. But if a friend is associated with a friend, if they are **benefics** <note>original: "boni" (good). In astrology, Jupiter and Venus are the primary benefics, known for helpful and harmonious influences.</note>, their operation in goodness will be increased, nor will one resist the other in their work. However, if among friends one is **malefic** <note>original: "malus" (bad). Saturn and Mars are the primary malefics, known for challenging or destructive influences.</note> and the other is benefic, then the benefic partially mitigates the malice of the malefic; you will distinguish this friendship and opposition in the following.

the house of Saturn <note>original: "domui Saturni." This refers to the signs Capricorn and Aquarius, which Saturn rules.</note>. In a similar way, Saturn, the Sun, and other planets have houses situated opposite one another. There is also enmity between planets by reason of their **exaltations** <note>A sign where a planet’s influence is particularly high or "honored," distinct from the signs it rules.</note>; thus Jupiter is an enemy to Mars, since Jupiter's exaltation is in Cancer, and Mars's is in Capricorn, which are opposite signs. However, the friendship of planets is greater and stronger when planet agrees with planet in nature, quality, substance, and power. In this way, Mars agrees with the Sun, because both are hot, dry, and light, and Mars is the lord of the house of the Sun’s exaltation <note>Aries</note>, in which the Sun's strength appears. So also Venus and the Moon agree in coldness and moisture, and Venus is the mistress of the house of the Moon's exaltation <note>Taurus</note>. Jupiter and Venus also agree in nature and substance, which is why they are also called friends.

## ON ORIENTALITY AND OCCIDENTALI-
## ty in relation to the Sun.

A planet that rises before the Sun is called **Oriental** <note>From the Latin "oriens," meaning rising or east.</note>, while one that emerges above the horizon after the rising of the Sun shall be called **Occidental** <note>From the Latin "occidens," meaning setting or west.</note>. Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are strengthened when they are Oriental, and they are weak when Occidental. Venus and Mercury, however, are strengthened by being Occidental, and they will be weak in an Oriental rising.

There is also another dignity called <term>Hayx</term> <note>Often spelled "Hayz," this is an Arabic term for a specific type of planetary "honor" or comfort. It occurs when a planet's gender and the time of day align with its position.</note>. It is when a masculine planet is above the earth by day in a masculine sign, or below the earth at night. And a feminine planet is in a feminine sign by night above the earth, and by day below the earth. And that which is similar to <term>Hayx</term> is when a masculine planet is moving in a masculine sign, and a feminine planet in a feminine sign; and that a diurnal <note>day-active</note> planet is above the earth by day, and a nocturnal <note>night-active</note> planet is below the earth by night.

<term>Almugea</term> <note>Also called "Almugeia," this refers to a specific relative distance between a planet and a "luminary" (the Sun or Moon).</note> is said to be a "face-to-face vision" in respect to the two luminaries. It occurs when the distance between any planet and the Sun or Moon is equal to the distance between that planet’s house and the house of the Sun or Moon—such as when a planet is Occidental to the Sun and Oriental to the Moon, for the sake of example. Libra, which is the house of Venus, is the third sign from Leo, which is the house of the Sun. Therefore, when Venus is in the third sign from the Sun (counting according to the succession of the signs, as by placing the Sun in Gemini and Venus in Leo), then the Sun is said to see Venus "face to face," and Venus is then said to be in the <term>Almugea</term> of the Sun.

Regarding the Moon, you will understand it briefly thus: Virgo, which is the house of Mercury, is the third sign from the house of the Moon—namely, from Cancer. Therefore, when the Moon is in the third sign, counting from Mercury according to the succession of the signs...

In astrology, a planet is "besieged" when it is positioned between two "malefic" or harmful planets (Saturn and Mars), which is thought to restrict its positive influence.</note>. Or when Saturn is in the 10th degree of Aries, and the Moon is in the 12th degree of Aries, having separated from Saturn and moving toward <note>original: "applicans." In astrology, "application" occurs when a faster-moving planet approaches an aspect with a slower one.</note> Mars, which is located in the 13th degree of Cancer, and so on for other such cases.

**Conjunction.** A planet is said to be joined to another when it is with it in the same sign, degree, and minute; and this is the truest form of conjunction. Alternatively, when a planet "gazes" at another planet and strikes that planet's degree with its light, it is said to be joined to it. Unless it strikes the other with its light, it is not called "joined," but is instead described as "moving toward a conjunction." For example: let the Sun be in the first degree of Gemini, with its rays extending fifteen degrees, and let Saturn be in the 13th degree of the same sign. In this case, the Sun and Saturn are said to be joined. This type of conjunction is commonly used by those **forecasting changes in the weather** <note>original: "prognosticantes aeris mutationem." Astrology was historically the primary tool for meteorology.</note> and other events that happen throughout the year. However, regarding the first type of conjunction [by exact degree], this is used by those who predict the future from a person's birth <note>Natal astrology.</note>, where in the **directions** <note>original: "directionibus." A complex calculation where one degree of movement represents one year of life; thus, a tiny mathematical error results in a significant error in timing a prediction.</note> an error of one degree will cause an error of a year. Finally, there are some who interpret the conjunction of the wandering stars <note>Planets.</note> more broadly than those mentioned above; they hold that planets are joined whenever they touch each other with their rays. For instance, if the Sun is in the first degree of Aries, casting its rays out fifteen degrees, and Saturn is in the 22nd degree of Aries, casting its rays to the left to the ninth degree: in this case, the rays of both planets are joined, and therefore the planets themselves are said to be joined. From this it follows that the effects of the planets in conjunction are sometimes felt in anticipation when their rays touch—something I have very often experienced myself in the changing of the weather.

# BOOK [ONE]

**Application** <note>original: "Applicatio." In astrology, this describes a faster planet moving toward an aspect or conjunction with a slower planet.</note> is said to occur when a **lighter** <note>In traditional astrology, "light" planets move quickly (like the Moon or Mercury), while "heavy" planets move slowly (like Saturn).</note> planet is distant from a **heavier** one by only as far as its **rays** <note>original: "radij." This refers to the "orb" or field of influence surrounding a planet.</note> extend. For example, when Jupiter is in the first degree of **Taurus**, and Saturn is in the ninth, Jupiter—in this case casting its rays nine degrees forward and backward—is said to be **applying** to Saturn and seeking a conjunction with it.

**Separation**. A planet is said to be **separated** <note>original: "Separatio."</note> from another planet in a conjunction when it moves away from it by the distance of the degrees of its rays. For instance, if Saturn and Mars were joined in the first degree of **Scorpio**, Mars is said to be separated from Saturn [once it moves past]. Others say that when the lighter planet has moved away from the heavier one by even a single **minute** <note>A unit of measurement; 1/60th of a degree.</note>, it is then called separated; however, the first method is more rational.

**Prohibition** is understood in two ways. The first way is when there are three or more planets in one sign but at different degrees; in this case, the one in the middle **prohibits** the one at the lower degree from joining the heavier one until it has passed it. For example, let Saturn be in the 22nd degree of **Scorpio**, Jupiter in the 14th degree, and the Moon in the 18th degree. In this case, Jupiter seeks to be joined to Saturn, but the Moon, being in the middle, prohibits it.

The second way **prohibition** is understood concerns the **aspect** <note>original: "aspectus." An aspect is a specific geometric angle between planets (like a trine or square) that allows them to "see" and influence each other.</note>. This occurs when two planets are in one sign and the lighter one is joining the heavier one, but another planet joins that same heavier planet through an aspect. Therefore, the one that was in the same sign as the heavier planet prohibits the one making the aspect and destroys its conjunction, provided their degrees are equal. However, if the degrees of the planet making the aspect are closer to the conjunction than the degrees of the one joining in the same sign, the conjunction of the one making the aspect will take precedence, because it joins the planet before the other can. You will understand this better by an example: Let Saturn be in the 12th degree of **Virgo**, and Mars in the 8th degree of the same sign, and let Jupiter cast **trine** <note>original: "trinos radios." A trine is a harmonious aspect of 120 degrees.</note> rays from **Taurus** to the 8th degree of **Virgo**. In this case, Mars prohibits the aspect of Jupiter. But if Jupiter were to cast his rays to the 9th degree of **Virgo**, he would gaze upon Saturn and prohibit the conjunction of Mars. Yet, if Jupiter were to cast his rays to the 7th degree of **Virgo**, then Mars would be said to be joined to Saturn and would prohibit the aspect of Jupiter.

# BOOK [ONE]

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, concluding a definition from the previous page.</note> ...it is transferred, and it transfers that nature to the one to which it is joined.

In another way, **translation** <note>original: "translatio." This occurs when a fast planet moves from a conjunction with one planet to a conjunction with another, "carrying" the influence between them.</note> occurs when a **light** <note>original: "leuis." In astrology, "light" planets move quickly (like the Moon), while "heavy" planets move slowly (like Saturn).</note> planet is joined to a **heavy** one, and that heavy planet is further joined to another planet. In this case, the heavy planet transfers the nature of the light one to the planet to which it is joined. To use an example: suppose the **Moon** aspects **Jupiter**, and Jupiter also aspects **Saturn**. In this case, Jupiter transfers the nature of the Moon to Saturn.

**Returning of Light** <note>original: "Redditus Luminis." This is a specific astrological condition where a third planet acts as a bridge or intermediary for two planets that do not "see" each other directly.</note> occurs when planets are so arranged that one of them is not joined to the other, but both are joined to a certain third planet. Then, when that third planet aspects a particular place in the circle of the zodiac, it projects the light of those two planets to that aforementioned place. If any planet should be in the location of its **rays** <note>The "reach" or influence of a planet's aspect.</note>, it returns the light of those two to that planet. 

For example: let the **Sun** be in **Capricorn**, and **Venus** be in **Pisces**, with no aspect between them. Let **Mars** be in **Cancer**, aspecting the Sun by an **opposite aspect** <note>An opposition, or 180 degrees apart.</note>, and Venus by a **trine** <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, usually considered harmonious.</note>. In this case, Mars receives the light of the Sun and Venus, and returns their light to the places in the circle where the rays of Mars fall—namely, to **Virgo**, **Libra**, and **Scorpio**. For Mars aspects Virgo by a **sextile** <note>An aspect of 60 degrees.</note>, Libra by a **fourth aspect** <note>original: "quarto," referring to a quartile or square aspect of 90 degrees.</note>, and Scorpio by a trine aspect, as shown in the figure.

# BOOK [ONE]

## PULSATION or the Sending of Nature <note>original: "PVLSATIO feu Misio naturæ"</note>

This is said to occur when any of the **planets** is joined by an **aspect** <note>A geometric angle between two planets.</note> to the lord of the sign in which it is located, or to the lord of its **exaltation, triplicity, term, or face** <note>These are "essential dignities," or specific zones in the zodiac where certain planets have increased power or "rights."</note>. In this case, it "sends" the nature of the lord of that dignity to that planet which holds the dignity. For example, when the **Sun** is in **Capricorn** and aspects **Saturn** in **Virgo**, because the Sun is in the **house** <note>The primary sign ruled by a planet.</note> of Saturn, the Sun sends the nature of Saturn back to Saturn himself.

If a **light** <note>A faster-moving planet, like the Moon or Mercury.</note> planet is in its own house or exaltation, etc., and aspects a planet **heavier** <note>A slower-moving planet, like Saturn or Jupiter.</note> than itself which has no dignity in that location, the light planet is said to send its nature to the heavy one.

But if the heavier planet holds a dignity in the location of the lighter one, then the lighter planet sends its own proper nature and the nature of the heavier planet together to that heavier planet.

**Reception** <term>Reception (receptio): A cooperative relationship where a planet is "welcomed" by the ruler of the sign it is visiting.</term> occurs when planets are joined from their own houses, exaltations, or terms; they then "receive" each other. Reception from a house is the strongest, followed by exaltation, and so on through the other essential dignities. For example, when the Sun is in **Aries** (which is its exaltation and the house of **Mars**) and aspects Mars with any aspect, the Sun sends its own nature along with the nature of Mars to Mars. However, when it happens that the **inferior** <note>The faster/lower planet.</note> is in the dignity of the **superior** <note>The slower/higher planet.</note>, and the superior is in the dignity of the inferior, that is considered a complete and perfect reception.

**Restoration of Virtue** <term>Restoration of Virtue (redditus virtutis): When a planet "returns" power it cannot use due to its own weakness.</term>. This is said to happen when an inferior planet aspects a superior one that is **combust** <note>Too close to the Sun, thus "burned up" or weakened.</note>, or "under the Sun's rays," or **retrograde** <note>Appearing to move backward in the sky.</note>. In this case, the superior planet returns to the inferior the virtue which was sent to it, because it cannot retain it due to its own weakness. If both are in an **angle** <note>The 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses of a chart, which are areas of high activity.</note> or in a **succedent** house <note>The houses following the angles (2nd, 5th, 8th, 11th).</note>, the restoration will be profitable. Similarly, the restoration is useful if the inferior is in an angle and the superior is not, provided that the superior receives the inferior. A restoration is also useful when the inferior is **cadent** <note>The weakest houses (3rd, 6th, 9th, 12th).</note> and the superior is in an angle; but if both are cadent, the restoration results in loss.

**Aspects of the planets** are specific distances between planets in the locations of the **Zodiac**, in which they notably help or hinder one another. In "good" aspects they help each other, and in "bad" ones they hinder. There are four in number: **Sextile**, **Trine**, **Square** <note>original: "Quartus"</note>, and **Opposition**.

**Sextile** is the distance of the planets from one another by a sixth part of the circle; that is, by two signs or 60 degrees. By dividing the circle of the signs—that is, twelve signs—by six, you will have two signs in the quotient. Or, by dividing the degrees of the zodiac—that is, 360 degrees—by six, 60 degrees results in the quotient, which constitutes two signs.

**Trine aspect** <term>Trine (trinus): A harmonious aspect where planets are separated by 120 degrees, forming a triangle within the zodiac.</term>. This is a fixed distance of the Planets across a third part of the circle, which is four signs, or 120 degrees.

**Square aspect** <term>Square (quartus): A challenging aspect where planets are separated by 90 degrees, creating tension.</term>. This is the distance of the Planets across a fourth part of the circle, which is three signs, or 90 degrees.

Finally, the **Opposition aspect**. This is when Planets are distant across the opposite part of the circle, which is six signs, or 180 degrees.

And there is a twofold aspect: **left** <note>original: "sinister"</note> and **right** <note>original: "dexter"</note>. The **Left** aspect is that which occurs according to the succession of the signs <note>Moving forward through the zodiac: Aries, then Taurus, then Gemini, etc.</note>. The **Right** aspect is that which occurs against the succession of the signs. In this case, a Planet located in **Aries** gazes upon a Planet located in **Cancer** with a **left square aspect**, and a Planet in **Capricorn** with a **right square aspect**; and so it is for the others. And the planet which is in the right aspect is said to be **superior**, and the one in the left aspect **inferior**. For example, when **Saturn** is in **Aries** and **Jupiter** is in **Cancer**, gazing at each other in a square, in this case Jupiter is said to be inferior and Saturn superior, as seen in the following figure.

And speaking properly of aspects, a **Conjunction** is not called an aspect, since in it the planets are not distant, but are in one sign and degree. And when a planet passes another planet by one degree, it is said to be **separated** from it.

And when it is distant from it according to the number of rays <note>The "orb" or reach of a planet's influence.</note>, it is said to be **applying** <term>Application (applicatio): When a faster planet moves toward a specific aspect with a slower planet.</term> to it from a conjunction. **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century foundational authority on astronomy and astrology.</note> says that Application is not more than three degrees.

### EXPLANATIONS.

**1** **Combustion** <term>Combustion (combustio): The "burning up" of a planet's power when it gets too close to the Sun.</term>; others feel differently about this. For they think a planet is combust while it is moved toward the **Sun** <note>original symbol: ☉</note> either beyond or within the space of half the "orb" of the planet that is near the Sun. For example, if a planet were in the 15th degree of **Aries**, but the Sun was at the 3rd degree through to the 27th degree, the planet is said to be **combust**. Except while it is distant by only 16 minutes before and after the Sun, or less, which they then say is in **cazimi** <note>An Arabic term meaning "in the heart" of the Sun; the planet is thought to be strengthened rather than burned here.</note> or **in the heart of the sun**. But when it enters the Sun's orb—for instance, if it were from the end of **Pisces** <note>original symbol: ♓</note> up to the beginning of combustion—then it is said to be **under the rays** <note>original: "sub radijs"</note>, both before and after.

3. **Reception** <term>Reception (receptio): A condition where a planet is located in a part of the zodiac where another planet has "dignity" or essential power, and the two are connected by an aspect.</term>. Briefly, as they say <note>original: "sicco ut aiunt pede," literally "with a dry foot," an idiom meaning to touch upon a subject without lingering or getting "soaked" in its complexities</note>, our author speaks here of reception; for this reason, this section must also be clarified. But since **Valentinus Nabod** <note>A 16th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>, who has served the study of astrology well in his commentary on **Alcabitius** <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer whose work was a standard textbook in European universities</note>, explains this matter clearly enough, I would like you to hear him speaking as follows: 

**Reception** occurs when a planet existing in its own **dignity** <term>Dignity (dignitas): The essential strength a planet has based on its position in the zodiac (such as being in its own Home or Exaltation).</term> gazes upon another planet which holds a dignity in that same location. For example, if the **Sun** is in **Aries** (which is the **House** of **Mars** and the Sun's own **Exaltation**) and sees **Mars** in **Capricorn** via a **Sextile** aspect <note>original: "✶," the symbol for a 60-degree aspect</note>, then the Sun communicates both of its natures: its own, and the nature which Mars holds in Aries by reason of it being his House. 

If an "inferior" planet <note>Planets closer to Earth, like Venus or Mercury</note> exists in the dignity of a "superior" planet <note>Planets further away, like Saturn or Jupiter</note>, and vice versa—the superior in the dignity of the inferior—then a **mutual and perfect reception** occurs, such as the **Sun** being in **Aries** and **Mars** being in **Leo**. In this case, the Sun is in the House of Mars, and Mars is in the House of the Sun.

It should also be noted that **mutual reception** holds the first (most powerful) place. The second place is held by non-mutual reception, but based on the **House**; the third place is from **Exaltation**; the fourth from **Term**; and the last place is held by **Face**. 

<term>Term (terminus): A subdivision of a zodiac sign, usually one of five unequal parts, where a specific planet holds power.</term>
<term>Face (facies): Also known as a Decan, this is a 10-degree subdivision of a sign (each sign having three "faces"). This is the weakest form of essential dignity.</term>

### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER VIII.

He defines the **House of Heaven** <term>House (domus): One of the twelve divisions of the sky representing specific areas of life, such as wealth, health, or marriage.</term>, and teaches which signs are **Northern** and which are **Southern**. He shows which planets benefit the houses by their presence and which affect them poorly. He distinguishes the twelve houses into four parts and relates them to the four ages of man and the seasons of the year.

**THE CELESTIAL HOUSES** <term>Domus Coeli: In astrology, the "houses" are twelve divisions of the sky representing different areas of life (such as wealth, travel, or career). Unlike the zodiac signs, which are always 30 degrees, houses can vary in size depending on the system used.</term> is a twelfth part of the firmament <note>The "firmament" refers to the vault of the heavens or the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, consisting of unequal degrees. For when the northern signs <term>signa septentrionalia: The signs from Aries to Virgo, which are north of the celestial equator.</term> rise, the houses are larger and encompass more degrees than when the southern signs <term>meridionalia signa: The signs from Libra to Pisces, which are south of the celestial equator.</term> seek their rising. 

For example, under a polar elevation <note>A historical term for geographic latitude</note> of 50 degrees, when the beginning of Aries rises, the 22nd degree of Taurus falls at the second house. But when the beginning of Libra rises, the 23rd degree of Libra falls at the cusp <note>The boundary line or starting point of an astrological house</note> of the second house. Likewise, when the beginning of Taurus ascends in the east, the tenth degree of Gemini will arrive at the second house. However, when Scorpio touches the eastern line, its 24th degree will enter the second house; and so it goes for the others, where one house always possesses more degrees in the northern signs than in the southern.

The **FIRST house**, which begins from the rising of the Sun <note>This refers to the Ascendant, the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, signifies life, the body of the newborn in nativities <term>nativities: birth charts</term>, and the person of the inquirer in questions <term>horary questions: a branch of astrology where a chart is cast to answer a specific question</term>, as well as the sick or the infirm. The first lord of this triplicity <term>triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element (fire, earth, air, or water). Each triplicity has three "lords" or planetary rulers</term> signifies the life of the newborn, what they love and hate, and what good or evil shall meet them in the beginning of life. The second lord of the triplicity indicates life, the body, and what will happen to them in the middle of life. Finally, the third lord of the triplicity signifies what ought to happen to them in the final age of their years.

The **second house**, which is also called the "infernal gate" and "anaphora" <note>Greek for "rising up" or "carrying up"</note>, signifies substance, livelihood, servants, helpers, wealth, trade, and the increase of possessions. The first lord of the triplicity of this house signifies substance in the first part of life; the second in the second part; and the third in the third part. It is called the "lazy place" <note>original: "locus piger"</note> because it is joined to the Horoscope <note>In this period, "Horoscope" often referred specifically to the first house or the Ascendant point</note> by no radiation <note>meaning it does not form a major geometric "aspect" like a square or triangle to the first house</note>.

The **third house** is called the "Goddess" <note>original: "Dea"</note>. It indicates brothers and sisters, friends of the same, religion, commands, messengers, changes of place from one to another, journeys, relatives <note>original: "nora," likely a variant of "notos" or "cognatos"</note>, kin, letters, all sects, and heretics; it is joined with the Horoscope by a sextile aspect <term>sextile: an aspect of 60 degrees, usually considered harmonious</term>. The first lord of this triplicity signifies the elder brothers; the second, the middle ones; the third, the younger.

The **fourth house**, which is called the "Bottom of Heaven" <note>original: "Imum coeli"</note> or the "Pit of the Earth," signifies fathers, parents, fields, houses, lands, waters, grandfathers, and all ancestors and direct descendants. It signifies all immovable things which are beneath the earth or above the earth, all buildings, the labor of buildings, towers, cities, castles, hidden treasures, and all inheritances except those of the dead. This house also signifies medicine in the case of illness; along with its lord, and according to the mind of Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, a famous 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>, the end of the sick person and the illness is taken from the fourth house. This house is placed in the fourth aspect <note>a square aspect of 90 degrees</note> of the ascendant. The first lord of the triplicity signifies fathers; the second, cities and lands; the third, the end of things and prisons.

The **fifth house** is called "Good Fortune" <note>original: "bona fortuna"</note> because Venus rejoices in it. It signifies children, messengers, gifts, joy, clothing, papers...

Indeed, the fortune of any house is greater and more stable when a planet suited to it blesses it, and its misfortune will be judged greater and of more damage when it is harmed by a planet suited to harming that house. For example, when the Sun is in the **fourth house** (the house of the father), it blesses it more because the Sun is more suited to this house than if Jupiter or Venus were located there.

Finally, the twelve houses of the heaven are distinguished into four parts, each of which is composed of three houses.

The **first part**, which is composed of the twelfth, eleventh, and tenth houses, is called the eastern quarter. It is masculine, youthful, sanguine <note>Referring to the "sanguine" temperament associated with blood, air, and a cheerful disposition</note>, vernal <note>original: "vernalis," relating to the spring</note>: and it signifies the beginning of life.

### EXPLANATIONS.

1. Regarding what the author says about the meanings of the **lords of the houses**, he has drawn from the teachings of the **Arabs**. <term>Alcabitius</term> <note>original: "Alcabitius"; the Latinized name of Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer whose "Introduction to the Craft of Astrology" was a foundational textbook in Europe</note> teaches the same thing, attributing three lords to each of the **triplicities** <note>groups of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element</note>, just as our author has done. **Ptolemy**, however, followed a different reasoning, and it will be no trouble to write his words here in English <note>original: "latinè"; the text transitions into a Latin translation of Ptolemy’s Greek work, the *Tetrabiblos*</note>:

"The first of these [triplicities] is drawn through **Aries**, **Leo**, and **Sagittarius**, three masculine signs which are the houses of the **Sun**, **Mars**, and **Jupiter**. This triangle is assigned to the Sun and Jupiter; Mars was excluded because of his differing nature <note>original: "alienam conditionem"; referring to Mars's status as a 'malefic' planet which did not fit the sect of the Sun and Jupiter in this specific grouping</note>. In the administration of this triplicity, the Sun takes the lead by **day**, and Jupiter by **night**. The location of Aries is equinoctial, Leo is of the summer, and Sagittarius is of the winter. This same triangle is primarily **Northern** because of the lordship of Jupiter, who is the author of fertility and of breaths <note>original: "spirituum"; often referring to the 'pneuma' or vital winds</note>, just like the northern winds."

And a little later: "The second triangle is drawn through **Taurus**, **Virgo**, and **Capricorn**; because it consists of three feminine signs, it is given to **Venus** and the **Moon**." Then, after some intervening remarks, he says: "The third triangle, **Gemini**, **Libra**, and **Aquarius**, encompasses three masculine signs. It is entirely foreign to Mars, but belongs properly to **Saturn** and **Mercury**." After other points, he says of the fourth: "The fourth, through **Cancer**, **Scorpio**, and **Pisces**, is left to **Mars**, who alone remains, and who claims the right to this for himself because of his house <note>Scorpio is the traditional home of Mars</note>. However, the **Moon** by night and **Venus** by day are joined to him as associates in administration, both because of their nature and because these are feminine signs." All of this is depicted in this table:

| Triplicity | Signs | Rulers |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Fiery** | Aries (♈), Leo (♌), Sagittarius (♐) | The **Sun** (☉) by day; **Jupiter** (♃) by night. |
| **Earthy** | Taurus (♉), Virgo (♍), Capricorn (♑) | The **Moon** (☽) and **Venus** (♀). |
| **Airy** | Gemini (♊), Libra (♎), Aquarius (♒) | **Saturn** (♄) and **Mercury** (☿). |
| **Watery** | Cancer (♋), Scorpio (♏), Pisces (♓) | **Mars** (♂), joined by the **Moon** (☽) by night and **Venus** (♀) by day. |

*It presents a twofold way in which the complexion <note>original: "complexio"; the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's physical and mental temperament</note> of the human body, as they say, can be discerned, one of which is derived from the cause; the other from the effects, to which one must resort when the first is missing. # ON RECOGNIZING AND HEALING DISEASES
## From the Position of the Celestial Bodies,
### BOOK TWO.
### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER I.

*He presents a twofold way by which the human body’s <term>complexion</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "complexion" or "temperament" referred to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual, which determined their health and personality</note>, as they call it, can be identified. One way is derived from the cause; the other from the effects, to which one must resort when the first is lacking. The first derives knowledge from the <term>birth chart</term> <note>original: "natalicio themate"; a map of the sky at the exact moment of a person's birth</note>, while the second comes both from the human figure and colors, as well as from the emotions of the mind. He affirms that this latter method is the primary one in the order followed by physicians.*
