### BOOK <note>likely the Second Book, continued from the previous page</note>

...they show whether the one born is a child of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, or the Moon.

A **Saturnine** person <note>Someone born under the dominant influence of the planet Saturn</note> has a large, unattractive face, average-sized eyes <note>original: "oculos mediocres"</note> looking down toward the ground, one larger than the other, and a spot or deformity in one of the eyes. They have thick nostrils, thick lips, joined eyebrows, and hair that is black, hard, rough, and somewhat curly. Their teeth are uneven, and they are commonly beardless or have sparse hair in their beard; elsewhere on the body, especially around the chest, they are hairy. They are sinewy and lean with dry skin, long legs, distorted hands and feet, and cracks in their heels. The body is of moderate size, honey-colored <note>original: "melleique coloris"; a yellowish-pale hue</note>, and quite foul-smelling—like goats—as is said to appear in the Jews <note>This reflects a common medieval and early modern antisemitic stereotype that associated Jewish people with the "melancholic" and "foul" traits of Saturn</note>. In their <term>complexion</term> <note>The balance of bodily humors</note>, coldness and moisture predominate. However, when Saturn is occidental <note>Setting in the west after the sun</note>, the person will be emaciated, small-bodied, with thin and flat hair, black eyes, and a dry temperament.

But regarding the soul, those of Saturn are given to much deep reflection and good counsel, and their advice can hardly be improved upon. They are rarely fond of people, but when they do begin to love, their affection is intense; and when they hate, they pursue their hatred most vehemently, and can hardly be moved from it. They are easily angered and retain that anger for a long time. They are gluttonous and heavy drinkers, heavy-bodied, walking with a slow gait, greedy, fraudulent, deceitful, unjust, treacherous, thieves, practitioners of magic and sorcery, very stingy, and silent—speaking little or not at all. They are also usurers, burying their money in the earth, and spreaders of evil and of novelties—though they pretend they bring such news against their will. They walk about sadly, having no confidence in God or men, leading a solitary life and seeking out corners.

## BOOK 2

...and in them joined eyebrows: signs or spots on the face.

As for the mind, the son of the **Moon** will be a wanderer: unstable, running here and there; forgetful; fearful; small-souled <note>original: "pusillanimus"; lacking courage or spirit</note>; a revealer of secrets; a lover of delightful things; loving spells, histories, stories, and banquets. He is universally unstable, adaptable to all things, and is of no service. For the most part, such people are **phlegmatic** <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>The "cold and moist" temperament, associated with the humor of phlegm; it was thought to make a person passive, slow, or calm</note>: for which reason they grasp a thing quickly but quickly commit it to oblivion, nor do they retain it for long. They desire sexual intercourse little, but are capable of much; they rejoice in sleep, and are made lazy and heavy in their walking, hardly daring, and not at all generous, being mockers and deriders.

> Sleep captures the phlegmatic, and much laziness,
> He spits much from his mouth, he coughs with much effort:
> The sense is dull, the face fat, a white color clings:
> Under the command of the Moon: an informer <note>original: "delator"</note>: great in body:
> He is fickle, and chaste, bathed in whiteness.
<note>This poem summarizes the medieval medical view of the phlegmatic person, whose "cold" nature was thought to produce excess fluids (spitting/coughing) and a pale, "white" appearance.</note>

However, the natures and **complexions** <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined a person's physical and mental health</note> of mortals vary according to the diversity of regions and places. For a cold region will increase the effect of a cold complexion but diminish a warm one, and a warm region will increase the effect of a warm complexion and diminish a cold one. A region that is equal and temperate will harmonize with the effect of a temperate complexion: such as the regions that are under the **equinoctial circle** <note>the equator</note>, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard medical text in Europe for centuries</note> proves in his chapter on Complexions.

Suppose, then, someone was born in **Venice**, whose birth had the following celestial constitution.*

# [BOOK] SECOND.

Medicinal WEIGHTS are determined according to average grains of wheat, and they vary first according to the difference of provinces: for the *kist* <term>xestes</term> <note>original: "Kist"; a liquid measure, here discussed in terms of its weight equivalent in grains.</note> is one thing among the Greeks, and another among the Italians. The Greeks take a *kist* for 20 grains, and the Italians for 18. Secondly, they vary by reason of the medicine itself: because a *chus* <note>An ancient Greek liquid measure.</note>, or *congius* <note>An ancient Roman liquid measure.</note> of wine is 9 pounds, but a *chus* of honey is 12 and a half pounds. And a spoonful <term>cochlear</term> of honey is 4 *aurei* <note>original: "aurei"; literally "gold pieces," used here as a weight standard.</note>, but a spoonful of medicine is one *aureus*. Thirdly, they vary by reason of the different authors. For Nicolaus <note>Likely Nicolaus Salernitanus, author of the influential medieval "Antidotarium Nicolai."</note> says a *Sextarius* is 2 and a half pounds. But Serapio <note>An Arabic medical authority (Yahya ibn Sarafyun) whose works were fundamental to medieval European medicine.</note> says a *sextarius* is 3 and a half pounds and 2 *danics* <note>An Arabic unit of weight, usually one-sixth of a drachm.</note> or 4 and 5 *aurei*.

But for the sake of harmony, you should know that when a *kist* is found in a Greek book, the Roman *kist* should be used, namely 20 grains. But in Italian books, the Italian *kist*, which is 18 grains. And when a *sextarius* of wine or oil is found in Nicolaus, let 2 and a half pounds be used. But if a *sextarius* of poppy or something else is found in Rhazes, or in Serapio, or Avicenna, let it be 6 drachms and 2 *danics*. And whoever wishes to know this diversity of weights, let him read the authors of Medicine, and especially Serapio at the end of his *Breviary*, and Saladinus of Ascoli in his *Compendium for Apothecaries*, Part 3.

And I have placed here these weights which occur daily in the practice of medicine, such as the Scruple and the Drachm, as shown below, which are composed of grains of wheat and not of barley—unless barley is specifically mentioned, as if one were to say "5 grains of barley." Otherwise, you should always understand grains of wheat, according to Saladinus. Nevertheless, almost all practitioners commonly use grains of barley, and they take 16 ounces for one pound.

## SUMMARY OF CHAPTER III.

*When the Physician wishes to cure a disease which is in the whole body, let a fortunate sign of Libra <note>The Scales; associated with balance and equilibrium in the body.</note> arise [on the horizon], and let the Moon (☽) not be in the horoscope <term>ascendant</term> <note>The "horoscope" here refers to the specific degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of treatment.</note>; let it nevertheless be well-disposed by the "good" planets, and not in conjunction (☌) with the lord of the ascendant or the lord of the eighth house; nor should it be descending. If you wish to cure a chronic <note>original: "veterem"; literally "old" or long-standing.</note> disease, let the Moon be in Taurus (♉), or in its triplicity <note>The group of three signs belonging to the same element; for Taurus (Earth), these are Virgo and Capricorn.</note> and well-disposed, and in one of the angles. If it is a recent disease, let it be in Cancer (♋), or Aquarius (♒), and especially in Pisces (♓). If the disease is in a specific limb, make the rising sign the one that rules that limb which you wish to cure; let the sign and its ruler be well-disposed, and let the Moon be increasing in number and light when you wish to heal the afflicted members; and thus the Moon should be in a suitable part of the heavens, and the text teaches which part this should be.*

<margin>1</margin>
If the patient's sickness is in the whole body, and the learned physician wishes to heal this sickness, let him set the sign of Libra at the horoscope, and let it be fortunate without any "infection" from the "malicious" planets <note>The "malicious" or "malefic" planets are typically Saturn and Mars, thought to cause harm in astrological medicine.</note>; similarly, let the lord of Libra (which is Venus) be so disposed. And beware in curing every disease that the Moon is not in the horoscope; let it be elsewhere in a fortunate aspect, such as in trine or sextile <note>Trine (120 degrees) and sextile (60 degrees) were considered harmonious and helpful planetary alignments.</note> with the fortunate planets, and let it not be joined with Jupiter. For Ptolemy says in the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "centiloquio"; a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to the astronomer Ptolemy.</note>: "If anyone takes a purgative <term>laxative</term> while the Moon is with Jupiter, its action will be shortened and its effect diminished." One must also take care in every cure that the Moon is not in conjunction (☌)...

5 Furthermore, every sickness that occurs from the head down to the <term>groin</term> <note>original: "pectinem"; literally the pubic bone or the pelvic region, serving as the anatomical midpoint in this system.</note> is cured while the Moon is moving from the <term>angle of the earth</term> <note>Also known as the *Imum Coeli* or the 4th house, the lowest point of the chart.</note> toward the <term>midheaven</term> <note>The *Medium Coeli* or 10th house, the highest point of the chart.</note>, which is the ascending part of the sky. However, if the Moon moves through the other houses, it will be cured with difficulty.

You should always take care, however, never to touch a limb with iron <note>referring to surgery</note> or fire <note>referring to cautery</note> while the Moon is in the zodiac sign that governs that specific limb. In applying other types of cures, the presence of the Moon in those signs is not avoided.

->EXPLANATIONS.<-

1 One who is not constantly practiced in astronomical matters will not easily find at what hour a certain sign—be it **Libra**, **Taurus**, or another—rises or climbs above our horizon. Because we wish to be helpful to everyone, we provide here a double method by which this can be known without any labor. One method is by using an **ephemeris** <note>A table showing the daily positions of celestial bodies.</note>; the other is by the following **rotula** <note>A "little wheel"—a paper instrument with moving parts used for calculations.</note>, which is highly suited for this and many other purposes. First, then, regarding the ephemeris: I seek to understand today, the 10th of June 1584 (the day I was writing this), at what hour the first degree of **Libra** will rise above our horizon so that I may drive out a disease from someone's body that is greatly harming the whole person. This is how to proceed: First, find the sign of **Libra** in the tables of houses for the latitude of 45 degrees (for I was writing in **Venice**, which is at that latitude). Look for it under the heading of the "ascendant." In that row, in the column titled "Time from Noon," I see that the first degree of **Libra** (which I want to rise) corresponds to 6 hours and 4 minutes. I write this time down separately. Then, I look in the ephemeris and see that on June 10th, the Sun is at 19 degrees of **Gemini**. I enter the tables of houses again with this degree, looking for 19 degrees of **Gemini** in the tenth house; the time from noon that corresponds to it in the time column is 5 hours and 12 minutes. I write this below the first time I found and subtract it from the one above. The remainder is 0 hours and 52 minutes. This will be the hour after noon on that same day in which the first degree of **Libra** was rising. If you wish to convert this time to our clock hours, see what hour noon is, which then was...

*You will also be able to do this by another method, and more easily, by the following **small wheel** <note>original: "rotula"; a paper instrument with rotating parts, also known as a volvelle.</note>, which I am about to teach after I have explained its individual parts, so that the instruction may be clearer: especially since understanding it is of the greatest use for many other things which are treated in this booklet.*

*The first part of this figure is that larger wheel, which is immobile and is bound together with the other pages of the book. This is divided into 24 equal parts, and the numbers are inscribed from 1 up to 24. The first number is on the right side, and the order of the numbers is written through the lower part of the wheel toward the left side, in the astronomical manner. These numbers indicate our <term>Italian hours</term> <note>Unlike modern hours that start at midnight, "Italian hours" began at sunset. Hour 24 (or 0) was the moment the sun went down.</note>, which begin from the setting sun and end in the same place.*

*Above this is placed another wheel, but smaller, on the edge of which is the same division into 24 hours; however, it does not begin from the sunset like the upper one, but from the <term>meridian line</term> <note>The line representing high noon.</note>. These are the hours used by astrologers, and the <term>ephemerides</term> <note>Tables showing the daily positions of celestial bodies.</note> are written according to these hours.*

*There are, furthermore, three circular lines or three circumferences. The first is where those semicircular lines end which are in the area of the circle, and this indicates to us the <term>Tropic of Capricorn</term> <note>original: "♑"</note> of the sphere. The other is narrower than this and divided into 12 equal parts, and this is the **equinoctial line** <note>The celestial equator.</note>. The third is narrower still and is entirely covered by that smaller wheel, and this is the <term>Tropic of Cancer</term> <note>original: "♋"</note>.*

*There are also two straight lines whose ends touch the Tropic of Capricorn and divide each other at right angles in the center of this second wheel. The one inscribed at one end with the number 10 and at the other with 4 is the **meridian line**. The one that divides this is the **horizon in the Right Sphere**. There are five other semicircular lines which, along with these two, divide the equator line into twelve equal parts and the whole sky into **twelve houses** <note>The divisions of the sky used in astrology to determine the influence of planets on different areas of life.</note>, each of which is inscribed with its own numbers, so that the first is to the left and in the opposite order to how the hours are written.*

*Furthermore, that line inscribed **HORIZON** divides the six houses which are above the earth from those six which are below the earth; it is the **Horizon of our Oblique Sphere** at a latitude of 45 degrees. There are also several lines made of points [dotted lines], which we will speak of at another time. The outermost line of the third wheel (even smaller than the other two) is the **ecliptic line**, properly divided into twelve parts, marked with the signs of the **Zodiac**, and distributed into 360 degrees.*

->On the use of this little wheel.<-

This figure offers us a manifold use, but omitting those which are of little use for either understanding our author or for performing what he teaches, we will explain: at what hour of the day any part of the Zodiac rises for us; how, once the hour of the day is known (whether after noon or by the clock), the <term>celestial theme</term> <note>original: "cæleste thema"; a chart or horoscope showing the positions of the stars and planets at a specific moment.</note> may be drawn up immediately; and how it can be easily seen daily at what hour the sun rises and reaches the <term>meridian</term> <note>The highest point in the sky reached by a celestial body.</note> according to <term>Italian Hours</term> <note>A system where the 24-hour day begins at sunset.</note>, and at what hour it sets and rises according to <term>Astrological Hours</term>—and not only the sun, but the remaining planets as well. S E C O N D [B O O K]. 29

...pertains to the first objective proposed: a physician wants to know when the sign of Libra will begin to rise on the 21st day of December, 1584. First, one must look in an <term>ephemeris</term> <note>A table providing the calculated positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals.</note> to see what part of the Zodiac the Sun occupies on that day; I find it to be in the first part of Capricorn. I locate this part on the smaller wheel and on the ecliptic line, and I align the <term>line of trust</term> <note>original: "lineam fiduciæ"; a straight-edge used for alignment.</note> over it. Next, these two parts are rotated so that the point where the line of trust divides the ecliptic reaches above the Horizon on the right side (which is on the second wheel). Then, these two wheels are rotated together with the line of trust until the line of trust falls upon the beginning of the first hour of the first wheel, which is the larger one. Once you have done this, use a little wax to fix the second wheel onto the third so they remain immobile. Likewise, fix the line of trust upon the Zodiac wheel with wax or by some other means. Afterward, turn the Zodiac wheel along with the line of trust until the first degree of Libra <note>original: "♎"</note> rises on the left side. The line of trust will then show you on the larger wheel the hour of the clock, and on the second wheel the hour after noon or the <term>astrological hour</term> at which the sign of Libra will begin to rise on December 21, 1584. For it will be the 12th hour after noon by the Sun clock, namely at 7:45 in the middle of the night. <note>The author is navigating between different systems of time-keeping used in the 16th century, such as "equal hours" from a mechanical clock and "astrological hours."</note> This method is easier and faster than others performed with numbers and calculations; although it is not as precise, it possesses enough accuracy for the business at hand.

## How the celestial theme is erected.

Of all the complaints that physicians level against astrologers when they are urged not to undertake the care of any man without first inspecting the <term>celestial theme</term> <note>original: "cæli themate"; a horoscope or chart of the heavens.</note> of the hour of the patient's <term>decubitus</term> <note>original: "decubitus"; the moment a patient first takes to their bed due to illness, considered vital for prognosis.</note>—nor to bleed a vein, nor administer treatment, nor use baths, nor do anything else for the sake of healing unless the heavens seem favorable for it—the main one is that there is not enough time for physicians, who treat many sick people, to cast a celestial figure for each one. I wished to help this situation as much as I could by providing a way in which they might be able to accomplish this easily. But first, let us teach how it is cast, specifically at noon. First, the position of the Sun is observed in the ephemeris. Then, the line of trust is aligned over the position of the Sun <note>original: "☉"</note> at noon of that day on the ecliptic, as was said above, and the point where the line of trust divides the ecliptic is placed over the Horizon line, and the line of trust falls over the first part of the first hour of the first and larger wheel. Then, let the second wheel and the first remain in the same position, joined by wax. Next, let the line of trust and the Zodiac wheel remain together in their position, yet in such a way that they can be rotated together. Afterward, they are rotated until they reach the beginning of the first hour after noon, which is on the second wheel. Finally, let all the wheels be fixed so they do not move from their place at all. When this is finished, see which degree of the ecliptic falls upon the tenth house, and transfer that into a <term>quadrangular figure</term> <note>The standard square-shaped astrological chart used in the Renaissance.</note> as is the custom; likewise, see which falls upon the eleventh, and so on for the remaining lines, and thus you shall have

...twelve houses <note>The twelve divisions of the sky in an astrological chart, each governing different aspects of life or health.</note> have been constructed. Then, you should distribute the planets through the signs as you will see written in the <term>ephemeris</term> <note>A table of calculated celestial positions.</note>. While keeping all parts beneath the **line of trust** <note>original: "linea fiduciæ"; the movable straight-edge or pointer on the instrument.</note>, you will find the hour of noon on the larger wheel. Turn the line of trust again above the Horizon, and you will see on the larger wheel, beneath the line of trust, the setting of the sun. If you do the same on the left side, the line of trust will show you the hour of sunset on the larger wheel (as has been said often), and on the smaller wheel, the <term>astrological hour</term>.

If you wish to erect a <term>celestial theme</term> <note>A horoscope or birth chart.</note> at other hours of the day, just as you turned the line of trust to the line of noon, so turn it to your hour of the clock, and you will achieve your goal. For you will see which degrees of the zodiac run with the lines of the twelve houses; you should copy these into a square figure, as was said regarding the figure to be erected at noon. 

For the sake of example, I wish to erect a celestial figure on the 21st day of December at the 21st hour of the clock. First, I fit the second and third wheels with the line of trust (as was said above) using wax; then I attach the second wheel to the first, and the line of trust to the small wheel containing the zodiac. Afterward, I rotate the line of trust, thus attached, to the beginning of the 21st hour. Finally, I observe which degrees of the zodiac are above the tenth house, and I find it at the 5th degree. I find Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄</note> at 11 degrees 22 minutes; Jupiter <note>original symbol: ♃</note> at 12 degrees 20 minutes; Mars <note>original symbol: ♂</note> at 1 degree 10 minutes; Aries <note>original symbol: ♈</note> at 2 degrees 22 minutes; Taurus <note>original symbol: ♉</note> at 3 degrees 18 minutes; and Gemini <note>original symbol: ♊</note>. In the opposite houses, you place the opposite signs. Once found, you must copy these onto a small page prepared for this purpose, as was said of the others.

However, so that you may record the planets without great labor, and with a method sufficiently accurate for a physician, I believe it should be done this way: write down all the planets in the manner they are found in the ephemeris, except for the Moon. Because the movements of the other planets are slower, they cannot cause error for a prudent physician. For the Moon <note>original symbol: ☽</note>, however, see what hour it is after noon on the wheel, as we have taught, and for every two hours, add one degree to the position of the Moon found in the ephemeris; place the Moon in that spot in the figure. In this way, you will easily have what you seek.

<margin>2</margin> Take care that the Moon is not in <term>opposition</term> <note>An astrological aspect where two bodies are 180 degrees apart, often considered difficult.</note> to the lord of the sixth or eighth house. For the lord of the eighth house, if poorly positioned, threatens death according to the <term>genethliaci</term> <note>Astrologers who cast birth charts (from the Greek 'genesis').</note>, and the lord of the sixth house threatens disease. If the lord is poorly positioned, it is always made worse by a <term>square</term> <note>original symbol: □; a 90-degree aspect.</note> or <term>opposition</term> <note>original symbol: ☍</note> from the Moon. A question arises here as to which lord of the 8th or 6th house is meant: the one from the time of birth, or the one from the celestial figure of the illness currently being suffered. I believe he is speaking of the figure of the illness, since he wishes to heal those whose hour of birth is unknown, as he taught in the previous sections. Nevertheless, if you have both the person's birth chart and the celestial theme of their birth—since all things (as Ptolemy and the entire school of astrologers believe) depend on that beginning and sprout from that root—it will be useful to ensure that the Moon is not poorly affected by the lords of those houses, or that the Moon does not affect them poorly, along with those factors present in the figure of the illness.

...or for the other houses, as you ought to find first in the <term>ephemeris</term> <note>A table showing the daily positions of celestial bodies.</note> what we wish to ascend in the tables of houses under the title of the first house. Thus, if you wish for some sign to be at or enter the second house, you would find it under the title of the second house, and so on for the remaining houses. However, with our <term>rotula</term> <note>original: "rotula"; the small rotating wheel on the instrument.</note> it may be done as follows. Suppose today is the 2nd of June, and I wish to know at what hour the 10th degree of Taurus <note>original: "♉"</note> reaches the <term>cusp</term> <note>The line or point that marks the beginning of an astrological house.</note> of the second house. First, I enter the ephemeris and seek the position of the Sun <note>original: "☉"</note>. On the 11th of June <note>The text shifts from June 2 to June 11 in the example.</note>, I find it to be at the 20th degree of Gemini <note>original: "♊"</note>. Next, I align the **line of trust** <note>original: "lineam fiduciæ"; the movable pointer or rule on the instrument.</note> over that same degree on the smaller wheel, upon which the Zodiac is distributed.

Afterward, I align that same point—formed by the intersection of the line of trust and the line of the ecliptic—over the Horizon line on the right side. Furthermore, while keeping these three parts fixed and moving them all together, the line of trust must fall over the first part of the first hour on the larger wheel. Finally, once the line of trust is fixed with wax or by some other means over the Zodiac, and the wheel of the celestial houses (which is closer to the first, that is, the larger wheel) is rotated over that larger wheel, you must move the Zodiac with the line of trust until it reaches the tenth degree of Taurus—which we want to reach the second house. Then the line of trust will show you on the larger wheel the hours of our clock, which will be nearly six hours elapsed. On the second wheel, however, which shows the hours from noon, you will see that almost twelve and a half hours have elapsed when the 10th degree of Taurus reaches the cusp of the second house. Use this same method for the other signs and houses.

<margin>4</margin> Let the Sun be "increased in number and light." For the sake of <term>beginners</term> <note>original: "tironibus"; students or novices in astrology.</note>, let us undertake an explanation of this matter. Look in the ephemeris of the most distinguished young man Giovanni Antonio Magini <note>original: "Antonij Magni"; referring to the famous astronomer and mapmaker (1555–1617).</note> or in others, for the position of the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "☽"</note>, and consider the distance of the Moon from the Sun. If this distance, when doubled, is less than a semicircle, then the Moon is "increased in number"; if it is greater, it is "diminished"—greater, I say, than a semicircle if it exceeds the number of 180 degrees, for a semicircle contains that many degrees.

Any planet is said to be "increased in light" while either the planet moves forward from the Sun, or the Moon moves from a planet. For instance, the Moon is said to be increased in light, or to grow in light, from the moment it leaves the Sun's orb—which we have said, according to Cardano <note>original: "Cardanum"; referring to Girolamo Cardano, the famous 16th-century polymath.</note>, is 17 degrees—until it reaches <term>opposition</term> <note>original: "☍"; when the Moon is 180 degrees from the Sun, i.e., a full moon.</note> with the Sun. It is "diminished in light" from the opposition until the <term>conjunction</term> <note>The new moon.</note>.

<margin>5</margin> Regarding the "descending Moon": once the figure of the heavens has been made as we advised above, look in the ephemeris to see which part of the Zodiac the Moon is in. Then, in the <term>erected theme</term> <note>A cast horoscope or chart.</note>, look at where that part of the Zodiac is located in the figure, and you will have your answer. For if the Moon is between the tenth and the fourth house, it is descending; if it is between the fourth and the tenth, it is ascending.

# SECOND BOOK

*...the significator of the ascendant or of the sick person. The House in which the unfortunate planet <note>In astrology, "unfortunate" or "malefic" planets—usually Saturn or Mars—were believed to cause harm or illness when poorly positioned.</note> is located signifies the affected part of the patient; if the <term>Almuten</term> <note>The planet that holds the most "dignity" or power over a specific degree of the zodiac.</note> is unfortunate and above the earth, the disease is on the right side; if below the earth, on the left; if in a sign of long ascension, it is in the whole body; in a sign of equal ascension, in the heart. In a sign of short ascension, it is a wasting <note>original: "diminutio"; a shrinking or weakening.</note> of a limb. The "Part of Infirmity" <note>A mathematical point in a chart used to locate disease, calculated by measuring the distance between two celestial points and adding it to a third.</note> is taken from the degree of the Lord of the Hour to the degree of the Sun <note>☉</note>, and is projected from the beginning of Aries <note>♈︎</note>. It also teaches that the disease can be known from the sixth house <note>Traditionally the house governing sickness and servants.</note>, its lord, and the planet from which the Moon is separating. He explains all these things with an example.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a scholar or physician in robes and a cap seated on a bench or chair within an interior space.</image-desc>

IF the hour in which the sickness first troubled the patient is known to you, let a <term>celestial figure</term> <note>A horoscope or chart showing the positions of the stars at a specific moment.</note> be erected for that hour, as is customary. From there, let the Almuten be observed over the ascendant, over
<margin>1</margin>
<margin>2</margin>
the Sun and Moon, and the lord of the <term>Part of Fortune</term>, and the Lord of the Hour; he himself shall be the significator of the sick person. According to his state of strength or weakness, the weakness or strength of the patient is indicated. Let it be seen in which of the houses this
<margin>3</margin>
Almuten is afflicted. It indicates that the infirmity is in that limb signified by the house: giving the ascendant <note>The first house.</note> to the head; the second house to the neck; the third house to the hands and shoulders, as was held in the first treatise. And this infirmity will be of the nature of the afflicting house—namely, the one which looks upon them with a better aspect. And if the Almuten or significator is afflicted above the earth, the infirmity is on the right side. But if it is afflicted below the earth, the sickness is on the left side. And if it is in a sign of long ascension—which are Leo, Virgo, Cancer, Sagittarius, Scorpio, and Libra—the infirmity will be in the whole body. And if it is in a sign of equal ascension, say that the infirmity is in the heart. And if it is in a sign of short ascension, say that the infirmity is a wasting of a limb. Furthermore, the "Part" through which the location of the infirmity may be known is taken from the degree of the Lord of the Hour to the degree of the Sun, and is projected from the beginning of the sign of Aries; and where the count ends, say that the infirmity is in the limb of that sign.

A bodily sickness attacked a certain person in the year 1529, on the fifteenth day of December, after noon, at one o’clock and 30 minutes, in the <term>hour of the Moon</term> <note>In planetary hours, each hour of the day is ruled by a different planet; this system was vital for timing medical treatments.</note>. I wished to know the <term>Almuten</term> <note>The planet that holds the highest score of "essential dignities" (power based on its zodiacal position) at a specific point in a chart.</note> of the sick person. I examined which of the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note> had more essential dignities in the Ascendant, the location of the Sun, the location of the Moon, etc. 

And I found that Saturn had no dignity in Taurus at its 19th degree, which was rising at the hour of the sickness; I found that Jupiter has the <term>term</term> <note>A subdivision of a zodiac sign; a planet in its own "term" gains a small amount of dignity or strength.</note> there, for which I gave him two dignities. I found Mars has his <term>detriment</term> <note>original: "exilium" (exile); a sign where a planet is weakened because it is opposite the sign it naturally rules.</note> there, and the Sun has no dignity. But I discovered that Venus has her <term>house</term> <note>The sign where a planet is "at home" and most comfortable; Venus rules Taurus.</note>, from which I assigned her five dignities. After this, I found Mercury had no dignity. Finally, the Moon had her <term>exaltation</term> <note>A sign where a planet’s influence is heightened or "honored"; the Moon is exalted in Taurus.</note> in Taurus, for which she is supported by four dignities; she also had the <term>triplicity</term> <note>A grouping of three signs belonging to the same element; Taurus is part of the Earth triplicity.</note>, for which I gave her three dignities, so that the Moon had seven total dignities in

These illnesses arise from a "cold and moist" cause <note>The author is using the system of Humors; cold and moist conditions were often associated with phlegm or stagnation.</note>.

I also looked at the "Part of the Place of Sickness" and found it in Virgo (♍), which corresponds to the belly and the intestines; therefore, I said he also suffered pain in these, which is the teaching of Haly <note>original: "Hali"; refers to Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose work was central to European medical astrology.</note>. 

However, illnesses are commonly identified from the sixth house, and so on. According to this method, because of Virgo in the sixth house, he will similarly suffer in the belly, as will the lord of the sixth. Mercury, being in the ninth house and in Capricorn (♑), shows that he suffers in the liver and hips, or suffers from "Mercurial illnesses" which we have discussed previously. Nevertheless, Jupiter being in the sixth house foretells that the sick person will emerge safely and recover from all these illnesses.

### 2. And to the lord of the hour.

Many methods can be taught for finding the "lord of the hour," but because we strive for brevity, use the same instrument you used previously to cast the celestial chart. First, however, you must notice that on the second disk (where we said the twelve houses of heaven are located), there are also several dotted lines marked with the numbers 1 through 12. These indicate the twelve planetary or "unequal" hours <note>Unlike our modern 60-minute hours, "unequal hours" divide the periods of daylight and darkness into 12 parts each. Thus, a summer day-hour is much longer than a winter day-hour.</note>. To know which hour it is at a given time, you must first set the disks as I taught above. 

For example, if you want to know the unequal hour for the 13th day of August at the 21st hour according to our <term>Italian clock</term> <note>The "Italian Clock" or "Bohemian hour" system started the day at sunset, counting 24 hours until the next sunset.</note> in Venice: first, look up the position of the Sun (☉) in the ephemeris, which is the 20th degree of Leo (♌). Then find that degree on the smaller disk marked with the signs of the zodiac and place the <term>fiducial line</term> <note>The fiducial line (linea fiduciae) is the straight edge or pointer on an astronomical instrument used for precise alignment.</note> over it. Take the intersection made by the fiducial line over the ecliptic and place it over the Western Horizon. Then rotate these two disks along with the fiducial line until the line falls on the beginning of the first hour on the larger disk. 

Afterward, fix the second wheel onto the first with a little wax, and the fiducial line over the smallest. Rotate this until the fiducial line falls on the beginning of the 21st hour on the larger disk. With everything fixed in this way, the <term>Nadir of the Sun</term> <note>The "Nadir" here refers to the point directly opposite the Sun's position in the zodiac (180 degrees away).</note>—that is, the degree opposite the Sun's location—will show you the hour, which is the 8th hour and almost a half; it is therefore the time of the 9th hour. 

To know the "lord" of that hour, you must do the following: first, consider what day of the week it is. In this case, it is Monday (the Day of the Moon). The lord of the 1st hour is the Moon (☽); the 2nd, Saturn (♄); the 3rd, Jupiter (♃); the 4th, Mars (♂); the 5th, the Sun (☉); the 6th, Venus (♀); the 7th, Mercury (☿); the 8th, the Moon (☽) again; and the 9th, Saturn (♄). Therefore, Saturn (♄) is the lord of this hour. Note also that if you wish to do this at night, the Sun's position will show you what its Nadir did by day. 

You will find this lord more easily through the following tables: enter the table of unequal hours of the day, and at the top, look for the hour found by the disks (which is the 9th hour). On the left side, look for the day (Monday). At the meeting point of the two, Saturn (♄) is present as the lord of the hour. If you also want the nighttime hours, use the table of unequal hours of the night, and you will achieve your desire.

### *...whether soon or late; and it teaches the way by which you may know on what day and at what hour the stars signify death to him.*

<margin>1</margin>
<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'S' depicting a figure seated in a landscape setting with trees.</image-desc>
**I**f you desire to know whether a sick person <note>original: "infirmus"</note> will survive their illness, look at the hour in which the sickness first seized them, or at the <term>hour of the question<note>The "hour of the question" refers to horary astrology, where a chart is cast for the exact moment a specific question is asked of the practitioner.</note></term>. Observe the Sun, the Moon, and the <term>Almuten of the Ascendant<note>The "Almuten" is the planet that holds the most combined dignity and power over a specific degree of the zodiac—in this case, the sign rising on the eastern horizon (the Ascendant).</note></term>. If you find them free from <term>malefics<note>original: "infortunijs"; refers to planets like Saturn and Mars which were traditionally believed to bring bad luck or hardship.</note></term>, and if they do not "aspect" <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between planets that determines how they influence one another.</note> the Lord of the <term>House of Death<note>The Eighth House of an astrological chart, which governs death and decay.</note></term>, you may be certain that he will recover from his ailments. Even if only two of these are so disposed, he shall still recover.

But if even one of these two significators is safe from the malefics, and the other two have no aspect with the Lord of the House of Death, he will likewise recover. However, if two of them are afflicted by a malefic planet that happens to be the ruler of the Fourth, Eighth, or Second Houses, the sick man will undergo death. If it is the Almuten of the Ascendant, or the Moon—and especially if they are the "ruler of the time" (that is, if the illness begins at night, which the Moon governs, or if the Sun is the ruler of the time)—and they are joined with malefics or with the Lord of the House of Death, or in a bad aspect to him, the patient will die. If the Moon or the Lord of the Ascendant is joined to Saturn, the sickness will be prolonged. If the Lord of the Ascendant is "under the earth" <note>Below the horizon in the astrological chart.</note> and the Moon is joined to a planet located in the Third, Sixth, Ninth, or Twelfth houses, it indicates death. If the Lord of the Ascendant is joined to the Lord of the Eighth House and the Moon is "impeded" <note>Weakened by a bad position or a harsh aspect from another planet.</note>, or similarly if the Moon is joined to the Lord of the Eighth and the Lord of the Ascendant is impeded, he shall not easily escape death. If the Lord of the Ascendant is <term>received<note>"Reception" occurs when a planet is located in a sign of the zodiac over which another planet has secondary or primary rule.</note></term> by the Lord of the Eighth House, but the Lord of the Ascendant does not receive the Lord of the Eighth, it indicates a dangerous but not fatal sickness.

But if the Lord of the Ascendant or the Moon "receives" the Lord of the Eighth, he will scarcely be delivered from death.

If any planet "transfers the light" <note>A term for when a faster planet moves from an aspect with one planet to an aspect with another, essentially connecting their influences.</note> of the Lord of the Ascendant to the Lord of the Eighth, there will be fear that the sick man is in great peril; nevertheless, he may be delivered through the good care of those standing by and the physician.

The Lord of the Ascendant located in the Eighth House, received by the Lord of the Eighth without being received back, indicates recovery after a state of despair. But if the Lord of the Ascendant "receives" him, it portends death.

If the Lord of the Eighth is "heavier" <note>Moving more slowly in its orbit compared to the other planet.</note> than the Lord of the Ascendant, and they are joined so that the Lord of the Ascendant receives the Lord of the Eighth, it foretells death. This will be the same even if they look upon each other by any aspect, even a <term>Sextile or Trine<note>Harmonious aspects of 60 or 120 degrees; the author suggests that even "good" aspects can be fatal if the planetary "reception" involves the house of death.</note></term>.

# BOOK 2

**I**

<meta>catchword: 3 The Lord</meta>

The Lord of the Ascendant <note>original: "Dominus ascendentis"; the planet that rules the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time of the chart.</note> being located in any of the <term>angles<note>The "angles" are the four most powerful houses in an astrological chart: the 1st (Ascendant), 4th (Imum Coeli), 7th (Descendant), and 10th (Midheaven).</note></term> indicates death. This is true when the Lord of the Eighth House reaches the degree of the Ascendant at the hour the question was asked or the sickness began, or when the Lord of the Eighth reaches the degree where the Lord of the Ascendant had been standing.

If the Lord of the Ascendant is also the Lord of the Eighth House <note>The Eighth House is traditionally the "House of Death."</note>, it foreshadows death when it reaches the degree where the Lord of the Eighth was located. If the Lord of the Eighth House is in the Ascendant, and the Lord of the Ascendant and the Moon are <term>afflicted<note>original: "impediti"; hindered or weakened by a difficult relationship with a "malefic" planet like Mars or Saturn.</note></term>, the sickness will increase greatly and the patient will be in danger, but they will escape through good care.

If the Lord of the Ascendant is "below the earth" <note>This refers to the half of the chart below the horizon line, representing the night side.</note> and joined to the Lord of the Eighth in the fourth house—or if it is "above the earth" in the eighth house, joined to the Lord of the Eighth and <term>receiving<note>original: "recipiens"; "Reception" occurs when one planet is in a sign governed by another, creating a supportive relationship between them.</note></term> it—this indicates death. However, if it does not receive it, and the Lord of the Ascendant does not receive the Lord of the Eighth, but the Lord of the Eighth receives the Lord of the Ascendant, the illness will grow heavy and the patient will be in danger of death, but they will be set free.

If the Lord of the Ascendant and the Lord of the Eighth do not "aspect" each other <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between planets that allows them to communicate or influence one another.</note>, but some other planet "transfers light" between them, and the Lord of the Ascendant is in a <term>cadent house<note>A "cadent" house is one of the weaker areas of the chart (the 3rd, 6th, 9th, or 12th houses), suggesting a lack of strength or vitality.</note></term> while the Lord of the Eighth is in one of the angles, it signifies that the sick person will die. If the Lord of the Ascendant is one of the superior planets <note>Mars, Jupiter, or Saturn.</note> and is <term>combust<note>original: "combustus"; a planet is "combust" when it is so close to the Sun that its influence is overwhelmed or "burned up" by the Sun's heat.</note></term> thirteen degrees or less before the Sun, or four degrees or less after the Sun; or if it is one of the inferior planets <note>Venus or Mercury.</note> and is three degrees or less before the Sun, or fourteen degrees or less after the Sun, it foretells death. Yet, if the Lord of the Ascendant is "received" by the planet it is joined to, the patient will be delivered from death after all hope is lost; they may even seem to be dead when they are not. The Lord of the Eighth House in the fourth house, if it is unfortunate, indicates death. The Moon with Mars in the fourth house, if not protected by a beneficial planet, indicates death. The Moon in the "combustion" of the Sun also indicates death. If a malefic planet is in the degree of the Ascendant, or within two degrees of it, it is a sign of death. To determine the timing, look at the number of degrees of that distance: if they are in <term>moveable signs<note>Aries, Cancer, Libra, or Capricorn; signs that represent change and quick movement.</note></term>, count the days; if <term>fixed signs<note>Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius; signs that represent stability and long duration.</note></term>, count months or weeks.

There is great fear for the sick person when, at the hour of the question or the hour they first took to their bed, both <term>luminaries<note>The Sun and the Moon.</note></term> were below the earth.

The <term>Part of Fortune<note>A calculated point in a chart representing well-being and prosperity.</note></term> located below the earth near the <term>Tail of the Dragon<note>original: "cauda Draconis"; the South Node of the Moon, traditionally associated with loss or decrease.</note></term> within four degrees, or in the eighth house, is an evil sign. If the Moon is in an unfavorable place in a fixed sign, the disease will be prolonged; in a moveable sign, they will be healed quickly; in a <term>common sign<note>Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces; signs that represent transition.</note></term>, they will be healed in a moderate amount of time, or the sickness will transition from one disease into another. A malefic planet in the Ascendant, or a malefic Lord of the Ascendant, signifies that the sick person will be poorly managed and will bring harm upon themselves.

The Lord of the Ascendant or the Lord of the Sixth House <note>The Sixth House governs sickness and the physical body.</note> being <term>retrograde<note>Appearing to move backward in the sky, which weakens a planet's power.</note></term>, combust, or in the house of death, joined to Mars or Saturn by a bad aspect, is a sign of evil and death.

Lord of the Ascendant, Lord of the Eighth House, death, Moon, Mars, Sun, combustion, Part of Fortune, Tail of the Dragon, moveable signs, fixed signs, sickness.

# SECOND [BOOK]

**I 2**

And it is necessary, if you wish to make a more certain judgment, to combine those things which you have recognized in the <term>figure of the disease</term> <note>The "figure of the disease" refers to a decumbiture chart, cast for the moment a patient first takes to their bed.</note> (as the author says, and as we have stated above) with the factors found in the <term>figure of the birth</term> <note>The natal chart or horoscope of the patient.</note>.

5. A planet is "swift in course" when its daily motion is greater than its average motion; if it moves less than that, it is called "slow." To determine this, find the daily motion of the planet in this manner: subtract the position of the planet on the day you wish to know from its position on the following day. The remainder from that subtraction will be the daily motion. For example: on the 11th day of June, 1584, the Moon is at 1 degree and 20 minutes [of Leo]. On the 12th day, it is at 16 degrees and 1 minute. From this, the position of the Moon on the 11th is subtracted as follows:

<margin>
16 [deg] : 1 [min] Leo
1 [deg] : 20 [min]
-------
14 [deg] : 41 [min]
</margin>

->Day 12: 16 degrees, 1 minute of Leo<-
->Day 11: 1 degree, 20 minutes [of Leo]<-
->-------------------<-
**Daily Motion** <gloss>5</gloss> <gloss>14 : 41</gloss> --- **of the 11th day: 14 degrees, 41 minutes.**

Therefore, the daily motion of the Moon on the 11th day is "swift," because it exceeds the average motion of the Moon itself, which is only 13 degrees, 11 minutes, and 27 seconds.

The <term>Almuten</term> <note>The planet that holds the most essential and accidental dignity (influence) over a specific degree or house in a chart.</note> of the ascendant: this was discussed in Chapter 4.

# BOOK SECOND

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a landscape with a building or tower and some foliage.</image-desc>

HAVING UNDERSTOOD and known which illnesses the patient suffers and in which member, and from which causes and <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health.</note> they arise, there follows the canonical and regular process to be held in curing the sick. And first, we speak of Lenitives <note>Medicines used to soften the body's tissues or act as mild laxatives.</note>. For before a physician administers <term>digestives</term> <note>Medicines intended to "cook" or prepare the humors for elimination.</note>, it is first necessary that he opens the passages and leads out the matter, and he reduces these through lenitives so that the dregs and common matter do not mix with the medicine, enter into its power, and weaken its strength and operation.

A lenitive medicine warms with temperance, so that by its operation it does not dissolve much, and its dryness is equal to its heat; and according to Galen <note>A Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose medical theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, in the fifth book of *Simple Medicines*, chapter 8: Lenitive medicine, which he calls "rarifying" <note>original: "rarificantem"; making the humors or tissues less dense.</note>. It is warmer than the heat of the limb, and it dissolves some of the humidity, yet not so much as to attract the subtle parts, and it dries out the remainder. And it is called lenitive because it softens or mellows a hard limb or hardened matter.

There are some lenitives that are strong, some moderate, and some light, with which one must first begin; for the light ones are more like food than medicine, and are given to the delicate. Among these are two or three soft-boiled eggs with sugar, taken an hour or half an hour before lunch. The second lenitive is to give 5 or 6 Damson plums <note>original: "pruna damascena"</note> before dinner. The third is to give 15 grains or one handful <note>original: "M. 1." likely "manipulus"</note> of fat black raisins. The fourth is to give 5 or 6 fresh figs, or 5 or 4 fat dried figs <note>original: "Caricas"</note> before food; or let the figs be boiled down and given in this way: Take one part white figs and ten parts water; let them be cooked over a slow fire until they reach the proper consistency <note>original: "statum regulæ"</note>, and give about 3 ounces <note>original: "℥ 3"</note> of this daily to those who are constipated.

A useful electuary <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note> for the elderly who have a hard belly: Take cleaned Safflower seed <note>original: "Seminis Carthami"</note> and Anise, 2 ounces of each; 30 fat, cleaned white figs; let them be pounded very finely in a wooden mortar. Take 3 ounces of Baurach <note>An ancient term for borax or nitre, used here as a laxative.</note>; grind and incorporate everything with the figs and clarified honey; and if they cannot be well incorporated, mix with them as much of the fig-water decoction as is sufficient; give a quantity the size of an egg in the morning.

Another lenitive: It is the broth <note>original: "brodium"</note> of a fat chick or hen, if given an hour before lunch. Another is broth of chickpeas or broth of cabbage, which is made thus: Take cabbage in the morning, before the dew is removed from them,

And lenitive medicine warms with moderation, so that by its action it does not dissolve much, and its dryness is equal to its heat; and according to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity whose theories dominated medieval medicine.</note>, in the fifth book of *On Simple Medicines*, chapter 8, [he describes] *Lenitive medicine*, which he calls "rarefying." # EXPLANATIONS.

1 **You should choose ruminant signs.** <note>original: "signa ruminantia." These are astrological signs associated with animals that "chew the cud" (regurgitate), specifically Aries, Taurus, and Capricorn. In medical astrology, it was believed that performing an emetic treatment while the Sun was in these signs would help the patient's body "bring up" the medicine and the toxins.</note> The author is going to say in the following sections that if a sick person drinks or eats a medicine while the Sun [☉] is in ruminant signs, they will eject the medicine. Therefore, when you wish for them to vomit, you must choose these times. You can determine when the Sun is in these signs from an **ephemeris** <term>Ephemeris: A table or book providing the daily positions of the Sun, Moon, and planets for a specific period.</term>.

2 **In the middle of the sky.** Once a chart of the heavens has been made, as we taught above, you will not only know at what hour the sign you desire rises, but also whether the Lord of the Ascendant <note>The planet that rules the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment.</note> is in the **Midheaven** <note>The highest point in the sky on an astrological chart, representing success and strength.</note> or not; and finally, you will recognize all other things handed down here concerning the selection of timing for vomiting.

## SUMMARY OF CHAPTER IX.

> Those things that evacuate downwards fall into two types: they are either **suppositories** or **clysters** <term>Clyster: An early form of enema used to inject fluids into the lower bowel for medicinal or cleansing purposes.</term>. Suppositories are either natural or artificial. Natural ones are either mild, strong, or moderate, and the author teaches which these are. Artificial ones are fourfold, and he treats them here.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter P. It depicts a figure in long robes, likely a scholar or physician, standing and holding a book, symbolizing the academic nature of this medical instruction.</image-desc>
After discussing those things that evacuate upwards, we must now speak of those that, when administered below, soothe and evacuate at the same time, such as Suppositories and Clysters. Beginning with suppositories, I say there are two types: Natural and Artificial. Natural ones are classified in three degrees: Mild, Strong, and Moderate.

Among the **Mild** substances are **Blite** <note>original: "Blitis," a leafy green similar to spinach or beets.</note>, **Cabbage** <note>original: "Caulis."</note>, and **Mercury herb** <note>original: "mercurialis," specifically *Mercurialis annua*, a plant long used as a gentle laxative.</note>, including the roots, the young shoots, and the stalks. These are shaped like a suppository and smeared with honey. Another is made from **lard**, both sweet and salted, but the salted is more highly praised; for by reason of its fatness it soothes, and by reason of the salt it stimulates the body's expulsive power. Another is made from **salted cheese**, which by reason of the milk soothes, while the salt incites the [body's] strength. It could also be made from unsalted cheese smeared with honey, which is effective against worms. Another is made from **mouse dung**, which greatly stimulates the expulsive power in both children and adults. Human blood, once

...once dried and formed into the shape of a suppository, it is effective. Finally, **barley sugar** <term>Penidiae: A twisted sugar candy, often used as a mild laxative or base for medicines.</term> used as a suppository in patients is very effective against worms, but this is more an artificial preparation than a natural one.

Moderate suppositories that are not "artificial" <note>The author distinguishes between "simple" preparations and "artificial" (compounded) ones.</note> consist either of honey alone, or of honey and salt. Take note of this **Rule** regarding this: for 1 ounce of honey, use 1 drachm or a half-drachm of salt. Boil them well over a fire. The prescription is written as follows: Take 1 ounce of honey and 1 drachm of salt; let the honey boil until it is cooked to a thick consistency. You may, however, take more or less salt depending on how much you wish to **sharpen** <note>original: "acuere" – to make the medicine more potent or irritating to the bowel to trigger a movement.</note> the effect. Pour it onto a stone slab or a polished wooden board and form suppositories the length of a little finger. They can also be made from egg yolk, salt, and a little saffron wrapped in a linen cloth. Or they may be made from white soap with **lard** <term>Axungia: Animal fat, usually pig lard, used as a base for ointments or to ease insertion.</term>, and this is one of the stronger types. Others are made from **rock salt** <term>Sal Gemma: Pure crystalline salt, valued in pharmacy for its drawing properties.</term>, or alum, or from the root of the **squirting cucumber** <term>Cucumeris asinini: A plant known for its violent purgative effects; the fruit literally "squirts" its seeds when ripe.</term>; we use these last ones in cases of severe illness.

Artificial suppositories are of four types. Some are composed of honey, "magistral" powders <note>Medicines prepared according to a master's or physician's specific recipe rather than a standard commercial formula.</note>, and common salt; some from honey and other strong powders and common salt; some from honey and liquids; and some from honey and special (rather than common) salt. 

An example of the first: Take honey and the powder of **Hiera Picra** <term>Hierapicra: Literally "sacred bitter," a traditional purgative compound typically made of aloes and other aromatic herbs.</term>, which are called "magistral species." There is a common **Rule** for this: for 1 ounce of honey, use 1 drachm or a half-drachm of the species. The second rule is that 1 drachm or a half-drachm of salt is added to this, depending on how much you wish to sharpen the medicine and stimulate the body's expulsive nature, as shown in the example:

<margin>Take</margin>
Honey, 1 oz.
Species of Hiera Picra, 1 drachm.
Common salt, ½ drachm.

Let the honey be boiled, and when it has been cooked, let the species and the salt be added, and let the suppository be made. Do not add the powders during the boiling of the honey, lest their medicinal virtue be dissolved and lost through the boiling; add them only after the honey is cooked.

An example of the second type: This is made from honey, common salt, and strong powders, such as the powder of **white hellebore**, **euphorbium** <term>Euphorbium: The dried, caustic sap of a succulent plant, used as a powerful stimulant and purgative.</term>, and the like. The common rule is that for 1 ounce of honey, one adds a half-scruple and 5 grains of that powder, and 1 drachm or a half-drachm of salt. For example: Take 2 ounces of honey, boil it, and mix in 1 scruple of euphorbium and 2 drachms of salt; make a suppository.

An example of the third type: This is made from juices and liquids combined with honey and common salt, such as the juice of **spurge** <term>Tithimallus: A plant of the Euphorbia genus, known for its milky, purgative sap.</term> with **gall** <note>original: "felle" – bile, used in early medicine to stimulate the bowels.</note>, especially ox-gall.

There is also a rule that for 1 ounce of honey, 5 scruples or 6 grains of juices should be added. For instance: take 2 ounces of honey and 1 scruple of **bull’s gall** <term>felli tauri: Ox gall, traditionally used in medicine for its bitter, purgative properties to stimulate the bowels.</term>; a little salt may be added; let it be boiled to form a suppository.

An example of a fourth type, which is made not from common salt, but from **Indian black salt** <term>Indo sale nigro: Likely a reference to Himalayan or volcanic salts used for their high mineral content.</term>, **borax** <term>Baurach: From the Arabic 'bauraq', referring to borax or similar alkaline salts used as flux or medicine.</term>, **sal ammoniac** <term>amoniaco: A mineral salt (ammonium chloride) used as a stimulant or purgative.</term>, and **nitre** <term>sale nitri: Saltpeter, used here to increase the "drawing" or irritating power of the medicine.</term>, along with honey. The rule is that for 1 ounce of honey, 5 grains or 5 scruples of these salts are added, and the suppository is formed.

How to tell if the honey is cooked enough: if it is placed with a spatula onto a stone or a polished board and it does not flow but remains still, then it is judged to be sufficiently cooked; if it flows, let it be boiled further. Suppositories should be stored in oil or in some kind of fat—especially that of a **castrated pig** <note>Lard from a barrow (castrated male pig) was often specified in early modern pharmacy for its supposed purity or specific consistency.</note>—so that they may be more easily inserted into the anus.

A rule highly worth noting: if an experienced physician wishes to strengthen the **expulsive power** <note>original: "expulsiuam virtutem" – the body's natural ability to drive out waste or toxins.</note>, he administers suppositories while the Moon is in the cold and moist signs, namely **Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces**.

# SECOND [BOOK]

However, the aspect of the **Moon** toward **Venus** is more praiseworthy than its aspect toward **Jupiter**.

The physician must take care, however, not to administer **clysters** <term>Clisteria: Enemas; the term refers to the procedure of injecting fluid into the rectum.</term> while the Moon is in conjunction with Jupiter or with Venus, lest the work of the medicine be cut too short by over-loosening or weakening the body, and lest the **good humors** <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that needed to be kept in balance for health.</note> be drawn out along with the bad. For **Ptolemy** says in his *Centiloquium* <note>original: "Centiloquio"; a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy.</note>: "If anyone takes a purgative while the Moon is with Jupiter, its work will be shortened and its effect diminished."

Commonly, the term "clyster" is used without being distinguished from an **enema** <term>Enema: From the Greek word for "injection"; here distinguished as the liquid itself.</term>. But properly speaking, the "clyster" is the instrument, and the "enema" is the liquid which is injected into the anus with that instrument. There are certain clysters that are mild, some that are strong, and some that are middling. The mild ones are divided into three types.

The **first mild type** is **barley water** <note>original: "aqua hordei"</note>, and this is used for fevers. **Hulled barley** <note>original: "ordeum excorticatum"</note> is more effective for altering the body's state, while unhulled barley is more effective for cleansing; the quantity of it is 1 pound or 1 and a half pounds, and we apply it with **violet oil**.

The **second mild clyster** is made from the broth of a chick or a hen, or of other meats or peas. Make the broth fatty when you wish to lubricate more, or not fatty if you desire more to wash the bowels, cooked with salt, in the amount of 1 and a half pounds. Up to 5 ounces of good sugar can be added, and it is beneficial for pregnant women, young girls, the elderly, and the weak. Some even maintain that if someone is unable to receive nourishment through the mouth, the said clysters administered with broths can nourish them for a long time.

The **third mild clyster** is made from milk; for instance: take 1 pound of milk, to which is added some sugar or honey (when there is no fever), in the amount of 5 ounces. This is suitable for **worms** in children. A rule regarding the presence of worms, or the fear of them: bitter things should never be placed through the lower opening, even if they are specifically suited for killing worms—such as **lupins**, **aloe**, **gentian**, **dittany**, **centaury**, etc.—because they would drive the worms upward. Instead, such things are given by mouth so that they force the worms to descend downward. Sweet things, which attract them, are to be administered through the lower opening. Nor should oil be added to clysters for children suffering from worms, because oil by its own property is hostile to worms; since worms are of a poisonous nature, they would flee the oil and ascend upward. Therefore, let oil be given to them by mouth.

**Middling clysters** are made from **decoctions** <term>decoctionibus: Concentrated extracts made by boiling medicinal substances in water.</term> and various ingredients. Regarding decoctions, the intentions are various: you may intend to better lubricate, or to alter, or to cleanse, or to restrict, sometimes even to target specific organs, and sometimes to strengthen them.

Concerning other medicines—those that heal wounds (<term>consolidatives</term>), those that ripen abscesses (<term>maturatives</term>), those that cut through thick humors (<term>incisives</term>), and those that wear away tissue (<term>corrosives</term>), etc.—you will find them written about everywhere in the works of authors; therefore, for the sake of brevity, I have omitted them here.

**General rule for decoctions.** Take a desired quantity of water, such as 3 or 4 <term>pounds</term> <note>original: "libra", a unit of weight approximately 12–16 ounces depending on the local standard.</note>; boil the ingredients in it until half or a third part is consumed. For children and infants, take half a pound to 1 pound.

**An example where you wish to soothe and also to cleanse.** Take <term>mallow</term>, <term>marshmallow</term>, and <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurialis"; the herb *Mercurialis annua*, used as a laxative, not the metal.</note>, 1 <term>handful</term> <note>original: "manipulus".</note> <term>of each</term> <note>original: "ana".</note>. Sometimes 2 or 3 egg yolks are added because they soothe and strengthen the intestines, and so that the enema adheres to the intestinal walls.

The **general rule** is that two handfuls of herbs require one pound of water. However, practitioners commonly write: *Take mallow, marshmallow, pellitory of the wall, and so on. Let them be boiled in sufficient water,* etc.

### [Digestive medicines] <note>The text begins mid-word; "stiua" is the conclusion of "Digestiva."</note> are listed together with those ingredients that are added to them, known as simple medicines; it also teaches their weights and measures.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'H' featuring two classical pillars or columns with ornate capitals, set against a dark hatched background.</image-desc>

HITHERTO we have discussed Enemas; now we must consequently proceed to the digestion of materials, according to the sayings of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>.

> Treat and move those things which are digested, not those which are raw <note>original: "Digesta medicari & mouere non cruda"; a foundational rule from Hippocrates's Aphorisms, meaning one should not try to expel "humors" until they have been properly "cooked" or matured by the body's heat.</note>. Digestion is the preparation of humors that are to be expelled, and this is appropriate in material diseases—that is, those beginning from raw matter. It is not appropriate for immaterial diseases, where no fault of the humors is found, but rather these diseases require only alteration <note>Changing the quality of the body (e.g., cooling it down) rather than removing substance.</note>. If a material disease, or a faulty humor, is correctable and can be returned to a healthy state, then neither evacuation nor digestion is appropriate (since digestion prepares for expulsion); instead, "alteratives" are suitable, by which the humor is restored to a healthy state. However, if it is not correctable, then digestion is appropriate first, followed by its evacuation and eradication, proceeding regularly according to Hippocrates. When it is said "Treat things that are digested," it refers to regular practice; for in cases of necessity involving a great deal of "furious" or poisonous matter, we evacuate without prior digestion, as is held in the said Aphorism of Hippocrates. Hence, physicians do poorly when they evacuate from the very beginning, because the disease is often rendered incurable. They also act poorly when giving digestives and evacuatives <note>Laxatives or purgatives.</note> to healthy bodies, as stated in the second book of the Aphorisms: "Those who have healthy bodies are weakened by being purged with medicines."

**A rule to be highly noted.** If you wish to strengthen the digestive power, let the **Moon** be in Gemini, in the first half of Libra, or in Aquarius, joined with **Jupiter** in a favorable aspect—especially when Jupiter is in signs similar to those of the Moon. And if the Moon is in a hot and moist sign, let Jupiter also be in a sign of this nature. There are three humors to be digested or evacuated: namely, the **Melancholic**, the **Choleric**, and the **Phlegmatic**. Regarding these: the star of **Saturn** governs the first. Therefore, when you wish to purge the Melancholic humor: 1. let Saturn be weak; 2. let Saturn be "falling" <note>A term in astrology referring to a planet in a weak position in the zodiac.</note>; 3. let it not be in the hour of Saturn, but in the hour of Jupiter, and let Jupiter be fortunate. **Mars** governs the second, the Choleric humor; therefore, if you wish to evacuate this humor, let Mars be weak, and let it not be in his hour but in the hour of **Venus**, with Venus being fortified. If, however, we intend to treat the Phlegmatic humor, let the Moon be weakly disposed, and let it not be in her hour, but in the hour of the **Sun**, with the Sun being fortified. For if the Moon, which governs the phlegmatic humor,

However, if it is not corrigible, then digestion is appropriate first, and afterwards its evacuation and eradication, operating regularly according to Hippocrates.

When it is said "treat what is digested," this refers to regular operation; because by necessity, in cases of great "furious" or poisonous matter, we evacuate without preceding digestion, as is held in the stated Aphorism of Hippocrates. For this reason, physicians do badly when they evacuate from the beginning, because the disease is often rendered incurable. # LIBER
<meta>catchword: Octaua</meta>

...[if the humor] were strong, then it would strengthen and increase the phlegm; once increased, it would resist the medicine with its own strength and frustrate its operation. This is also to be understood regarding the other planets. The **faulty humor** <note>original: "humor peccans"; the specific bodily fluid—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, or black bile—believed to be causing the illness.</note> sometimes causes harm by its thickness, sometimes by its viscosity, and sometimes by its thinness. Therefore, thick humor is **digested** <note>In this context, "digested" means "ripened" or "matured" by heat to make it easier to purge.</note> by hot and thinning agents. Viscous humor is treated with **incisives** <note>original: "incidentibus"; medicines believed to "cut" through and break up thick, sticky fluids.</note>. Thin humor is treated with thickening agents. Digestive medicines are administered in two forms: namely, **syrups** and **waters**. Some syrups are **magisterial** <note>original: "magistrales"; custom-compounded by a physician for a specific patient.</note>, and some are usual or common. Of the waters, some are distilled and some are decocted <note>boiled</note> from herbs. The syrups and waters appropriate to each humor will appear in the following sections, regarding which note the following rules:

**FIRST Rule.** Because a disease in which you wish to digest the humors is either through "community" or through "essence." If it is through community <note>meaning the disease has spread from one organ to another</note>, then first attend to the digestion and removal of the matter from the **sending member** <note>the primary organ from which the disease originated.</note>. If, however, it is through essence <note>the disease is rooted in the organ itself</note>, it is either a disease appropriate to one member, or it is common to several members. If the first, you shall give digestives appropriate to that member only. If the second, the matter is either of one kind or diverse; in the first case, you shall give one digestive. In the second case, you shall give a combination of digestives for various intentions.

**SECOND Rule.** A common syrup is not given by itself, but through the mixing of waters. First, lest it cause nausea on account of its sweetness. Second, it is rendered more liquid and thin for taking. Third, because the water gives the syrup **penetration** to reach distant parts of the body. Fourth, because water itself has a digestive power, and thus they mutually assist each other in the ripening process.

**THIRD Rule is,** that every dose of Syrups is 1 ounce, or slightly more, so as not to cause nausea in the one taking it.

The dose of waters is commonly 3 ounces. But when water is given separately, the dose for a single time is 4 ounces.

**Fourth rule,** The Physician, in the **clarification** <note>The process of clearing a liquid of impurities, often using egg whites or heat.</note> of syrups to make them more pleasing to the patient, ought to take a double quantity <note>original: "subduplam quantitatem"; here referring to adjusting the volume to account for loss during boiling.</note> beyond the predicted amount, so that once clarification by fire and resolution is complete, it remains at the stated dose; and the same is to be said of water. Also, if he wishes to **aromatize** <note>add pleasant-smelling herbs or spices</note> a common syrup or waters, he should increase the dose.

**Fifth rule.** It is better to give syrups that have not been clarified, because they work better, especially in **acute matter** <note>diseases that are sharp, fast-moving, or highly inflamed.</note>.

**Sixth rule.** The Physician must always put some **stomach-confortatives** <note>original: "confortantia stomachum"; ingredients intended to strengthen or "comfort" the stomach to prevent vomiting or irritation.</note> in his recipes, of which we speak below.

¶ **Seventh rule.** In every syrup, **Cordials** <note>medicines intended to stimulate or "strengthen" the heart and vital spirits.</note> should be placed, such as **Lemon Balm**, **Borage**, **Bugloss**, or their waters.

# BOOK SECOND

**Eighth rule.** A physician wishing to prescribe a standard syrup ought to select a water appropriate to the member <note>the specific organ or body part being treated</note> to which the syrup is proportioned; for this reason, some waters and syrups regard the head, others the chest, and others the stomach, as will be discussed below. For example: In a simple "cold" stomach ailment, he shall give Syrup of Wormwood <note>original: "Absinthio"</note> or of Mint in a dose of 1.5 ounces <note>original: "vnc. 1. 5."</note> with 3 ounces of Wormwood water. But in a "composite" or complex disease, you shall divide the syrup so that the larger quantity addresses the more severe ailment, and the lesser quantity the minor one; or, he may have the syrup address one and the water the other. And so that these things may be better understood, let us define an example for every part of the body, both in "hot" and "cold" matter, except for the blood: for in the blood, **digestion** <note>the process of maturing or thinning a humor so it can be expelled</note> or evacuation through medicines is not appropriate; rather, the separation of bad humors from the blood is required. 

Here is an example for **digesting phlegm** <note>phlegm was characterized as cold and moist; "digesting" it meant warming and thinning it</note>, to be given in four doses, intended for when digestive potions must be sent to remote places where there are no pharmacies <note>original: "apothecæ"</note>. Take 2.5 ounces each of Syrup of Hyssop and Simple Oxymel <note>a medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar</note>; 1 ounce of Compound Oxymel; 4 ounces each of Fennel and Parsley waters; and 2 ounces each of Couch-grass and Celery waters. Mix for four doses.
