***

And with the said syrups and waters, we also include "directives" <note>specific ingredients intended to guide the medicine to a particular organ</note>. For example: Take 1 ounce <note>original: "vnc. i."</note> each of compound syrup of Apples and syrup of Dodder of Thyme; 1 ounce each of the waters of Hart’s-tongue fern, Fumitory, and Bugloss; with half a drachm <note>original: "drag. s."</note> of aromatic nutmeg—as will be stated above regarding those substances that digest **cholera** <note>yellow bile; a hot, dry humor</note>—and let a syrup be made for one dose.

**Syrup for four doses.** Take 2 ounces each of syrup of Dodder of Thyme and Fumitory; 1 ounce each of Byzantine syrup and Borage syrup; 3 ounces each of the waters of Elderflower, Borage, and Bugloss; and 1.5 ounces each of the waters of Hart’s-tongue fern and Tamarisk. Mix these for four doses.

For the composition of syrups, prioritize those simple ingredients that require more **decoction** <note>prolonged boiling to extract medicinal properties</note> over those that require less. For example: first roots, second herbs, third fruits, fourth seeds, and fifth flowers.

**NOTE** that in recipes, roots are ordered by weight, herbs by handfuls <note>original: "manipulos"; a standard pharmaceutical measure of the amount of herb held in one hand</note>, fruits by number, and flowers and seeds by weight. And when we wish to make a syrup to perfection, we add for 1 pound of <term>decoction</term> <note>a liquid made by boiling down medicinal plants</note> or juice, 1 pound of sugar, boiling it until the liquid or syrup is reduced. Such syrups are primarily made when we wish to preserve them for many days. There is another syrup, which is called "long" or of "small decoction," so named because after it is boiled, there remains with the sugar as much of the decoction as there is sugar, or double, or less, according to your judgment.

The decoction shall be made until half of the water is boiled away; of this, take one pound, and with 1 pound of sugar, a syrup shall be made, boiled to perfection; or with 1 pound of sugar and half a pound <note>original: "lib. 5.", likely a transcription of "lib. s." meaning "semis" or half</note> of honey.

For you see that in the aforementioned digestive, there is twice as much decoction as there is syrup. There are, however, some people who do not add syrups to the said decoction, but only sweeten the decoction with sugar.

A **JULEP** <note>from the Persian 'gulab' (rose water); a sweet liquid medicine</note> is used at times in place of a syrup. It is made from distilled waters, either by boiling it to perfection or for a long duration, as was said regarding Syrups. Let a julep be made, up to 1 pound or 10 ounces. Sometimes a julep is a simple thing, and sometimes it is composed of many ingredients. It is only made with sugar and not with honey, and it requires more boiling than a syrup; in this, it differs from a syrup.

# BOOK TWO

Therefore, these syrups and waters are intended for the **digestion** <note>In Galenic medicine, 'digestion' or 'concoction' refers to the process of ripening or thinning a "humor" (like yellow bile) so the body can easily expel it.</note> of **choler** <note>Yellow bile; one of the four bodily humors, associated with a hot and dry temperament.</note>, whether the fault lies in the head or in any other part of the body. If you wish for their healing power to reach the head, you must add something that carries their influence to the brain. This is done in many ways. The **first** is that they are given two hours after dinner; while the vapors are rising from the food and reaching the brain, they carry the power of the syrup along with them. This method is praised by only a few. The **second way** is to mix a small dose of a "warming" brain-remedy with the aforementioned "cold" syrups, so that it serves only to guide the medicine to the head. For example, by adding **stoechas** <note>original: "sticados"; French lavender, often used for head ailments</note> or **marjoram** to any of the said syrups or simple ingredients. For instance: Take 1 ounce <note>original: "vnc. 1"</note> of syrup of endive, half an ounce <note>original: "vnc. s." for 'uncia semis'</note> of syrup of violets, and 1 ounce each <note>original: "ana"</note> of water of sorrel and endive.

The **third way** is to scent the medicine with aromatics that target that specific organ, which can be done in several ways. **First**, when the "master syrup" is being prepared: once it is finished, add the brain-targeting aromatics—such as **nutmeg**, stoechas, etc.—at the very end. **Second**, when you take the syrups and waters together, infuse 1.5 or 2 <term>scruples</term> <note>a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of nutmeg or another brain-remedy in them—either loose or in a small cloth bag—for three or four hours, and then strain it. **Third**, it is done by infusing the aromatic in the waters alone for 4 hours, then straining and administering. For example: Take 1.5 ounces (or 6 <term>drams</term> <note>a unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</note>) each of syrup of violets and syrup of roses, and 1.5 ounces each of endive and rose waters. Infuse 2 <term>scruples</term> of nutmeg in the waters for 4 hours, then strain and mix with the syrups.

It should be noted that in giving a single "digestive draft," 1.5 ounces of syrups requires three ounces of medicinal waters, as is done when directing Choler. **Example**: Take 1 ounce of syrup of endive, half an ounce of simple vinegar syrup, and 1.5 ounces each of endive and chicory waters. However, if you wish to provide a drink for four doses, you shall quadruple the amounts: take 2 ounces each of syrup of endive, simple vinegar syrup, and simple **oxysaccharum** <note>original: "oxizacara"; a medicinal syrup made of vinegar and sugar</note>; and 3 ounces each of endive, chicory, sorrel, and purslane waters. Behold, here you have 4 drafts, and each contains 1.5 ounces of syrups and 3 ounces of waters.

**Rule**: If you wish to scent a syrup, use 3 <term>drams</term> of aromatics for every 1 pound <note>original: "lib. 1"</note> of the decoction.

Next follow the digestives for matter located in the **respiratory organs** <note>original: "membris ſpiritualibus"; literally 'spiritual members,' referring to the heart and lungs where the 'vital spirit' was thought to reside</note>, and first for the choleric matter of the chest. They are:

|:---|:---|:---|

| | Rose & Julep | **Maidenhair Fern** <note>original: "Capillorum Veneris"</note> |

## SECOND BOOK

These syrups and waters are therefore used for the digestion <note>In Galenic medicine, "digestion" or "coction" refers to the process of ripening or thickening a harmful "humor" so it can be purged from the body.</note> of yellow bile <note>original: "choleræ"</note>, whether it causes trouble in the head or in any other limb. If you wish for their medicinal power to reach the head, it is necessary to add something that carries their virtue to the brain. This is done in many ways. 

The first way is that they are given two hours after dinner; while the vapors are rising from the food and reaching the brain, they carry the virtue of the syrup with them. This method is praised by few. The second way is to mix a small dose of a "warm" cerebral substance with the aforementioned "cold" things, so that it carries them to the head—for example, by adding stoechas <note>original: "sticados"; French Lavender (Lavandula stoechas), believed to strengthen the brain.</note> or marjoram to one of the said syrups and simples. For example: Take 1 ounce of syrup of endive, half an ounce of violet syrup, and 1 ounce each of sorrel and endive waters. <note>original: "vnc." is an ounce (uncia); "s." stands for "semis" or half.</note>

The third way is to scent the medicine with aromatics that target that specific limb, and this is done in several ways. First, when a master syrup is being prepared, and when it is finished, the aromatics targeting the brain—such as nutmeg, stoechas, etc.—are added at the end. Second, when you take the syrups and waters together, infuse 1.5 or 2 scruples <note>original: "℈" is the symbol for a scruple, about 1.3 grams.</note> of nutmeg or another cerebral herb in them, either loose or in a small cloth bag, for 3 or 4 hours, and afterwards strain them. Third, it is done by infusing the herbs in the waters alone for 4 hours, then straining and administering. For example: Take 1.5 ounces (or 6 drachms <note>original: "drag."; a drachm is 1/8th of an ounce.</note>) each of violet and rose syrups, and 1.5 ounces each of endive and rose waters; infuse 2 scruples of nutmeg in the waters for 4 hours, then strain and mix with the syrups.

It should be noted that in giving one medicinal draught, 1.5 ounces of syrups require 3 ounces of waters, as when directing the yellow bile. For example: Take 1 ounce of syrup of endive, half an ounce of simple vinegar-syrup, and 1.5 ounces each of endive and chicory waters. If, however, you wish to provide a drink for four doses, you shall quadruple the amounts: take 2 ounces each of syrup of endive, simple vinegar-syrup, and simple oxisaccharum <note>A syrup of vinegar and sugar.</note>; and 3 ounces each of endive, chicory, sorrel, and purslane waters. Here you have 4 draughts, and each contains 1.5 ounces of syrups and 3 ounces of waters.

**Rule.** If you wish to scent a syrup with aromatics, 3 drachms of aromatics should be added for every 1 pound of the decoction.

# BOOK TWO

Nightshade water <note>original: "Aqua solatri"; likely *Solanum nigrum*, used in small doses as a cooling agent.</note>, which is effective for the digestion <note>In Galenic medicine, "digestion" or "coction" refers to the process of ripening a harmful "humor" so it can be purged.</note> of yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>, is wonderfully effective at the start of treatment. If you were to argue that nightshade water is cold and styptic <note>A substance that causes body tissues to contract or "binds" the humors.</note>, and therefore it hinders the clearing of phlegm and should not be used in cases of pleurisy <note>An inflammation of the lining of the lungs.</note>, Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note> resolves this in the fourth book of the first volume of his *Canon* in the section on swellings. He says: "And Nightshade has properties for dissolving hidden, hot swellings <note>original: "apostemata"</note>, and it does this not through a visible quality, but through a hidden property."

Among the aforementioned syrups, violet syrup and jujube syrup are commonly applied at the onset of pleurisy because they reduce the fever and the sharpness of the humors. For a rupture of the veins at the start of pleurisy: Take 1 ounce <note>original: "vnc. 1"</note> of violet syrup, half an ounce <note>original: "vnc. s."; the OCR read "5", but "s" for "semis" or half is the standard medical notation here.</note> of jujube syrup, and 1 ounce each of the following: barley water (either boiled or distilled), violet water, and maidenhair fern water. Mix these for a single dose.

Scabious, in particular, has the natural property of opening swellings, especially in the chest. # BOOK TWO

From all these waters, you can make a pectoral water <note>original: "aquam pectoralem"; a remedy specifically for the chest and lungs.</note> which we commonly use as follows. Take 4 each of dried figs, dates, and sebestens <note>original: "sebesten"; a plum-like fruit from the *Cordia* tree used to soothe the throat.</note>; 5 ounces each of maidenhair fern <note>original: "capillorum veneris"</note>, raisins <note>original: "passulæ"</note>, and licorice; and 10 jujubes. Boil these in water until one third of the liquid has evaporated; at the end, add enough sugar to sweeten it. Some, beyond this, add one ounce of cinnamon, hyssop, and fennel when they wish to more effectively break up "windiness" <note>Gas or pressure</note> in the chest.

For digesting Melancholic matter <note>Black bile, the heavy, cold, and dry humor. "Digesting" or "coction" refers to the medical process of ripening or softening a harmful humor so the body can expel it.</note> in the chest: Take syrups that digest melancholy, as follows: take 6 drams <note>original: "drag. 6"</note> each of syrup of epithyme <note>original: "Epithymo"; a parasitic plant (dodder) believed to purge black bile.</note> and syrup of apples; 1.5 ounces each of colt’s foot water <note>original: "aquæ farfaræ"</note> and hyssop water. Mix and flavor with a little cinnamon and licorice. However, it is very rare for melancholy to cause an affliction in the chest.

**Note.** No syrup containing vinegar should be used for ailments of the chest, except in cases of Asthma, where the matter is very viscous <note>Thick and sticky</note>; in such cases, the matter can be digested with oxymel of squill <note>original: "Oximelle squillitico"; a mixture of honey, vinegar, and the sea-onion (squill), used as a powerful expectorant.</note>. And if "hot matters" <note>Referring to yellow bile or blood</note> are contained in the chest, let them be digested with a decoction of lettuce, water-lily flowers <note>original: "nenufaris"</note>, seeds of melons, watermelons <note>original: "citrulli"</note>, and gourds, purging cassia <note>original: "cassię fist."</note>, fresh violet flowers, barley, and seeded raisins.

## EXPLANATIONS.

1. Jupiter [is] in [its] signs, in Cancer ♋ and Pisces ♓. For they are cold and moist, just as Jupiter is. <note>In medieval astrology, planets were most effective when placed in zodiac signs that shared their "elemental" qualities. Jupiter was associated with the "sanguine" temperament (hot and moist), but here the author links its strength to these specific watery signs.</note>
2. Saturn [is] weak and falling, falling either by reason of the sign: for it falls in Aries ♈, but this happens rarely (for it reaches Aries only every thirtieth year); it cannot be that the author speaks of this "fall"; or by reason of the houses in the figure of the heavens: in this way any planet "falls" in four houses: 3, 6, 9, 12. Care should be taken, therefore, that Saturn is in one of these four houses. <note>A "falling" (cadent) planet was considered weak or poorly placed. For medical procedures, one often wanted the "malefic" planet Saturn to be weak so it would not hinder the cure.</note>
3. Nor should it be in the hour of Saturn; we taught above how the planetary hours are found. <note>Each hour of the day was traditionally ruled by one of the seven planets. Physicians avoided the hour of Saturn for administering medicine because Saturn was associated with cold, contraction, and death.</note>

---

### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER XII.

*A magisterial syrup is composed of various medi-*
*cines regarding different diseases: this is either*
*digestive, or laxative, or restorative.*
*Certain ones are boiled to perfection, others not:*
*he teaches how each is made.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' with foliate scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>
A MAGISTERIAL SYRUP <note>original: "Sirupus magistralis"; a "magisterial" formula is one custom-prescribed by a master physician for a specific patient, rather than a standard "officinal" recipe kept in stock by apothecaries.</note> is a syrup composed of various medicines regarding different illnesses; for example, a syrup composed of wormwood and French lavender <note>original: "absinthio, & sticados"; French lavender (*Lavandula stoechas*) was often called 'Stoechas'.</note> is called magisterial, being suitable for the stomach because of the wormwood, and for the head because of the lavender, especially if taken in the same dose. But in a broad sense, a syrup made of many things, even those corresponding to the same limb, is called magisterial. And in composite illnesses, nothing is better for a physician than to compose a magisterial syrup: for through it he will have multiple intentions <note>Medical "intentions" are the specific goals of a treatment, such as "to cool the liver" or "to purge phlegm."</note>; take an example of this. If a woman suffers from a cold mal-disposition of the womb <note>original: "matricis"; the uterus.</note> caused by phlegm, and of the stomach from a hot cause, then from wormwood and feverfew <note>original: "matricaria"; its name derives from 'matrix' (womb) because of its use in feminine health.</note> a medicine will result that is suitable for both dispositions. However, in this there is a specific caution. If you make a syrup for two or more ailments, of which one is more intense and worse than the other, you ought to put a greater quantity of the medicines regarding the weaker [ailment], <note>The author suggests a counter-intuitive balancing act: the weaker ailment needs more "bulk" of medicine to assist the body, or perhaps to ensure the stronger medicine for the worse ailment doesn't overwhelm the system.</note> for example. Someone suffers from pain of the stomach and head, and the pain of the stomach

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

                      { Digestive
**Magisterial Syrups**  { Solutive <note>These are laxative syrups intended to "loosen" the bowels.</note>
**are of certain types:** { Restorative
                      { Boiled to perfection
                      { Some [are] not

Digestive syrups are made in two ways. First, from a decoction <note>A decoction is a medicinal liquor produced by boiling herbs or other substances in water to extract their properties.</note> of herbs, roots, flowers, seeds, barks, and woods, with sugar or honey; these are called "magisterial syrups" in the absolute sense. Sometimes they are made acidic, and they are then called "acidic magisterial syrups."

Second, they are prepared from juices, sugar, or honey, and are called "juiced syrups" <note>original: "succosati"</note>. Concerning this, a rule is established for their composition: first, when boiling a syrup from herbs, it is better to take green or fresh herbs, for in dry ones the medicinal power <note>original: "virtus"</note> is somewhat exhausted.

The second rule: when boiling roots, let them first be crushed and placed in the decoction a little before the other ingredients, because they require more boiling. Next, let the herbs be added and boiled until they lose their greenness. Then let the seeds and powders be added, and finally the flowers. After this, let the mixture rest until the decoction becomes lukewarm; let it be pressed and strained through a cloth, and keep and use this strained liquid.

To clarify the syrup, take two or three egg whites, well beaten in water, and stir them in. Allow it to come to a small boil, and strain it again through a well-washed cloth; it will then be clarified. And if you wish to make it drinkable <note>In this context, "drinkable" refers to a thinner consistency meant for immediate consumption rather than long-term storage.</note>, then add the sugar or honey at the end. In this, the rule is that for one pound of water, 4 or 5 ounces of sugar should be added.

If, however, it is boiled to perfection so that it may be preserved without spoiling, then for 3 pounds of the decocted water, 1 pound of sugar or honey should be added. Return it to a slow fire and boil it sufficiently so that it produces foam and the coarse part rises; then strain it again through a thin cloth, and thus the syrup is clarified. Once this is done, boil it again over the fire until it is perfectly cooked. The sign of [complete] cooking is when it clings to the spatula while boiling. Another sign is if, when a drop is placed on a fingernail, it does not run off. Another: if you rub it between your fingers and it sticks, it is well cooked.

If you wish to make the syrup acidic, take for every 4 pounds of boiled syrup...

<meta>This page continues the specific instructions for creating Magisterial Syrups. The previous page concluded by explaining that the choice of ingredients depends on the intensity of the ailment and the vital importance of the organs being treated, particularly the stomach.</meta>

<header>BOOK 2</header>

...one pound of vinegar, but this remains at the physician's discretion <note>original: "arbitrio medici"</note>, according to whether he wishes to make it more or less acidic.

### An example of the aforementioned for cold matter of the stomach.

Take two handfuls of spearmint <note>original: "menthæ viridis"</note>, and one handful each of wormwood <note>original: "absinthij"</note> and agrimony <note>original: "eupatorij"</note>. Let them boil for a short time in water. Add half an ounce and three drachms of watermelon seed <note>original: "seminis citrulli"</note>, and one drachm each of sweet flag <note>original: "calamiaronci," likely a corruption of calamus aromaticus</note> and mastic. Then add one pinch of roses and wild vine <note>original: "labruscæ"</note>. Let them boil a little longer, then remove them from the heat so that the decoction <note>A medicinal liquid made by boiling herbs to extract their properties.</note> may cool. Squeeze and strain it; if you wish to clarify it, do so with egg white, though the medicine will be stronger if it is not clarified. 

And if you wish to have a drinkable syrup, take one pound of the aforementioned decoction and sweeten it with as much skimmed honey or honey of roses as is sufficient; or add three or four ounces of syrup of mint to create a drinkable syrup. If, however, you wish to boil it to perfection <note>That is, boiling it down with sugar until it reaches a thick, shelf-stable consistency.</note>, then let the clarified decoction boil again so that the dregs may rise after adding the honey and sugar; strain it again, and then boil it until it reaches its final consistency. 

Another example, for cold matter of the stomach and the head: Take one handful of mint and wormwood; half a handful each of sage, betony, and marjoram; and one pinch of Arabian lavender <note>original: "sticados"</note>. Let them boil in water according to the method described, and add sugar or honey for the syrup.

### Rule concerning laxative syrups.

Once the decoction of the aforementioned items is made, and before the boiling is completed, add two ounces of laxative or "solutive" medicines into one pound of the decoction—such as turbith <note>A root used as a purgative.</note>, agaric <note>A medicinal fungus.</note>, rhubarb, senna, or polypody fern with its proper corrective ingredients. Then let it be sufficiently boiled. 

If you wish to use this as a drinkable syrup, give three ounces with a sweetener. Or, if you want it boiled to perfection, give one and a half ounces and write the prescription thus: "Take one and a half ounces of that syrup boiled to perfection, and three ounces of mint water; mix them." The waters produced by decoction work more effectively than those produced by sublimation <note>A process of dry distillation; the author suggests boiling the herbs directly is better than using distilled spirits.</note>, which is why it is better to provide them.

Restorative syrups are made in this way: let the herbs be placed in the decoction, or in their place use powders or other substances. Let us take two ounces of powder for every one pound of water and make a decoction. Afterward, let it be strained, and at the end add sugar or honey. For example, we might add one or two ounces of the "electuary of gems" <note>A luxury medicine containing finely powdered precious stones, believed to have heart-strengthening properties.</note>. 

Another example: take one ounce each of the three types of sandalwood <note>Red, yellow, and white sandalwood.</note>, aromatic spices, and rose-scented powder; half an ounce of spodium <note>Likely "spodium ex ebore," which is burnt ivory used to cool the body.</note>; half an ounce of roses and violets; and one drachm each of the flowers of bugloss and borage <note>Plants traditionally used to "gladden the heart" and combat melancholy.</note>. Boil these in two or three pounds of water, strain, and return to the fire. Add one pound of sugar and boil again so the dregs rise to be cast off; then strain and preserve it.

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

Syrups from juices are made in this way. For from any juice expressed from herbs, flowers, or roots, a syrup can be constructed in two ways. First, take the juice—either clarified or unclarified—then add clarified sugar <note>original: "zuccarum clarificatum"</note>, and let them boil together. For example: Take 3 pounds of juice and 1 pound of sugar clarified with egg whites; let them boil sufficiently over the fire, and let a syrup be made.

Second, take 3 pounds of the juice expressed from the said herbs, including both the thick and thin parts <note>The "gross" and "subtle" parts, meaning the pulp and the liquid</note>, and add 1 pound of sugar. Clarify this with egg white, mixing it well, and cook them together. Then strain it, and a syrup will be made. This second method is better than the first because the sugar and the juice are clarified at the same time, and the medicine will receive greater potency.

## SUMMARY OF CHAPTER XIII

### Example of the aforementioned for cold matter of the stomach.
<note>In medieval medicine, a "cold" stomach was thought to cause poor digestion and a buildup of phlegm. Treatments involved "hot" herbs like mint and wormwood to restore balance.</note>

Take 2 handfuls <note>original: "manip." (manipulus), a common measurement for herbs</note> of green mint, and 1 handful each of wormwood <note>original: "absinthij"</note> and agrimony <note>original: "eupatorij"</note>. Let them boil in water for a short time. Add half an ounce and 3 drachms of watermelon seed, and 1 drachm each of sweet flag <note>original: "calamiaronci," likely a variation of calamus aromaticus</note> and mastic <note>a resin from the pistachio tree</note>. Then add a pinch <note>original: "pugillum," the amount held between three fingers</note> of roses and wild vine <note>original: "labrusceanæ"</note>; let them boil a little longer. Afterward, set it aside so the decoction may cool, then squeeze and strain it. If you wish to clarify it, clarify with egg white, though it will be more potent if it is not clarified.

And if you wish to have a drinkable syrup, take 1 pound of the aforementioned decoction and let it be sweetened with as much skimmed honey <note>original: "despumato"</note> or rose honey as is sufficient, or add mint syrup in a dose of 3 or 4 ounces to make a drinkable syrup. If, however, you wish to boil it to "perfection" <note>meaning to a thick, shelf-stable consistency</note>, then once the decoction is clarified, let it boil again after adding the honey and sugar until the thick part rises, then strain it again and boil to perfection.

Another example for cold matter of the stomach and the head: Take 1 and a half handfuls each of mint and wormwood; half a handful each of sage, betony, and marjoram; and one pinch of Arabian lavender <note>original: "sticados" (Stoechas)</note>. Let them boil in water in the manner described, and add sugar or honey for the syrup.

### Rule for laxative syrups.

When the decoction of the said items is made, and before the boiling is finished, add 2 ounces of laxative or purgative substances to every one pound of the decoction—such as turpeth, agaric, rhubarb, senna, or polypody fern—along with their "correctives" <note>Spices like ginger or cinnamon added to prevent the cramping often caused by harsh laxatives</note>, and then let it be boiled sufficiently. If you want it as a drinkable syrup, give 3 ounces with sweetener; if you want it boiled to "perfection," give 1 and a half ounces and write the prescription thus: "Take 1 and a half ounces of this syrup boiled to perfection and 3 ounces of mint water; mix them." The waters from a decoction work more effectively than those from sublimation <note>distillation</note>, which is why it is better to give them.

Restorative syrups are made in this way: let the herbs be placed in the decoction, or in their place use powders or other substances. For every one pound of water, we take 2 ounces of powder and make a decoction; afterward, let it be strained. At the end, add sugar or honey. For example, we might add 1 or 2 ounces of the powder "Electuary of Gems" <note>a prestigious medicine containing crushed pearls and precious stones</note>. Another example: 1 ounce each of the "three sandalwoods" <note>red, white, and yellow sandalwood</note>, aromatic roses, and rose-scented spices; half an ounce of spodium <note>likely zinc oxide or burnt ivory, used as a coolant</note>; half an ounce of roses and violets; and 1 drachm each of bugloss and borage flowers. Boil these in 2 or 3 pounds of water, strain, and return to the fire. Add 1 pound of sugar and boil again until the thick part rises and is skimmed off, then strain and store.

**An example for purging yellow bile.** Take endive and sorrel <note>original: "acetosa"</note>, and make a decoction in which is dissolved 1 ounce of cassia-fistula, 1 dram of choice rhubarb, and 1 scruple of spikenard <note>an aromatic oil used here to balance the medicine</note>. **An example of when a laxative is given in a decoction or infusion.** Take 1 ½ drams of yellow myrobalans; let them be infused in the water of a decoction of raisins, or endive, or in goats' whey as much as is sufficient. Scammony <note>a harsh resinous purgative</note> is only dissolved in the drink, so that it is neither boiled nor infused.

# SECOND [BOOK]

Another example of a laxative decoction, for purging yellow bile <note>original: "choleram"</note>. Take endive, hops, and chicory, 3 or 4 handfuls <note>original: "manipulus"</note> of each. Great cold seeds <note>usually a cooling blend of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon seeds</note>, 1 ounce of each; 7 damson plums; the three common flowers <note>typically rose, violet, and borage</note>, 5 drams <note>original: "drachma"</note> of each; 2 ounces of barley. Make a decoction in a sufficient quantity of water, specifically boiling it until half the water is consumed. In the remaining liquid, infuse choice rhubarb and yellow myrobalans <note>an astringent fruit used as a purgative</note>, 1 dram of each; and 2 scruples <note>original: "scrupulus"</note> of spikenard; let these remain in the decoction for 12 hours. Then, perform a strong pressing <note>to squeeze out the medicinal juices</note>, to which you should add freshly extracted cassia fistula and tamarinds, 3 drams of each; and 1 ounce or 6 drams of violet syrup.

Another example in substance <note>meaning a solid form, such as a paste or powder, rather than a liquid drink</note>. Take rhubarb and the bark of yellow myrobalans, 2 scruples of each; 1 scruple of spikenard; 2 drams of sugar-rose electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with sugar and rose petals</note>; 6 drams of freshly extracted cassia fistula; and enough water of endive, chicory, borage, and scabious <note>a flowering herb often used for skin or respiratory ailments</note> to mix them.

It should be noted that in summer, myrobalans and rhubarb are mostly infused in endive water or goat's whey. In winter, they are infused in white wine. In the middle seasons, they are infused in a mixture of both.

Composite medicines that dissolve yellow bile from the head can be given in various ways. First, in pills—such as the pills that evacuate yellow bile from the head, whether common or "pestilential" <note>pills used during epidemics, thought to protect the heart and purge toxins</note>. These include those made of washed aloe, *Azaiaret* <note>a traditional Arabic pill formulation</note>, pills of the five types of myrobalans, and "Golden Pills" of rhubarb. The common eradicative <note>strong, "root-pulling"</note> dose of pills is 1 dram for adults; the minorative <note>milder</note> dose is 2 scruples. The exceptions are pills of mezereon <note>a toxic shrub</note>, which are effective for dropsy <note>original: "hydropisi"; the accumulation of fluid in the body</note>, and pills of squirting cucumber <note>original: "cucumero asinino"</note>, for which the dose is smaller. For children, a half-dose is given, and this is adjusted according to the nature of the region.

->Method of administering pills.<-

The pills should be rolled in a moistened wafer <note>original: "hostia"; a thin bread used to wrap bitter medicine for easier swallowing</note>, or honey, or some appropriate syrup, or a roasted apple; or they may be taken with wine or another liquid. According to the mind of the Prince <note>referring to Avicenna, often called the "Prince of Physicians"</note>, when evacuating the head, large pills should be given two hours after a light supper, so that the vapors rising from the food to the head may carry the medicinal power of the pills with them. But if you wish to evacuate the whole body, give them in the morning. If you wish to target the lower parts of the body, give them one hour before food; in this way, the pills are pressed down by the food so that their power passes only to the lower regions. However, many practitioners administer pills around midnight.

One must always pay attention to the speed or slowness of the pills' action. Those that work slowly should be taken early, upon going to bed. Those that work quickly should be taken around or after midnight; and when they begin to work, the patient should get up and walk around a little, here and there.

# BOOK 2

Then let him walk about until they perform their operation, and before this, he should eat nothing; instead, he shall take a pea broth without salt for a cleansing. Then, after an hour, he may eat. ### On the Sharpening of Pills
Commonly, pills are "sharpened" <note>This refers to *acuatio*, the process of adding a small amount of a more powerful substance to increase the speed or strength of the medicine's effect</note> with 3, 5, or 7 grains of colocynth pulp <note>The "bitter apple," a very strong purgative</note> for phlegm, or with 2 or 3 grains of diagridium <note>A preparation of scammony resin</note> for yellow bile. But pills that concern the joints and nerves ought to be sharpened with powdered bdellium <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum-resin similar to myrrh</note>.

It should also be noted that whenever pills are made, they ought to be formed with a powder appropriate to the place where the evacuation is sought. For example, if for the head, use powdered nutmeg; for the eyes, powdered fennel; for the chest, powdered licorice; for the stomach, powdered cinnamon; and for the nerves and joints, powdered ginger.

Strong pills, such as the *Hiera* of Rufus <note>original: "ieræ ruffini"; Hiera was a class of "holy" bitter electuaries or pills</note> or *Hieralogodion*, should not be given except to robust patients. Similarly, pills of hellebore and the pills of Democritus are given only to eradicate humors that are difficult to remove, such as in cases of leprosy, morphew <note>A skin disease causing scurfy eruptions or discoloration</note>, and warts.

Pills of mezereon <note>A flowering shrub whose bark is a drastic purgative</note> and other very strong pills that evacuate "yellow water" <note>serous fluid associated with edema</note> should never be sharpened, and they should not be given in doses larger than 1 dram or thereabouts; these are specifically for dropsy <note>original: "hydropisi"; a condition of swelling caused by excess fluid</note>. *Cochiae* pills <note>A standard purgative pill often containing aloes and colocynth</note> are strong, which is why they work well for weak people without needing sharpening. Golden Pills (*Aureae*) are close in strength, but in robust and strong people, they do nothing without sharpening; they are beneficial for the head, for matters in the front part of the head, and for the nerves.

Pills of euphorbium <note>A caustic resin from a succulent plant</note> are quite strong and are beneficial for ailments of the nerves and for paralysis. All other pills that are commonly given are weak, such as:

...but on account of its bitterness it should be given in pills, although it works better and more strongly in a potion. In a potion, it is safely given in the amount of half an ounce <note>original: "vnc. ς." – vnc. (uncia) is an ounce; the symbol ς (semis) represents a half</note>.

Pestilence pills <note>Medicines intended to protect against or treat the plague</note>, made of aloe, myrrh, and saffron, do not require one to stay at home or to abstain from food and drink; they can be taken in the morning, and if they do not cause a bowel movement, do not be afraid. For while remaining inside, they have the power to preserve the mass of humors from putrefaction and corruption. Pills taken before or after food provide no protection and are instead for ailments of the stomach.

Arthritic pills, and those made from hermodactyls <note>The root of a plant, likely meadow saffron, historically used for gout and joint pain</note>, are for ailments of the joints arising from a "cold" cause. If the humors are thick, "fetid pills" <note>original: "pillulæ fetidæ"; a specific class of strong-smelling purgative pills</note> are more useful; these are also effective against paralysis caused by a thick humor.

Pills of Fumitory <note>original: "Fumo terræ"; a plant used for skin conditions and liver health</note> are effective for scabies and skin infections, though they are very weak.

Pills of the five types of myrobalans <note>A plum-like fruit used in medieval medicine as a gentle purgative</note> are effective for ailments of the head caused by "hot" humors, especially if it involves the stomach or liver.

Rhubarb pills evacuate yellow bile <note>original: "cholerā"</note> from the head and liver, but they are very weak.

### The second method of purging yellow bile from the head.

This is done in the form of a powder, such as: take 2 drachms of rhubarb and 4 grains of spikenard <note>An aromatic essential oil/herb</note>; let a fine powder be made and given with broth or a decoction of marjoram.

Aloe, however, is not taken in powder form because of its bitterness; furthermore, if it is not "washed" <note>A process of refining the resin with water or juice to temper its harshness</note>, it harms the liver because it opens the veins, as the Prince <note>A reference to Avicenna (Ibn Sina), known as the "Prince of Physicians"</note> says in the chapter on Dropsy. Therefore, in cases of Dropsy, it is only given if washed with endive water. It is also harmful in any flow of blood—whether it be from an abscess, hemorrhoids, the intestines, or the chest—because it has the property of opening the orifices of the veins, as Mesue <note>A famous Persian or Arab physician, likely Mesue the Younger</note> says; wherefore physicians should then beware of giving medicines containing aloe.

### The third method of purging yellow bile from the head.

This is done in the form of an infusion, such as: take 2 drachms of rhubarb or half an ounce of yellow myrobalans; let them be infused in milk-water overnight, and in the morning let it be given to the patient.

The fourth method is done in the form of electuaries <note>A medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> of psyllium <note>Fleawort seeds</note>, juice of roses, *diaprunis* <note>A plum-based laxative</note>, and *diacatholicon* <note>A "universal" purge</note>. The common dose for adults is 4 drachms or half an ounce. It is given either in the form of a bolus <note>A large, soft pill</note>, or a "date" <note>dactili; a pill shaped like a date fruit</note>, as in: take 5 drachms of the laxative electuary of rose juice and make a bolus with sugar. It can be gilded <note>original: "deaurari"; coated in gold leaf to mask the taste or signify luxury</note>, or given in the form of a potion with some appropriate medicinal water, giving or preparing the said dose.

## Example of a bolus for yellow bile.

Take electuary of rose juice and laxative diaprunum <note>term: "diaprunum" - a medicinal paste made primarily from Damask plums</note>, two drams of each; add enough sugar to make a bolus <note>term: "bolus" - a large, soft medicinal pill, usually about the size of a grape or a large pea, swallowed whole</note>. Some preserves may be added, or appropriate powders and electuaries; the weight of the bolus may be one ounce and should not exceed two ounces.

Another example for yellow bile: Take six drams of freshly extracted cassia fistula <note>term: "cassia fistula" - the pulp of the "pudding-pipe tree," prized as a gentle and sweet-tasting laxative</note>, three drams of electuary of rose juice, one dram of choice rhubarb, one scruple <note>original: "℈ 1."</note> of spikenard, and enough violet syrup to make a bolus.

For phlegm: take three drams of diacarthamum <note>term: "diacarthamum" - a purgative electuary containing safflower seeds</note>, agaric troches <note>term: "agaric troches" - medicinal lozenges made from larch fungus, traditionally used to clear "cold" humors like phlegm</note>, and choice turpeth <note>term: "Turbit" - the root of a plant in the morning glory family, used as a powerful purgative</note>, two and a half drams <note>original: "drag. s. ʒ 3. scru. 5." — these are various medicinal weight units</note> of each, and enough fennel water to make a bolus.

For melancholy <note>the humor of black bile</note>: Take six drams of freshly extracted cassia fistula, confection of Hamech <note>term: "confection of Hamech" - a complex, bitter purgative specifically designed to treat melancholy and skin diseases</note>, and powdered senna, two and a half drams of each, one and a half ounces of borage, and enough sugar to make a bolus.

# BOOK SECOND.

First, the compounds are:

*   Alefangine pills <note>original: "Pillulæ alefanginæ" - a traditional compound made primarily of aloe, cinnamon, and nutmeg, used to cleanse the head and stomach</note>.
*   Aggregative pills <note>term: "aggregative pills" - a multi-purpose laxative intended to gather and expel multiple humors at once</note>.
*   Stomachic pills.
*   Pills of Alhandal <note>term: "Alhandal" - an Arabic name for colocynth, or bitter apple, a very potent purgative</note>.
*   Cochiae pills <note>term: "cochiae" - from the Greek "kokkos" meaning berry; these were small, potent pills usually containing scammony and aloe</note>.
*   Pills of sarcocolla <note>term: "sarcocolla" - a Persian tree resin used to treat wounds and as a purgative</note>.
*   Arthritic pills <note>for joint pain</note>.
*   Pills of simple and compound hiera <note>term: "hiera" - from "hiera picra" meaning "holy bitter," one of the oldest and most famous medicinal powders used as a laxative</note>.
*   Pills of hiera with agaric <note>term: "agaric" - a fungus that grows on larch trees, used in small doses to purge phlegm</note>.

Pills of simple hiera are made by taking the ingredients of Galen's <note>Galen was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated medicine for over 1,500 years</note> simple hiera and forming them into pills. However, compound hiera pills are made from the Hiera Picra of Nicholas <note>referring to Nicolaus Myrepsos or Nicolaus Salernitanus, authors of famous medieval pharmaceutical texts</note>; to every 1 ounce <note>original: "vnc. 1."</note> of the hiera ingredients, 1 dram <note>original: "drag. 1."</note> of scammony <note>term: "scammony" - a harsh resin from the root of Convolvulus scammonia, used as a powerful purgative</note> is added. On the other hand, pills of hiera with agaric are "magistral" <note>term: "magistral" - a custom formula prescribed by a doctor for a specific patient, rather than a standard pre-made recipe</note>, and they are made as follows. Take three parts of simple hiera. Take one part of agaric, both in troches <note>term: "troche" - a medicinal lozenge or flake</note> and not in troches; let pills be made with syrup of stoechas <note>original: "sticados" - French lavender</note>. These pills purge phlegm from the instruments of the senses <note>the eyes, ears, and nose</note> and appropriately dry out phlegm from the stomach. The "Pills of Light" <note>original: "pillulæ lucis" - prescribed for clearing the vision</note> do this same thing, as do the pills "without which I do not wish to be" <note>original: "sine quibus esse nolo" - a famous name for a specific multi-purpose laxative pill</note>.

Secondly, there are powders mixed with the aforementioned laxatives by adding their "correctives" <note>term: "corrective" - an ingredient added to a harsh medicine to "correct" its side effects, such as cramping or toxicity</note>. Each scruple <note>original: "ſcrup."</note> of laxative should have 1 grain <note>original: "gra. 1."</note> of corrective. For example, take 1 dram of laxative, 3 grains of ginger <note>original: "ʒʒ."</note>, or 3 drams of laxative with 1 grain each of mastic <note>a tree resin</note> and pepper; let a powder be made. If you wish to give agaric, give it in troche form in a dose of 1 dram or 1.5 drams.

Thirdly, there are infusions. For example, by infusing 2 drams of agaric for 10 hours with its corrective; afterward, squeeze it out, strain it, and administer it. For example: take 2 drams (or 2 ounces, 5 drams, and 3 scruples) of agaric, and 1 scruple of rock salt <note>original: "ſalis gemmę"</note>; infuse this in 1.5 ounces of sage and marjoram water for 12 hours. Then squeeze, strain, and administer; it can be sweetened slightly with syrup of stoechas.

The corrective for agaric, according to some, should be one-third the amount of the agaric itself. For example: take 1 dram of agaric, 1 scruple of rock salt, and a little cinnamon; mix them and let pills be made.

However, if agaric is given in liquid form, its corrective is oxymel <note>term: "oxymel" - a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note> or rock salt. If it is given in pills, its corrective is oxymel and rock salt together; a stomach medicine should always be mixed with it, such as cinnamon, cloves <note>original: "gariofi."</note>, aromatic calamus <note>sweet flag</note>, or mastic.

Colocynth <note>original: "Coloquintida" - bitter apple</note> is especially praised for apoplexy <note>stroke</note> and paralysis, and therefore it should by no means be omitted in those cases. Its true corrective is mastic, followed by ginger, and cinnamon. It should never be given without a "cordial" medicine <note>term: "cordial" - a medicine intended to invigorate or protect the heart</note>, because by its very nature it harms the heart. Also, labdanum, bdellium <note>bitter tree resins</note>, and tragacanth <note>a plant gum</note> correct colocynth, as do lapis lazuli <note>a blue semi-precious stone, believed to have medicinal properties</note>, bugloss <note>an herb in the borage family</note>, the bones from a deer's heart <note>a rare and prized medieval remedy for heart ailments</note>, and citron peels. The dose for the pills is 1 dram; for the powder, 1 dram.

Senna <note>a well-known leaf-based laxative still used today</note> should be given with chicken broth, or meat broth, or a light wine, or with rock salt. The dose is 6 drams, or [it can be given] with ginger <note>original: "ʒʒ" - a common apothecary shorthand for "Zingiber" (ginger)</note>. When combined with safflower and nettle seed, it purges phlegm.

Hellebore <note>a very potent and potentially toxic root</note> should be given with pepper, wild carrot, parsley, anise, oregano, and calamint. The dose is 1.5 scruples; in pill form, 1 scruple.

Hermodactyls <note>original: "Hermodactilos" - the "fingers of Hermes," likely the root of a meadow saffron used for joint pain</note> are corrected by myrobalans <note>astringent, plum-like fruits from India</note>, roses, cumin, mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree</note>, pepper, and anise. Mastic corrects its excessive moisture, while ginger and pepper correct its tendency to cause gas. Myrobalans correct its slow onset of action, and to remove potential harm to the stomach, an equal amount of ginger and saffron should be added. However, the addition of anise, ginger, and mastic helps to strengthen the stomach when [the hermodactyl] is given by itself. The dose is 1.5 drams; if given with other medicines, it is 1 dram.

The corrective for Turpeth <note>original: "Turbit" - the root of a plant in the morning glory family used as a purgative</note> is ginger. According to the mind of the Prince <note>referring to Avicenna (Ibn Sina), known as the "Prince of Physicians"</note>, they should be given in equal weight. Mesue <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note>, however, prescribes two parts ginger and one part turpeth, with as much sugar as the total of all the other ingredients. Others prescribe two parts turpeth and one part ginger. Turpeth in an infusion, according to Mesue, should be given in a dose from 1 to 2 drams; in a decoction, up to 4 drams.

Fourth are the decoctions <note>medicines made by boiling plant materials in water</note>. Strain it and give it to the patient, or dissolve the electuaries listed below in it, in a dose of 1.5 drams or up to 5 drams <note>original: "3. v." - the symbol "3" or "ʒ" denotes a dram</note>. Such as: the Indian electuary, Diaphoenicon <note>a purgative made with dates</note>, Galen's simple hiera, Hiera Picra <note>literally "holy bitter," a famous ancient laxative powder</note>, Hiera Logodio, and Hiera of Hermes. In the form of a confection <note>a solid medicinal sweet</note>, there are Diaturbith, Diacartamum <note>made with safflower</note>, and Diaphoenicon; these are given in a solid dose of 4 or 5 drams.

### An example of when a laxative is given.

In a decoction for purging melancholy, take half an ounce each of the roots of butcher’s broom <note>original: "bruscij"</note>, asparagus, and tamarisk; half a handful each of borage and bugloss; 1 or 2 drams each of senna and epithyme; half an ounce of raisins; and 7 Damask plums. Let a decoction be made until half the water is consumed, and in sufficient quantity, dissolve 5 drams of cassia fistula, 3 drams of the confection of Hamech <note>a complex medicinal paste named after a famous physician, used specifically for melancholy</note>, and 1 ounce of syrup of violets; let a drink be made.

**Note.** Epithyme ought not to be added except at the end of the decoction. **Explanation of the recipe.** The roots of butcher's broom, asparagus, and tamarisk, along with borage and bugloss, are included because they regard <note>act upon</note> melancholy. Senna and epithyme are used because they evacuate the melancholic humor; raisins and plums are added to remove the dryness of the other ingredients, and likewise syrup of violets for soothing <note>original: "linitionem" — a softening or lubricating effect</note>. The confection of Hamech is added because it is quick-acting. It is better that senna or epithyme be given with other laxative medicines rather than alone, lest the potion become revolting; in place of the syrup of violets, you may add honey of roses or another appropriate syrup.

# BOOK

But among the compound medicines that evacuate melancholy <note>Black bile, one of the four humors; an excess was thought to cause sadness or "melancholy."</note> are these: First, the **Indian pills**, **pills of lapis lazuli**, **pills of Armenian stone**, and **pills of fumitory** <note>original: "fumo terræ" — a flowering plant used to treat skin conditions and "purify" the blood.</note>, which are nevertheless more effective in the cure of scabies <note>A general term for itchy skin eruptions or mange.</note>. However, if substances are added to direct them toward the head, they will serve our purpose. Second are the **powders** of the aforementioned simple medicines: for example, take half a pound of senna pods, 5 ounces of safflower <note>original: "carthami"</note>, 1 dram of rock salt, half a dram of mace, 2 drams of ginger <note>original: "ʒ ʒ" — apothecary shorthand for "Zingiber."</note>, and 1 scruple of cloves. Take from 2 to 4 drams of this powder with water, or some prepare it with an appropriate wine. One may use senna alone with ginger and rock salt, as previously stated.

Third are **infusions** or **decoctions** <note>Liquids made by boiling down medicinal ingredients.</note>: for example, take half an ounce of senna, 2 drams of epithyme <note>original: "epithymi" — dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant used to purge melancholy.</note>, and 4 Indian myrobalans <note>original: "mirobala: ind." — a fruit from the Terminalia tree used as a laxative.</note>. Infuse these overnight in water, strain in the morning and administer; or better yet, boil until half the liquid is consumed and give 3 ounces of this decoction, or use it to dissolve the electuaries mentioned below, such as *diacassia*, *diacatholicon*, or *diasene*.

Fourth are **electuaries** <note>Medicinal pastes made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note>, such as the electuary of epithyme or **Hamech** <note>Confectio Hamech: a famous, complex purgative formula used specifically for black bile.</note>. These electuaries are given in the form of a "date" or a "bolus" <note>A large pill, often the size of a date fruit.</note>: for example, take half an ounce of the electuary of Hamech and let a gilded bolus be made with sugar. Among the *hiera* <note>original: "hieras" — literally "holy" medicines; a class of bitter purgative powders mixed with honey.</note>, there is *hieralogodion* in a dose of 1.5 ounces, and the *hiera of Hermes* in a dose of 2 to 2.5 drams. But because not all laxatives target the head—indeed, some are indifferent to all parts of the body—it is good to include "directing" ingredients with them. Regarding the stomach, we evacuate humors in the same way and with the same medicines, using the appropriate simples and compounds mentioned, and there is no need to add directing ingredients because the medicine naturally reaches the stomach on its own.

### Regarding other members besides those mentioned.

In the **liver** and the **spleen**, we evacuate with the stated medicines appropriate to those humors, but combined with their specific "digestives" <note>Medicines that "cook" or prepare a humor for evacuation.</note>. For example: For the liver, use an appropriate decoction such as: take 1.5 drams each of Indian myrobalans and red sandalwood, 1 scruple of spodium <note>original: "spodij" — medicinal ash, often from ivory or minerals.</note>, and 1 dram of citron myrobalans. Boil these in 6 pounds of water until half is consumed. Then take half an ounce of electuary of juice of roses, dissolve it in the decoction, and administer in cases of a "hot" liver.

For the **spleen**: take 5 handfuls of tamarisk, 5 handfuls each of caper bark, hart's-tongue fern <note>original: "scolopen." — Scolopendrium.</note>, and hops. Boil as above, then dissolve half an ounce of *dialene* or 6 drams of *diacatholicon* into 2 ounces of the decoction. One dram of the confection of Hamech also evacuates melancholy from it. We should do the same for other parts of the body by adding "directing" ingredients. For the **kidneys**, there is a specific medicine called *benedicta laxativa* and pills of the same.

Take 5 drams each of the powders *dyarodon abbatis* <note>A rose-based compound.</note> and *dialacca maior* <note>A compound containing lac (resin), used for the liver and spleen.</note>, and 1 scruple each of hemp-agrimony juice, aloe wood, and celery seed.

->SECOND BOOK.<-

Sometimes preserves are also added, such as: preserves of calamus <note>original: "acori" — a fragrant marsh plant used for digestion</note>, candied citron peel, 2 scruples <note>A unit of weight; 1 scruple is about 1.3 grams.</note> or 1 dram <note>A unit of weight; 1 dram is about 3.9 grams.</note> of each. With a sufficient amount of sugar dissolved in fennel water, let an electuary <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or lozenge made by mixing powdered herbs with a sweet base</term> be made in the form of tablets.

**Note.** For 1 ounce of powder, use 5 pounds of sugar. <note>original: "li. 5" — this suggests a very dilute preparation for lozenges.</note> And for 5 ounces of powder, use 3 ounces of sugar in solid or liquid form, as you prefer. However, in liquid form, the weights of the ingredients should be increased for a large quantity, but not in the solid form; for in the solid ones, sugar takes up a great deal of space. Indeed, for 1 ounce of the species <term>species: the raw powdered botanical ingredients of a compound medicine</term>, 1 pound or 8 ounces of sugar is added; but in a liquid form, 3 ounces of sugar suffices for 1 ounce of the species. Usually, liquid forms are made with some syrup, as in this example for a **hot liver**: take 1 dram of each of the "three-sandalwoods" compound <note>original: "triasandali" — a cooling mixture of red, white, and yellow sandalwood</note> and the "pearl" compound <note>original: "dyamargariton" — a restorative made from crushed pearls and herbs</note> (without the hot ingredients). Take 1 and a half drams each of red roses, spodium <note>original: "spodij" — likely zinc oxide or the ash of burnt ivory, used to cool the body</note>, and sorrel seed. Take 1 dram each of preserves of chicory, borage, and violets. Add 3 ounces of endive syrup, or a sufficient amount, to make an electuary in liquid form. You can add a greater weight of preserves in liquid electuaries, but only a small weight in others—namely, the alteratives <note>medicines intended to restore healthy balance rather than purge</note>—so that the electuary can better be reduced to a solid form.

### Note on laxative electuaries.

Laxative electuaries can be composed of the same things from which alterative electuaries are made, by adding more or less of the laxative ingredients along with their "correctives" <note>ingredients added to buffer the harsh effects of a purge, such as preventing cramps</note>, depending on how much you wish to evacuate through such laxatives. These can be made in solid or liquid substance, as was said regarding the alteratives. Note that for 1 ounce of powder, 3 ounces of sugar or syrup are used in liquid electuaries.

### Example for cholera. <note>Yellow bile, the humor associated with heat, anger, and digestive fire.</note>

Take 1 ounce of the "three-sandalwoods" compound. Take 5 drams of the Abbot’s rose-based compound <note>original: "dyarodon abbatis"</note>. Take 1 and a half ounces of water lily preserve. Take 3 drams of choice rhubarb, 5 drams of spikenard, 3 drams of yellow myrobalan <note>A fruit used as a gentle laxative</note> rinds, and 1 scruple of prepared scammony <note>original: "diagridij" — a powerful resinous purgative</note>. With 2 and a half ounces of sugar dissolved in endive water, or as much as suffices, let a liquid electuary be made. The dose is 5 ounces; for in every 5 ounces, there enters 1 dram of myrobalans and rhubarb, and about 4 grains of scammony. Therefore, it will be a laxative without violence <note>i.e., a gentle purge that does not cause excessive pain or strain</note>. But if you wish to make it stronger, add some "syrup of roses" electuary or another medicine that evacuates yellow bile.

### Example for phlegm.

Take 5 drams each of the hyssop compound <note>original: "diaisopi"</note> and the cumin compound. Take 1 scruple each of the galingale compound <note>original: "diagalagæ"</note>, mastic, and cloves. Take 5 ounces each of the safflower compound <note>original: "dyacartami"</note> and the date-based compound <note>original: "dyafinicon"</note>. Take 2 drams of troches of agaric <note>original: "agarici trociscati" — tablets made from larch fungus, used to purge phlegm</note>. Take 5 ounces of calamus preserve and 1 and a half ounces of mint syrup, or as much as suffices. Mix them. The dose is 5 ounces; it is stronger than the preceding one, yet still without violence. But if you wish to sharpen its effect, add 2, 3, or 4 grains of prepared scammony.

-># BOOK<-

But among the compound medicines that evacuate melancholy <note>original: "melancholiam" — in Galenic medicine, one of the four humors, associated with black bile and cold, dry qualities</note> are the following. First are the "Indian pills," those made from lapis lazuli <note>original: "lapide lazuli" — a deep blue stone used as a pigment and a medicine</note>, from Armenian stone <note>original: "lapide armeno" — a blue carbonate of copper</note>, and pills of fumitory <note>original: "fumo terræ" — literally "smoke of the earth," a plant used for skin conditions</note>, which are nevertheless more effective in the cure of scabies; however, if "directives" <note>ingredients added to guide the medicine's effect to a specific body part</note> for the head are included, they will serve our purpose. Second are the powders of the aforementioned simple ingredients, for which use this recipe: take half a pound of senna pods, half an ounce of safflower <note>original: "carthami"</note>, 1 dram of rock salt <note>original: "salis gemme"</note>, half a dram of mace, 2 drams of ginger <note>original: "ʒʒ" — a standard abbreviation for zingiber</note>, and 1 scruple of cloves. Some prepare 2 to 4 drams of this powder with suitable waters or wine. Some use only senna with ginger and rock salt, as was stated.

Third are the infusions or decoctions <term>decoction: a concentrated liquor made by boiling herbal ingredients in water</term>; for example: take half an ounce of senna, 2 drams of dodder of thyme <note>original: "epithymi"</note>, and 4 Indian myrobalans <note>original: "mirobala: ind." — a dried plum-like fruit used as a laxative</note>. Infuse these overnight in water, strain in the morning and administer; or better yet, boil until the liquid is reduced by half, and give 3 ounces of this decoction, or mix into it the electuaries mentioned below, such as *diacassia*, *dyacatholicon*, or *dyasene*.

Fourth are the electuaries, such as the electuary of dodder of thyme or the Hamech confection. These electuaries are given in the form of a "date" or a bolus <term>bolus: a large, soft pill, often the size of a grape</term>; for example: take half an ounce of the Hamech electuary and make it into a gilded bolus <note>original: "bolus deauratus" — pills were often coated in gold leaf to mask bitterness and add prestige</note> with sugar. Among the *hiera* <note>original: "hieras" — a class of "holy" bitter purgative powders mixed with honey</note>, there is *hieralogodion* in a dose of 1 and a half ounces, or the *hiera* of Hermes in a dose of 2 to 3 drams. But because not all purgatives are directed toward the head—indeed, some act indiscriminately on all members—it is good to include "directives" with them. For the stomach, we evacuate the humors in the same way and with the same medicines, using the aforementioned suitable simple and compound ingredients; here, it is not necessary to add directives, because the medicine naturally arrives at the stomach on its own.

Regarding organs other than those mentioned: for the liver and spleen, we evacuate with the stated medicines suited to the humors, yet combined with their "digestives" <note>medicines intended to "cook" or prepare a humor for evacuation</note>. For example: for the liver, use an appropriate decoction such as: take 1 and a half drams each of Indian myrobalans and red sandalwood, and 1 scruple of spodium <note>original: "spodij" — likely ash from burnt ivory</note>, and 1 dram of citron myrobalan. Boil these in 6 pounds of water until reduced by half, then take half an ounce of the electuary of rose juice, dissolve it in the decoction, and administer for a "hot cause" of the liver. For the spleen: take half a handful <note>original: "manip." — manipulus</note> of tamarisk, and half a handful each of caper bark, hart’s-tongue fern <note>original: "scolopen."</note>, and hops. Boil as above, then dissolve half an ounce of *dyalene* or 6 drams of *dyacatholicon* with 1 dram of the Hamech confection into 2 ounces of the decoction. This evacuates melancholy from the spleen; we shall do the same for other organs by adding directives. For the kidneys, there is a specific medicine called *benedicta laxativa* and "pills of *benedicta*."

### Example for the liver in a "cold cause."

Take half a dram each of the powders *dyarodon abbatis* <note>The "Abbot’s Rose" compound</note> and the "greater *dialacca*" <note>A resin-based compound used for the liver and spleen</note>, and 1 scruple each of eupatory juice, aloe wood, and celery seed <note>original: "feminis apij"</note>.

# BOOK TWO. 56

Sometimes preserves are also added, as follows: 2 scruples of each of sweet flag <note>original: "acori" — calamus root, used for digestion</note> preserves and candied citron peel, or 1 dram of sugar dissolved in a sufficient amount of fennel water; let an electuary <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or lozenge made by mixing powders with honey, syrup, or sugar</term> be made in tablets.

Note: For 1 ounce of powder, use 5 ounces <note>original: "li. 5" — likely a scribal error for "vnc. 5" (5 ounces), as a 1:5 or 1:6 ratio of medicine to sugar was standard for solid tablets</note> of sugar. And for half an ounce of powder, use 3 ounces of sugar in either solid or liquid form, as you prefer. However, in liquid form, it is necessary to increase the weight of the medicinal ingredients for a large quantity, but not in solid form. For in those [solid forms], sugar occupies a large space; for instance, for 1 ounce of species <term>species: a mixture of various powdered herbs or spices used as a base for a medicine</term>, 1 pound of sugar is used, or 8 ounces; however, in liquid form, 3 ounces of sugar is sufficient for 1 ounce of species, and for the most part, liquid forms are made with some syrup.

As in this example for a **hot liver**: take 1 dram each of the "three-sandalwoods" <note>original: "triasandali" — a cooling mixture of red, yellow, and white sandalwood</note> species and *diamargariton* <note>original: "dyamargariton" — a restorative powder made from crushed pearls</note> without the hot spices; 1.5 drams each of red roses, *spodium* <note>original: "spodij" — traditionally bone ash or zinc oxide, used as a cooling agent</note>, and sorrel seed; 1 dram each of chicory, borage, and violet preserves; 3 ounces of endive syrup, or better yet, as much as is sufficient. Let an electuary be made in liquid form. You can use a greater weight of preserves in liquid electuaries, but only a small weight in others—namely the "alterative" <note>medicines intended to gradually restore healthy body functions</note> ones—so that the electuary can better be reduced to a solid form.

->Note on laxative electuaries.<-

Laxative electuaries can be composed of the same things from which alterative electuaries are made, by adding more or less of the laxative ingredients along with their "correctives" <note>ingredients added to mitigate the harsh side effects of a purge</note>, according to how much you wish to evacuate the body through such laxatives. They can be made in solid or liquid substance, as was said regarding the alteratives. Note that for 1 ounce of powder, 3 ounces of sugar or syrup is used in liquid electuaries.

->Example for yellow bile <note>original: "cholera" — in Galenic medicine, the hot and dry humor</note>.<-

Take 1 ounce of the "three-sandalwoods" species; 5 drams of the "Abbot’s Rose" <note>original: "dyarodon abbatis" — a famous rose-based digestive powder</note> species; 1.5 ounces of water lily <note>original: "nenupharis"</note> preserve; 3 drams of choice rhubarb; 5 drams of spikenard; 3 drams of yellow myrobalan <note>original: "mirobalanorū citrinorum" — a dried fruit from India used as a gentle purgative</note> rinds; 1 scruple of *diagridium* <note>original: "diagridij" — a purified form of scammony resin, a potent laxative</note>; 2.5 ounces of sugar dissolved in endive water, or as much as is sufficient. Let an electuary be made in liquid form. The dose is 5 ounces <note>The weight of the final mixture, not a single serving</note>; for in every 5 ounces there enters 1 dram of myrobalans and rhubarb, and about 4 grains of *diagridium*; therefore, it will be a laxative without violence. But if you wish to make it stronger, add some of the "electuary of rose juice" or another medicine that evacuates yellow bile.

->Example for phlegm.<-

Take 5 drams each of the *diaisopum* <note>original: "diaisopi" — hyssop-based powder for the chest</note> and *diacyminum* <note>original: "diacimini" — cumin-based powder for wind</note> species; 1 scruple each of the *diagalanga* <note>original: "diagalagæ" — galangal-based powder</note> species, mastic, and cloves; 5 ounces each of the *diacarthamum* <note>original: "dyacartami" — safflower-based</note> and *diaphoenicon* <note>original: "dyafinicon" — date-based</note> electuaries; 2 drams of agaric <note>original: "agarici trociscati" — a medicinal mushroom prepared in small cakes</note>; 5 ounces of sweet flag <note>original: "acori"</note> preserve; 1.5 ounces of mint syrup, or as much as is sufficient. Mix them; the dose is 5 ounces, and it is stronger than the preceding one, yet still without violence. If you wish to sharpen it, add 2, 3, or 4 grains of *diagridium*.

# BOOK TWO

-> Example for melancholy. <-

Take 5 drams each of the species for caper electuary and *diacurcuma* <note>original: "diacurcumę" — a medicinal powder based on saffron or turmeric used for the liver and spleen</note>; 1 dram of bugloss <note>original: "buglossæ" — oxtongue, an herb believed to gladden the heart</note> preserves; 5 drams each of confection of Hamech <note>original: "confectionis hamech" — a famous bitter purgative used to expel black bile</note> and *diasena*; 4 scruples of washed Armenian stone <note>original: "lapidis armeni loti" — a blue carbonate of copper used as a potent purgative for melancholy</note>; 3 drams of senna pods; and as much fumitory syrup as is sufficient. Mix these. The dose is 5 ounces or 5 drams; however, you may increase or decrease the dose according to your discretion by increasing or decreasing the laxatives.

Electuaries in solid substance are made in the same way as alterative electuaries, with the addition of laxatives.

-> Example for cholera. <- <note>In this context, "cholera" refers to an excess of yellow bile, not the modern bacterial infection</note>

Take 5 drams of the "three-sandalwoods" species; 1.5 drams of choice rhubarb; 2 drams of yellow myrobalans <note>original: "miroba. citrinorum" — an astringent fruit from India used in purging</note>; 2 scruples of spikenard; 4 grains of *diagridium* <term>diagridium: a purified form of scammony, a harsh plant resin, often prepared with quince juice to lessen its griping effects</term>; and as much sugar dissolved in sorrel water as is sufficient. Let a solid electuary be made in tablets; the dose is 5 drams or 5 ounces.

-> Method for retaining the medicine. <-

The first method is for the patient to smell fragrant things—indeed, the patient should pinch the nostrils so as not to perceive the odor of the medicine. Second, let a cloth soaked in cold water be taken and tied around, or at least applied to the front of the neck, while simultaneously splashing cold water on the face. Third, let something be placed in the mouth, such as an apple or similar fruit, or let a piece of burnt bread be held before the mouth and nostrils. Finally, let a cupping glass with fire <term>cupping glass: a vessel used to create suction on the skin; "with fire" refers to the practice of burning air out of the cup to create a vacuum</term> be placed over the stomach, and the medicine will be retained. When there is much sleep after the bowels have been moved, it demonstrates that the evacuation has now perfectly cleansed the body and been beneficial.

The signs of a perfect evacuation are: first, when it evacuates without pain or twisting <note>original: "torfione" — likely *torsione*, referring to intestinal cramping</note>. Second, if joy, lightness, and rest follow the evacuation. Third, if thirst follows—not because of the humors being evacuated, nor because of the heat and dryness of the medicine, but when it comes because of and after the completion of digestion and the consumption of the medicine, then the thirst is good and appropriate. Regarding this, the aphorism from the fourth section <note>original: "aphorismus quartę particulæ" — referring to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, a foundational medical text</note> says: "Those who, during purging by drugs, do not become thirsty, do not cease until they become thirsty."

Removing harm induced either by windiness <note>original: "ventositatem" — gas or bloating</note> or by medicines: If you see harm, give the patient 15 drams of the best *mithridatum* or theriac <term>theriac: a "universal" medicinal paste made of dozens of ingredients, used as an antitoxin and restorative</term> in the best choice wine on the following morning, because in this way the residual windiness is removed. Or take 2 drams of aged theriac and 1.5 drams of rose sugar, and give it to the patient in the morning on an empty stomach; or if the patient is very hot, give rose water alone.

# SECOND [BOOK]

### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 14.

*Laxative medicines should be given least of all during times that are either very hot or very cold; the upper parts <note>referring to the use of emetics to induce vomiting</note> should be purged in summer, and the lower parts <note>referring to the use of laxatives</note> in winter. Medicines should be given very sparingly to children and the elderly. Young people should take medicines rarely, and the elderly should avoid them: Different medicines require different times, and he enumerates what they are. The signs of the Zodiac influence the power of simple medicines.*
*♄ <note>Saturn</note> rules the humor that is at fault in quartan fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, traditionally associated with black bile</note>.*
*♃ <note>Jupiter</note> rules synochal fevers <term>synochal: a type of continuous fever that does not remit</term>.*
*♂ <note>Mars</note> rules tertian fevers <note>a fever that recurs every three days, associated with yellow bile</note>.*
*☉ <note>The Sun</note> rules hectic fever <note>a persistent, wasting fever</note>, ☿ <note>Mercury</note> rules ephemeral fever <note>a fever lasting only a single day</note>.*
*When these planets are in a strong position, the cure for those diseases they rule must not be begun. One must also observe the signs; the ☉ <note>Sun</note> and ☽ <note>Moon</note> govern the stages of life, just as both the planets and the signs govern the virtues <note>natural powers or functions</note> of the body, and he [the author] passes down which planets govern which virtues.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting a landscape with figures in the foreground and classical architecture in the background.</image-desc> It should be noted that in the use of laxative medicine, two things are primarily considered. First, the timing in the administration of the laxative medicine. For it should not be given on the hottest or coldest days: for during the "Dog Days" <note>original: "sub cane" — the sweltering period of summer when the Dog Star, Sirius, rises with the sun</note> and just before them, purgings are troublesome and the use of medicines is difficult. Hippocrates, Section 4, Aphorism 5.

I And it is more suitable in the seasons of autumn and spring than in summer and winter: for Hippocrates says in Section 6, Aphorism 46: Those who are being purged with medicine...

# BOOK [TWO]

...secondly, medicine should be administered to these people in the springtime. For in the summer, because of the heat, a boiling of the humors <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> occurs, which causes harm to the body through their movement. However, Hippocrates <note>original: Hipocra.</note> prefers the winter season over the summer for this, in what he says in Part 4, Aphorism 4: "In summer, purge the upper parts <note>referring to the use of emetics to induce vomiting</note>, but in winter, the lower parts <note>referring to the use of laxatives</note>." By this he means that in the summer, if necessary, vomiting should be induced, while in the winter, we should use purgative medicines <note>original: pharmacijs</note>. For slender people, such as those of a choleric temperament who vomit easily, it is necessary to purge from above, avoiding the winter—that is, at any time except in winter. But those who vomit with difficulty, such as the melancholic, the phlegmatic, and those of moderate fleshiness, [should be purged] from below, avoiding the summer.

Secondly, when giving purgatives or laxative medicines, age must be considered: for children and the very old are unfit for purging, according to Aphorism 12 of Arnaldus de Villa Nova <note>a famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note>, when he says: "In children and the elderly, one must fear to administer purgatives. In young people, too, it is suspicious to take medicine frequently." Whosoever takes purgatives too often in their youth will quickly weep for the discomforts of old age.

Thirdly, one must consider the manner of administering laxative medicine, and to whom it should be given. For those who have healthy bodies should not use laxative medicine, as Hippocrates says in Part 2, Aphorism 36.

It is also to be known that the chosen times for taking medicines are determined by the movement of the Moon in the "watery" signs <note>original: signis aquaticis</note>, which are Cancer, Scorpio, Pisces, Libra, and Aquarius.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ In Cancer, it is good to give medicine in electuaries <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</term>.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ In Scorpio, it is good in potions.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ In Pisces, pills should be given.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;{ In Libra and Aquarius, give whatever you wish.
Among these signs, Scorpio is better, Cancer is worse.

## Concerning the Rules and conditions to be observed in Laxative Medicine.

First rule. In administering laxative medicine, care must be taken that the Moon is not in the "ruminating" signs <note>original: signis ruminantibus; signs associated with animals that chew the cud</note>, which are Aries, Taurus, and Capricorn; for these signify the vomiting up of the medicine. And this is what Hermes <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure associated with medical astrology</note> says in Proposition 84: "When the Moon is in ruminating signs, or joined to a retrograde planet, it is not good to use purges; for these cause vomiting or other injuries."
