# [BOOK] SECOND

<margin>3</margin> **The second rule.** Do not give medicine during unfavorable alignments of the Moon with the "infortunates" <note>original: "infortunatos," referring to the malefic planets Saturn and Mars</note>. For **Saturn** hinders and frustrates the work of medicine by thickening and condensing the humors <note>the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> and by closing the pores. This is because **Saturn** is cold by nature, and it is the property of cold to constrict. **Mars**, however, because of its heat and dryness, causes the humors to become unruly, sharpening them sometimes to the point of drawing blood, especially if the medicine used is strong.

**The third rule.** Care must be taken that the **Moon** is not joined with **Jupiter**, because this will shorten the medicine’s duration of action. For **Ptolemy** says in the 19th proposition of the *Centiloquium* <note>original: "Centiloquij," a famous collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>: "If anyone takes a purgative <note>original: "purgatorium"</note> while the Moon is with Jupiter, its work will be shortened and its effect diminished." The reason for this is that **Jupiter** is a friend to nature and favorable to the life of living beings. He is warm and moist—the qualities in which the life of living things consists. Therefore, when a medicine acts against nature to remove something, nature becomes strong by reason of **Jupiter**, and it prevents the operation and effect of that medicine.

**The fourth rule.** It is praiseworthy to give medicine when the **Moon** is in **Scorpio** or **Pisces**, and when the "Lord of the Ascendant" <note>the planet ruling the zodiac sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> is joined to a planet below the earth through a conjunction or a favorable aspect. However, if the Lord of the Ascendant is joined to a planet located in the "mid-heaven" <note>original: "medio cœli," the highest point in the sky</note>, the patient will suffer nausea and the medicine will be vomited up and will not remain within him. **Ptolemy** states this in the 21st "word" of his *Centiloquium*.

<margin>4</margin> **The fifth rule.** If you wish to purge the **spleen**, see that **Saturn** is not fortified in the heavens; instead, you should treat it in the **hour of Jupiter** <note>a system where each hour of the day is ruled by a specific planet</note> when he himself is fortified.

**The sixth rule.** Do not purge the **liver** in the hour of **Jupiter** when he is fortified in the heavens, but [in that hour] you may purge the **spleen**.

**The seventh rule.** Do not purge the **heart** in the **hour of the Sun** or when the **Sun** is fortified. However, if the **Sun** is in the Ascendant, or in the mid-heaven, or in the "angle of the seventh" <note>the western horizon or descendant</note>, it is good to give a cordial medicine that strengthens, but not one that is laxative or purgative.

**The eighth rule.** You shall not evacuate the **lung** in the **hour of Mercury** when he is fortified in the heavens.

**The ninth rule.** Do not treat the **gall** <note>bile</note> and the **kidneys** in the **hour of Mars** when he is well-disposed.

**The tenth rule.** The **testicles** should not be purged in the **hour of Venus** or during her favorable disposition.

**The eleventh rule.** It is bad to purge the **brain** in the **hour of the Moon** when the **Moon** itself is fortified in the heavens.

**The twelfth rule.** If you give a laxative, ensure that **Leo** is not the ascending sign at that hour, lest the sick person suffer nausea and vomit the medicine.

We can, however, [prepare] in the hours of the planets when they are fortified in the heavens...

It should also be noted that just as the planets relate to the evacuation of our body’s humors <note>the four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, so too do the signs of heaven. In evacuating a humor, one must avoid the influence and strength of a planet that shares the same quality or power over that specific humor. The rule for the zodiac signs, however, is different. For when evacuating a humor, a sign should be chosen that shares a likeness with that humor, such that this sign is the "Ascendant" <note>the sign rising on the eastern horizon</note> or the **Moon** is within it—except for the signs of **Aries**, **Taurus**, **Leo**, **Capricorn**, the last half of **Libra** (which is the **Burnt Path** <term>Via Combusta: a specific region of the zodiac between 15° Libra and 15° Scorpio traditionally viewed as unlucky or "burnt"</term>), and the first three degrees of **Scorpio**.

**Note diligently:** Just as the signs and planets influence the human body, so too do they influence medicines, whether they be "simples" <note>medicines made of a single herb</note> or compounds.

Therefore, if you wish to administer it, let the **Moon** be well-disposed in those signs.

**Aries (♈):** This sign also governs **hepatic aloes** <note>a dark, liver-colored variety of aloe</note> and **myrobalans** <note>dried astringent fruits from India</note>, which evacuate humors from the head.

**Sagittarius (♐):** **Colocynth** and **Hermodactyls** <note>a plant historically used to treat joint pain and gout</note>, which purge the feet.

### BOOK TWO

...are [treated] by cold humors, and especially by **melancholy** <note>black bile, one of the four bodily humors thought to cause sadness or sluggishness</note>, and they are ruled by the **Sun**.

- **Saturn** rules the humor that is at fault in a **quartan fever** <note>a fever where paroxysms occur every fourth day, often associated with black bile</note>.
- **Jupiter** rules continuous fevers <note>original: "sinochum & sinocham," referring to types of non-remitting fevers caused by blood or heat</note>.
- **Mars** rules **tertian fevers** <note>fevers recurring every three days</note> and all others that exist in the body by reason of **yellow bile** <note>original: "choleræ"</note>.
- The **Sun** rules **hectic fever** <note>a persistent, wasting fever often associated with chronic illness</note>.
- **Mercury** rules **ephemeral fever** <note>a fever lasting only one day</note>.

When these planets are "fortified" <note>positioned in a powerful or influential part of the astrological chart</note>, treatment must not be begun; nor should the time of their dominance be chosen for starting a cure or for the administration of medicine.

It must be considered that the suitability of time for **purging** <note>original: "pharmacandum," the medical evacuation of humors</note> is observed in the water signs <note>Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces</note> through the presence of the **Moon**, as has been said. For when the **Moon** is found in a water sign and is **void of course** <term>Void of course: a period when the Moon makes no further major geometric relationships (aspects) with other planets before moving into the next sign; traditionally seen as a time when "nothing will come of it."</term>, we should judge the purging to be mediocre. A "mediocre" purging is one where there are as many testimonies from "fortunate" planets as there are from "unfortunate" ones.

<margin>Aspects</margin>
- A **square** <note>a 90° angle</note> of **Jupiter** or **Venus** to the **Moon** will make for a good purging.
- A **sextile** <note>a 60° angle</note> of the **Sun** or **Mars**, or a **trine** <note>a 120° angle</note> of them to the **Moon**.
- A **sextile** or **trine** of **Jupiter** to the **Moon** likewise—and provided **Venus** is not **combust** <term>Combust: when a planet is so close to the Sun (within 8.5 degrees) that its power is thought to be "burnt up" or hidden</term>—will make for the best purging.
- A **square** of the **Sun**, **Saturn**, or **Mars** to the **Moon**, or their **conjunction** <note>occupying the same degree</note> with the **Moon**, prohibits the giving of medicine.

One should also note the rule of **Ptolemy** <note>the famous 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer/astrologer</note> in the 56th saying of his *Centiloquium* <note>a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>, and that of **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arabic astrologer</note>. Namely, that the humors in the first and third weeks of the lunar cycle recede from the internal parts of the body to the exterior; however, in the second and fourth weeks, they move from the exterior to the interior. Therefore, in the first and third weeks, one should use external evacuations, such as **bloodletting** <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note>. In the [second] and fourth weeks <note>The Latin text here repeats "third and fourth," but the logic of the previous sentence implies the second and fourth for internal treatment</note>, use internal evacuations, such as purging medicine.

**Haly** provides the reason for this rule when he says: the fluids of bodies, from the hour of the **conjunction** of the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>the New Moon</note> until the first quarter aspect, "advance" because they go out from their inner parts to become visible. They are like rivers whose waters rise, and that increase is called the **flood** <note>original: "accessio"</note>. From the first quarter until the "prevention" or **opposition** <note>the Full Moon</note>, they are drawn back from the extremities of the body to its interior; they are like rivers whose waters recede. From the opposition until the second quarter aspect, it is as in the first quarter; and from the second quarter aspect until the conjunction, they recede again, according to the proportion of the second quarter.

# BOOK

### On Strengthening the Virtues <note>original: "Virtutes"; in this context, "virtues" refers to the innate powers or physiological functions of the body, rather than moral qualities.</note>.

The virtues of the body are twofold: the principal ones, which are further divided. One is that which preserves the species <note>referring to the survival of the human race through reproduction</note>, and this flourishes in the reproductive organs and is ruled by **Venus**.
   Others are those that preserve the individual, and there are three of these: the **Vital** virtue, which resides in the heart and is governed by the **Sun**; the **Natural** virtue, which resides in the liver and is ruled by **Jupiter**; and the **Animal** virtue <note>from the Latin "anima," meaning the soul or breath; this refers to cognitive and nervous functions</note>, which **Mercury** governs. For the various alignments of **Mercury** with the other planets change the mind in different ways—at times dulling it, and at other times wonderfully sharpening and strengthening the intellect. There are other less principal or "administering" virtues, namely the **attractive**, **digestive**, and so on, as follows:

| The Virtues | Action | Governing Planets |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Attractive** <note>The power to draw in nourishment</note> | | ☉ The Sun |
| **Digestive** <note>The power to process nourishment</note> | Governs & strengthens | ♃ Jupiter |
| **Retentive** <note>The power to hold nourishment</note> | | ♄ Saturn |
| **Expulsive** <note>The power to eliminate waste</note> | | ☽ The Moon |

In a similar way, the signs of the zodiac rule these virtues:
♈ Aries and ♐ Sagittarius govern the **Attractive** virtue.
♉ Taurus, ♍ Virgo, and ♑ Capricorn govern the **Retentive** virtue.
The first half of ♊ Gemini and ♎ Libra, along with ♒ Aquarius, govern the **Digestive** virtue.
♋ Cancer, ♏ Scorpio, and ♓ Pisces govern the **Expulsive** virtue.

   And if you wish to strengthen the **attractive virtue**, which flourishes through heat and dryness (just as the **Sun** does), let this be done while the **Moon** is in a hot and dry sign, such as ♈ Aries or ♐ Sagittarius; ♌ Leo is bad for this purpose <note>likely because Leo, being the Sun's own sign, creates an excess of heat that could be harmful rather than strengthening</note>.
   Alternatively, strengthen it when the [Sun] is in ♈ Aries or ♐ Sagittarius if you cannot wait for the **Moon**. The same logic applies to the other virtues.
   **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century scholar whose works formed the basis of medieval astronomy and astrology</note> spoke of these virtues in the 86th proposition of his *Centiloquium* <note>original: "centiloquij"; a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>, where he says the **Sun** is the origin of the **vital virtue**, which belongs to the heart, as seen below:

☉ The **Sun** is the Origin of the **vital virtue**, which belongs to the **Heart**.
☽ The **Moon** is the Origin of the **natural virtue** of the **liver**.
♄ **Saturn** is the Origin of the **receptive virtue**.
♃ **Jupiter** is the Origin of the **growing and nourishing virtue**.
♂ **Mars** is the Origin of the **irascible** <note>related to spirit or anger</note> and **attractive virtue**.
♀ **Venus** is the Origin of the **concupiscible** <note>related to physical desire</note> and **appetitive virtue**.
☿ **Mercury** is the Origin of the **imaginative**, **phantastic** <note>the faculty of forming mental images</note>, and **thinking virtue**.

SECOND BOOK. 60

### EXPLANATIONS.

1 And it is agreed, *Astrologers judge the four seasons of the year one way, and physicians another*: astrologers begin Spring from the entry of the Sun into the first degree of **Aries** ♈, Summer from its entry into the first degree of **Cancer** ♋, Autumn from its entry into the first degree of **Libra** ♎, and Winter from its entry into the first degree of **Capricorn** ♑. Physicians feel otherwise, but since the author confirms his own opinion by the authority of **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, I believe the physician ought to see what both Hippocrates and his followers think on this matter, and divide the seasons according to their opinions.

2 Lest the **Moon** ☽ be in the signs: he said above that the Moon should be in "ruminating" signs <note>original: "signis ruminantibus"; these are zodiac signs associated with animals that chew the cud, like Aries, Taurus, and Capricorn, which were thought to cause medicine to be vomited back up.</note> when you wish to induce vomiting.

3 To the unfortunate ones, that is, to the "malefics" <note>original: "infortunas"; planets traditionally thought to have a negative influence.</note>, which are **Saturn** ♄ and **Mars** ♂, as he himself asserts. Otherwise, all planets can be unfortunate in certain positions, as was said above.

4 The fifth rule: a universal rule can be gathered from this, that physicians should never purge that body part over which the current planet is a strong lord, nor do so in that planet's specific hour. This is handled differently, however, when signs are "dominating" the limbs. For it is good if such a sign is "ascending" <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time.</note> or if the Moon is in it—except for **Aries** ♈, **Taurus** ♉, **Leo** ♌, **Sagittarius** ♐, and the latter half of **Scorpio** ♏.
"Void of course" <note>original: "Vacua cursu"; a term for when the Moon makes no further major aspects to other planets before leaving its current sign, often suggesting a time when actions will not have the intended result.</note>: regarding this, see the first treatise, chapter 7.

<header>BOOK</header>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a seated scholar or physician holding a vessel, framed by ornamental scrollwork.</image-desc>

**Bloodletting** <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> is a general method of cleansing that removes an excess of **humors** <note>The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health.</note> when they increase beyond their proper balance within the veins. As **Avicenna** <note>The influential Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of the *Canon of Medicine*.</note> declares in the fourth book of his first volume, chapter 20, four factors must be considered regarding bloodletting.

First is the **time**. Bloodletting is to be feared during the hottest and coldest days. For as **Hippocrates** says in the fourth part of his *Aphorisms*, the fifth entry: "During and before the Dog Days <note>original: "sub cane"; referring to the period of late summer when the star Sirius, the Dog Star, rises with the sun, traditionally associated with oppressive heat.</note>, purgings are troublesome." There are three reasons for this. First, regarding the state of the body's vitality: a great deal of "resolution" <note>A weakening or thinning of the body’s substances due to heat.</note> has already occurred, and the medicine or the bloodletting adds to this depletion. Second, it is due to the inflammation of the spirits and humors, as the medicine further inflames them.

Third, because that summer air is like a bath that draws the humors from the center of the body to the surface; medicine, however, draws from the surface back to the center. This causes a kind of conflict that weakens the body's vitality and inflames the spirits, leading to fevers.

Second, the **age** of those to be bled must be considered: bloodletting is not advisable before the 14th year or after the 60th or 70th year. This is primarily due to the thinness of the veins in youths, and secondly due to the weakness of vitality in the elderly—unless those elderly people are fleshy, full of blood, and vigorous.

Third, **habit** must be considered; the elderly and those unaccustomed to the practice should not be bled lest they fall into illness, except in cases of great necessity.

Fourth, **vitality** <note>original: "virtus"</note> must be observed: the strong may be bled, but the weak by no means.

It should be noted that there are two types of timing for bloodletting. One is the **time of necessity**, namely when a disease demands it. For example, in cases of <term>Quinsy</term> <note>original: "Squinantia"; a severe, potentially life-threatening inflammation of the throat or tonsils.</note>, bleeding the cephalic vein or the vein under the tongue is very beneficial, even if the timing is not chosen according to the heavens. For Quinsy is an extremely acute disease that allows no delay because it kills very quickly; regarding this time of bleeding, it is not our main subject, because "necessity has no law."

The other is the **elected time**, which according to the wise masters of the stars is taken from the position of the **Moon** ☽ in the signs of the zodiac, and the various aspects of the Moon to the **Sun** ☉ and other planets, as described below.

As for the signs, those of a <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>One of the four temperaments, associated with water, cold, and moisture.</note> nature ought to be bled when the Moon is in **Aries** ♈︎ or **Sagittarius** ♐︎. However, an exception is made for the head in **Aries** and the thighs in **Sagittarius**, in which parts bloodletting is not advisable, as shown in the figure <note>A reference to the "Zodiac Man," a common medical diagram showing which signs govern which body parts.</note>.

<summary>This page outlines the four essential criteria for bloodletting—timing, age, habit, and physical strength—while distinguishing between emergency medical necessity and astrologically "elected" times for treatment.</summary>

**Bloodletting** <note>original: "Minuant"; literally "They may diminish [the blood]."</note> **is advised for:**

| Temperament | Zodiac Signs | Restrictions |

In Leo, bloodletting is forbidden because Leo is the house of the **Sun**, and the Sun’s nature is entirely contrary to that of the **Moon**.

In Gemini, bloodletting is forbidden for this reason: bloodletting is commonly performed in the arms and hands, which are the parts of the body governed by Gemini. One must fear touching a limb with iron <note>The surgical scalpel or lancet.</note> while the Moon is in the sign that rules that specific limb; this same rule is stated by **Al-Mansur** <note>original: "Almanfor"; referring to the Persian physician Al-Razi (Rhazes) and his famous medical text *Liber ad Almansorem*.</note> in his *Book of 150 Chapters*, chapter 24. It will not be a good bloodletting when the Moon is in Gemini, nor will it be suitable to use **cupping glasses** <note>original: "ventosis"; heated glass jars used to draw blood to the surface.</note> when the Moon is in Taurus. Furthermore, Gemini and the latter half of Libra are excluded because the **galaxy** <note>original: "galaxia"; the Milky Way, which was thought to have a turbulent, Mars-like astrological influence.</note> passes through them; in that region are many stars with the nature of **Mars**. Therefore, the Moon is said to be **combust** <note>Weakened or "burned" by proximity to harsh celestial influences.</note> in those signs, and phlebotomy should be avoided. Many also reject Scorpio for bloodletting because it is opposite to Taurus (where the Moon is exalted) and because Scorpio is the house of Mars, who is more contrary to the Moon than even the Sun. However, when the Moon passes through the first 12 degrees of Scorpio, which the galaxy also passes through, a moderate bloodletting may be performed. In the other **earthly signs**, namely ♉ Taurus, ♍ Virgo, and ♑ Capricorn, bloodletting is in no way effective.

### BOOK TWO

**Bloodletting** <note>original: "minutio"; literally a "diminishing" of the blood.</note>, according to the teaching of physicians, is sometimes performed through **metathesis** <note>original: "metathesim"; a technique of drawing blood from the same side as the ailment to encourage local healing.</note>. This is said to occur when blood is drawn from that same part in which the sickness resides; for example, if there is pain in the left side, the bloodletting should be performed on the left side of the body. Sometimes it is performed through **antispasis** <note>original: "antispasim"; a technique of "revulsion" where blood is drawn from the opposite side of the body to divert the flow of harmful humors away from the site of disease.</note>. *Antispasis* is named for the "contrary" method: if the suffering occurs in the left side, the bloodletting shall be done on the right.

And if the pain is new <note>acute</note>, let the bloodletting be done through *antispasis*. If it is long-standing <note>chronic</note>, let it be done through *metathesis*. Galen <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose works formed the backbone of medieval medical theory.</note> says in his **Microtechne** <note>original: "micratechgni"; likely referring to the "Ars Medica" or "Small Art," a foundational medical textbook.</note>: If anyone has a weak or failing stomach, they must beware of phlebotomy <note>bloodletting</note>, and especially from the veins located in the bend of the arm. Similarly, those who have a failing liver and those in whom "coldness" dominates should abstain from phlebotomy, unless the disease is dangerous, such as <term>quinsy</term> <note>original: "squinantia"; a severe, potentially suffocating throat infection.</note>, <term>pleurisy</term>, <term>pneumonia</term>, and the like.

Note that concerning the veins which are opened most often, the first we encounter is the **cephalic** <note>original: "cephalica"; from the Greek word for "head."</note>, which is in the upper part of the arm. There is less danger in opening this one because there is no significant nerve or artery beneath it that might be accidentally touched during the procedure, which would be perilous. The incision of this vein is effective against discharge from the eyes, all pains of the head, and against the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "morbum caducum"; an old term for epilepsy.</note>. This vein relates to the upper parts of the body, and if it cannot be used, the **salvatella** vein <note>original: "saluatella"; a vein on the back of the hand.</note> should be taken, which is at the base of the thumb.

The **basilic** <note>original: "basilica"; from the Greek for "royal."</note> is in the lower part of the arm. It is also called the **hepatic** <note>liver</note> vein. It is opened for ailments of the liver and spleen, and this is done more perfectly in the left hand. Under this vein is a large artery; therefore, the opening of the basilic must not be deep, lest the artery be touched. In place of the basilic, if it cannot be easily found, the **seylen** <note>original: "seylen"; a Latinized Arabic term for a specific vein in the hand.</note> should be opened, which is between the little finger and the ring finger. However, it must be opened with fear <note>extreme caution</note> because a nerve lies beneath it. The hand should be placed in warm water so the vein appears more clearly, and the blood is thinned so it may exit more freely. This vein evacuates from the lower parts of the body. The basilic in the right arm is called the "vein of the liver," and in the left, the "vein of the spleen," because they draw blood from those organs. According to the teaching of many, the *seylen* and the *salvatella* are the same vein.

The **common** or **middle vein** is also called the vein of the heart or the womb. It is also called the **black** or **purple vein**. It is called "common" because it draws blood from both the upper and lower parts of the body. It is "of the heart" because it evacuates directly from the heart and chest area, and "of the womb" because it diverts blood from the womb. It is called **median** because it is in the middle between the cephalic and the basilic, and is formed from branches of both. It is called "black-purple" because its color tends more toward those shades.

The **quidegi veins** <note>original: "venæ quidegi"; from the Arabic "al-wadaj," referring to the jugular veins.</note>. These are two large veins in the neck, one on the right, the other...

### On the judgment of the blood and its inspection.

Blood emitted or flowing out from the veins must be felt; if it is found to be cold, the flow should be stopped immediately. Likewise, if it is found to be hot and thin <term>subtle</term>, the bloodletting should be ceased lest the patient faint <term>syncope</term> <note>original: "sincopizet"</note>.

Also, let one drop of blood be placed upon the fingernail; if it flows off, it is very watery, and for this reason the bleeding should be stopped. But if it stays in place, it is too thick, and a small amount more should be extracted until it becomes thinner.

And if you wish to distinguish between the thickness and the wateriness of the blood <term>cruor</term> <note>original: "cruoris, seu sanguinis"; "cruor" often refers to blood once it has left the body or clotted</note>, let one drop be thrown into water. If it sinks to the bottom, it is judged to be thick; but if it floats on top, it is considered watery. If it remains in the middle, it is a good sign.

Blood of a black color settling at the bottom of the bowl <term>scutella</term> <note>a shallow medical dish</note> testifies to an excess of **melancholy** <term>black bile</term> and to fearfulness. Whoever possesses such blood should use things that cleanse the blood and increase "good blood."

A mucilaginous whiteness, tasteless and similar to the white of an egg—if it is found in the blood after the "melancholic" blood and in excessive quantity—signifies that **phlegm** <note>the cold, moist humor</note> is dominant.

Pure blood, purple, red, or reddish, appearing in great quantity, indicates the **sanguine** humor <note>the humor of blood itself, associated with a social and energetic temperament</note>.

Foam on the blood, if it is of a saffron color tending toward a sparkling redness and in smaller quantity than the blood, indicates **choler** <term>yellow bile</term> <note>the hot, dry humor associated with anger</note>.

The watery substance that floats on top of clotted blood—just like the whey in milk when it has curdled—if it appears as a wateriness similar to the urine of a healthy person, it is a good sign. The more perfectly that wateriness is separated from the blood, the better the digestion in the **liver** <term>hepar</term> is signaled, and vice-versa. Thus, it is not good for the blood to be totally deprived of such urinary wateriness, for from this one judges dryness and thickness of the blood. Such a lack of wateriness is usually found in the blood of those who fast and keep watch <note>stay awake for prayer or study</note> a great deal, who eat dry and hot foods, and who exercise and study much; likewise in those recovering from illness.

But if this urinary moisture is excessive, it signifies a failure of digestion and a weakness of the body. Commonly, such people have a cold stomach and liver, and such blood—

### SECOND BOOK. 63.

...stones <note>referring to kidney or bladder stones</note>, and is beneficial for women who have not been properly cleansed after childbirth, and for those who are not well-disposed toward receiving seed <note>a historical reference to fertility and conception</note>.

The opening of the veins in the arm should be done lengthwise, as should those in the corners of the eyes; however, the vein in the middle of the forehead should be opened crosswise <term>transverse</term>.

In spring and summer, bloodletting shall be performed on the right side. In autumn and winter, it shall be done on the left.

->**On the judgment of the blood, and its inspection.**<-

Blood emitted or flowing from the veins must be touched; if it is found to be cold, the flow should be stopped immediately. Likewise, if it is found to be hot and thin <term>subtile</term>, care must be taken so that the one being bled does not faint <term>sincopizet</term> <note>original: "sincopizet"; from the Greek 'syncope', meaning a temporary loss of consciousness</note>.

Likewise, let a single drop of blood be placed upon the fingernail: if it runs off, it is very watery, and therefore the flow should be stopped; but if it stays in place, it is too thick, and a small amount should be extracted until it becomes thinner.

And if you wish to discern the thickness or wateriness of the blood <note>original: "cruoris, seu sanguinis"</note>, let a drop be cast into water. If it sinks to the bottom, it is judged to be thick; if it floats on the surface, it shall be considered watery; but if it remains in the middle, it is good.

Blood of a **black color** settling at the bottom of the basin testifies to **melancholy** <note>one of the four humors, associated with black bile, the earth element, and a cold/dry temperament</note> and to fearfulness; whoever possesses such blood should use things that cleanse the blood and increase the production of good blood.

A **mucilaginous whiteness**, tasteless and similar to the white of an egg—if it appears in the blood after the melancholic blood and in great quantity—signifies that **phlegm** <note>the humor associated with water, coldness, and moisture</note> is dominant.

Pure blood, **purple, red, or reddish**, in great quantity, indicates the **sanguine** humor <note>the humor associated with air, heat, and moisture; generally considered the most "balanced" state</note>.

The **foam of the blood**, if it is of a saffron color <term>croceus</term> verging toward a sparkling redness and in a smaller quantity than the blood itself, indicates **choler** <note>also called yellow bile; the humor associated with fire, heat, and dryness</note>.

The **watery substance** that floats upon clotted blood—just like whey in milk when it has curdled—is a good sign if it appears as wateriness similar to the urine of a healthy person. The more perfectly that wateriness is separated from the blood, the better the digestion in the liver <term>hepar</term> is shown to be, and vice versa. For this reason, it is not good for blood to be entirely deprived of such "urinal" wateriness; for from its absence, one judges the dryness and thickness of the blood. ### On the judgment of blood and its inspection.

Blood that has been drawn or is flowing from the veins must be touched. If it is felt to be cold, the flow should be stopped immediately. Likewise, if it is found to be [excessively] hot and thin, the flow should be restricted so that the person being bled does not faint <note>original: "sincopizet"; to experience syncope or a loss of consciousness</note>.

Furthermore, let a single drop of blood be placed upon the fingernail. If it flows off, it is very watery, and the bleeding should therefore be stopped. But if it stays in place, it is too thick, and a small amount should be drawn until it becomes thinner.

And if you wish to discern the thickness or wateriness of the gore <note>original: "cruoris"; often used to describe blood once it has left the body or begun to clot</note> or blood, let one drop be cast into water. If it sinks to the bottom, it is judged to be thick. If it floats on the surface, it will be considered watery. But if it remains in the middle, it is a good sign.

Blood of a black color settling at the bottom of the bowl testifies to an excess of black bile <term>melancholia</term> and a fearful disposition. He whose blood is like this should use medicines that purify the blood and increase the supply of good blood.

Pure, purple, red, or reddish blood in large quantities indicates the [predominance of the] blood humor <note>the "sanguine" temperament, associated with a lively and optimistic nature</note>.

Foam on the blood, if it is saffron-colored leaning toward a shimmering redness, and in smaller quantity than the blood itself, indicates yellow bile <term>cholera</term>.

The watery substance that floats upon clotted blood—like whey in milk when it has curdled—which appears as wateriness similar to the urine of a healthy person, is a good sign. The more perfectly that wateriness is separated from the blood, the better the digestion in the liver <term>hepar</term> is indicated, and vice versa. Hence, it is not good for the blood to be entirely deprived of such urine-like wateriness; for from such a lack, dryness and thickness of the blood are diagnosed. Such a lack of wateriness is common in the blood of those who fast and keep watch much, who eat dry and hot foods, and who exercise or study a great deal; it is similar in those recovering from illness.

But if this urine-like moisture is excessive, it signifies a failure of digestion and a weakness of the body.

And commonly such people have a cold stomach <term>stomachus</term> and liver, and such blood...

### *On the thickness and thinness of the blood.*

Blood that clots too quickly is called thick; but that which clots slowly is evidence of thinness and indigestion. 

Likewise, let the blood be cut with a knife; for if it does not resist but yields easily to the cut, it is called thin. But if, on the contrary, it is cut and divided with difficulty, it is called thick and viscous. 

But if the blood in no way withstands the cut—as is seen with water and oil, which are easily divided but cannot be "cut"—such blood is excessively thin and signifies indigestion.

### Remedy against the Swelling of the Veins.

After bloodletting <term>phlebotomiam</term> <note>original: "phlebotomiam"; the surgical practice of withdrawing blood to balance the humors</note>, take rue <note>original: "rutam"</note>, wormwood <note>original: "absinthium"</note>, and barley <note>original: "hordeum"</note>; crush them and prepare from them a plaster <term>emplastri</term> <note>original: "emplastri"; a medicinal paste applied to the skin</note> in a warm pan. *An epithem is a certain mixture of juices, or distilled waters, and powders placed upon a limb with a linen or woolen cloth soaked in them; it is applied when the internal matter has been "digested" <note>digesta: in medieval medicine, this meant the stage where the harmful humors have been processed by the body's natural heat</note> and when the disease is in decline. And the discourse will be concerning the epithem of the heart, liver, brain, and testicles, because these are the principal organs for which an epithem is made.

->Rule for a single epithem.<-

To one pound <term>libra</term> of water, between 1.5 <note>original: "drag. 1. s." - one and a half drams</note> to 2 or 3 drams <term>drachma</term> of medicinal species <note>powdered herbs or ingredients</note> should be taken. Others take 1.5 pounds of waters and 1.5 drams of species.

->An example for the strengthening of the heart.<-

Take of rose and bugloss <note>original: "Buglossæ"; an herb used to treat "melancholy" of the heart</note> waters, half a pound <term>libra semis</term> of each. Of yellow sandalwood, citrus peel, and zedoary <note>a root similar to ginger</note>, 1 scruple <term>scrupulus</term> of each; let them be ground and mixed with the aforementioned waters. And a cordial epithem is made from heart-strengthening waters and species, or cordial powders, such as the *electuary of gems* <note>original: "electuarij de gemmis"; a medicine containing crushed pearls and precious stones</note>, *diambræ* <note>an ambergris-based compound</note>, or *diamusci* <note>a musk-based compound</note> in cases of extreme cold.

Note that in an epithem for the heart, the physician should never omit adding a little Malmsey wine <note>a sweet, fortified wine used as a carrier</note>, or muscatel, or a little saffron; indeed, physicians always include saffron. However, in an epithem for the liver, saffron should not be used because of its heat (as Avicenna <note>the 11th-century Persian "Prince of Physicians"</note> directs), but instead a little vinegar should be added for the sake of easier penetration.

The dose of Malmsey wine for 1 pound <term>libra</term> is 1 ounce <term>uncia</term>, but only a little saffron should be used—say 2 or 3 grains <term>grana</term>—and this is for strengthening, or sometimes to temper coldness.

An example of the above for making an epithem for the liver of one suffering from a choleric fever. Take waters of endive, liverwort, chicory, and nightshade <term>solatri</term>, 3 ounces <term>uncia</term> of each; 5 ounces of vinegar; and 1 dram <term>drachma</term> of the "Three Sandalwoods" powder <note>original: "triasandali"; a standard cooling preparation</note>. Let the epithem be made.

An example for the liver. Take 5 ounces of chicory water; 4 ounces of celery juice <term>apij</term>; 5 drams of the *dialacca maior* species <note>a compound medicine containing lac resin, used for liver obstructions</note>; 2 scruples of wormwood juice; let them be ground and mixed.

->Epithem for the Spleen.<-

Take waters of hart's-tongue fern <term>scolopendriæ</term> and fumitory, half a pound <term>libra semis</term> of each; bark of caper roots and tamarisk, 2 scruples <term>scrupulus</term> of each; let them be ground and mixed.

It should be noted that an epithem for the liver should be made with juices or waters appropriate for the liver, and with powders or species that regard the liver, such as "Three Sandalwoods" in cases of heat, or *diarodon* <note>a rose-based compound</note> or *diaciminum* <note>a cumin-based compound</note> in cases of cold; the same is to be said of the spleen.

Also, if the patient is inclined to sweat, or is actually sweating, an epithem should not be applied, lest the crisis <note>the critical turning point or "judgment" of the disease</note> be hindered.

Also, in non-acute fevers, the time for applying the epithem is before food, and it should be warm. But in acute pestilential fevers, the time is not fixed; rather, it should be continued in those cases, as it is then most helpful, and this is done out of necessity.

We also use an epithem for the testicles, especially when we see blood...

**The method of using an epithem.** Let a linen or woolen cloth be dipped in the appropriate warm waters and squeezed out a little; apply it gently and do not allow it to cool, repeating the application according to necessity three or four times.

->The whole matter is medical.<-

### S V M M A  C A P. XVII.

*An embrocation or fomentation is a compound made from the*
*decoction of herbs, or other things, in water*
*or wine, applied to a limb by means*
*of a sponge or felt. Some fomentations are for the*
*stomach, others for the liver, and others for the head; and*
*he teaches how they are made.*

<note>The ornamental initial "N" marks the beginning of the "Nota" (Note).</note> NOTE, that a fomentation properly so called is that which is made from a decoction of herbs, either in water or in wine, although such a thing is commonly called an embrocation <term>embrocatio</term> <note>a liquid medicine rubbed or poured onto the body</note>; however, strictly speaking, it is called an embrocation when that decoction is poured down from a height <note>this refers to "douching," where liquid is poured over the body part rather than just soaked</note>.

Therefore, a fomentation or embrocation is a compound made from the decoction of herbs or other things—namely roots, seeds, flowers, or similar—in water or wine, with application to the limb by means of a sponge or felt. It is first said to be a "compound," etc., to distinguish it from an epithem, which is made by sublimation <note>here referring to the refined essence of the ingredients</note> and not by decoction.

It is said to be applied "by means of a sponge or felt" to distinguish it from an epithem, which is applied with a cloth.

<summary>This page concludes instructions for using cold compresses to stop bleeding and treat fevers, then defines the technical differences between epithems, fomentations, and embrocations. It highlights that while these terms are often confused, they differ in their preparation (decoction vs. essence) and method of application (cloth vs. sponge or pouring).</summary>

It is said to be made with wine or water. For sometimes we use common river water, sometimes cistern water, and this water is better because it is more purified; then river water is better [than the next], and finally rainwater.

It should be noted that some fomentations <term>fomentatio</term> <note>a warm medicinal application, usually using a cloth or sponge soaked in a decoction</note> are for the stomach, because they are made for the area of the stomach; some are for the liver <note>original: "hepaticæ"</note>, and some are for the head <note>original: "capitales"</note>.

Stomach fomentations are made from stomach-strengthening things. Liver ones from liver-strengthening things, and likewise in other members from things appropriate to them.

The rule for their composition is that 1 pound <term>libra</term> of water requires 2 handfuls <term>manipulus</term> of herbs. For example: Take <term>recipe</term> 2 handfuls of violets, 1 handful each of maidenhair fern <note>original: "capilli Veneris"</note> and melilot, and 5 ounces <term>uncia</term> of fenugreek seeds. Let them boil in 2 pounds of water. The matter ought to be boiled until half is consumed, or at least a third; soak a sponge, and thus apply it warm to the chest four times, or thereabouts; it softens, dissolves [matter], and mitigates pain. But in the case of coarser matter <note>referring to thick humors or phlegm</note>, add dill <note>original: "anethum"</note> and similar things.

->A stomach fomentation for a cold lapse <note>a condition caused by an excess of cold humors</note>.<-

Take 1 handful each of mint, wormwood <note>original: "absinthij"</note>, and chamomile; 5 drams <term>drachma</term> each of wild vine flowers <note>original: "florũ lambrufcę"</note> and dill; let them boil in 2 pounds of water until reduced by half.

For the liver after a fever, it is made from endive, sorrel, nightshade, and water lily <note>original: "Nenuff" / "nenuphar"</note>.

For the spleen, from bugloss, spleenwort <note>original: "scolopendria"</note>, tamarisk, and capers; and there, in the decoction, let half wine or vinegar and half water be placed.

->For worms.<-

Take 1 handful each of wormwood and peach leaves; 5 handfuls of mint; 5 drams each of dittany, gentian, wormseed <note>original: "sementinæ, id est feminis sancti"</note>, pistachios <note>original: "fisticorum"</note>, and aloes. Let them boil in water, and after the fomentation let the place be wiped with a cloth; a liniment or anointing should follow it if it is expedient. For the pores are opened by the fomentation itself, and thus the virtue of the ointment penetrates better. And an embrocation <term>embrocatio</term> <note>a liquid medicine poured over a body part or applied with friction</note> is commonly to be taken after an epithem, because it is of stronger operation since it is made from boiled water (decoction), which is stronger than distilled water <note>original: "aqua sublimationis"</note>; likewise, wine is stronger. From these things it is gathered that the cause for administering an embrocation or fomentation is twofold. First, because an embrocation is a stronger medicine than an epithem; therefore, where an epithem does not suffice, an embrocation shall be made. Second, because distilled waters, from which an epithem is made, are not found prepared everywhere, in which case we make an embrocation from a decoction of things.

And the use of embrocation is especially suitable for settling pain, whether from a hot or cold cause, compared to other medicines, and especially for arthritis <note>original: "artetico"</note> and colic; and the embrocation ought to be applied in the stage of decline <note>the "status declinationis" is the phase when a disease's symptoms begin to fade</note>. And a stomach, heart, liver, or head fomentation is more safely administered before food, but the others may be administered indifferently.

# EXPLANATIONS.

## SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 18.

The words are clear enough in themselves.

*An ointment <term>unguentum</term> <note>original: "vnguentum"</note> is a mixture of liquids and wax or gums, with fine powders added and ground to a smooth consistency; it differs from cerates <term>cerotis</term> <note>a stiffer preparation with more wax and resin</note> for this reason. The dosage is handed down here. A liniment <term>linimentum</term> is made from the same things but with only a small amount of wax, so that a liniment is effectively a soft ointment; the author shows the method by which this is made.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' depicting a figure standing in a landscape with classical architectural elements in the background, set within a square frame.</image-desc>IT SHOULD BE KNOWN that an ointment is a collection of liquids, and wax or gums, with fine powders added and reduced to a smooth consistency.

The liquids <note>original: "liquores"</note> are oils, fats, and juices. Wax is mentioned to distinguish it from a cerate, which is commonly made with resin. However, in place of wax in an ointment, sometimes sagapenum <note>original: "serapinum"; a gum-resin from the Persian plant Ferula persica</note>, gum ammoniac <note>original: "amoniacum"</note>, and similar things are used; for this reason, "or gums" is added to the definition. It is said to be "reduced to a smooth consistency."

In this, an ointment differs from a plaster <term>emplastrum</term>: because in an ointment, the components are reduced to a fine or medium consistency. In a plaster, however, they are reduced to a coarse and hard consistency. Finally, it is said in the definition "and with powders added"; this is understood to be the case for the most part, because an ointment can be made from liquids and wax alone. An example is used for pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the chest lining</note>: Take <term>recipe</term> 1 ounce <term>uncia</term> of oil of violets, 5 ounces each <term>ana</term> of oil of chamomile and washed butter, with a small amount of wax; let an ointment be made, and let the painful area be anointed after an embrocation <note>a liquid wash</note> has been performed. Or, in the case of coarse matter <note>referring to thick, stubborn humors</note>: Take 5 drams <term>drachma</term> <note>original: "drag."</note> each of oil of dill, white lilies, and iris; 5 drams of nettle powders; and 5 drams of wax. Let an ointment be made.

### *For the composition of ointments.*

Note that the simple ingredients composing an ointment, before they are brought into the form of an ointment, ought to be powdered separately and then placed with the liquid and the melted wax.

The rule for such preparations is that every 1 ounce <term>vnc.</term> of liquid requires 1.5 drachms <term>drag.</term> of powder.

Regarding wax, there is no fixed rule, because if we want to make a soft ointment, we add only a little wax; if a thick one, we add just enough wax to bring it to that thickness. However, it is a general rule that for every 2 ounces of liquid, half an ounce <note>original: ".s." for "semis"</note> of wax is taken. Yet, writers usually leave this to the judgment of the apothecary; therefore, we write "as much wax as suffices" <note>original: "ceræ quantum sufficit"</note>. These powders are to be placed in ointments according to what is appropriate for the limb being anointed. Furthermore, wax is of four types: namely white, yellow, green, and red.

White wax is colder, and thus it is used in ointments for those suffering from fevers. But red is hotter, and green likewise, because of the verdigris <note>original: "viride æris"; a green pigment and medicinal substance made from copper</note> from which it is composed.

Specifically for the care of the stomach, the cold oils are myrtle, rose, and quince <note>original: "citoniorum"</note>. The hot oils are those of wormwood, mint, spikenard <note>original: "spica"</note>, and mastic.

An example for a "cold lapse" <note>an imbalance where the organ has become too cold</note> of the stomach: Take oil of wormwood and spikenard, 1 ounce of each; cloves <note>original: "gariof."</note>, sweet flag <note>original: "Calami aromatici"</note>, and cinnamon, 2 scruples <term>℈</term> of each; as much wax as suffices, or half an ounce. Let them all be ground by themselves to make an ointment. And if you wish to use it against worms, in place of the aforementioned powders, use dittany, gentian, hops, wormseed <note>original: "sementinæ"</note>, and aloes, 1 scruple of each.

An example for a "hot lapse" of the liver, such as after a fever: Take rose and violet oils, half an ounce of each; water lily <note>original: "nenuffa."</note> oil, 3 drachms; wormwood oil, 2 drachms; "three-sandalwoods" powder <term>triasandali</term> <note>A traditional cooling compound of red, white, and yellow sandalwood</note>, 1 drachm; with a little wax, it shall be made into an ointment. Juices of endive and hyssop can be added, and the kidneys can be anointed up to the shoulder blade <note>original: "spatulam"</note>. This is done so that the *vena cava* and the aorta <note>original: "arteria aorti"</note> may be cooled; once these are cooled, the whole body is cooled, because they carry blood to the entire body.

The common dosage for a master-formulated ointment <note>original: "vnguenti magistralis"</note> is 1 ounce, or half an ounce, or 2 ounces.

<header>BOOK SECOND</header>

A liniment is made from the same ingredients [as an ointment], though with only a small amount of wax, so that a liniment is essentially a soft ointment. It is necessary that the wax and the liquids be placed over a slow fire, dissolved, and brought to a boil; afterwards, the medicinal powders <note>original: "species"; refers here to the aromatic or active dry ingredients</note> should be added and the mixture left to thicken. If you wish to have a quick thickening, place the small jar in cold water. The best time for applying ointments is after general evacuations <note>referring to the humorist practice of purging or bloodletting to balance the body</note>, and especially after an embrocation <note>a liquid medicinal rub</note> when the pores are open. However, the specific time can be any time indifferently, provided that three hours pass between one application and the next; additionally, they should be applied hot or warm, except in the case of wounds.

The common rule of almost all practitioners is that for 1 ounce <term>vnc.</term> of oil, 1 drachm <term>drag.</term> of powder should be added, and an equal amount of wax, as in the example for strengthening the stomach: Take mastic oil, mint, and wormwood, 1 ounce <term>vnc.</term> of each <note>original: "ana"</note>; dried marjoram and hyssop, 1 drachm <term>drag.</term> of each; nutmeg, cloves, and long pepper, 1 scruple <term>℈.</term> of each; 3 drachms of wax; let an ointment be made. If you wish to have an ointment in a fairly hard form, for 1 ounce of oil use 3 drachms of powders and 2.5 drachms <note>original: "2. s." for "semis," meaning half</note> of wax. If you want it soft, for 1 ounce of oil use 2 drachms of wax and 1 drachm of powders.

# BOOK SECOND

A **CERATE** <term>Cerotum; a stiff, waxy medicinal preparation</term> is a compound made from liquids and coarse powders with resin or wax, reduced to a solid and dense form. In the detail that it uses "coarse powders," it differs from an ointment, which is composed with fine powders. It also differs in being "reduced to a solid form," because an ointment is brought to a thin consistency; since wax alone would not bring it to a solid form, resin is added.

Concerning this, it should be noted that some cerates are for the stomach <note>original: "stomachale"</note>, made from stomach-soothing ingredients; some are for the liver <note>original: "hepaticum"</note>, some for the heart <note>original: "cordiale"</note>, and some for the womb <note>original: "matricale"</note>. Each of these is made from ingredients appropriate to its purpose, but they differ in shape based on the body parts to which they are applied; thus, a stomach cerate is made in the shape of a shield.

Recipe: take quince oil <note>original: "olei citoniorum"</note> and myrtle oil, 1 ounce <term>vnc.</term> of each <note>original: "ana"</note>; cloves and mastic, 1 drachm <term>drag.</term> of each; let a cerate be made with resin. The dosage for cerates is not fixed, as it is increased or decreased according to the intention of the physician and the body part to which it is applied. Secondly, it should be noted that they follow this order: namely, ointment, cerate, and plaster <term>emplastrum</term>. For a cerate has a stronger effect than an ointment, and a plaster is stronger still, although it is less tedious for patients. Therefore, wise physicians first begin with an ointment; then, when that is not sufficient, they progress to a cerate, and finally to a plas-

### EXPLANATIONS.

The words are plain enough.

#### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 20.

*A plaster is a mixture of herbs, roots, flowers, and powders, coarsely ground and either mixed or boiled together with liquids. The dosage—which physicians call the measure of weights—along with the method of preparation is contained within three rules. It also lists those materials from which plasters are typically made, provides instructions on how they should be applied to our bodies, and reviews other things that are usually applied externally.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial letter E, depicting a seated scholar or physician in a room, framed by architectural elements and foliage.</image-desc> A **plaster** <term>emplastrum</term> is a combination of herbs, roots, flowers, and powders, coarsely ground, and mixed or boiled together with liquids. By specifying "coarsely ground," it is distinguished from an ointment; for medications ground for an ointment must be more finely powdered than for a plaster or a cerate. Therefore, at the end of an ointment recipe, practitioners commonly say "let the ingredients be finely powdered," which they do not say at the end of a cerate or plaster, even those made from dry materials. Some plasters are made from "cold" things, and some from "dry" things <note>referring to the Galenic qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>.

#### *On the composition of plasters.*

Note that when prescribing an ointment or a plaster, physicians commonly maintain this distinction: in an ointment, they first name the li-

->First Rule.<-

Herbs and flowers should be specified by handfuls <term>manipulus; a measurement of a loose handful of material</term>. Roots should be specified by ounces <term>uncia</term> or drachms <note>original: "3."; the standard symbol for a drachm, which is one-eighth of an ounce</note>. Similarly for powders and flours.

->Second Rule.<-

One handful of the aforementioned items requires 1 ounce or 1 and a half <note>original: "S."; short for 'semis', meaning half</note> of liquid, according to the physician’s judgment.

->Third Rule.<-

When a physician orders a plaster made from green herbs and roots, he should not direct them to be powdered, but rather to be boiled, and this until they reach a thick consistency. Once boiled, the liquid is added—for example, pork fat, lard <term>axungia</term>, butter, or oils, according to the physician’s intent for resolving <term>resoluendo; dispersing a swelling</term> or maturing <term>maturando; bringing a boil or abscess to a head</term>.

**Example of a maturing plaster.** Take 1 handful of mallow, half a handful <note>original: "manip. S."</note> or 1 ounce of finely cut marshmallow <term>altheæ</term> root; let them boil in water until thickened, then add 2 ounces or 1 and a half of chicken fat; boil again, and let a plaster be made.

**Example of a resolving plaster.** Take half a handful each of chamomile flowers, melilot <note>original: "melli"; likely meliloti, a sweet clover used to reduce inflammation</note>, and dill <term>aneti</term>; boil as above, then take 1 and a half ounces each of chamomile oil and white lily oil; boil for a plaster.

Another rule for a specific example: with honey, for 1 pound <term>libra</term> of honey, 4 ounces of medicinal powders <note>original: "specierum"; literally 'species', referring to the dry ingredients</note> should be used.

If, however, you desire a plaster made of dry items that can be powdered, they should not be finely powdered, but coarsely ground, or only crushed. Take 1 ounce of liquid for every 1 drachm <note>original: "drag. 1."</note> of powder, or a little more or less as needed, whether the ingredients are herbs, roots, seeds, or flours, etc.

**Example:** Take half a handful each of flaxseed flour and fenugreek; take as much as suffices of sesame oil and chicken fat. Let it boil a little, and make a plaster. If, however, the apothecary <term>aromatarius; a preparer of drugs and spices</term> is not experienced, then set the weight of the liquids according to the preceding rule.

->Method of applying the plaster.<-

After the plaster is finished, let it be placed upon a cloth, and then let a heated stone be prepared, upon which it shall be warmed; then let it be applied to the limb. It must never be applied cold.

There are also other local medicines, such as the **poultice** <term>cataplasma</term>, which is made from crushed green herbs or boiled dry ones applied together. And the **sitz-bath** <term>encathisma</term>, which is a localized bath reaching up to the navel, prepared over appropriate boiled herbs.

# EXPLANATIONS.

<margin>The author has spoken clearly enough.</margin>

## SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 21.

*A confection is made from sugar and reduced into a solid form. An electuary is made from sugar, honey, or syrup; some confections are for common use, and some are "magistral" <term>magistralis; a custom preparation formulated by a master physician for a specific patient</term>. Some of these benefit the heart, some the brain, and some the stomach. Of the magistral ones, some are laxative, some are restorative, and some are transformative; the author provides the weights for all of these, along with the method of preparation.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a floral and vine motif within a square border.</image-desc>

IT SHOULD BE KNOWN that powders (or appropriate spices), waters, sugar, and honey essentially enter into the composition and making of confections and electuaries, yet they differ from one another. A confection is made only from sugar and is reduced into a solid form. An electuary, however, is made from sugar, honey, or syrup. Beyond these essential ingredients, other things are sometimes added, such as pulps, capon meat <note>original: "caponum"; shredded meat from a castrated rooster was often used in medicinal pastes for its perceived nourishing properties</note>, or seeds, such as pistachios <term>fistici</term>, pine nuts <term>pineæ</term>, raisins, and the common "cold seeds" <note>original: "semina communia frigida"; a standard grouping in early pharmacy usually consisting of cucumber, melon, gourd, and pumpkin seeds, used to balance heat in the body</note>.

Furthermore, some confections are "magistral," while others are "usual" <term>vsualis; standard formulas kept in stock</term> found in apothecary shops. Some are designated for the heart, such as the "confection of gems" <note>original: "confectio de gemmis"; a luxury preparation containing crushed pearls or emeralds</note> or "Galen’s Joy" <note>original: "lætitia Galeni"; a restorative tonic named after the famous Roman physician</note>. Some are for the brain, such as *pliris arcoticon* or *diambra* <note>a preparation based on ambergris</note>. Some are for the stomach, such as *diagalanga* <note>a mixture based on galangal root</note>, and some for the liver, such as *triasandali* <note>a preparation made from three types of sandalwood</note>.

Regarding the magistral preparations, some are laxative—namely those composed of laxative substances, such as *diaturbith* <note>a preparation based on the root of the turbith plant</note> or *diasenna* <note>based on senna leaves</note>, which have been mentioned previously. But non-laxative ones are made from non-laxative ingredients; of these, some are restorative <term>confortatiuæ</term>, some are transformative <term>alteratiuæ; intended to change the body's 'humoral' state</term>, and some are both restorative and transformative at the same time.

### First Rule.

Herbs and flowers should be measured by the handful <term>manipulus; a standard pharmaceutical unit representing the amount a hand can grasp</term>. Roots should be measured by the ounce <term>uncia</term>, or by 3 ounces. Powders and flours are measured similarly.

### Second Rule.

One handful of the aforementioned items requires 1 ounce or 1.5 ounces <note>original: "vnc. 1. aut 1. & s."; the 's' stands for 'semis,' meaning half</note> of liquid, according to the physician's judgment.

### Third Rule.

When a physician prescribes a plaster made from fresh herbs and roots, he should not say they are to be pulverized, but rather boiled until they reach a thick consistency. Once boiled, the liquid is added—for example, pig fat, lard <term>axungia</term>, butter, or oils—depending on whether the physician intends to "resolve" <note>to dissipate or break down a swelling</note> or to "mature" <note>to bring an abscess or boil to a head</note> the ailment.

**Example of a maturing remedy:** Take <note>original: "Recipe"; the traditional start of a prescription</note> 1 handful of mallow and 1 ounce (or half a handful) of marshmallow root cut into small pieces. Boil them in water until the mixture thickens, then add 2 ounces (or 1.5 ounces) of chicken fat. Boil again and let a plaster be made.

**Example of a resolving remedy:** Take half a handful each of chamomile flowers, melilot <note>original: "melli"</note>, and dill. Boil as described above; then take 1.5 ounces each of chamomile oil and white lily oil. Boil together for a plaster.

Another rule to keep in mind: when using honey, 4 ounces of spices should be used for every 1 pound of honey.

If, however, you desire a plaster made from dry ingredients that can be pulverized, they should not be ground finely, but coarsely, or merely crushed. Take 1 ounce of liquid for every 1 drachma <term>dragma; a unit of weight roughly equal to 1/8th of an ounce</term> of powder, or a little more or less as needed, whether the ingredients are herbs, roots, seeds, or flours.

**Example:** Take half a handful each of linseed flour and fenugreek. Add enough sesame oil and chicken lard to suffice. Let it boil a little and make a plaster. If the apothecary <note>original: "aromatarius"; a spice-seller or pharmacist</note> is not experienced, then use the weights for liquids according to the previous rule.

### Method of applying the plaster.

After the plaster is prepared, it should be placed upon a cloth. Then, a heated stone should be ready, upon which the plaster is warmed; it should then be applied to the limb. It must never be applied cold.

There are also other local medicines, such as the poultice <term>cataplasma</term>, which is made from crushed fresh herbs or boiled dry herbs applied together. There is also the sitz bath <term>encathisma</term>, which is a partial bath up to the navel using appropriate boiled herbs.

That 1 drachm <term>drachma; approx. 3.9 grams</term> of powdered **species** <note>original: "specierum"; the dry herbal base of a medicine</note> requires 2 ounces <term>uncia; approx. 28.3 grams</term> of **sugar** in a confection, because it must be reduced to a solid form. ### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER XXII.

*A **mixture** is made from items already prepared in their own form; in this, it differs from a **confection** and an **electuary**, because the latter are prepared from simple powders or species. **Preserve**, **conserve**, **mixture**, and **electuary** are the same thing, but they differ in their purpose.*

A **mixture** differs from **electuaries** and **confections** because a mixture is always made from items already prepared in their own form. But a **confection** or **electuary** is made from simple powders or **species** <note>original: "speciebus"; the dry herbal base of a medicine</note>. ### SUMMARY CHAPTER XXII.

*A **mixture** is made from things already prepared in their own form, which is how it differs from a **confection** and an **electuary**, because the latter are prepared from simple powders or **species** <note>original: "speciebus"; the dry herbal base of a medicine</note>. Preserves, conserves, mixtures, and electuaries are the same thing, but they differ in their classification.*

A **MIXTURE** differs from electuaries and confections because a mixture is always made from things already prepared in their own form. But a confection or electuary is made from simple powders or species; for instance, in making a mixture I say: take of **borage** conserve and **rose** conserve, equal parts <term>ana; a medical shorthand for equal parts of each ingredient</term>, and mix. Or thus: Take 2 ounces of rose conserve, 1 drachm of the **species for the electuary of gems** <note>a luxury medicine containing crushed pearls and precious stones</note>. Let a mixture be made with sugar or rose syrup, and let it be **gilded** <note>original: "deauretur"; the practice of coating medicine in gold leaf, believed to strengthen the heart</note>; it is effective in burning fevers. No rule is set regarding the dose, but it is given as desired; the mixture is made with syrup of roses, or of **verjuice** <term>agresta; the tart juice of unripe grapes</term>, or others, and it can be gilded.

And preserves, conserves, mixtures, and electuaries are the same; they differ only in their classification.

**Lochs** <term>loch; from the Arabic "la'uq," a thick, syrupy medicine</term> are named from **licking** <note>original: "a lambendo"</note>. Some of these are pleasant to the taste, while others are unpleasant and somewhat bitter. Note that if the same recipe is made with **sugar** <note>original: "zuccaro"</note>, it can be classified as either a confection, an **electuary** <term>electuarium; a medicinal paste made of powders and honey or sugar</term>, or a loch. However, they differ in their physical substance and their method of action. Through more or less boiling <note>original: "decoctionem"</note> and the mixing of certain viscous ingredients, a noticeable variation and distinct mixture is created. For a confection, a longer boiling of the sugar is required so that it hardens; for an electuary, less is needed. But for a loch, much less is required than for both of those; it is cooked slightly more than a **julep** <term>iuleb; a thin medicinal syrup</term> but less than an electuary. Many viscous substances are added to a loch so that they stick to the throat. Furthermore, more lochs are made with honey than with sugar, because honey cleanses more strongly, opens the passages, adheres better, and provides warmth. We use lochs only for ailments of the chest, the lungs, and the **esophagus** <note>original: "meri"; the gullet</note>, whereas confections and electuaries are used for all ailments of all body parts. Some lochs evacuate thick humors from the chest and many **catarrhal** <note>original: "catarrhales"; relating to mucus drainage</note> fluids, such as the "healthy loch" <note>original: "loch sanum"; a standard medicinal formula</note>; some treat even thicker and more viscous fluids, such as **loch of squill** <note>made from the sea onion, used as an expectorant</note>; and some are effective for cleansing fluids from lung ulcers, such as **loch of pine**. Others thicken the thin fluids flowing from the head to the **respiratory organs** <note>original: "partes spirituales"; literally 'spiritual parts,' referring to the lungs and windpipe where 'vital spirits' were thought to circulate</note> which cause irritation and a dry cough, such as **loch of poppy**.

The dose of a loch is the size of a hazelnut or chestnut. The time for taking it can be anytime, day or night, before or after food. However, it should not be taken immediately after eating, so as not to cause the food to "evaporate" upwards <note>referring to indigestion or reflux</note>. The best time is on an empty stomach, except for the loch of poppy; since we use that to induce sleep or to thicken thin fluids in the head, it is better given one hour after dinner when going to bed.

The method of taking it is by licking, holding it in the mouth until it melts, and then tilting the head forward and swallowing gradually, so it passes through the passages. Me

*A troche is a certain round medicinal preparation with a slight depression, like a lupin bean, in which they differ from pills, which are perfectly round; they also differ in their action and flavor. This can be made from anything that can be reduced to powder. Some troches are for the stomach, some for the brain, some for the heart; and finally, they receive their name from the part of the body to which they bring health; for this reason, they are made of various substances and weights.*

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'T' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

A **TROCHE** <term>trociscus; a medicinal tablet or lozenge</term> is a certain round medicinal preparation with a depression in the manner of a lupin bean <note>lupins are flat, round legumes, providing the model for the shape of these tablets</note>. Sometimes it is also made with a certain length and roundness. The reason for their composition is so that the ingredients within may be preserved longer and better. Thus, their difference from pills is clear in their shape, because pills are entirely round—named from *pila*, that is, a ball or roundness. Secondly, they differ in their action, because all pills either loosen the bowels or soothe them. But troches often do neither of those. Thirdly, they are not as repulsive to take as pills. Note, however, that troches are not given in their own form, because that shape is unsuitable for swallowing; instead, they are given in the form of a powder, an **electuary** <term>electuario; a medicinal paste</term>, a medicinal mixture, or a **decoction** <term>decoctione; a concentrated liquor made by boiling</term>, according to what the physician intends—or even in pills, especially when they are given for the head. And from every medicine that can be pulverized, a troche can be made by dosing the medicines according to the physician's intention, using more stomach-strengthening ingredients <note>original: "stomachica"</note>, or those for the brain <note>original: "cerebralia"</note>, or others as it seems fit. And so, some troches are for the stomach, some for the brain, some for the heart <note>original: "cordiales"</note>, and likewise for other members. Those for the stomach are made from stomach-strengthening substances...

Some of these troches address "hot" matter, others "cold" <note>Referring to the Four Humors theory where illnesses were classified by temperature and moisture</note>. For there is no obstruction <note>original: opilatio</note> caused by matter so cold or viscous that it cannot be removed by troches of lacca or myrrh; for this reason, troches of myrrh are highly praised for the oldest cases of suppressed menstruation <note>original: retentione menstruorum</note>.

**Restrictive troches:** Made of "sealed earth" <term>terra sigillata; a medicinal clay from Lemnos</term> or Armenian bole <note>a red medicinal clay</note>.

**Restorative troches:** Troches of wormwood <note>original: absinthio</note>, of mint, or *diarodon* <note>a compound made of roses</note>. These are especially suitable during the decline of a fever caused by "cold" matter, as they wonderfully remove the weakness of the entire body, open any obstructions that may exist, and digest thick matter. The time for administering them is one or two hours before food.

Troches are also made for fumigation <note>burning to produce medicinal smoke</note>. This is done either for afflictions of the womb using ingredients related to the matrix, or for the purification of the air—for example, during a plague <note>original: pestilentia</note>. Take of cinnamon, cloves, and red roses, 2 ounces of each; aloeswood, frankincense, mastic, and ladanum <note>a sticky resin from rockrose</note>, 1 ounce of each; red and white sandalwood, 1.5 drams. Let troches be made with turpentine in a dose of 5 drams. Let them be ground in a mortar. "French troches" <note>original: trocisci galliæ</note> and musk-scented alipta <note>a type of aromatic paste</note> may also be added as the physician pleases. One or more of these troches should be placed upon hot coals.

A PESSARY <term>pessarium; a medicated plug or suppository for vaginal use</term> is made in an oblong and sometimes round shape. It is inserted into the womb <note>original: uuluam</note> to check or induce menstruation. It is made of appropriate substances that have been powdered and mixed with some liquid or an electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>, then wrapped in a very thin cloth.

An example of a pessary for inducing menstruation: take of myrrh, mugwort <note>original: arthimisiæ</note>, southernwood <note>original: abrotani</note>, and black cumin seed <note>original: seminis nigellæ</note> in equal parts. Let them all be powdered, and let the pessary be formed with Great Triphera <note>a complex pharmaceutical paste</note> or mithridatum <note>a famous ancient "universal" antidote and cure-all</note>. The size of a pessary is commonly made to the size of the little finger; let it be wrapped in a thin linen cloth and placed in the womb <note>original: matricem</note>. Commonly, a double thread is tied to it so that it hangs outside the womb, allowing it to be extracted as needed.

An example of a constrictive pessary for menstruation flowing beyond what is natural <note>i.e., excessive bleeding</note>: Take of amber <note>original: carabæ</note>, cypress nut, gum arabic, and pomegranate flowers <note>original: balaustiæ</note>, 3 drams of each; of frankincense, 2 drams. Let the pessaries be made with a decoction of sumach, or plantain juice, or a mucilage of fleawort <note>original: psilij</note>, using 2 drams of each, and let them be placed in the womb.

### S V M M A R Y  O F  C H A P T E R  X X V I .

> *A decoction occurs when herbs, flowers, seeds, roots, or anything of any kind is boiled down either in common water, distilled water, or another liquid, so that their essence is extracted into the liquid through the boiling process. An infusion occurs when a medical substance is placed in a liquid but is not boiled in it; he provides an example of how this is done.*

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'D' with intricate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>
A DECOCTION is so named when herbs, flowers, seeds, roots, or anything of any other kind is boiled in common water, distilled water, or some other liquid, so that the virtue <note>original: virtus; the medicinal potency or "spirit" of the plant</note> of these things is received into the waters in which they are boiled. Finally, such a decoction is strained, sometimes with expression <note>original: expresione; squeezing or pressing the ingredients to extract all liquid</note> and sometimes without expression, according to the requirements of the substance. The liquid strained in this way is called a decoction.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the preparation of medicines.
