->### BOOK<-

[they are] called, and enough has been said about this previously.

An **infusion** <term>infusio; a method of extracting medicinal properties by soaking</term>, however, is when certain medicinal things are placed—either powdered, crushed, or cut, and either alone or in water, wine, or another liquor—without any boiling <term>decoctio; a decoction or boiling</term>. They remain there for a time and are afterwards strained, either with or without pressing, depending on whether we seek for a greater or lesser strength to remain in the liquor. Such a liquor, thus strained and prepared, is called an infusion. However, more of the strength of the substances remains in a decoction than in an infusion; therefore, after the infusion of some simple medicine, such as agaric <note>original: agarici; a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note>, turbith <note>original: turbit; the root of a plant in the morning glory family, used as a laxative</note>, or another, we often perform a gentle boiling so that the strength may be more powerfully drawn out.

### *Example of an infusion for drawing out phlegm.*

Take agaric and turbith, of each 1 and a half drams; spikenard <note>original: Spicæ</note> and rock salt <note>original: salis gemmæ</note>, of each 4 grains. Infuse these in 2 and a half ounces of wormwood water for 12 hours. Then, press it out strongly and strain it. To the strained liquid, mix 2 drams of diaphoenicon <note>a medicinal paste made from dates</note> and administer it. And if it is preferred, a gentle boiling of the simple ingredients could be done in water so that the strength is better received; administer this at dawn. I say the same regarding rhubarb <note>original: rabarbaro</note> for the evacuation of bile <note>original: cholerę</note>, when it is infused in endive water. And if the bile is thick, a little wine or fennel water should be added. At the end, we commonly add some syrup in a dose of half an ounce for sweetening, as in an infusion of agaric one might add half an ounce of oxymel <note>original: Oximellis; a mixture of honey and vinegar</note>.

These decoctions ought also to be sweetened with sugar, honey, or appropriate syrups, so that they are more pleasant to those taking them. Therefore, for every 3 or 4 drams, add 1 ounce of honey, sugar, or syrup. By this means they are also preserved for a longer time; for unless they were prepared in this way, they could not last even for three days.

### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER XXVII.

*The Physician ought to know the powers of simple medicines, not only in general, but also what they call the degrees of quality <note>referring to the Galenic system of ranking medicines as hot, cold, moist, or dry on a scale of 1 to 4</note>, and which part of the body they benefit. That simple medicament which is called the "basis" of the medicine—which has the greatest power for that which we intend—ought to be double the amount of the other ingredients we use, and it enters the medicine for the purpose of strengthening that part of the body which we intend to heal.*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the preparation of medicines, moving from simple infusions and decoctions into the principles of "compounding"—the art of combining multiple ingredients into a single drug. It begins the Second Book or section of the treatise.</meta>

->### SECOND [BOOK]<-

*For seven reasons, several things are mixed with that which is the base of the medicine: for strengthening it, for removing the medicine's poison <note>original: venenum; in this context, it often refers to harsh side effects or "toxicity" of a potent drug</note>, for pleasing the patient, so that paths may be opened for the medicine, so that the medicine might be protected from digestive heat, so that a common medicine may be made specific to a particular part, or so that what is not useful in the base may be removed. Sometimes several bases are placed in one medicine, and the seven rules for how they should be mixed are handed down. Likewise, five things enter into a compound drug <note>original: pharmacum compositum</note>, and the dosage of these is provided.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "I" featuring floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

In the compounding of medicines, it is required that the composer knows the virtues of simple medicines through both universal and particular knowledge. For it is not enough that he knows which medicine is hot, cold, moist, or dry, or which is cleansing <note>original: abstersiua</note>, opening <note>original: apperitiua</note>, or soothing <note>original: lenitiua</note>, etc.; rather, it is necessary that he knows in what degree the medicines perform these operations—namely, whether they do this much or little. It is also necessary to know which organ each medicine regards: which the head, heart, chest, stomach, liver, etc. And whether it regards that organ weakly or strongly. It is also necessary to observe which humor <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine health</note> he wishes to evacuate, and which medicines primarily evacuate a humor of this kind, just as turbith <note>original: turbit; the root of a plant in the morning glory family used as a laxative</note> purges phlegm, and scammony <note>original: scamonea; a harsh purgative resin</note> purges yellow bile <note>original: cholera</note>, and so on. And this primary medicine is called by authors the **base** <term>basis; the "active ingredient" or main component of a prescription</term>, or the **root** <note>original: radix</note>.

For the **base** is that medicine which has the most noble effect for evacuating a humor, just as the base in Galen’s *hierapicra* <note>original: hierapicra Galeni; "Sacred Bitter," a famous ancient purgative formula</note> is aloe; for this confection is made to purge phlegm in the stomach, upon which aloe has an ineffably effective regard. Sometimes several bases are found in one medicament, so that the virtue of one may be fortified by another, as in the *benedicta* <note>original: benedicta; "The Blessed Medicine," a compound laxative elective</note>, in which turbith, hermodactyls <note>original: hermodactili; "fingers of Hermes," a plant root used for joint pain</note>, and scammony are the base. For it is a medicine that evacuates phlegm from the joints and remote locations, but turbith and hermodactyls are weak in their operation; therefore, scammony is added to assist their operations.

# BOOK

...for according to the authors of medicine, it is included in medicines based on aloe <note>original: "aloeticis"</note> so that it might hasten their operations.

It should be noted here that of the medicine which serves as the **base** <note>original: "basis"; the primary active ingredient</note>, one ought to include twice as much as the medicine included to **strengthen** <note>original: "confortante"</note> its operation. For example, when **turpeth** <note>original: "turbit"; a root used as a potent purgative</note> is used as the root or base in any medicine, half the amount of **ginger** <note>original: "Zinzibere"</note> is added. Thus, if 1 ounce <note>original: "3. 1."</note> of turpeth is used, let half a drachm <note>original: "drag. S."</note> of ginger be added, for ginger strengthens the operation of turpeth. This rule holds true if the medicines are of the same weight and density. For if the strengthening medicine is of a lighter weight than the root or base, then less than half should be added. For instance, if **aloe** is used as the base and the pulp of **colocynth** <note>original: "coloquintidæ"; also known as bitter apple, a very harsh laxative</note> is the strengthening agent, then less than half the amount of pulp is added because of its lightness compared to the heaviness of the aloe. As much **opium** is added to a medicine as **castoreum** <note>original: "castoreo"; a yellowish secretion from beaver sacs used as a stimulant</note>, because they are both heavy. Likewise, as much **scammony** <note>original: "scamonea"; a binding resin used as a purgative</note> as **bdellium** <note>original: "bdellio"; a semi-transparent oleo-gum resin</note>.

Sometimes a medicine composed of a base and those things that strengthen it is sufficient to achieve the effect we seek, and then it is the best medicine. However, sometimes it is not sufficient, which is why it is necessary to add other things to fulfill what is lacking and prepare the body to receive the operation of the base. These medicines are called **"those following the operation of the root"** because they are not placed in the medicine for their own sake, but for the sake of the root, to which they provide assistance.

->*These medicines which follow the operation of the root are added to the compound for seven reasons.*<-

The **first reason** is so that the organs may be strengthened. This is done especially when the base is a laxative medicine that is poisonous <note>original: "venenosa"; meaning "toxic" or "harsh" in this context</note>, bringing harm to the organs. In such cases, the organ is strengthened by **cordial** medicines <note>medicines intended to stimulate or "comfort" the heart and vital spirits</note> which strengthen the spirits, such as medicines with **aromaticity** <note>original: "aromaticitas"</note>, like roses, **agarwood** <note>original: "xilo aloes"</note>, sandalwood, saffron, and so on.

The **second reason** is so that the "malice" <note>harmful side effects or toxicity</note> of a medicine may be removed; for example, the malice of opium is removed by castoreum, and that of scammony by bdellium and **tragacanth** <note>original: "dragantum"</note>. The malice of **hellebore** is removed by **wild carrot** <note>original: "daucum"</note> and **laserwort** <note>original: "siler montanum"</note>.

The **third reason** is so that the "abomination" <note>the foul taste or smell</note> of the medicine may be removed. For this reason, we mix sugar or honey with medicines of bad flavor more than we do with medicines of good, non-horrible flavor.

The **fourth reason** is so that the paths through which the medicine is drawn may be opened. As in cases of **paralysis** and **apoplexy**, where the paths are narrow and thus they draw the medicine with difficulty, it is necessary then to mix in **diuretic** <note>original: "diureticas"</note> medicines so that the paths may be opened.

The **fifth reason** is so that the medicine may be protected from the heat of digestion, lest it be weakened on its way. For this reason, opium is included in **theriac** <note>original: "theriaca"; a famous ancient "universal" antidote and medicine containing dozens of ingredients</note>.

The **sixth reason** is so that a medicine which is common to many organs may be made specific to one. For example, if a medicine opens an **obstruction** <note>original: "opilationem"</note> of the veins...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of pharmaceutical compounding, moving from the proportions of ingredients to the specific medicinal vehicles required to direct a drug to certain organs (liver, spleen, chest), and concludes with the general rules for formulating recipes.</meta>

# BOOK SECOND

...and provokes urine. If we wish to provoke urine, we must mix with the medicine something that directs it to that location, such as Spanish flies <term>cantarides</term> <note>original: "cantarides"; dried blister beetles used historically to stimulate the urinary tract, though highly toxic in large doses</note>. If we wish to use "opening" medicines <note>medicines intended to clear blockages or "open" the pores and vessels</note> in the liver, they should be given alone; if in the spleen, they should be given with vinegar; if in the chest, they should be given with honey-water, or barley water, or with sweet wine. And with diuretic medicines <term>diureticis</term> we mix radish <term>rafanum</term> when we want them to remain in the liver for a long time during its de-obstruction <note>original: "de opilatione"; the clearing of "opilations" or blockages in the humors</note>.

The seventh reason [for compounding] is so that a quality of the root or "base" which is harmful to the disease may be removed, while nothing is taken away from its medicinal power. For example, scammony <term>scamonea</term> <note>original: "scamonea"; a harsh purgative resin</note> is harmful to a fever because of its quality; therefore, we mix myrobalans <term>mirobalanos</term> <note>original: "mirobalanos"; astringent plum-like fruits used to temper harsh drugs</note> with it, because they do not diminish the power of purging but do restrain its sharpness.

And very often several bases are placed in one medicine. 
First, so that in the same type of sickness, the medicine may perform different operations. For example, in disorders of the nerves, pellitory <term>piretrum</term> <note>original: "piretrum"; a root used for its warming and stimulating properties</note> and castoreum <term>castoreum</term> <note>original: "castoreum"; a substance from beaver sacs used as a stimulant</note> are used as the base: pellitory to consume and dissolve phlegm, and castoreum to provide strength.

Second, because a composite medicine may address different ailments in different members, or even in a single member. If one base were sufficient and had no harmfulness in itself, it would not be necessary to mix anything else with it. However, because a single ingredient is often insufficient in its operation or carries a harmful effect, something must be mixed in to make its operation strong and to corroborate it.

This strength consists in two things. One is in the identity of the medicinal power—and for this reason dittany <term>diptamus</term> and "sealed earth" <term>terra sigillata</term> <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay from Lemnos, famously stamped with a seal and used as a universal antidote</note> are placed in theriac <term>theriaca</term> <note>original: "theriaca"; a complex "wonder-drug" used against poisons and many diseases</note>. The other is in the preparation of the matter, and in this way ginger <note>original: "33."; a common medical shorthand for "Zingiber" or ginger</note> strengthens the operation of turpeth <term>turbit</term> <note>original: "turbit"; a root used as a potent purgative</note>.

->Now follow the rules for composing recipes.<-

**The first rule.** If any medicine is of strong power, only a little of it should be put in the recipe or compound. For a strong agent can do as much in a short time as a weak one in a long time; and conversely, a strong agent can do as much in a small quantity as a weak one in a large quantity.

**The second rule.** If any medicine has many benefits, a large amount of it should be placed in the compound, especially if it is fast-acting. But if it has few benefits and is slow-acting, only a little of it should be used.

**The third rule.** A medicine which acts on remote parts <note>parts of the body far from the stomach, such as the extremities</note> should be added in a large amount; if, however, it acts on nearby parts, only a little should be added. For the power of a medicine is greatly weakened on a long journey before it reaches its destination, but when its substance is multiplied, [it maintains its strength].

# BOOK 2
T 2
<meta>catchword: Five</meta>

...and its power will be multiplied.

**The fourth rule.** A noble medicine <note>original: "medicina nobilis"; a drug of high quality or one that acts upon the most vital organs</note>, which provides much assistance, should be used in a large dose; if it is common <note>original: "ignobilis"</note>, a small amount should be used. A medicine is called "noble" when it works upon a noble organ <note>The "noble organs" in medieval medicine typically included the heart, brain, and liver</note>, or performs a noble operation—for example, it is more noble to strengthen an organ while cleansing it <term>abstersione</term> <note>the process of scouring or wiping away waste humors</note> than to strengthen it without cleansing.

**The fifth rule.** If a certain medicine has a benefit that is already found in the other medicines placed within the compound, only a small amount of it should be added; if the opposite is true, a large amount should be used.

**The sixth rule.** If there is any medicine to whose benefit a specific harm is attached, only a small amount should be added; if the opposite is true, add more.

**The seventh rule.** If any medicine in the compound encounters another medicine that corrupts its power <term>virtutem</term>, a large amount of it must be used; if the opposite is true, use a small amount.

From these rules, it is gathered that if there are four simple medicines in a compound that work equally within the body, they are measured with the same weight—for example, fennel seed <term>semen feniculi</term>, dill <term>anethi</term>, and similar herbs. However, if they are of unequal power and operation, they must be added in unequal amounts. For example, if I wish to purge yellow bile <term>cholera</term> and phlegm <term>phlegma</term> through a medicine composed of aloe <term>aloe</term> and scammony <term>scamonea</term> <note>a harsh, resinous purgative</note>, more of the aloe and less of the scammony must be added, because of the weakness of the aloe and the strength of the scammony.

### Three things a physician must avoid in the compounding of laxative medicines.

First, that the "dissolution" <note>the movement of the bowels</note> does not become unequal. This happens through compound medicines that have a great diversity in the time it takes to loosen the belly; for then the movement of the bowels is disturbed, as the first ingredient loosens the belly before the second, and sometimes the first ingredient even expels the second. Avicenna <note>The 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina, the primary authority for medieval medicine</note> mentions this in the fourth part of the first book, chapter four.

Second, that a mixture of medicines is not made where the method of loosening of one weakens the other. An example is a compound of softening <term>lenitiuæ</term> and compressing <term>compressiuæ</term> medicines, such as myrobalans <term>mirobalani</term> and violets <term>violæ</term>. For the medicine that softens will complete its operation before the one that presses. Avicenna says in the fourth part of the first book, chapter nine: "That which acts freely should not be joined to that which assists by pressing, in such a way that their powers are equal," etc.

Third, that a mixture of those things whose individual property corrupts the property of another is not made—specifically when it corrupts the very power we seek. For this reason, cashews <term>anacardi</term> <note>original: "anacardi"; likely refers to the Marking Nut (*Semecarpus anacardium*), used in various medicinal confections</note> are not put into theriac <term>theriaca</term> <note>a famous "universal" antidote and cure-all</note>, because they corrupt the viper flesh <term>carnes tyri</term> <note>original: "carnes tyri"; processed viper meat was a key ingredient in the recipe for Theriac</note>.

<header>SECOND [BOOK].</header>

<margin>
Five things must be placed in a composite medicine
</margin>

<image-desc>A large opening curly brace on the left margin groups the following five numbered points, indicating they are the components of a composite medicine.</image-desc>

The first is the **root** or **base**, which must be added in double the amount of the strengthening medicine.

The second is the **strengthening medicine** <term>medicina confortans</term> <note>a tonic intended to support the body's natural "virtue" or power</note>, which should be half the amount of the base.

The third is the **medicine following the operation of the root** <note>an adjuvant that assists the primary ingredient</note>.

The fourth is the **medicine restraining the harm of the root** <note>a corrective used to mitigate side effects</note>.

The fifth is the **medicine altering the whole compound**, or the quality of the entire medicine.

**Concerning the third type**, those medicines following the operation of the root, a certain rule of dosage cannot be given; instead, more or less is added depending on the scale of the "service" required. For example: if a medicine is added alongside the root so that its power <term>virtus</term> may be directed toward the extremities of the body, a larger amount should be added than if it were intended for the parts nearby, as was stated in the preceding rules.

**Concerning the fourth type**, the medicine restraining the harm of the root, the dose of such a medicine should be equal in weight to the root itself. For example, when opium <note>original: "opium"</note> is placed in a medicine, an equal amount of castoreum <note>original: "castoreo"; a substance secreted by beavers, historically used to counter the "cold" and sedative effects of opium</note> should be mixed with it. And with scammony <note>original: "scamonea"; a harsh herbal purgative</note>, an equal amount of bdellium <note>original: "bdellio"; a semi-translucent gum resin</note> is added, unless the "malice" <note>the toxic or overly aggressive properties</note> of the root has already been removed, in which case less should be added.

**Concerning the fifth type**, the medicine altering the whole compound: its dose is as much as is added of all the others combined. For instance, when a medicine is composed of 10 drams and 3 [scruples] of turbith <note>original: "turbit"; a root used as a laxative</note>, since that compound possesses a certain sharpness <term>acuitatem</term>, one and a half drams of sugar <note>original: "zuccari"</note> should be added to restrain this. From all these statements, you can determine the "digestive" <note>a medicine that prepares the humors for expulsion</note> for any humor, regardless of which organ it is located in. For example, if you wish to digest yellow bile <term>cholera</term> that is causing harm through its heat, observe in which organ it is situated—whether in the stomach, the liver, or other members. Once this is known, take a medicine that restrains the sharpness of the bile for that specific organ: such as endive, hart's-tongue fern <note>original: "scolopendria"</note>, lettuce, or purslane for the liver. For the spleen, use bugloss, borage, watercress, or calamint; and likewise for other humors.

*Both simple and composite medicines are presented, which benefit the individual parts of our body for both purging and strengthening.*

<header>BOOK 2</header>

...and its power <term>virtus</term> <note>original: "virtus"; the inherent medicinal efficacy of a substance</note> will be multiplied.

**Fourth rule.** A noble medicine <note>original: "medicina nobilis"; referring to a medicine that acts on vital organs or performs complex actions</note>, which provides great benefit, should be administered in a large dose; if it is of low status, a small amount should be used. A medicine is called "noble" when it acts upon a noble limb <note>such as the heart, brain, or liver</note>, or performs a noble operation—for example, it is nobler to strengthen a part of the body while also cleansing it <term>abstersio</term> <note>original: "abstersione"; the process of wiping away or purging impurities</note> than to strengthen it without cleansing.

**Fifth rule.** If a medicine possesses a benefit already found in the other medicines being placed in the compound, a small amount of it should be added; however, if it provides a benefit the others lack, a large amount should be added.

**Sexta regula.** If there is a medicine whose benefit is linked to some harm <note>original: "nocumentum"; side effects or toxic properties</note>, a small amount should be added; if the opposite is true, then the opposite should be done.

**Seventh rule.** If any medicine in the compound finds another medicine that corrupts its power, a large amount of it must be added; if the opposite is true, let a small amount be added.

From these rules, it is gathered that if there are four simple medicines in the body working equally, they should be measured by the same weight—for example, **fennel seed**, **dill**, and similar items. If, however, they are of unequal power and operation, they must be added in unequal amounts. For instance, if I wish to purge **yellow bile** <term>cholera</term> and **phlegm** <term>phlegma</term> through a composite medicine made of **aloe** and **scammony** <note>a harsh purgative resin</note>, more of the aloe and less of the scammony must be added because of the weakness of the aloe and the strength of the scammony.

### *The doctor must beware of three things in the composition of dissolving <note>laxative</note> medicines.*

**First**, that the dissolution <note>the emptying of the bowels</note> does not become unequal. This happens when composite medicines have great diversity in the time they take to move the belly; the bowels are disturbed because the first medicine moves the belly before the second, and sometimes the first expels the second itself. Avicenna discusses this in the fourth [book] of the first [canon], chapter 4.

**Second.** Let there be no mixing of medicines where the method of dissolving of one weakens the other—such as the composition of a **lenitive** <note>soothing</note> medicine and a **constrictive** <note>compressing</note> one, like **myrobalans** <note>original: "mirobalani"; astringent fruit used in tanning and medicine</note> and **violets**. For the medicine that softens will complete its work before the one that constricts. Avicenna says in the fourth [book] of the first [canon], chapter 9: that which acts freely should not be joined to that which aids by compressing in such a way that their powers are equal.

**Third.** Let there be no mixing of those items where the property of one ruins the property of the other, especially when it ruins the very power we are seeking. Because of this, **marking nuts** <note>original: "anacardi"; the fruit of the Semecarpus anacardium</note> are not put into **theriac** <note>a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all"</note>, because they ruin the **viper flesh** <note>original: "carnes tyri"; literally "Tyrian flesh," referring to the vipers of Tyre used as a key ingredient in theriac</note>.

<header>BOOK THE SECOND</header>

<margin>
Five things must be included in a compound medicine
</margin>

The first is the **root** or **base** <term>radix</term> <note>original: "radix"; the primary active ingredient in a medical formula</note>, which should be added in twice the amount of the strengthening medicine.

The second is the **strengthening medicine** <term>medicina confortans</term> which supports the power <term>virtus</term> of the remedy; its dose should be half that of the base.

The third is the **medicine that follows the operation of the root** <note>an ingredient that assists the primary drug in reaching its target or performing its specific function</note>.

The fourth is the **medicine that suppresses the harm** of the root <note>a corrective ingredient meant to mitigate side effects or toxicity</note>.

The fifth is the **medicine that alters the entire compound**, or the quality of the whole medicine.

*Regarding the third item*, the medicine following the operation of the root: no fixed rule for the dose can be given. Instead, it is added in a greater or lesser quantity according to the amount of "service" <note>the degree of assistance required to transport or activate the drug</note> required. For example: if a medicine is added with the root so that its power might be directed to the extremities of the body, more of it should be added than if it were directed to parts closer to the center, as was stated in the preceding rules.

*Regarding the fourth item*, the medicine that counteracts the harm of the root: the dose of such a medicine should be equal in weight to the root itself. For instance, when **opium** is placed in a medicine, an equal amount of **castoreum** <note>a substance secreted by beavers, historically used to counter the sedative effects of opium</note> should be mixed with it. Likewise, with **scammony** <note>a harsh purgative resin</note>, an equal amount of **bdellium** <note>a bitter tree resin</note> is used, unless the "malice" <note>the toxic or irritating properties</note> of the root is already removed; in that case, less should be added.

*Regarding the fifth item*, the medicine altering the entire compound: its dose is as much as is needed for the whole mixture. For example, when a medicine is composed of ten drachms <term>drachma</term> of **turpeth** <note>a tropical root used as a laxative</note> and five of **ginger** <note>original: "ʒʒ." abbreviation for "zingiberis"</note>, since this compound possesses a certain sharpness, one and a half drachms <note>original: "drag. 1. s." where 's' stands for 'semis' or half</note> of **sugar** <note>original: "zuccari"</note> should be added to suppress it. From all these statements, you can determine the "digestive" <note>a medicine that prepares "humors" or bodily fluids for evacuation</note> for any humor, regardless of which limb it resides in. If you wish to digest **choler** <note>yellow bile, associated with heat</note> that is causing harm through its excessive heat, observe which limb it is located in—whether the stomach, the liver, or other parts. Once this is known, take a medicine that suppresses the sharpness of the choler in that specific limb: such as **endive**, **hart's tongue fern** <note>original: "scolopendria"</note>, **lettuce**, or **purslane** for the liver. For the spleen, use **bugloss**, **borage**, **watercress** <note>original: "nasturtium"</note>, or **calamint**. The same applies to other humors.

And so that the new apprentices of the medical art might have at hand those things that are necessary for the composition of medicines, I have set down both the simple and compound medicines that are more commonly in use. And all evacuative medicines <note>purgatives intended to clear the body of excess fluids or "humors"</note> are evacuants by their own inherent property, and they do not only evacuate from the specific organs mentioned above. Rather, all evacuative medicines for bile, phlegm, and melancholy <note>the three primary "waste" humors in the medieval medical system</note> evacuate the aforementioned humors from any part of the body, provided they are given alongside medicines that "guide" their power to those specific parts. For example: Turpeth <note>a root used as a strong laxative</note>, which purges phlegm; if it is given with medicines that guide its power to the joints, such as with ginger, sea onion, etc., it will purge phlegm specifically from the joints, and the same applies to other parts of the body.

Now that we have discussed digestive, evacuative, and guiding medicines, we must speak of strengthening medicines, as well as those that alter a "bad complexion" <note>an imbalance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry</note> left behind in the said organs. First, we discuss those that strengthen and warm the head.

# ON THE
# RECOGNITION,
## AND TREATMENT
## OF DISEASES,

->*From the position of the celestial bodies,*<-

### *BOOK THREE.*

## SUMMARY OF CHAPTER I.

*A **crisis** <note>original: "Crisis"; in ancient and early modern medicine, the "crisis" was the critical turning point of a disease where the patient either began to recover or took a turn for the worse.</note> is a struggle between **nature** <note>original: "naturae"; here referring to the body's internal healing force or "vital heat."</note> and **disease**. If nature overcomes the disease, the outcome is good; if it is overcome, the outcome is bad. There are three parts to this: first, in which nature separates the **matter of the disease** <note>In Galenic medicine, diseases were thought to be caused by "corrupt humors" or matter that the body had to isolate.</note> and, through this separation, sets in motion the harmful elements away from those that are helpful, so that it directs the harm to a specific part of the body. The second part is when nature entirely expels from the body that which it has separated. The third part is the sudden change that arrives, leading either toward health or toward death.*

*Furthermore, a crisis is either **simple** or **compound**. A simple crisis is one that happens quickly. A compound crisis is one that happens gradually, leading either toward health or toward death. This latter type is two-fold: one in which a great change toward health occurs first, followed by a gradual improvement until the patient is made strong again; the other, however, is the opposite—namely, leading toward death.*

<vocab>Turning point, disease, nature, position of the heavens, medicine, astrological medicine</vocab>

<summary>This page introduces Book Three, defining the "crisis" of a disease as a three-stage struggle between the body's natural healing power and the illness. It categorizes these turning points as either simple (rapid) or compound (gradual) based on how the body isolates and expels morbid matter.</summary>
<keywords>crisis, nature vs disease, pathology, iatroastrology, humoral theory, recovery, medical theory</keywords>

--- Page 226 ---
<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book Three. While the previous book focused on the properties of seeds and medicines, this section transitions into clinical theory, specifically the concept of the "crisis"—the decisive turning point in an illness. It establishes the definitions used by classical and medieval authorities like Galen and Avicenna to predict whether a patient will recover or perish.</meta>

# THIRD [BOOK].

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'E' containing a seated figure, likely a scholar or physician, surrounded by foliage.</image-desc>

First, therefore, a **crisis** <note>original: "crisis"; from the Greek word for "judgment" or "decision." In early medicine, this was the critical moment when a disease reached its peak and the body either began to heal or succumbed.</note> is the resistance of **nature** <note>original: "naturae"; the body's innate vital force or healing power</note> and disease. If nature overcomes the disease, the crisis is called **praiseworthy** <note>original: "laudabilis"; a favorable sign indicating recovery</note>; but if the disease overcomes nature, the crisis will be bad and deadly. Or, it is a furious consumption of the sickness in which great labor and anxiety come upon the infirm person. And this is what **Avicenna** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> says in the second [tractate] of the fourth [book]: A crisis is a sudden change made either toward the side of health or toward the side of death. 

A crisis has three parts. First, in which nature separates the **matter of the disease** <note>original: "materiam morbi"; refers to the "corrupt humors" believed to cause illness</note> and sets it in motion, separating the harmful from the helpful, and directing the harmful toward the places of expulsion outside the body, or toward some limb or the **lesser members** <note>original: "membra vilia"; parts of the body considered less vital to life, where nature might "dump" toxins to protect the heart or brain.</note> of the body; this part is called the **antecedent movement**.

The second part is that in which nature evacuates and expels from the body the harmful matter itself, which has already been separated and directed to the places of expulsion; this is called **evacuation**. The third part is the suddenly arriving change toward health or toward death. Thus, in the broad sense of "crisis," it encompasses these three parts. But in the strict sense, a crisis is only the sudden change itself, made either toward health or toward death.

Furthermore, secondly, there is a two-fold crisis: **simple** and **compound**. A simple crisis is one that happens quickly toward health or quickly toward death, or gradually toward health or gradually toward death. A compound crisis is when the disease is diminished only partially, but is completed afterward with a resolution toward good or evil. And this crisis is divided into two. One, in which a great change toward health occurs at first, and then it is gradually completed until the sick person is healed.

The second is one in which a great change toward death occurs at first, and then it is gradually completed until the person dies. In a good and praiseworthy crisis, it is necessary for **concoction** <note>original: "coctionem"; the process where the body "cooks" or ripens the raw, diseased humors so they can be expelled.</note> to come first, then to divide [the humors], and then to expel them, as is held in the commentary on the 22nd Aphorism of the fourth section. Therefore, a crisis never happens at the beginning, nor during the **increase** <note>original: "augmento"; the phase where symptoms are worsening.</note> of a universal disease, nor does it happen during the universal **decline** <note>original: "declinatione"; the period after the peak of the illness.</note> of a healthy disease. This is because when the movement occurs in the matter, the **accidents** <note>original: "accidentia"; the outward symptoms or signs of the disease.</note> are intensified; however, when the symptoms are intense, it is not a decline, for in a decline the symptoms are lessened.

However, a crisis taken as an evacuation in a healthy disease can begin at the **peak** <note>original: "statu"; the "status" or acme of the illness when it is at its highest intensity.</note> after the movement of the matter and the separation of the harmful substance and its direction toward the places of expulsion; and this will be at the end of that peak itself. And this is what **Galen** <note>The 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> says in the third book of *On Crises*: The best crisis is at the hour of the peak of the sickness.

# BOOK [THREE]

->SUMMARY OF CHAPTER 11.<-

*A **crisis** <note>original: "Crisium"; the decisive turning point of a disease.</note> has a double cause, either general or particular: the general cause is found through the signs of the disease’s nature, which is sometimes aided by **celestial influence** <note>original: "influentia cœlesti"; the belief that the positions of stars and planets directly affected human health and the "humors" of the body.</note>, and sometimes merely provoked by it. The particular cause, however, is the **vital power** <note>original: "virtus"; the internal strength or life force of the patient.</note> dominating the matter, the **matter of the disease** <note>original: "materia morbi"; the corrupt fluids or "humors" thought to cause the sickness.</note> provoking that power, and the alignment of the heavenly bodies. A crisis, insofar as it is a crisis, tends more toward health than toward death; however, in malignant fevers, a crisis is most often toward death. A crisis produced by a change in the matter is worse than one produced by the body’s natural evacuation. The **critical days** <note>original: "dies critici"; specific days during an illness when a change was expected to occur.</note> in chronic diseases follow the motion of the Sun, but in acute diseases, they follow the motion of the Moon.*

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'H' featuring an architectural setting with a seated figure inside a vaulted space.</image-desc>FOR the crisis itself has double causes, both general and particular. The general causes are the struggle that occurs between **nature** <note>The body's internal healing force.</note> and the disease, from which nature is moved to attack the disease and its causes, and conversely, the disease attacks nature. This movement is produced by nature as the principal agent, aided by celestial influence, but it is not produced by the disease itself. Sometimes, however, nature brings about a crisis without the aid of celestial influence, being only stimulated by it. 

The particular causes of a **crisis of evacuation** <note>original: "crisis euacuationis"; a turning point where the body successfully expels corrupt matter through sweat, vomit, or other means.</note> are a strong vital power dominating the matter, either in its entirety or in its greatest part, along with the disease matter provoking that power, and the alignment of the celestial bodies. 

The causes of a **crisis of derivation** <note>original: "crisis deriuationis"; a turning point where the disease matter is not expelled from the body, but shifted from one part or organ to another.</note>, however, involve a vital power that is not "simply" strong. This is because a simply strong power—such as that found in a crisis of evacuation—does not keep the matter inside the body, but expels and evacuates it. Rather, this power is called "strong" only in comparison to a power that entirely succumbs in the struggle, being unable to evacuate the matter or trans-

### [BOOK] THREE

<page-num>81</page-num>
<header>THIRD [BOOK].</header>

...to transform it, which is called simply weak, so that it can be called a middle state between a **vital power** <note>original: "virtutem"; the patient's internal life force or strength.</note> that is simply strong and one that is simply weak, and bad **matter** <note>original: "materia"; the corrupt fluids or "humors" believed to cause the disease.</note>: not yet much of a stimulus to the power, yet obedient to it, so that it may be expelled from the body to the outside, and with these the aspect of the celestial bodies. However, the aforementioned types of crisis are weakened according to the strength and weakness of the power and the celestial aspect, and according to the obedience of nature and its rebellion against the abundance or scarcity of matter.

And a crisis, insofar as it is a crisis, more often ends in health than in death, and pertains primarily to health rather than death. The reason for this is that a crisis is in itself an effort of nature operating naturally for a purpose; nature, so operating, does not attempt to move the matter, nor to separate the harmful from the helpful, unless the matter is **digested** <note>original: "digesta"; in early medicine, this meant the humors had been "cooked" or processed by the body's heat until they were ready to be expelled.</note>, over which nature is for the most part victorious; and this rarely fails when the crisis is complete.

In pestilential fevers, however, or where the matter is very malignant, the crisis is for the most part toward death, because the vital power cannot overcome the very malignant matter.

And a crisis achieved through the natural evacuation of the body is better than one achieved through a change of the matter <note>referring to when the disease shifts to another part of the body rather than leaving it.</note>, because it occurs from a stronger power and from matter more obedient to nature, and it is better tolerated by the sick person; nor is there fear of a harmful injury occurring to any limb, as is feared in a crisis of change.

And **critical days** <note>original: "dies critici"; specific days during an illness when a major change in the patient's condition was expected.</note> are observed in chronic and acute diseases; the days counted in chronic diseases follow the motion of the Sun, and those in acute diseases imitate the motion of the Moon. For these planets most clearly change lower bodies <note>meaning earthly bodies, including humans.</note> by their movements, light, and influence in the twelve signs of the **zodiac** <note>original: "zodiaci"; the belt of constellations through which the sun and planets appear to move.</note>, but the Moon more so because of its proximity to us, whereby it can more strongly impress itself upon our bodies. For Galen says in the third book on critical days: The Moon signifies how the disposition of a man will be on those days, in his sickness and in his health: for if the fortunate **wandering stars** <note>original: "stellæ erraticæ"; the planets.</note> are aligned with the Moon, those days will be favorable for the man, and the crisis ends for the most part in good.

* And if unfortunate stars are aligned with it, those days will be days of injury and sorrow for the man, and the crisis will end in evil. Galen gives an example of this: when a man is born, and fortune <note>a benefic planet like Jupiter or Venus</note> is found in **Aries** <note>the Ram</note>, and misfortune <note>a malefic planet like Saturn or Mars</note> in **Taurus** <note>the Bull</note>, then this man, without a doubt, when the Moon is in Aries, or in **Cancer** <note>the Crab</note>, or in **Libra** <note>the Scales</note>, or **Capricorn** <note>the Horned Goat</note>, will have a good disposition.

But when it is in Taurus or in the signs **square** <note>original: "quadratis"; an astrological aspect of 90 degrees, usually considered challenging or stressful.</note> to Taurus, or in the **opposite sign** <note>an aspect of 180 degrees.</note>, such as **Leo** <note>the Lion</note>, **Scorpio** <note>the Scorpion</note>, or **Aquarius** <note>the Water-Bearer</note>, then his disposition will be bad, as will the sicknesses of that man which occur to him.

# BOOK [TWO]

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

When the Moon is in Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius <note>These are known as the "fixed" signs of the Zodiac; in medieval medicine, they were thought to make a disease stubborn or long-lasting.</note>, the outcomes of its illnesses are worse.

And those illnesses which begin while the Moon is moving in Aries, Cancer, Libra, or Capricorn <note>These are the "movable" or cardinal signs, representing change and movement, which suggests a quicker resolution to the illness.</note> are healthier in their outcomes, and the patient is more likely to recover from them. Galen also says: "We have found that for everything that happens in the cycle of days, in all matters, there is no cause except the Moon."

### EXPLANATIONS.

**1 If they apply:** <term>Application</term> <note>original: "applicatio"</note> occurs either by body or by ray. Application "by body" happens when a faster planet approaches the position where a slower planet is located; the application begins when it enters the "orb" (the range of influence) of the planet it is seeking to join. Or, it happens when its own orb touches the planet it is applying to. For example, if **Saturn** ♄ were at 12 degrees of **Aries** ♈, and the **Moon** ☽ were at the 1st degree, then the Moon is said to be "applying" to Saturn. The application is stronger at the 3rd degree, for then the orb of the Moon would touch Saturn, which proceeds in a straight line. Both can also be <term>retrograde</term> <note>appearing to move backward from our perspective on Earth</note>, provided that one is faster than the other. Because of this, one must carefully observe in the <term>ephemeris</term> <note>a table of daily planetary positions</note> whether a planet is **direct** or **retrograde**. For if the number of degrees and minutes on the following day is larger, it is direct; if smaller, it is retrograde. Application also occurs by "rays" or by <term>aspect</term> <note>a specific geometric angle between planets</note>; for instance, if Saturn were at 12 degrees of **Capricorn** ♑ and the Moon was at the 1st degree of Aries ♈, then the Moon’s application to Saturn would be by a **square** ⬜ aspect. The same applies to the other aspects.

However, one should note here that since the Moon is faster than the other planets, it is very rare for another planet to "apply" to the Moon. Rather, the Moon applies to all of them. Therefore, when the author says "if the **wandering stars** <note>original: "stella erraticæ"; the ancient term for planets.</note> apply to the Moon," it must be understood in the reverse order—that is, if the Moon applies to any of the wandering stars. For if the Moon is in the 1st degree of Aries and Saturn is in the 12th, although in reality the Moon applies to Saturn (since the Moon is faster than Saturn), our author still describes it as Saturn applying to the Moon.

**2 We have found:** They are lying, therefore, who claim that Galen was ignorant of astrology. I believe this is said by many so that they may protect, or rather hide, their own ignorance. They think that if they appear like Galen in their ignorance of this art, they will be better regarded by their listeners. I would wish that these enemies of astrology would observe daily what the heavens effect in diseases, and only then say what they wish against astrology. For, as the **Philosopher** <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle.</note> testifies in the first book of the *Ethics*, "no one is a good judge of things he does not know." Therefore, let those who are ignorant of this art not speak a single word about it.

# BOOK THREE

<sig>X 2</sig>
<header>THIRD.</header>

->SUMMARY OF CHAPTER III.<-

*The critical motion <note>original: "motus criticus"; the biological process leading toward a medical "crisis" or turning point in a disease</note> arises from the movement and influence of the superior bodies, and especially the Sun and Moon. While the Sun travels through the first quarter of the oblique circle <note>the ecliptic or zodiacal path</note>, blood is moved within our bodies; through the second quarter, yellow bile; through the third, black bile; and through the fourth, phlegm. This also occurs by the Moon’s motion, whether general or specific. By the general principle of the waxing or waning of its light: in the first quarter while it is growing, blood is specifically moved; in the second, yellow bile; in the third, black bile; and in the fourth, phlegm. However, the Sun and Moon, along with the rest of the planets and fixed stars, cause the crisis in different ways. The Sun acts through the manifest change of the air, and through good or bad fortune, as do the rest of the planets. The Moon acts through the manifest change of the air, by its operation while passing through opposite points in the Zodiac, and through good or bad <term>aspects</term> <note>the geometric angles between planets</note> or <term>conjunctions</term> <note>when two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky</note> with the other planets. The remaining planets operate only through aspects or conjunctions.*

->[concerning] meteors <note>original: "meteororum"; likely a reference to Aristotle's *Meteorologica*, which discussed atmospheric and natural phenomena</note>. But the critical motion <note>the process leading to the "crisis" or turning point of a disease</note> adheres to one path and one order, as is evident through experience; therefore, this arises from the movement of the superior bodies and from their influence, especially that of the Sun and the Moon. For just as the Sun produces changes through its motion in the four quarters of the circle of signs <note>the Zodiac</note> in chronic <note>long-term</note> diseases, so the Moon effects changes in acute <note>short-term/sudden</note> diseases through its motion through the four quarters of the signs of the zodiac as it moves within them. And by the quarters of the sun, the four seasons of the year are distinguished, according to which the air is differently altered by the sun’s progress. 2 And from this it happens that a sickness which begins in winter is terminated in summer, and that which occurs in spring is terminated in autumn. And each of these quarters moves the humors <note>the four vital fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm</note> in the human body with their own qualities, proportional to the quality of the air of that quarter. Whence blood, which is temperate with a tendency toward heat and moisture, is proportioned to and moved by the complexion of spring. And yellow bile <term>cholera</term> in summer, black bile <term>melancholia</term> in autumn, and phlegm <term>phlegma</term> in winter.<-

The motion of the Moon, however, moves the humors in two ways: namely, by a general and common motion, according to which the Moon increases and decreases in light. 3 For as it grows in light, every liquid <note>original: "humidum"</note> increases—in water, animals, and trees. And thus the humors and moistures in the bodies of men increase until the full moon <term>plenilunium</term>, and as the Moon wanes, they decrease and are diminished. By its special and proper motion, however, the Moon moves through the twelve signs of the zodiac, in which it creates four quarters diversified 4 by its qualities and phases <note>original: "figuris"</note>; and in those quarters, the humor proportional to the qualities of that quarter is moved. Hence they say that blood is moved in the first, yellow bile in the second, black bile in the third, and phlegm in the fourth. Nevertheless, the Sun, the Moon, and the remaining planets, 5 as well as the fixed stars, operate in different ways in producing a crisis. For the Sun specifically operates 6 through the manifest change of the air, through which it terminates long diseases; however, by its motion in the circle of signs passing to opposite places, it has no effect on the crisis through any occult property—or if it has any, it is very little. Yet the Sun, through its operation which is 7 by way of fortune or misfortune <note>astrological favor (benefic) or affliction (malefic)</note>, does have an effect on the crisis, just like any other planet. And thus the Moon operates in three modes in the termination of diseases: namely, through its manifest operation by changing the air; through the operation it has by passing through opposite places in the zodiac; and the operation according to which it is a fortune or a misfortune—that is, through which it is made fortunate or suffers misfortune. The Sun, however, possesses only the first and third of these operations. ### EXPLANATIONS.

*1 Regarding the movement: even if this reasoning has the power to demonstrate it, I would nevertheless urge physicians to use that art which they have used thus far and have learned, and to believe that the causes of this matter are those which they have considered them to be until now. Yet they should persuade themselves that it is possible for the matter to be otherwise. Because of this cause, through diligent observation of those changes and movements of the celestial bodies, they should see daily whether the matter stands as our author <note>The writer of the main text being commented upon.</note> teaches or not. For in this way it will happen that they see, as if with their own eyes, that which is both weakened and confirmed by many arguments: namely, the opinion concerning critical days <note>original: "diebus criticis"; the specific days when a disease was expected to reach a "crisis" or turning point.</note>, both that of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician (c. 129–216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> and that of the other Astrologers. I would not want the reader to expect me to either approve or disapprove of the authorities of either Fracastoro <note>Girolamo Fracastoro (c. 1478–1553), a physician and scholar who wrote on "contagion" and astronomy.</note> or of him who recently wrote against Galen on this opinion. For this is not what we have set out to do, but rather to explain the more obscure words and opinions of the author; let others, therefore, if they wish, take this task upon themselves.*

*2 And from this it happens that diseases which begin in winter end in summer—specifically when the Sun <note>original symbol: ☉</note> reaches the opposition <note>original symbol: ☍; an astrological aspect where two bodies are 180 degrees apart, often signifying a turning point or confrontation.</note> of that place in the zodiac in which it was when the patient fell into the illness. For contraries are cured by contraries <note>original: "contraria contrarijs curantur"; a fundamental principle of Galenic medicine suggesting that an illness caused by heat should be treated with cold, etc.</note>. Therefore, to someone who once objected to me that there is no need for either a doctor or medicines if the heaven alone is the cause of disease and the heaven alone can heal, I replied—and I would wish this to be the answer to everyone else: if the Sun, by traveling through Aries <note>original symbol: ♈; the first sign of the zodiac, associated with heat and the element of fire.</note>, has adversely affected someone's blood, that same Sun can bring help when it reaches Libra <note>original symbol: ♎; the sign opposite Aries, associated with balance and air.</note>, which is a sign contrary to Aries in both location and nature; and a prudent physician can bring help to that same person. Marsilio Ficino <note>A celebrated Italian philosopher and priest (1433–1499) who sought to integrate Platonism, medicine, and astrology.</note> persuades me of this in his book On Obtaining Life from the Heavens <note>original: "de vita celitus comparanda".</note>, which teaches how we can transfer the powers of the planets to ourselves through medicines. In reality, all people understand that if our bodies use cold things, they become cold on any day of the year; however, if they use those same things in winter, they become colder than in summer. What is the cause of this matter? The heaven and food. Food or medicines can heal the sick, and so can the heaven; when the heaven and medicines work together toward the same end, they can restore lost health more safely, easily, and quickly. But if the heaven was not the cause of the disease, but rather the person's own will—which, since it is free, can not only cast itself into diseases but even bring about its own death—then both the heaven and the physician can assist him. For if someone’s skin pores and passages were constricted by cold such that they fell into a fever, if this happened in winter, the physician will help him while the heaven resists; if it happened in summer, both the physician provides help and the season of the year supports him, and thus the sick person will recover lost health more safely and easily. But perhaps we have digressed too much.*

<header>BOOK I</header>
<page-num>2</page-num>

3 **For as the light increases,** this is so well known that it requires no interpretation—not just the words themselves, but the truth behind the words. Fishermen observe this in <term>shellfish<note>It was a common ancient and medieval belief, cited by authors like Pliny the Elder, that the flesh of oysters and other shellfish grew and shrank in sync with the phases of the moon.</note></term>. Farmers see it in those timbers which, if cut during the first quarter of the moon, are quickly eaten away by rot; however, they understand that wood cut during the final phase of the moon—when its light is diminished—does not easily decay because of its dryness. One may see the same principle in sowing, in harvesting, and in other rustic tasks. And what of the ebb and flow of the sea? These things are sufficiently well known.

4 **By qualities and figures:** By "qualities" we mean that from the <term>conjunction<note>original: "☌"; when the Moon and Sun are in the same degree of the zodiac (New Moon).</note></term> to the first <term>square<note>original: "□"; a 90-degree angle between celestial bodies, representing the first quarter moon.</note></term>, the moon is hot and moist. From the first square to the <term>opposition<note>original: "⍘"; when the Moon is 180 degrees from the Sun (Full Moon).</note></term>, it is hot and dry. From the opposition to the second square, it is cold and dry, and from the second square back to the conjunction, it is cold and moist. Regarding "figure," in the first quarter it is only half-full; at opposition, it is entirely full of light; in the second square, it is again half-full, but on the side opposite the first; and at the conjunction, nothing is seen at all.

5 **And the fixed stars:** Therefore, the fixed stars must also be carefully observed, whether they are joined to the Sun or to other planets that gaze upon the moon, whose powers are either weakened or intensified because of this. But in what manner? You will be able to draw this not only from the tables of the fixed stars, but also from the <term>ephemerides<note>Books listing the daily positions of celestial bodies.</note></term> of the most excellent **Antonio Magini**, <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617) was an influential Italian astronomer and mathematician who competed with Galileo for a chair at Bologna.</note> who adapted these calculations for almost every single day.

6 **Through a manifest change in the air:** when the Sun enters Aries, Cancer, Libra, or Capricorn <note>original: "♈ ♋ ♎ ♑"; these are the Cardinal signs, marking the start of the four seasons.</note>, it will cause a clear change in the weather; for these are <term>movable signs<note>Also known as "cardinal" signs, they represent the turning points of the seasons and are associated with change.</note></term>, as was stated in the first book.

7 **By way of fortune or misfortune:** namely, when the moon is joined with the <term>malefics<note>original: "infortunis"; planets traditionally considered "unlucky" or harsh in their influence, usually Mars and Saturn.</note></term>, or is harmed by "bad rays" (harsh aspects), or when the moon itself harms Venus or Mars <note>original: "♀, uel ♂".</note>.

---

->**SUMMARY OF CHAPTER IV**<-

Of <term>critical days<note>original: "Dierum criticorum"; specific days in the progression of a disease when a "crisis" occurs, determining if the patient will recover or decline.</note></term>, some are **radical**, others are **indicative**, and others are **intercedent** (intervening). These days are observed only in acute, very acute, and extremely acute diseases, and they occur without a "higher nature" <note>The author likely means they follow the physical cycles of the moon rather than more abstract spiritual forces.</note>. They occur from third day to third day; the **indicative** days run by the number four, which comes from the division of the week or the "squaring" of the moon. There are four **radical** days in a month—the 2nd, 14th, 20th, and 27th—and all of these are observed based on the motion of the moon, as the author teaches.

<page-num>84</page-num>

Physicians also distinguish <term>critical days<note>In traditional medicine, these are specific days during an illness when a significant change (a "crisis") is expected to occur, leading toward either recovery or death.</note></term> in three ways. For they call some "radical," some "indicative," and some "intercedent." The **intercedent days** are those in which a crisis happens solely through the irritation of nature against the <term>matter of the disease<note>The physical substance, such as excess humors, believed to be causing the sickness.</note></term>; nature, being provoked, rises up to expel it. These days are only observed in acute and very acute diseases, because only the matter of such diseases is of a kind that can stimulate nature so that it is moved to expel it without waiting for the nature of the higher bodies <note>This likely refers to the slower influence of the stars and planets compared to the rapid movement of the "choleric" humor.</note>. This is because such matter is <term>choleric<note>Associated with yellow bile; characterized by heat and a tendency toward rapid movement.</note></term>, whose nature is to move from the third day to the third day, and thus to stimulate nature in that same pattern. Therefore, these days are calculated by the number three with a repetition of the third day. The calculation is as follows: 1, 2, 3; then 3, 4, 5; and again, 5, 6, 7; and so on until the 14th day. These days are also called <note>original: "critici mendosi"</note> **false critical days** by <term>Rhazes<note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925 AD), a famous Persian physician whose work "The Comprehensive Book" (Latin: *Continens*) was a standard medical text in Europe.</note></term> in the nineteenth book of his *Comprehensive Book*, of which he said those "falling in the middle" are understood to be those which are neither the seventh nor the fourth. And a crisis in acute diseases, for the most part, occurs on these intercedent days.

**Indicative days** are the days in which traces are seen that are signs of the alteration of the matter—that is, its <term>digestion<note>In this context, the "ripening" or processing of the disease-causing humors by the body's heat.</note></term> or lack thereof—or they are days signifying the victory of one of the two struggling forces: namely, the body’s strength and the disease.

And these indicative days run by the number four, resulting from the division of the week (or the <term>quadrature of the Moon<note>The quarter-phases of the lunar cycle.</note></term>) into two parts.

There are four such days in every lunar month: the 4th, 11th, 17th, and 24th. These days always proceed by the number four with a repetition of the fourth, except in the second group of four in every <term>vigenary<note>original: "vigenarius"; a cycle of twenty days.</note></term> number. Thus the seventh day, which is the second fourth-day of the first twenty-day cycle, is not repeated. They are therefore counted like this: 1, 2, 3, 4; then 4, 5, 6, 7. The seventh day is not repeated, and the third group of four begins on the eighth day, and is counted thus: 8, 9, 10, 11; and again, 11, 12, 13, 14; and so on: 14, 15, 16, 17; and again, 17, 18, 19, 20. The same calculation must be used in the other twenty-day numbers, such as 21, 22, 23, 24; and again 24, 25, 26, 27; and so on until the final vigenary, which is the 120th day—again not repeating the 27th, but beginning from 28, 29, 30, 31.

**Radical critical days**, which run by sevens, occur four times in a month: namely, the 7th, 14th, 20th, and 27th. They are calculated thus: in every twenty-day number, there are three weeks. The first seven-day number, or the first week, is not repeated with the first day of the second week, but they are counted separately. But the second seventh day, which is the end...

...of the second week is repeated in the third week, and becomes its beginning, and the weeks are calculated thus: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; and afterward: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14; then by repeating: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20.

And similarly, the remaining <term>vigenary numbers<note>Numbers based on a count of twenty.</note></term> are calculated, which are called by physicians the **universal periods** in <term>crises<note>The turning point of a disease, where the patient either begins to recover or declines toward death.</note></term>, or critical days. They are calculated as follows: the first limit is 20, the second limit is day 40, the third is day 60, the fourth is day 80, the fifth is day 100, and the last is day 120.

Regarding these <term>radical days<note>The "root" or foundational days from which medical progressions are measured.</note></term>, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical works dominated European universities for centuries.</note> said that the influence of the Moon, which occurs during critical days, becomes more powerful when the Moon is in the position of its opposition—that is, when it is in opposition to, or in the full moon of, the sun.

Then it follows the **quadrature** <note>original: "quadrationem"; an astrological aspect where celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart, forming a quarter-circle.</note>, which is when it is in the fourth aspect of the sun; and this is done by dividing the revolution of the Moon into halves, and then into halves of halves.

In this way, Avicenna touched upon two **aspects** of the Moon relative to the starting point where it began; both of these are aspects of "enmity" toward the newly begun disease, and for that reason, they assist nature against the illness.

1 And the first aspect is **opposition**. This occurs when the Moon, by its own motion, arrives at the sign in the **Zodiac** that is opposite the sign it was in at the hour the sickness began. For example, if the Moon was in **Aries**, the opposite sign is **Libra**.

If it was in **Taurus**, the opposite sign is **Scorpio**, as was established in the first treatise.

The second aspect, the "half of a half," is called the **fourth aspect**. This is when the Moon has traveled through three signs from the point or sign where the disease began. For instance, when it was in **Cancer** and arrives at **Libra**, it has then completed the quadrature of the circle of signs, or the fourth aspect. This is considered to have less "malice" <note>original: "malitiæ"; in medical astrology, this refers to the severity or harmful intensity of a planetary influence.</note> than the opposition.

Now, when the Moon reaches the first and fifth shapes mentioned above, it is said to be in the **sextile aspect**. ### EXPLANATIONS.

**1** And the first **aspect** <note>An "aspect" is a specific geometric angle between two celestial points, believed in early medicine to influence the human body.</note> is the **opposition**. This occurs not merely when the moon is in the zodiac sign opposite the one it occupied at the hour of the patient's <term>onset of illness<note>original: *decubitus*; literally "lying down," referring to the moment a patient is forced to take to their bed by disease.</note></term>, but rather when it is at the exact opposite degree. For example, if someone falls ill when the Moon is at the 3rd degree of **Aries** (♈), the Moon is said to be in **opposition** (☍) when it reaches the 3rd degree of **Libra** (♎). The same principle applies to the other aspects mentioned in the first treatise. These aspects are either "good" or "bad": the good ones are the **Trine** (△) and the **Sextile** (⚹), though the Trine is better; the bad ones are the **Opposition** (☍), **Conjunction** (☌), and **Square** (□), with the Opposition being the worst. Because of this, they are figuratively called by the names of "friendship" and "hostility"—thus there is perfect and imperfect friendship, and the same is said of the types of hostility.

**2** When the Moon is at a distance—since we have undertaken this burden for the sake of <term>novices<note>original: *tironibus*; students or beginners in the medical-astrological arts.</note></term>, it will not be useless to follow the individual and minute details; for the experts, it will be enough to read through what the author has written, leaving aside our explanations. Therefore, whoever wishes to know on which day, and at what hour of the day, any lunar aspect will occur, must proceed as follows: Carefully observe the position of the Moon at the hour the disease began. For example, someone begins to be ill at noon on June 20th. I see in the <term>ephemeris<note>A table providing the daily predicted positions of celestial bodies. The text mentions the tables of Giovanni Paolo Magini, a famous Italian astronomer.</note></term> of Magini that the Moon is at 0 degrees and 20 minutes of **Cancer** (♋). I want to know at what hour it will be 45 degrees distant from this place, which is the time of the first **critical day**—which physicians call the fourth day, as they ignore the specific hours in this matter. You should proceed like this: add 45 degrees to the position of the moon, and see where the resulting number ends according to the order of the signs; when the Moon is at that spot, or at that time, it will be the "critical hour," in this manner:

->Position of the Moon at the start of illness: 0 deg. 20 min. Cancer (♋)<-
->Distance from that place which creates the crisis: 45 deg. 0 min.<-

Search for this degree in the ephemeris to see if it appears on the third, fourth, or fifth following day; if that exact number is not there, look for the next lower number, and that will be the critical day. This specific number is not in the ephemeris, but the closest lower number is on the 23rd day. Therefore, this is the critical day. ### SUMMARY OF CHAPTER V.

Once the location where the moon triggers a <term>crisis<note>In early medicine, the "crisis" was the decisive moment when a disease either began to resolve or became fatal.</note></term> is found, as well as the hour, let a <term>celestial theme<note>original: *cœleste thema*; a chart showing the positions of the stars and planets at a specific moment, much like a horoscope.</note></term> be erected. Let the Moon's condition be observed: if it is favorable, it will be good for the patient; if unfavorable, it will be bad, as often happens on other days, even those that are not <term>critical days<note>Specific days during an illness (traditionally the 7th, 14th, etc.) when the patient's condition was expected to change drastically.</note></term>. The Moon in a **square** aspect (□) to the position it held at the <term>onset of illness<note>original: *initio morbi*</note></term> triggers a crisis; it does the same in **opposition** (☍), in the second **square**, and in **conjunction** (☌). However, this does not occur on an equal number of days because of the Moon's unequal motion; although it moves through equal spaces in the heavens—namely, 90 degrees—it does not do so in equal time. From this, it happens that those ignorant of this art believe the ninth day is always critical, whereas that only happens occasionally, specifically when the Moon is slow in its motion.

To find the critical days most easily—for instance, the 7th, 14th, 20th, and 27th—observe in which sign and degree the Moon is at the beginning of the illness. Add 90 degrees to its position for the 7th day, 180 degrees for the 14th day, 270 degrees for the 20th or 21st day, and 360 degrees for the 28th day. Thus, you will have the location of the Moon at the critical day by beginning the calculation of the <term>signs<note>The twelve divisions of the zodiac.</note></term> from the sign in which the Moon was at the start of the illness. If the Moon were at the tenth degree of <term>Aries<note>The first sign of the zodiac, associated in medical astrology with the head and the element of Fire (hot and dry).</note></term>, and I wished to find the first <term>critical day<note>original: *dies criticus*; a day when the patient's condition is expected to change significantly.</note></term>, which is the seventh day, I added 90 degrees to the position of the Moon—that is, to the tenth degree of Aries. This results in 100 degrees, which makes 3 signs and 10 degrees, allowing 30 degrees for each sign. Now, when three signs and twelve <note>original: *duodecim*; the author likely means ten degrees to be consistent with the 100-degree total, but the text reads twelve.</note> degrees are counted from Aries, the Moon will arrive at the 12th degree of the sign of <term>Cancer<note>The fourth sign of the zodiac, associated with the element of Water (cold and moist).</note></term> on the seventh day from the start of the illness. 

But to find the 14th day, I added 180 degrees to the position of the Moon on the day the disease began (namely, at the tenth degree of Aries), and the result was 190 degrees, which makes six signs and 10 degrees. By counting 6 signs and 10 degrees from Aries, the Moon arrives on the 14th day at the 10th degree of the sign of <term>Libra<note>The seventh sign of the zodiac, directly opposite Aries.</note></term>, and so on for the others. 

And if the Moon is well-disposed on any of those critical days, the patient will then be relieved, they will feel better, and the crisis will end well, unless the <term>malefics<note>original: *mali*; referring to the "unlucky" planets Saturn and Mars.</note></term> hinder it physically, or through an <term>opposition<note>An aspect of 180 degrees, usually considered stressful or confrontational in astrology.</note></term>, or a <term>square aspect<note>original: *quartum aspectum*; an angle of 90 degrees, traditionally viewed as a point of tension or crisis.</note></term> without <term>reception<note>A condition where one planet is in a sign ruled by another, suggesting a degree of cooperation or "hospitality" between them.</note></term>.

1 But if on any of those days the Moon is hindered and poorly disposed by Saturn or Mars, then the patient will grow worse and fare poorly. This is especially true if the Moon is then in <term>conjunction<note>When two celestial bodies appear in the same place in the sky.</note></term> with the lord of the <term>sixth house<note>In astrology, the "houses" divide the sky into twelve sections; the sixth house specifically governs sickness and infirmity.</note></term> at the hour of the onset of the illness or the patient's birth, because in such a case, the recovery of the sick person will be in doubt.

If indeed that hindering malefic planet is the lord of the <term>eighth house<note>The house associated with death and transformation.</note></term>, then the patient will die.

2 Other days besides the critical ones are also considered in illnesses. If the Moon is joined to any "good" planet on that day, the patient will be relieved and it will be healthier for them. From this, it happens that sometimes a crisis results in a good outcome for the patient on a day when it was not expected, nor did it seem likely to occur. 

And when the Moon on any given day reaches the malefics through conjunction, opposition, or square, the patient will grow more burdened. If a crisis occurs then, it will lead to harm rather than health. This is why physicians who are ignorant of <term>astronomy<note>In this period, "astronomy" and "astrology" were often treated as a single discipline essential for medical practice.</note></term> are so often deceived; they judge the crisis differently than it actually turns out because they do not pay attention to the Moon's <term>application<note>The movement of a faster planet toward an aspect with a slower one.</note></term> to the other planets. 

Therefore, whoever wishes to judge a crisis correctly should carefully examine the true position of the Moon in longitude and latitude, and its speed or slowness; for the patient's crises vary according to these movements. For when the Moon is in the <term>fourth aspect<note>The square aspect (90 degrees).</note></term> relative to the place it occupied at the start of the illness, it triggers a crisis. This commonly happens on the seventh day from the start of the illness, because the Moon then reaches a sign contrary to the sign in which it was at the beginning of the disease. For example, let us suppose the Moon was in Aries at the start of the illness; when it reaches the fourth aspect—that is, Cancer—it will generate a crisis because Aries is a hot and dry sign, while Cancer is cold and moist, which are contrary qualities.
