This is especially true if it is also near a conjunction, where indeed, the conjunction having been released, it moves toward the full moon; and if it is carried into a greater quantity of its course, it kills [the disease or the patient] near the one hundred and eightieth degree.

If, however, when someone has fallen ill, the Moon moves by subtracting [slowing down], the disease will cause a commotion until it reaches the opposite point. [For the Moon, having turned toward the opposite, that is, the one hundred and eightieth degree] turns the disease toward a more healthy state. ### On the configuration of the Moon in Aries. Chapter III.

If the <term>decubitus</term> occurs when the Moon is in Aries, and it is configured with Mars or the Sun, the disease will originate from the head due to the Sun's heat; the <term>meninges</term><note>The membranes enveloping the brain and spinal cord.</note> will be in pain, and there will be continuous fevers, insomnia, burning heat, thirst, a rough tongue, and a burning of the chest, or pain in the liver, and the pulses will be elevated and disordered. But if no beneficial planet is joined with the Moon, and Saturn holds the same configuration, the patient will die at the first square aspect by the seventh day, especially if the Moon is increasing in its degrees or light. If, however, the decubitus occurs when the Moon is in Aries and any of the <term>malefic</term><note>Planets traditionally viewed as harmful, specifically Saturn and Mars.</note> stars is configured from the opposite or square position, or appears with the Moon itself, one must observe which star it is. And if indeed it is Saturn, the causes are in the head: <term>lethargy</term><note>In ancient medicine, this referred to a specific state of drowsy unconsciousness.</note>, loss of sensation, being oppressed by a deep sound <note>Likely referring to heavy or stertorous breathing/snoring in a semi-conscious state.</note>, and coldness; furthermore, they will be inconsistent, with the disease now easing and now intensifying.

If that star also subtracts from the light, or the degrees, or both, as I told you before, at the said 90th degree, the patient will have the greatest crisis. But join the remaining stars as well. For if Jupiter or Venus signifies anything by their configuration, the patient will come to the highest danger, but having passed the opposition, they will be saved. If, however, Mercury alone is configured to the proposed arrangement, the patient will die without a doubt. And if fiery Mars is also configured to the proposed arrangement, you shall rather consider them to be the redeemers. Wherefore

If, however, one falls ill when the Moon is in Taurus, especially when it is day, and Mars is together with it, or in its opposition or square, the disease will be from a fullness of blood and constriction; there will be burning, pain in the neck and bones, excessive insomnia, and a great desire for wine and cold water.

Let this inequality be determined by you in this way: in whichever sign the Moon resides, in that sign it assumes command. ### *On the configuration of the Moon in Cancer. Chapter VI.*

If someone takes to their bed when the Moon is in **Cancer**, and **Mars** is with it, or views it from an opposition or square, the origin of the disease will be from vomiting, <term>cholera</term><note>In this context, an excess of yellow bile leading to digestive distress, rather than the specific modern bacterial infection.</note>, and an upset stomach. For these patients, everything that cools and binds is suitable. ### On the configuration of the Moon in Leo. Chapter VII.

If indeed anyone should fall ill <note>original: "decubuerit." Referring to the moment the patient takes to their bed at the onset of sickness.</note> when the Moon is in **Leo** and [**Mars** is with her,] or regards her from an opposition or a square <note>These are astrological "aspects," or geometric angles: 180 degrees and 90 degrees, usually considered unfavorable.</note>, the onset of the disease will be from fullness <note>an excess of bodily humors</note> and indigestion. For there will be pain in the chest and the hypochondria <note>the upper abdominal region below the ribs</note>, and there will be intense fevers, and a heat that is greater in the internal depths than on the surface, and the bowels will be constricted. For these patients, therefore, all things that warm and relax the body are appropriate. If the **benefics** <note>Helpful planets, typically Jupiter and Venus.</note> do not regard the Moon, the patient will perish by the time the Moon reaches the opposition. But if the benefics do regard the Moon, though having suffered many evils, the patient will be saved.

If indeed someone falls ill when the Moon is in **Leo** and **Mars** is together with her, or regards her from an opposition or a square, the onset of the disease will be from a fullness of blood. And there will be flowing fevers, and pulses that are weak and hidden, as well as fainting fits <note>original: "animi defectus"</note>, collapsed appetites, heaviness, <term>cataphora</term> <note>a state of lethargy or semi-coma</note>, a languor of the whole body, and a cardiac condition <note>original: "cardiaca dispositio." In this period, this often referred to a dangerous state of collapse or "heart-faintness."</note>. For these patients, therefore, all things that constrict and cool are appropriate. If none of the benefics regards the Moon, the patient will perish by the ninth day. But if the benefics regard her, after having been in great danger, the patient will be saved following the opposition.

If indeed someone falls ill when the Moon is in **Leo** in any degree whatever (this itself may be observed in other signs as well, although I do not judge concerning them) with **Leo** being in the <term>horoscope</term> <note>the Ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of falling ill</note>, the disease will be from a vital principle <note>original: "animali principio," relating to the anima or spirit</note>, and from troublesome labors, or business, and other anxieties. The chest indeed will be burning, but the extremities cold; the causes will be in the head, the eyes will be hollowed, and the nostrils pinched <note>a classic sign of the "Hippocratic face," indicating near-death</note>, and the sick will seem to be without a pulse, and they will show a long-lasting disease, and they will be strong in their powers as far as their fullness is concerned. It is necessary, therefore, to draw blood immediately <note>original: "sanguinem detrahere." Bloodletting was the standard treatment for "fullness" or plethora.</note> (if indeed it can be done) while the Moon moves in that sign, and especially if she has begun to move toward greater degrees; if not, then until the third day; and to rub the extremities and stimulate all things that are below the thorax. 

If **Mars** and the **Sun** are configured to a Moon increasing in both degree <note>original: "numeris"</note> and light, there will be a cardiac affliction without a doubt until the fifth day; but if she ceases from her degrees <note>slows down</note> or even increases at the square, and is configured to **Saturn**, the patient will become well. If indeed **Jupiter** or **Venus** are configured to the Moon at the onset of illness, when the Moon herself comes to the square, he will be saved. But if she is also alone and decreasing in degree, he will become well. Moreover, administrations of wine and "white" medicines <note>original: "blanca," likely referring to a light-colored potion or powder</note> will be useful, and after the third or fifth day, <term>gestations</term> <note>original: "gestationes." A medical treatment involving passive movement, such as being carried in a chair or litter.</note>. 

If indeed in the proposed figure, when the Moon is in **Leo** at the onset of illness and is moving toward greater degrees or adding to her light, **Saturn** is configured to her along with **Venus** or one of the benefics, those things which were predicted will happen up until the square; nevertheless, there will be pains in the bladder and bloating of the stomach, yet the patient is saved.

# GIOVANNI PAOLO

### TO THE READER.

*Whatever things have been written by the divine Ficino <note>original: "diuino Ficino"; referring to Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the celebrated Florentine philosopher who revived Neoplatonism and sought to harmonize medicine with astrology.</note> in these booklets, they have emanated from three sources: Philosophy, Medicine, and Astrology. Although all these things seem to require interpretation, nevertheless, since they are now published for the sake of those who, having obtained the insignia of physicians <note>referring to those who have completed their formal medical degrees or doctoral honors.</note>, are preparing themselves for practice, it will be easy for them to understand both natural matters and medical ones without a commentator. It would remain, therefore, for us to explain the astrological matters, as we have done in previous sections, but we have deliberately omitted that too. For whoever has diligently applied effort to our previous explanations, together with those things written by both Hasfurtus <note>Johann Virdung von Hassfurt (c. 1463–1538), a German physician and judicial astrologer.</note> and by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational texts on alchemy and astrology were attributed.</note>, will certainly grasp the meaning of both Galen and Ficino. For this reason, we wished for Hasfurtus to hold the first place in this work, not out of status, but in order of arrangement.*

# PREFACE.

A priest has scarcely one mother and one father. I, the least of priests, have had two fathers: Ficino the physician and Cosimo de' Medici <note>Cosimo "the Elder" de' Medici (1389–1464), the de facto ruler of Florence and Ficino’s primary patron.</note>. From the former I was born; from the latter I was reborn. The first indeed commended me to Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the foundational Greek physician whose works dominated medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note>, who was both a physician and a Platonist; the second, however, consecrated me to the divine Plato. Thus, in a similar fashion, both of them destined Marsilio for medicine: Galen indeed for the medicine of bodies, but Plato for the medicine of souls. For a long time, therefore, I have practiced the health-giving medicine of souls under Plato. After completing the translation of all his books, I soon composed eighteen books on the immortality of souls and eternal happiness. In this way, I satisfied my duty to my father the physician to the best of my ability.

Thinking it then necessary to satisfy my father the physician further, I composed a book on *Caring for the Health of Scholars* <note>original: "De litteratorum valitudine curanda"; this is Book I of the "De vita."</note>. Afterward, men of letters desired not only to be well at certain times, but also to live long while remaining in good health. To them, therefore, I gave the book *On Long Life* <note>original: "De vita longa"; Book II of "De vita."</note>. However, since they mistrusted earthly medicines and remedies in such a great matter, I added a book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "De vita coelitus comparanda"; Book III, which explores astrological influences and natural magic.</note>, so that from the living body of the world itself, a more vigorous life might be propagated into our own body—as if into a member of the world—just like a shoot from a vine. 

I pray you, most indulgent Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), "The Magnificent," Cosimo’s grandson.</note>, forgive these books of medicine. If, while I wish to be a physician, I am somehow also a poet—though not often a good one—it is because Phoebus <note>The sun god Apollo, patron of both medicine and poetry.</note> is the discoverer of medicine and the master of poetry alike. He bestows his life upon us not so much through herbs as through the lyre and song. Indeed, even Venus, among the astrologers, produces both the musician and the physician in equal measure. 

But until now, while I have been carefully looking after the lives of scholars and similar citizens, I have neglected the safety of my own books by allowing them to remain separated from one another. For this reason, I now for the first time join them into a single body, so that life may immediately be present in limbs already joined into one form. This physical work—this "body" of mine—cannot receive life except from my own, and such a life depends solely upon my soul. This soul of mine has already lived for a long time with you, my patron Lorenzo, especially in that magnificent part of your house where my work on the immortality of souls <note>Referring to his "Theologia Platonica" (Platonic Theology).</note> is kept alongside Plato, dedicated long ago to your name. But this soul of mine, although it leads a life in a happy homeland near you, is meanwhile restless (as the theologians say) until it receives this physical work as its own body. 

Receive, therefore, most excellent Lorenzo, these books on the body after those on the soul. Breathe upon them with the same favor with which you recently breathed upon the others. In this way, this body shall live under your spirit through its own soul, and my soul, in turn, will rest within your household together with this body of its own.

A priest has barely one mother and one father. I, the least of priests, have had two fathers: Ficino the physician <note>Diotifeci d’Agnolo di Giusto, Marsilio’s biological father and personal physician to the Medici family.</note> and Cosimo de' Medici. I was born from the former, but reborn from the latter. The former commended me to Galen <note>A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD) whose works dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note>, who was both a physician and a follower of Plato; the latter, however, consecrated me to the divine Plato. And just as the former destined Marsilio for medicine, so too did the latter—Galen for the medicine of bodies, but Plato as the physician of souls. For a long time, therefore, I have practiced the health-giving medicine of souls under Plato. After translating all of his books <note>Ficino completed the first full Latin translation of Plato's works in 1484.</note>, I soon composed eighteen books on the immortality of souls and eternal happiness. In this way, I satisfied my physician father to the best of my ability.

Thinking thereafter that I should satisfy my other physician father, I composed a book on caring for the health of scholars <note>This refers to Book I of *De Vita*, "On Caring for the Health of Men of Letters."</note>. Beyond this, learned men desired not only to be well at certain times but also to live a long life while remaining healthy. To them, therefore, I next gave a book on long life <note>Book II of *De Vita*, "On Long Life."</note>. However, they lacked confidence in earthly medicines and remedies in such a great matter; so I added a book on obtaining life from the heavens <note>Book III of *De Vita*, "On Obtaining Life from the Heavens," which deals with astrological medicine and Neoplatonic magic.</note>, so that from the living body of the world itself, a more vigorous life might be propagated into our body—as if into a member of the world—just as life is spread from a vine. 

I pray, most indulgent Lorenzo, that you forgive these medical books of mine if, while I wish to be a physician, I am also somehow a poet even when I do not intend to be, though often not a good one. For Phoebus <note>Another name for Apollo, the god of both healing and poetry.</note> is the same discoverer of medicine and master of poetry; he grants his life to us not so much through herbs as through the lyre and song. Even Venus herself, according to the astrologers, gives birth equally to the musician and the physician. 

But until now, while I have been carefully looking after the lives of scholars and similar citizens, I have neglected the safety <note>original: "salutem," which implies both health and preservation.</note> of my own books, as I have allowed them to remain separated from one another. For this reason, I now first join them together into one body, so that life may immediately be present in its limbs, which are now joined into a single form. This physical work—which is, as it were, my body—cannot receive life unless it is my own; and such a life depends solely upon my soul. For a long time now, my soul has lived with you, my patron Lorenzo, under your great name; specifically in that part of your vast house where our work on the immortality of souls <note>Ficino's *Theologia Platonica*, dedicated to Lorenzo.</note> is kept together with Plato, having been dedicated to your name long ago. 

But that soul of mine, even if it leads a life with you in a sort of blessed homeland, is nevertheless restless in the meantime (as the theologians would have it) until it receives this physical work as its own body. Receive, therefore, most excellent Lorenzo, these books on the body after those on the soul. Breathe happily upon these with the same inspiration with which you breathed upon those before. In this way, this body will live through its own soul under your spirit, and our soul, in turn, will rest in your household along with this, its own body.

# PREFACE.

A priest usually has but one mother and scarcely one father. I, the humblest of priests, have had two fathers: Ficino the physician, and Cosimo de’ Medici. From the former I was born; by the latter I was reborn. Indeed, the one commended me to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity.</note>, both as a doctor and a follower of Plato; the other consecrated me to the divine Plato himself. And this one, just like the other, destined Marsilio for medicine—Galen indeed for the medicine of bodies, but Plato for the medicine of souls. For a long time now, I have practiced the health-giving medicine of souls under Plato’s guidance; for after translating all his books, I soon composed eighteen books on the immortality of souls and eternal happiness. Thus, having satisfied my father’s wishes as a physician as far as I was able, I then thought I should further satisfy the physician-father by composing a book on caring for the health of scholars <note>This refers to *De Vita Sana* (On Healthy Life), the first book of the trilogy.</note>.

Furthermore, after this, learned men desired not only to be well at times, but also to live long while in good health. To them, therefore, I gave a book on long life <note>*De Vita Longa*, the second book of the series.</note>. However, they lacked confidence in earthly medicines and remedies for so great a matter, so I joined to it a book on obtaining a life both vigorous and long from the heavens <note>*De Vita Coelitus Comparanda*, the third book, which deals with harnessing astrological influences for health.</note>, so that from the living body of the world itself, a more vigorous life might be propagated into our own body—as if into a limb of the world—just as life spreads from a vine. 

I pray you, most indulgent Lorenzo, forgive these medical books if, while I wish to be a physician, I am also (somehow) a poet—even if not often a good one. For Phoebus <note>A name for Apollo, the god of both healing and poetry.</note> is the same discoverer of medicine and master of poetry; he grants us his life not so much through herbs as through the lyre and song. Even Venus herself, according to the Astrologers, brings forth the musician and the Physician alike. 

But until now, while I have been looking after the lives of scholars and fellow citizens quite carefully, I have neglected the safety of my books so long as I allowed them to be separated from one another. For this reason, I am now for the first time joining them into one body, so that life may immediately be present in its limbs, which are now joined into a single form. This physical work <note>original: "opus physicum"</note> cannot receive life, as if it were my own body, unless it receives my own; and such a life depends solely on my soul. But my soul, my patron Lorenzo, has already lived for a long time with you—the "Great" by name—especially in that part of your most ample palace where, together with Plato, that work of ours on the immortality of souls is kept, dedicated to your name long ago. 

Yet that soul of mine, even if it leads a life in a kind of blessed homeland with you, is nevertheless—as the theologians say—restless in the meantime until it receives this physical work as its own body. Therefore, best Lorenzo, receive these books on the body after those on the soul; breathe favorably upon these with the same inspiration you gave those others long ago. In this way, this "body" will live through its own soul under your spirit, and our soul, in turn, will find rest in your household <note>original: "laribus," referring to the Lares, the Roman deities who protected the home.</note> now united with its own body.

## THE FIRST BOOK.

### On the healthy life: or, on the care of health for those who apply themselves to the study of letters.

#### On the nine guides for scholars. Chapter I.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring an illustration of a rider on a horse moving through a wooded landscape, enclosed within an ornate square frame.</image-desc>

WHOSOEVER enters upon the rough, arduous, and long journey which, through tireless labor, finally leads to the lofty temple of the nine Muses <note>The Muses were the Greek goddesses of inspiration for the arts and sciences; reaching their "temple" represents achieving true wisdom and mastery.</note>, they seem to require nine guides in all for this journey. Of these, the first three lead us in the heavens, the next three in the mind, and the final three upon the earth. In the beginning, in the heavens, **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius". In Ficino’s astrological medicine, Mercury governs the intellect, speech, and the initial stage of any inquiry.</note> encourages us to undertake the path of the Muses through investigation—since indeed the duty of all inquiry is attributed to Mercury. Next, **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the sun god, representing the "light" of understanding that makes discovery possible.</note> himself so illuminates both the searching minds and the things being sought with his abundant splendor that what was being searched for is clearly found by us. Then comes most graceful **Venus**, the mother of the Graces; with her nourishing and joyful rays, she so seasons and adorns the whole matter that whatever was sought by the instigation of Mercury, and already found by the showing of Phoebus, might always delight and be of use, infused with a certain miraculous and health-giving beauty <note>original: "venustate", a wordplay on the name Venus, suggesting both aesthetic charm and the physical "grace" of a healthy body.</note> of Venus. There follow the three guides of this journey in the mind: namely, a **burning and stable will**, **sharpness of intellect**, and a **tenacious memory**. The three last ones are on the earth,

# BOOK I.

...the most prudent head of the household, the most proven teacher, and the most skilled physician. Without these nine guides, no one has been or ever will be able to reach the temple of the nine Muses <note>The Muses represent the peak of human knowledge and artistic inspiration. Ficino is arguing that genius is not purely internal; it requires a support system of celestial influence, mental discipline, and physical care.</note>. Almighty God and nature have granted us the first guides <note>The celestial and mental guides mentioned on the previous page.</note> from our very beginning; however, our own diligence must provide the final three. Many wise men of the past have treated the precepts and duties pertaining to the head of the household and the teacher regarding the study of letters—especially our **Plato**, both in many other places and most diligently in his books on *The Republic* and *The Laws*. After him, **Aristotle** wrote on this in his *Politics*; **Plutarch** also, and **Quintilian** wrote excellently on the subject. 

Yet, until now, students of letters have lacked only a physician—one who might stretch out a hand to those on their journey, and assist with healthful counsel and medicines those whom neither the heavens, nor their own minds, nor their fathers or teachers have abandoned. Therefore, pitying the most laborious lot of those who live with difficulty while **Minerva** <note>Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, here represents the exhausting nature of deep intellectual work, which Ficino believed "thinned the nerves" and drained the body's vitality.</note> weakens their nerves, I am the first to stand by the weak and the infirm as their physician. I only wish my skill were as complete as my will is favorable toward them. 

Arise now, young men, with God as your guide, arise eagerly! Arise, young and old alike, whom the burning study of Minerva too greatly weakens. Come willingly to the physician who, with God showing the way and favoring the work, will bestow upon you the counsels and healthful remedies for the perfection of your pursuit.

---

### *How diligent care must be had for the brain, heart, stomach, and spirit. Chapter II.*

In the beginning, just as runners are accustomed to care for their legs, athletes for their arms, and musicians for their voices, so at the very least students of letters ought to care for their brain, heart, liver, and stomach. Indeed, they should care for them as much more as these organs are more excellent than those limbs; for they use these organs more frequently and for more important matters than athletes or musicians use their own. 

Furthermore, any skillful artisan cares for his instruments most diligently: the painter his brushes; the blacksmith his hammers and anvils; the soldier his horses and armor; the hunter his dogs and birds; the lutanist his lute; and everyone else their own in similar fashion. Yet the priests of the Muses alone—the seekers of the highest good and truth—are so negligent (oh, the shame of it!) and so unfortunate, that they seem to utterly neglect that instrument by which they are able, in a certain way, to measure and grasp the entire universe. 

An instrument of this kind is the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritus". In Ficino’s medical-philosophical system, "spirit" is not the soul, but a very fine, physical vapor of blood that acts as the bridge between the body and the soul, allowing the mind to control the physical limbs and the senses to report back to the mind.</note> itself, which is defined among physicians as a certain vapor of blood: pure, subtle, and lucid. It is procreated from the subtler blood by the heat of the heart itself...

This physiological foundation leads into his famous exploration of why scholars are uniquely susceptible to illness, specifically the condition of melancholy.</meta>

# ON THE HEALTHY LIFE

...[the spirit] flies to the brain, and there the mind uses it constantly to exercise the senses, both internal and external. Therefore, the blood serves the spirit, the spirit serves the senses, and finally the senses serve reason. Moreover, blood is produced by the natural power that flourishes in the liver and stomach. The thinnest part of the blood flows into the fountain of the heart, where the vital power flourishes; from there, the created spirits ascend to the brain and (if I may say so) the citadels of Pallas <note>Pallas refers to Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom; Ficino uses this poetic imagery to describe the brain as the high fortress of the intellect.</note>, in which the animal <note>In Renaissance medicine, "animal" (from the Latin *anima*, meaning soul) refers to functions of the soul, specifically movement and sensation.</note> power—that is, the power of sensing and moving—dominates. Thus, contemplation is almost exactly as the service of the senses allows it to be; and the senses are as the spirit is. The spirit, in turn, is as the blood is, and as those three powers we mentioned—namely, the natural, the vital, and the animal—by which, through which, and in which the spirits themselves are conceived, born, and nourished.

### *Scholars are prone to phlegm and black bile. Chapter III.*

Truly, those who desire learning must not only care most diligently for those organs, powers, and spirits, but they are also commanded to avoid <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily humors, traditionally considered cold and moist.</note> and <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; the humor associated with melancholy.</note> at all times, just as sailors most cautiously avoid Scylla and Charybdis <note>Two legendary sea monsters from Greek mythology that forced sailors to navigate a narrow, dangerous strait.</note>. For as much as they are idle in the rest of their body, they are that much more occupied in the brain and mind. Because of this, they are forced to produce phlegm (which the Greeks call <note>original: "phlegmate"</note> *phlegm*) and black bile (which they call <note>original: "melancholiam"</note> *melancholy*). The former often dulls and suffocates the intellect; the latter, however, if it should abound too much or burn, vexes the soul with constant anxiety and frequent delusions, and disturbs the judgment. So it can be said, not without merit, that scholars would be exceptionally healthy if not for troublesome phlegm, and the happiest and wisest of all people, if not for the vice of black bile, which forces them to often mourn or sometimes lose their wits.

### *How many causes there are for which scholars are, or become, melancholic. Chapter IV.*

Now, for scholars to be melancholic, there are three types of causes: the first is celestial, the second is natural, and the third is human. The celestial cause exists because **Mercury**, who invites us to investigate doctrines, and **Saturn**, who makes us persevere in investigating those doctrines and preserve them once found, are said by astronomers to be in some way cold and dry—or if Mercury is perhaps not cold, he is often very dry due to his proximity to the Sun. This is exactly the nature physicians call "melancholic," and Mercury and Saturn themselves impart this same nature to their followers, the students of letters, from the beginning, and they maintain and increase it daily. The natural cause, however, seems to be that in order to pursue sciences—especially difficult ones—it is necessary for the soul to withdraw from external things to internal ones, as if from a circumference to the center; and while it speculates in this very center of man (if I may call it that), it remains most stably...

...to remain. Truly, to gather oneself from the circumference toward the center and to be fixed in the center is the most specific property of the earth itself. <term>Black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; also known as melancholy, this humor was thought to be cold, dry, and earthy.</note> is very similar to this property. Therefore, black bile gathers the soul into itself, unites it in one place, and fixes it there. It constantly provokes the soul to contemplate and, being like the center of the world, it forces the soul to investigate the center of individual things. It raises the soul to comprehend the highest matters, since it corresponds most closely with **Saturn**, the highest of the planets. 

In turn, contemplation itself, through a certain constant gathering and a kind of compression, draws together a nature very similar to black bile. The human cause—that is, the cause arising from within us—is that the frequent agitation of the mind violently dries out the brain. Therefore, once the moisture is largely consumed (which serves as the fuel for natural heat), the heat itself is also usually extinguished. From this, the nature of the brain becomes dry and cold, which is indeed called an "earthy" and "melancholic" quality. 

Furthermore, because of the very frequent movement of inquiry, the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus"; in this context, the subtle, vaporous substance that acts as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> being produced are continually dissolved. It is then necessary for these dissolved spirits to be restored from the thinner part of the blood. Consequently, as the thinner and clearer parts of the blood are often consumed, the remaining blood is necessarily rendered thick, dry, and black. 

Added to this is the fact that nature, when intent upon the brain and heart during contemplation, abandons the stomach and liver. Therefore, when food (especially the more abundant or harder kind) is poorly digested, the blood produced from it becomes cold, thick, and black. Finally, through excessive idleness of the limbs, neither are superfluities excreted, nor do the thick, dark vapors evaporate. 

All these things tend to produce a melancholic spirit and a sorrowful, fearful mind; for indeed, internal darkness occupies and terrifies the soul much more than external darkness. Of all men of letters, those most oppressed by black bile are those devoted to the diligent study of philosophy, who call away the mind from the body and bodily things and join it to incorporeal things. This is both because it is a very difficult task requiring greater mental focus, and because insofar as they join the mind to incorporeal truth, they are compelled to disconnect it from the body. Hence, their body is sometimes rendered as if half-dead and melancholic. 

Our **Plato** indicates this in the *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato’s most influential dialogues, dealing with the creation of the universe and the nature of the physical world and the soul.</note>, saying that a soul contemplating divine things very often and very intently grows so much upon such nourishment and becomes so powerful that it surpasses its body beyond what the body's nature can endure. By its more violent agitations, the soul sometimes either escapes from the body in a way or seems occasionally to dissolve it.

### Why the melancholic are gifted, and what kinds of melancholics are like this, and which are the opposite: Chapter V.

So far, it should suffice to have shown by first celestial, second natural, and third human reasons why the **priests of the Muses** <note>Ficino uses this poetic term to refer to scholars, philosophers, and poets who dedicate their lives to learning.</note> are either melancholic from the beginning or become so through study. Indeed, **Aristotle** confirms this in his book of *Problems*. For he says that all men who have been outstanding in any discipline were melancholic. In this matter, he confirmed that Platonic saying written in the book *On Knowledge*: namely, that the most gifted people are usually highly excitable and "frenzied." **Democritus** also says that no men can ever be great in talent except those who are stirred by a certain "frenzy." Our **Plato** seems to approve of this in the *Phaedrus*, saying that the doors of poetry are knocked upon in vain without frenzy. And if he perhaps wishes "divine frenzy" <note>original: "divinum furorem"; the Platonic idea that inspiration is a form of "sane" madness granted by the gods.</note> to be understood here, nevertheless, among the **natural philosophers** <note>original: "Physicos"; those who study the laws of nature and the body.</note>, such frenzy is never incited in any others except the melancholic.

Next, we must assign the reasons why Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle assert that some melancholic people sometimes so far excel everyone else in talent that they seem not human, but rather divine. Democritus, Plato, and Aristotle asserted this without doubt, but they do not seem to have sufficiently explained the reason for such a great matter. However, with God showing the way, we must dare to investigate the causes.

**Melancholy**, that is, **black bile**, is of two kinds. One is called "natural" by physicians, while the other occurs through "combustion" <note>original: "adustione"; a medical concept where a humor is "overcooked" or burnt by excessive heat, changing its properties from helpful to harmful.</note>. That **natural** kind is nothing other than a certain denser and drier part of the blood. The **burnt** kind, however, is distributed into four species: it is conceived by the combustion of either natural melancholy, or of the purer blood, or of yellow bile, or of "false phlegm."

Whichever type is born from combustion harms judgment and wisdom. Truly, while that humor is being ignited and burns, it usually makes people excited and "frenzied"—which the Greeks call **Mania**, and we call **frenzy** <note>original: "furorem".</note>. But when it is finally extinguished, the subtler and clearer parts having been dissolved and only a foul soot remaining, it renders them dull and stupid. This state they properly call "melancholy," as well as "madness" and "folly."

Therefore, only that **black bile** which we called **natural** contributes to our judgment and wisdom—and yet, not always. Certainly, if it is alone, and if it darkens the **spirits** <note>The "spirits" are the subtle vapors that carry thought and sensation through the body.</note> with an excessively dark and dense mass, it terrifies the soul, and blunts the talent. But if it is mixed with simple phlegm, since "cold blood stands around the heart," <note>Ficino is quoting a famous line from the Roman poet Virgil (*Georgics* 2.484), which was used to explain why some people are intellectually slow.</note> it brings on sluggishness and torpor through a certain thick coldness. And as is the nature of every very dense matter, whenever such melancholy grows cold, it is pushed to the extreme of coldness. In this state, nothing is hoped for, all things are feared, and one is weary of "beholding the arches of the sky" <note>A poetic way of describing deep depression or suicidal ideation.</note>.

BOOK I.

...when **black bile** <term>original: "bilis atra"; one of the four bodily humors, associated with the earth element and a cold, dry temperament.</term>, whether by itself or mixed with other fluids, begins to rot, it gives rise to **quartan fever** <note>A malarial-like fever where the paroxysm occurs every fourth day; historically attributed to an excess of black bile.</note>, tumors of the spleen, and many other ailments of that kind. Where it is less excessive—whether it exists alone or is joined with **phlegm** <term>original: "pituitæ"; the cold, moist humor.</term>—it makes the **spirits** <note>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine, these are the thin, vaporous substances that connect the physical body to the immaterial soul.</note> thicker and colder. This continually affects the soul with weariness, blunts the edge of the mind, and **the blood does not leap around the heart in the Arcadian fashion.** <note>A reference to the Roman satirist Persius (Satire 3.9); "Arcadian" implies stupidity or dullness, suggesting the heart lacks the lively heat of intelligence.</note> 

However, it is necessary that the black bile be neither so scarce that the blood, yellow bile, and spirits lack a "bridle" (which leads to an unstable nature and a slipping memory), nor so abundant that we seem to doze off, weighed down by too much weight, and require "spurs" to wake us. Consequently, it is absolutely necessary that this bile be as refined as its nature allows. For if it is made thin according to its nature, it can perhaps even be abundant without causing harm—even so much that it appears to equal the yellow bile in weight. Let the black bile be abundant, then, but let it be extremely refined. 

It should not lack the moisture of refined phlegm surrounding it, lest it dry out completely and turn quite hard; yet it should not be mixed entirely with phlegm (especially if that phlegm is cold or abundant), lest it grow chilled. Instead, it should be mixed with yellow bile and blood in such a way that one single body is made from the three, composed with a **double proportion of blood** to the other two. In this state, there should be eight parts of blood, two of yellow bile, and two of black bile. Let the black bile be somewhat ignited by those other two, and being ignited, let it shine, but not be scorched. Otherwise, just as harder materials do when they boil too much, it might burn and agitate too vehemently; and when it cools down, it would likewise become extremely cold. 

For black bile is like iron: when it is stretched toward the cold, it is cold in the extreme; when, on the contrary, it moves toward the hot, it is hot in the extreme. Nor should it seem strange that black bile can be easily ignited and, once lit, burn more fiercely; for we see that **lime** <note>original: "calcem"; quicklime or calcium oxide, which reacts violently and generates heat when touched by water.</note>, which is similar to it, boils immediately when sprinkled with water and burns everything. Melancholy has such power toward either extreme because of its stable and fixed nature—an extremity that does not happen to the other humors. 

When it is extremely hot, it produces the greatest boldness—indeed, even ferocity; but when it is extremely cold, it produces fear and extreme sluggishness. Yet when it is affected by the middle degrees between cold and heat, it produces various dispositions, not unlike how especially strong **undiluted wine** <note>original: "merum"; pure, unmixed wine.</note> tends to bring about various moods in those drinking to the point of drunkenness, or even those drinking a little too freely. 

Therefore, it is necessary that the black bile be appropriately tempered. When it is thus moderated (as we have said) and mixed with yellow bile and blood, it is easily ignited by them because it is dry by nature and as refined as its condition allows. Because it is solid and very tenacious, once ignited, it burns for a very long time; because it is most powerful in the unity of its tenacious dryness, it heats up more vehemently. Just as wood, if both it and straw are set on fire, glows and burns hotter and longer than the straw. And indeed, from long-lasting and vehement heat, brilliance is produced...

...and a vehement and long-lasting movement proceeds. This points toward that saying of **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine of change and fire as the central element.</note>: "A dry light is the wisest soul." <note>original: "lux sicca anima sapientissima." This reflects the ancient belief that moisture in the brain (phlegm) caused dullness, while the "dryness" associated with bile sharpened the intellect.</note>

## In what way black bile benefits the intellect. Chapter VI.

Someone might ask what kind of body this humor has, being composed of those three humors in the proportion we described. In color, it is nearly like gold, as we see it, but leans slightly toward purple; and when it is ignited—whether by natural heat or by the movement of the body or mind—it glows and shines much like fiery, reddened gold mixed with purple. Like a **rainbow** <term>original: "iris"</term>, it draws out various colors from the burning heart. Someone may ask again: in what way does such a humor benefit the intellect? Indeed, the **spirits** <term>original: "spiritus"; in Renaissance medicine, these are thin, vaporous substances that bridge the gap between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</term> created from this humor are, first, refined, much like that water called the **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitae"; referring to distilled alcohol or spirits, which were thought to have medicinal properties.</note> or "water of the vine," or "burning water," as is usually expressed from thick, unmixed wine through distillation by fire. For the spirits, compressed within the narrow passages of such black bile, are thinned out by a heat made intense through its concentration; and once forced through these narrow channels, they burst forth even more refined. Secondly, they are similarly hotter; thirdly, they are brighter; fourthly, they are agile in motion and most powerful in action; and finally, because they emanate continuously from a solid and stable humor, they serve the mind's action for a very long time.

Relying on such service, our mind investigates forcefully, perseveres longer in its search, finds whatever it seeks, perceives clearly, judges purely, and retains its judgments for a long time. Additionally, as we indicated above, the mind uses this instrument or stimulus—which in a way corresponds to the center of the world and (so to speak) draws the mind into its own center—and always seeks the center of all things and penetrates their innermost secrets. Furthermore, it corresponds with **Mercury** and **Saturn** <note>In astrological medicine, Mercury governs the quickness of the mind, while Saturn governs deep, heavy, and profound contemplation.</note>. Saturn, the highest of all planets, carries the investigator to the highest things. Hence, singular philosophers emerge, especially when the soul is withdrawn from external movements and its own body, becoming near to the gods and an instrument for divine things. Thus filled with divine influences and oracles from on high, the soul always thinks up new and unusual things and predicts the future. This is not only affirmed by **Democritus** and **Plato**, but is also confessed by **Aristotle** in his book of *Problems*, and by **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians and philosophers of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> in his *Book of Divine Things* and his *Book on the Soul*. 

Why so much about this black bile humor? So we remember that just as this "bright" or "shining" bile must be sought and nourished as the best, the opposite (as we said) is to be avoided as the worst. For it is such a dreadful thing that **Serapio** <note>Likely Serapion the Elder, a 9th-century physician whose works were standard texts in medieval European medical schools.</note> said its onset is stirred by an evil demon, and the wise **Avicenna** did not deny it.

BOOK I.

### Five are the principal enemies of scholars: phlegm, black bile, sexual intercourse, satiety, and morning sleep. Chapter VII.

To return to the point from which we have already strayed somewhat, the road that leads to truth and wisdom is very long, and it is full of heavy labors on both land and sea. Whoever undertakes this journey, as a poet might say, is often endangered on land and at sea. For if they sail the sea, they are constantly tossed among the waves—that is, between two humors: **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily fluids, associated with coldness and sluggishness.</note> and that harmful **melancholy** <note>original: "atra bilis" or "black bile." In its burnt or "adust" state, it was thought to cause depression or madness.</note>—as if caught between **Scylla and Charybdis** <note>In Greek mythology, two immortal sea monsters situated on opposite sides of a narrow strait, representing a choice between two equally dangerous situations.</note>. If they travel by land (so to speak), three monsters immediately present themselves: first, the earthly **Venus** <note>Representing sexual desire and lust.</note> meets them; second, **Bacchus** <note>God of wine.</note> and **Ceres** <note>Goddess of grain and food, representing gluttony.</note>; and third, the nocturnal **Hecate** <note>Goddess of the night and crossroads, here representing late-night vigils and the resulting morning sleep.</note> frequently opposes them. Therefore, **Apollo** must be called from the heavens, **Neptune** from the sea, and **Hercules** from the earth, so that Apollo might pierce these monsters—enemies of **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom.</note>—with his arrows, Neptune might subdue them with his trident, and Hercules might crush and tear them with his club.

The first monster is indeed **sexual intercourse** <term>original: "coitus"</term>, especially if it exceeds one’s strength even slightly. For it suddenly exhausts the **spirits** <term>original: "spiritus"; the subtle vapors that Renaissance doctors believed carried life and thought through the body.</term>, particularly the most refined ones, and it weakens the brain, shatters the stomach, and debilitates the heart; nothing can be more adverse to genius than this evil. Why did **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> judge intercourse to be similar to the **falling sickness** <note>original: "comitiali morbo"; epilepsy. Ancient doctors believed the physical exhaustion of sex mirrored the seizures of epilepsy.</note>? It is because it shocks the mind, which is sacred, and is so harmful that **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> said in his *Book on Animals* that if more semen flows out through intercourse than nature can tolerate, it is more harmful than if forty times as much blood had flowed out. It is not without reason that the ancients insisted the **Muses** and **Minerva** <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note> were virgins.

That Platonic saying looks to this: when Venus threatened the Muses that if they did not honor her sacred rites, she would arm her son against them, the Muses replied: "O Venus, threaten **Mars** <note>The god of war.</note> with such things; your Cupid does not fly among us." Finally, nature has separated no sense further from the intelligence than the sense of touch.

The second monster is the **satiety** <note>The state of being overfilled or stuffed.</note> of food and wine. Indeed, if wine is either too much, too hot, or too potent, it will fill the head with humors and the worst kind of fumes—not to mention that drunkenness makes men insane. Truly, excessive food first calls all the power of nature to the stomach for the act of digestion itself; as a result, the body is unable to apply itself to the head and to **contemplation** <term>original: "speculationi"</term> at the same time. Furthermore, if the food is poorly digested, it blunts the sharp edge of the mind with many thick vapors and humors. Even if it is digested well enough, as **Galen** <note>An influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> says, a soul suffocated by fat and blood cannot foresee anything divine.

The third monster, finally, is staying awake for much of the night, especially frequently after dinner, which forces you to sleep even after the sun has risen. Because very many scholars err and are deceived in this, I shall explain more extensively how much it harms genius, and I will provide the reasons.

I will put forward seven principal reasons [for this]. I have derived the first from heaven itself, the second from the elements, the third from the **humors** <term>humors: the four vital bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to determine health and temperament.</term>, the fourth from the order of things, the fifth from the nature of the stomach, the sixth from the **spirits** <term>spirits: the subtle, vaporous substances—natural, vital, and animal—that were thought to carry out the functions of the soul within the body.</term>, and the seventh from the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty that creates and processes mental images.</note>. 

In the first place, three planets—as we were saying in the previous sections—most favor contemplation and eloquence: the **Sun**, **Venus**, and **Mercurius** <note>Mercury, the planet associated with communication and intellect.</note>. Indeed, these planets run with almost equal steps; they flee from us as night approaches, but during the day, at the rising of the Sun, they are suddenly thrust into the twelfth region of the sky <note>original: "plagam coeli duodecimam"; in astrology, the twelfth house is traditionally associated with confinement or "prison."</note>, which is assigned by astronomers to prison and shadows. Therefore, it is not those who rise for contemplation and writing either at night (when the planets flee us) or during the day after the sun has risen (when the planets enter the house of prison and shadows), but those who rise just as the planets are seeking their ascent or are already rising, who observe most keenly and write and compose their findings most eloquently. 

The second reason, namely from the elements, is as follows: when the sun rises, the air is moved, thinned, and made clear; but when it sets, the opposite occurs. The blood and the **spirits** necessarily follow the movement and quality of the surrounding air, being similar to it in nature. 

The third reason, which is derived from the **humors**, is of this sort: at dawn, the blood is moved and reigns; through this motion, it is thinned, warmed, and made clear. The **spirits** are accustomed to following and imitating the blood. But as night approaches, that thicker and colder **melancholy** <note>original: "melancholia"; the humor of black bile.</note> and **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita"; the cold, moist humor.</note> dominate, which undoubtedly render the spirits most unfit for contemplation. 

The fourth reason, handed down from the order of things, will be this: the day is granted to wakefulness, and the night to sleep. For when the Sun either approaches our hemisphere or moves above it, it opens the passages of the body with its rays and dilates the humors and spirits from the center to the circumference; this indeed excites and leads toward wakefulness and action. Conversely, when the Sun recedes, everything is constricted, which by a certain natural order invites sleep, especially after the third or fourth part of the night. Therefore, whoever slumbers in the morning when the Sun and the world are waking up, but stays awake late into the night when nature commands us to sleep and rest from labors, undoubtedly fights against both the order of the universe and himself, while he is disturbed and distracted by contrary movements at the same time. Truly, while he is moved by the universe toward the outermost parts [of his body], he moves himself toward the innermost parts; and conversely, while he is drawn by the universe toward the innermost parts, he meanwhile withdraws himself toward the outermost. Therefore, by this perverse order and these contrary movements, the whole body, the spirits, and the intellect are utterly weakened. 

In the fifth place, we argue from the nature of the stomach in this manner: by the long-lasting action of the daytime air, the stomach is greatly dilated as the pores are opened, and by the escaping spirits, it is finally greatly weakened; therefore, as night comes on, it requires a new supply of spirits by which it may be fostered. For which reason, those who—

# BOOK I.

And when at that time one begins long and difficult contemplations, he strives to pull the **spirits** <term>spirits: subtle, vaporous substances believed to circulate through the body to perform vital functions and carry thoughts; they were the "fuel" for both digestion and thinking.</term> back to the head. These spirits, being thus distracted, serve neither the stomach nor the head sufficiently. It is especially harmful if, burning the midnight oil <note>original: "lucubrantes"; referring to the practice of studying by lamplight late into the night.</note> after dinner, we apply ourselves too intently to such studies; for at that time the stomach requires many spirits and much heat to digest the food. 

These two—heat and spirit—are diverted to the head by such nocturnal study, which results in a shortage for both the brain and the stomach. Additionally, because of this movement, the head is filled with the thicker vapors of the food, and the food in the stomach, deprived of heat and spirit, becomes raw and putrid, which in turn fills and harms the head. Finally, in the morning hours, when one should rise so that every limb can be purged of the wastes retained during sleep, the worst thing happens: the person who had completely interrupted their digestion by studying at night is forced to further delay the expulsion of wastes by sleeping late in the morning. All physicians judge this to be extremely harmful to both the intellect and the body. 

Rightly, therefore, those who use the night for the day and the day for the night, contrary to nature, are like **owls**. Even against their will, they imitate owls in this: just as the eyes of those birds are blinded by the light of the Sun, so too the sharp edge of the nocturnal scholar's mind is blinded under the splendor of truth.

In the sixth place, the same is proven by the **spirits**: by the fatigue of the day, all the most subtle spirits are eventually dissolved. Therefore, at night, only a few thick spirits remain, which are most unsuitable for the study of letters; the intellect can no more fly supported by these crippled wings than can bats or horned owls. On the contrary, after sleep in the morning, the spirits are refreshed and the limbs so strengthened that they require very little support from the spirits. Thus, many subtle spirits are available to serve the brain, and they can obey more readily because they are barely occupied with warming and governing the limbs.

Finally, the seventh reason is derived from the nature of the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"; the faculty of the soul that receives and stores sensory images.</note>. The imagination—whether it should be called fancy, thought, or by any other name—is distracted and disturbed by many long and conflicting images, thoughts, and cares while we are awake. This distraction and disturbance is entirely contrary to the coming contemplation, which requires a tranquil and serene mind. Only by the rest of the night is that agitation finally settled and calmed. Therefore, we approach our studies with a mind always troubled as night approaches, but for the most part, with a tranquil mind as the night recedes. Whoever tries to judge things with an over-agitated mind thinks that everything is spinning (as **Plato** says), just as those suffering from vertigo do, when in fact they are the ones spinning. 

For this reason, **Aristotle** cleverly commands in his *Economics* to rise before light, asserting that it is profitable both for the health of the body and for the study of philosophy...

But this must be understood in such a way that by a quick and moderate dinner, we most diligently avoid morning indigestion <note>original: "matutinam cruditatem"; literally "morning rawness," a medical term for the presence of undigested food in the stomach upon waking</note>. Finally, that sacred prophet David, the trumpet of the Almighty God, never says that he must sing to his God at evening, but always in the morning and at daybreak, rising with his lyre and psalms. We must certainly rise in mind at that hour, and soon after in body, provided that it can be done conveniently.

### Which hour is more suitable for beginning studies, and what manner of continuing them. Chapter VIII.

From those things which have been discussed above, it is now reasonably well-established that we should begin our studies at an opportune time, either exactly at sunrise, or at least one hour—or two at the most—before the sun rises. But before you rise from bed, rub your whole body gently with your palms for a short while, and then your head with your nails, though a little more lightly; let **Hippocrates** <note>Ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> advise you in this matter. For he says that by **friction** <term>friction: a form of medical massage or rubbing of the skin intended to move the "humors" and stimulate the body's heat</term>, if it be vigorous, the body is hardened; if light, it is softened; if much, it is diminished; and if moderate, it is filled. 

When you have risen from bed, do not apply yourself immediately to reading and meditation, but allow at least half an hour for any necessary purging <note>Refers to the morning evacuation of the bowels and bladder, as well as clearing the throat and nose.</note>. Soon after, gird yourself diligently for meditation, which you shall prolong according to your strength for about one hour. Then you shall relax the intensity of the mind for a little while, and in the meantime, carefully and moderately comb your head from the forehead toward the neck with an **ivory comb**, drawing the comb through forty times. Then rub the neck with a rather rough cloth. Finally, returning to meditation, dedicate two additional hours, or at least one hour, to study. 

Sometimes, however, studies can be extended—provided some intermittent breaks are made—until the hour of noon. Indeed, sometimes, though rarely (unless we are forced to take food in the meantime), they may continue for about two hours after noon. For the Sun is powerful near its rising, and powerful in the middle of the sky; also in that region of the heaven which closely follows the middle, which astronomers call the **ninth house** <term>ninth house: in astrology, the "House of Journeys and Religion," also known as the "House of Wisdom," where the Sun was thought to "rejoice."</term> and the **house of wisdom**, the Sun greatly rejoices. 

Since all poets hold that **Phoebus** <note>Another name for Apollo, the Greco-Roman god of the sun, music, and prophecy.</note> is the leader of the Muses and of the sciences, it is right that if something deep is to be thought out, it should be contemplated especially during these hours; if the Muses are to be sought, let them be sought in those same hours with Phoebus as the guide. For the remaining hours seem better suited to reading the works of the ancients and others, rather than for thinking out new and original things. We must always remember that in any given hour, the intensity of the mind should be relaxed at least once for a short time. For since the **spirits** are dispersed because of such intensity, you will surely become sluggish if you never cease to stretch them. While you labor with the mind, let the body rest in the meantime; exhaustion of the body is bad, that of the mind is worse, and that of both together is the worst of all, distracting a person with opposing movements and destroying life. Finally, let meditation proceed no further than there is pleasure in it—or rather, stop just short of that point.

BOOK I.

### How Phlegm Is To Be Avoided. Chapter IX.

It seems worthwhile to briefly repeat those things we have said are harmful to scholars, and to apply remedies to each. To prevent **phlegm** <term>phlegm: one of the four humors (pituita); associated with cold and moisture, an excess was thought to make a person dull or sluggish</term> from increasing too much, one should use exercise twice daily on a nearly empty stomach, yet never so laborious that the "sharp spirits" <note>refined vital energies believed to power the brain</note> are dissipated; rather, excrements must be most diligently purged from all the passages of the body. Grime should be thoroughly wiped away from the skin of the entire body, especially the head, through both washing and friction. One must avoid excessively cold foods, and—unless **black bile** <term>black bile: the humor associated with melancholy (atra bilis); while it aided deep thought, an excess was considered dangerous</term> stands in the way—avoid moist foods too, and generally everything that is fatty, virulent, viscous, oily, and gluey, or which tends to rot easily. If the stomach is cold, either by nature or by age, the drinking of water should be either given up entirely or certainly reduced. Food should be moderate, but drink even more moderate; the dwelling should be high up and far removed from heavy, cloudy air. Humidity is to be expelled through the use of both fire and warm scents, and cold must be kept away from the head, but especially from the neck and the feet. For cold greatly hinders the intellect, whereas the moderate use of spices in colder dishes is beneficial—especially nutmeg, cinnamon, and saffron, as well as preserved ginger taken in the morning on an empty stomach, which is most helpful for the senses and especially for the memory.

### By What Means Black Bile Is To Be Avoided. Chapter X.

That worst substance of all, which we expressed loathing for in the previous sections—**black bile**—is increased by thick and turbid wine, especially the black variety. It is also increased by foods that are hard, dry, salty, bitter, sharp, old, burnt, roasted, or fried; the meat of beef and hare; old cheese, salted fish, and legumes—especially beans and lentils; eggplants <note>original: "melongia"</note>, arugula, cabbage, mustard, radishes, garlic, onions, leeks, blackberries, dates <note>original: "cariotæ"</note>, and whatever things heat or cool while simultaneously drying the body; and everything that is black. Anger, fear, pity, grief, idleness, solitude, and whatever offends the sight, smell, and hearing also increase it—but most of all, darkness. Furthermore, it is increased by excessive drying of the body, whether born of long vigils <note>staying awake late for study or prayer</note>, much agitation or worry of the mind, frequent sexual intercourse, the use of many hot and dry things, or by some immoderate evacuation and purging, laborious exercise, or by hunger, thirst, heat, a drier wind, or cold. Since black bile is always very dry and also cold (though not equally so), one must certainly resist it with things that are moderately warm, but especially with those that are very moist. Use boiled foods regularly, which are easily digested and produce a refined and very clear blood. But meanwhile, so that the stomach and phlegm are taken into account just as much as the black bile, meals should be seasoned with cinnamon, saffron, and sandalwood. The seeds of melon and cucumber, and washed pine nuts, are helpful; all dairy products are suitable—milk, fresh cheese, and sweet almonds—as are the meats of birds, chickens, and four-footed...

# ON THE HEALTHY LIFE

...or the meat of suckling animals, especially soft-boiled eggs, and the brains of animals; sweet apples, pears, peaches, melons, Damascene plums, and the like. I recommend well-cooked squash and moist, non-viscous herbs; however, I have very little praise for cherries, figs, and grapes, and I truly detest nausea and over-satiety.

But against this plague <note>the "plague" refers here to an excess of black bile or melancholy</note> nothing is more powerful than wine that is light, clear, sweet, and fragrant, which is most suitable for generating **spirits** <term>spirits: "spiritus," the subtle vapors in the body believed to connect the soul to the physical organs and carry out mental functions</term> that are clearer than all others. For (as Plato and Aristotle agree) this **humor** <term>humor: one of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined health and temperament</term> is softened, sweetened, and cleared by this wine in no other way than lupin beans are softened by being soaked in water, or iron is cleared by being heated in flames. Truly, as much as its use benefits the spirits and the intellect, its abuse causes just as much harm.

Furthermore, it is agreed that it is beneficial to dip gold or silver heated to a high degree, or their leaves, into drinking cups or into the broth itself, and to eat and drink from golden or silver vessels. Likewise, it is very useful if liquorice juice is often swallowed on an empty stomach, as well as the juice of sweet pomegranates and sweet oranges. Sweet scents are of no small benefit, especially temperate ones; but if cold reigns, they should lean toward the warm, and if heat dominates, they should tend toward the cold. 

They should be tempered, therefore, from roses, violets, myrtle, camphor, sandalwood, and rosewater, which are cold. Conversely, they may be made from cinnamon, citron, orange, cloves, mint, lemon balm, saffron, aloeswood, ambergris, and musk, which are warm. Spring flowers are especially beneficial, as are the leaves of citron or orange, and fragrant apples—but most of all, wine. However, we do not approve of scents that are very warm and dry if they are used alone and continuously. 

A **jacinth** <note>original: "hyacintus"; this likely refers to the gemstone jacinth, believed to have medicinal properties, or possibly the flower</note> should be held in the mouth, for it greatly cheers the soul; likewise **holy herb** <note>original: "hierobotanum," identified here as wild clary sage</note>, that is, wild clary sage, is beneficial both as food and as a scent; also bugloss, borage, lemon balm, and the distilled water of these three. Furthermore, lettuce, endive, raisins, and almond milk should be staples of the table. One must flee from air that is either scorching, or too icy, or cloudy; instead, temperate and clear air should be very freely admitted. 

Hermes, Pythagoras, and Plato command us to settle and simultaneously uplift a discordant or mourning soul with the lute and with song that is as steady as it is harmonious; likewise, the holy poet David used the psaltery and psalms to free Saul from madness. I also—if I may compare the lowest things to the highest—frequently experience at home how much the sweetness of the lyre and song avails against the bitterness of **black bile** <term>black bile: "atra bilis," the cold, dry humor associated with the earth and with melancholy</term>. We praise the frequent sight of clear water, or the colors green and red; the enjoyment of gardens and groves; walking beside rivers and through pleasant meadows; and we strongly approve of gentle horse riding, being carried in a carriage, and smooth sailing. But above all, we praise variety: easy occupations, various non-burdensome business, and the constant company of pleasant people.

->### BOOK I. Care of the Stomach. Chapter XI.<-

It follows that we must take the most diligent care of the stomach, lest satiety ever bring on nausea or indigestion and offend the head. Food should be taken twice daily and in moderate amounts, lightly seasoned with cinnamon, mace, and nutmeg. However, dry food should always outweigh soft nourishment and drink in total weight, unless perhaps we greatly fear the dryness of **black bile** <note>original: "atrae bilis"; this refers to melancholy, one of the four humors believed to cause sadness and sluggishness if it became too dry or burnt</note>. Food should wait for hunger and drink for thirst (if this can be done conveniently); a bit of appetite should remain at the end of the meal, while disgust and over-fullness should be far away. One must abstain from those things which, because of excessive humidity or a poisonous, oily, and viscous nature, weaken the stomach by relaxing it, or those which are either very cold or very hot, or are difficult to digest because of their hardness. Also to be avoided are things that leave a bothersome aftertaste long after the meal, or those that cause gas, or those that strike the head with many vapors—especially all things that easily rot, whether inside or outside the bowels. We do not approve of sweet or sharp flavors if they are served alone; rather, we want sweets to be tempered by something sharp, pungent, or dry. 

Mastic, dry mint, fresh sage, raisins, quinces, cooked apples seasoned with sugar, chicory, rose, coral <note>ground coral was frequently used in Renaissance medicine as a tonic to strengthen the heart and stomach</note>, lotus, and capers seasoned in vinegar are very friendly to the stomach. Furthermore, pomegranates with a flavor midway between sour and sweet, and generally anything that is moderately dry and somewhat tart—which doctors call **styptic** <term>styptic: substances that contract organic tissue, used here to "tighten" or tone a weak stomach</term>—or things that are somewhat pungent, salty, or aromatic are beneficial; however, **myrobalans** <term>myrobalans: a dried, plum-like fruit from India, highly prized in medieval and Renaissance medicine for balancing the humors</term> surpass all these. 

Red wine is also better than white, with a flavor that is slightly bitter; unless heat or a "distillation" <note>likely referring to "catarrh" or the dripping of fluids from the head to the chest</note> requires otherwise, it will be best to drink **pure wine** <note>original: "merum"; wine not diluted with water</note> slowly, bit by bit. Generally, however, liquid dishes should be eaten before harder ones. Once the food is taken, it is helpful to have coriander, quinces preserved in sugar, pomegranates, tart pears, medlars, dried peaches, and the like. Indeed, one must chew every single thing very thoroughly before swallowing. If necessary, the stomach should be warmed from the outside with mastic, rose, mint, and coral. 

Care must be taken that for the next two or three hours after a meal, we do not apply ourselves to difficult thinking or diligent reading. Perhaps four hours of rest will be necessary if the food or drink was more abundant, or the food harder to digest. It is bad to distend the belly with food or drink; it is worst for the stomach, when so distended, to think about difficult things. Therefore, either take the lightest nourishment, or rest once it is taken until you have, as it were, cooked it <note>digestion was often described as a "cooking" or "concoction" process driven by the body's internal heat</note>. Nor should one sleep at midday after a meal unless the greatest necessity compels it, and even then, not before we have stayed awake for two hours. At night, however, once dinner is taken, one hour of wakefulness (as it seems) is sufficient. Sexual intercourse is pestilential to the stomach, especially if you lie together immediately when full, or when hungry; in idleness, the stomach grieves...

### *On those things which nourish the limbs, especially the powers of the spirit. Chapter XII.*

But now it seems better to bring forward several items from the physician’s workshop that either preserve the powers of the stomach, heart, brain, and the **spirits** <note>original: "spirituum"; in Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the soul, carrying out vital and mental functions</note> of the intellect in their entirety, or restore them. These remedies also drive far away any excess of **phlegm** <note>original: "pituita"</note> or **black bile** <note>original: "atra bilis"; also known as melancholy</note>, and repel any looming nausea. All physicians agree without controversy that nothing is more healthful than **theriac** <note>original: "theriaca"; a legendary ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium, used here as a general tonic</note> for nourishing and strengthening the individual limbs and powers, as well as the spirits and the intellect. We shall therefore use, in particular, half a drachm of this, or at least a third of a drachm, twice every week in winter and autumn; but in summer and spring, once—either alone or (if you prefer) in cold and damp seasons with a little clear, sweet, unmixed wine. In hot and dry times, however—especially if your nature or age is on the warmer side—it should be taken with two or three ounces of rose water, specifically on an empty stomach, six or seven hours before a meal. If theriac is unavailable, we shall give **mithridate** <note>original: "mithridatum"; a complex herbal remedy similar to theriac, named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus</note>; but whenever we take theriac or mithridate, one must completely abstain from anything hot on that day, and if it is summer or spring, cold things should be used instead. 

In the second place for this same purpose, all physicians approve of **aloe** <term>aloe: used in this period primarily as a purgative to "cleanse" the humors</term>, properly selected and washed. Take two drachms of **chebulic myrobalans** <note>original: "myrobalanarum chebularum"; an astringent fruit from India highly prized in medieval and Renaissance medicine</note>; one drachm each of purple roses, red sandalwood, emblic myrobalans, cinnamon, saffron, citron peel, been <note>likely *Centaurea behen*, a root thought to gladden the heart</note>, and lemon balm (that is, *citraria*); and twelve drachms of select, well-washed aloe. From these, fashion pills with the best unmixed wine, which you should use once a week at daybreak, in a dose that suits your nature—with rose water in the summer, and with wine at other times. 

On the days when you take neither the theriac nor the pills, use a confection of this kind morning and evening, two or three hours before food. Take four drachms of the finest cinnamon; two of chebulic myrobalans and two of emblic myrobalans; half a drachm of saffron and purple roses; two drachms of red sandalwood, and one drachm of similar corals; and as much very white sugar as is sufficient. Melt the sugar in rose water and the juice of citrons or lemons in equal portions; cook gently, then add a third of a drachm of **musk** <note>original: "musci"; a strong-smelling animal secretion used as a powerful stimulant for the heart and brain</note> and the same amount of **amber** <note>original: "ambrae"; likely ambergris, a substance from sperm whales used to strengthen the internal organs</note>; finally, form them into solid boluses, which are commonly called **morsels** <note>original: "morsulos"; small, medicinal lozenges or candied bites</note>, and wrap them in gold leaf <note>coating pills in gold was both a sign of luxury and a medical practice, as gold was believed to have cordial (heart-strengthening) properties</note>. 

We have found through experience that these three things, used as we have prescribed—the theriac, the aloe prepared as we said, and that confection—benefit every limb, power, and spirit; they sharpen the senses and the intellect, strengthen the memory, and easily draw out or correct phlegm, bile, and black bile through those pills. Furthermore, for [one's] age...
