### *Medicine against phlegm.* Cap. XIII.

If one must fight more sharply against overflowing **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitam"; one of the four humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note>, we shall give pills at dawn made from Galen’s *hierapicra* <note>original: "hierapicra"; a famous "holy bitter" laxative formula</note>, or those which **Mesue** <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician whose works were standard in Renaissance medicine</note> calls "Elephantine," specifically as many and as often as necessary. For a stronger constitution, one might even use pills composed of equal parts *Hiera* and **agaric** <note>original: "agarici"; a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note> troches, always taken with liquid honey of roses, **oxymel** <note>original: "oximelle"; a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</note>, and water of *maratrum* (that is, fennel). Certainly, this syrup is most beneficial for digesting phlegm both before and after taking the pills. If other humors are also disturbed along with the phlegm, we shall purge them opportunely with Mesue’s rhubarb pills, or those which later physicians call "pills without which" <note>original: "sine quibus"; referring to the *Pilulae sine quibus esse nolo*, or "pills without which I do not wish to be," a popular general-purpose laxative</note>. However, we utterly detest any violent or sudden purging, for it weakens the stomach and heart, exhausts many of the spirits, throws the humors into confusion, and darkens the spirits with the gloomy vapors of the humors.

### *On distillation, and its cure.* Cap. XIIII.

When the head is flooded with **distillations** <note>original: "distillationibus"; the movement of excess mucus or "catarrh" from the brain down into the throat or chest</note> due to phlegm, we shall sometimes give several of the pills described above at the hour of sleep. Furthermore, we shall command the patient to often chew frankincense at that hour and others, for it wonderfully aids against distillations and supports all the senses and the memory. Likewise, nutmeg and **theriac** <note>a complex ancient medicinal paste used as a universal tonic</note> held in the mouth are approved, as is marjoram (which he calls *amaracum*), or its water applied to the nostrils or poured in. After a meal, we shall restrain the vapors of the food with coriander and quinces.

### *On headache, and its cure.* Cap. XV.

If the head often aches from being weighed down by a cold humor, in addition to the things we have recounted, we shall command the patient to hold in the mouth that confection they call *diambra*, or *diachori*, or *plirisarchoticon*. Such a person should also often chew **mastic** <note>a resin from the mastic tree, used for oral hygiene and digestion</note>, and additionally rub the forehead, temples, and neck with the leaves of marjoram, fennel, and rue, crushed together with rose oil. Similarly, aloe perfectly dissolved in vinegar, oil, and rose water is effective.

### *On the care of vision.* Cap. XVI.

When the eyes grow dim but are not red, nor show any other sign of heat, then surely an **eyewash** <note>original: "collirium"</note> made from the water of fennel, marjoram, **celandine** <note>original: "celidoniæ"; a plant traditionally used for eye ailments</note>, and rue, with the addition of saffron and antimony, is beneficial; but such water must first be strained through a thick cloth. However, you should apply nothing to the eyes unless you have first purged them often with "pills of light" <note>original: "pillulis lucis"; a specific formula designed to clear the vision</note>. But if the dim eyes are red, purge them immediately with pills composed of **fumitory** <note>original: "fumo terræ"; literally "smoke of the earth," a plant used to clear the blood and skin</note>; then an eyewash of rose water and sugar is helpful. Sometimes, relief is brought as quickly as possible by adding egg white, **tutty** <note>original: "tucia"; zinc oxide used in eye salves</note>, and milk. In general, the daily use of fennel preserves and sharpens the sight; indeed, its seed is frequently—

It is excellent to take a preserved chebulic myrobalan <note>original: "myrobalanum chebulam"; a fruit from India highly valued for its ability to "purge" the head and sharpen the senses</note> daily on an empty stomach, and with it some bread made with sugar and powdered fennel. Furthermore, the use of **eyebright** <note>original: "eufragiæ"; a flower traditionally used to treat eye ailments</note> is a singular protection for the eyes and is wonderfully beneficial for the intellect and for prolonging life. In any case of either a headache or cloudiness of the eyes, the vapors must be diverted backward by means of frictions and cupping glasses; and if heat is the cause and blood is abundant, we shall apply leeches to the neck and shoulders.

### *On restoring the sense of taste. Cap. XVII.*

The stomach of those devoted to letters often loses almost all sense of taste. If this happens through the fault of **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitæ"; the cold, moist humor</note>, which is indicated by the flavor of the mouth or an abundance of sticky saliva, you should use the rose-based aromatic medicines we described above after the bowels have been moved. Specifically, use rose sugar mixed with rose honey and cinnamon alone, or with preserved ginger, or mint syrup, but especially **theriac** <note>original: "theriaca"; a famous "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium</note>. 

If, however, it happens due to a wealth of **bile** <note>original: "bilis"; specifically yellow bile, which is hot and dry</note>, which a bitter mouth usually indicates, you should similarly take—after a purging of aloe (prepared as we said) or rhubarb—either "three-sandalwoods" <note>original: "triasandalum"; a cooling mixture made from three types of sandalwood</note>, or *oxizacharum* <note>original: "oxizacharum"; a medicinal syrup made of vinegar and sugar</note>, or a mixture of white vinegar-sugar and the juice of a sharp pomegranate. You might also use peaches or pears, either preserved or made into a syrup as Mesue teaches, or our own such confection which is most healthy for the taste. 

Take four ounces of rose sugar, two ounces of *dimarenatum* <note>a preserve, likely of pomegranate or citrus</note>, the same amount (two ounces) of *diacitonite* <note>original: "diacitonitem"; a marmalade-like conserve made of quinces</note>, half an ounce of chebulic myrobalans, the same of emblic myrobalans, and half a drachm each of red sandalwood and red coral. Pour over this two or three ounces of **julep** <note>a sweet medicinal drink</note> made from citron or lemon juice. If the stomach is weak and cold, add two drachms of cinnamon. This should be used two hours before food. *Diacitonite* and the use of capers with vinegar always remove nausea arising from either humor; likewise, a modest drink of white rose-vinegar on an empty stomach, if mixed with twice its weight in sugar, or again, syrups of mint or wormwood. Likewise, mint either preserved in vinegar or diluted with the tart juice of a pomegranate.

### *On the exact cure of black bile. Cap. XVIII.*

But let us now set aside these lighter matters and return to that which is most dangerous: namely, to **black bile** <note>original: "atram bilem"; also known as melancholy. In Renaissance thought, this humor was associated with both profound intellect and deep depression or madness</note>. Whenever it abounds and rages, it undermines the whole body, and especially the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritum"; in this context, a subtle vapor that acts as the bridge between the physical body and the soul's intellect</note>—which is the instrument of the intellect—and the intellect and judgment themselves. Let the first precept in curing it be that which **Galen** <note>the most influential physician of antiquity</note> taught: that we should not strive to draw it out suddenly, lest perhaps once its more liquid and subtle part is withdrawn, the remainder becomes much denser and drier...

The second point is that meanwhile, the head and the entire body should be moistened as much as possible with wetter foods, as well as with sweet and moderate baths and similar ointments; this must be done with such caution, however, that neither "distillation" <note>original: "distillatio"; a medieval medical term for a downward flow of excess humors, often manifesting as a cold or catarrh</note> is provoked, nor the stomach or liver weakened, nor the passages of the body obstructed. The third point, which is indeed the most necessary, is that the heart should be continually nourished and strengthened with appropriate things—partly by substances taken internally, and partly by those applied externally to the chest or nostrils. One should also constantly look at and listen to, smell, and think about things that delight, while keeping contrary things far away.

## On Syrups. Cap. XIX.

Many things have been composed by many authors against this humor <note>referring to black bile or melancholy</note>. For the present, however, I will offer three types of remedies chosen as the most select and safest of all, first received from the ancients, then confirmed by more recent authors, and occasionally adapted by us for our own use. In the first group is the composition of an excellent syrup; in the second, most proven pills; in the third, the most healthful electuaries. When these three are applied opportunely, the melancholic humor is softened, digested, and dissolved; the spirits are sharpened and brightened, the intellect is nourished, and the memory is strengthened. 

The syrup is of this sort: take borage, bugloss, the flowers of both, lemon balm, maidenhair fern, endive, violets, dodder, polypody <note>a type of fern</note>, senna, and epithyme <note>a parasitic plant, "dodder of thyme," used as a purgative</note>—a handful of each; twenty Damascus plums, ten fragrant apples, one ounce of raisins, half an ounce of licorice; three drachms each of cinnamon, red sandalwood, and citron peel; and half a drachm of saffron. Let all be cooked in water except for the epithyme and the spices, until a third part is consumed. After the decoction has been strained, let it be cooked again moderately with sugar and the epithyme; finally, let the spices—namely the cinnamon and saffron—be infused. Three ounces of this syrup should be drunk warmed at dawn, together with two or three ounces of bugloss water; and along with these, some of the following pills ought to be taken—at least two, or more, as suits each individual—specifically so that the bowels are moved a little every day.

---

## On Pills. Cap. XX.

As far as our purpose is concerned, there are two types of pills: some are suitable for the delicate, others for the more robust. The first may be called "Golden" or "Magical" pills, composed partly in imitation of the Magi and partly by our own invention under the very influence of Jupiter and Venus. These draw out phlegm and black bile <note>original: "atram bilem"</note> without distress, strengthen individual members, and sharpen and illuminate the spirits. They dilate the spirits so that they do not produce sorrow through constriction, but rather rejoice in dilation and light; furthermore, they stabilize them so that they do not vanish through excessive extension. [Take] therefore twelve grains of gold, <note>original: "auri grana"; gold was believed in Renaissance medicine to have solar properties that could strengthen the heart and dispel gloom.</note> especially in the form of gold leaf; and if they are pure, take half a drachm each of: frankincense, myrrh, saffron, aloeswood, cinnamon, citron peel, lemon balm, raw crimson silk, mint, white ben, and red ben. <note>original: "been albi, been rubei"; "Ben" usually refers to the winged seeds of the Moringa tree or certain species of Centaurea used in cardiac tonics.</note> Take one drachm each of: purple roses, red sandalwood, red coral, and the three myrobalans—namely emblic, chebulic, and Indian. <note>original: "myrobalanorum... emblicarum, chebularum, indarum"; myrobalans are dried, plum-like fruits used in Ayurvedic and medieval European medicine as gentle laxatives to purge specific humors.</note> Take as much properly washed aloes as the total weight of all the other ingredients. Form these into pills with the most select unmixed wine. 

Following these are pills for dissolving melancholy that are somewhat stronger, yet not at all violent. Take one drachm each of: peony, myrrh, Arabian stoechas, <note>original: "sticados arabici"; a type of lavender (*Lavandula stoechas*) used to "cleanse" the brain.</note> lemon balm, frankincense, saffron, the three myrobalans (namely emblic, chebulic, and Indian), and roses. Take three drachms each of: agaric troches, <note>original: "trocifcorum agarici"; agaric is a larch fungus used as a purgative.</note> polypody, epithyme, <note>original: "epithimi"; dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant highly valued for purging black bile.</note> senna, properly washed and prepared lapis lazuli, and Armenian stone <note>original: "lapidis armeni"; like lapis lazuli, this blue mineral was used medicinally to purge melancholy.</note> prepared in the same way. Add two ounces of washed aloes and form the pills with a perfect wine. If a manifest heat dominates along with the melancholy, those ingredients in this composition that are cold should be increased by a third part of their weight. 

I have composed these pills (as befits devoted scholars) in imitation of the Greeks, Latins, and Arabs. I did not wish to mix in stronger ingredients, such as hellebore, <note>original: "veratrum"; a potent and toxic plant used since antiquity to treat madness, though risky due to its violence.</note> which the fanatic Carneades <note>Carneades (c. 214–129 BCE) was a Greek skeptic philosopher who reportedly used hellebore to purge his brain before debating.</note> used to use. For I advise only literary men, or those perhaps slightly more robust, for whom nothing is more destructive than violence. Therefore, I have omitted the "Indian pills," the famous "pills of lapis lazuli" or "Armenian stone," and the composition they call *hieralogodion*. <note>A complex, traditional purgative electuary.</note>

If, finally, it is appropriate to include a simpler composition, which I use more frequently: take one ounce of washed aloes; two drachms each of emblic and chebulic myrobalans; and two drachms each of mastic and roses (especially purple ones). Form these into pills with wine. Furthermore, regarding these or any other pills we have approved, no one should ever use them alone, lest they perhaps become too dried out. This dryness is indeed the worst thing in melancholy. Rather, they should be taken either with the syrup which we described above (following partly Mesuë <note>Mesuë the Younger (925–1015), an influential but semi-legendary Arabic medical author.</note> and partly Gentile da Foligno <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), a famous Italian physician and commentator on Avicenna.</note>), or with one, two, or three ounces of fragrant, light wine—as suits each person—or with water of honey, raisins, and liquorice. Or, if heat dominates anywhere, with violet julep <note>original: "iuleb"; a sweet medicinal drink, usually a syrup diluted with water.</note> and violet water. 

I entirely advise scholars, or whoever are more prone to "black bile," <note>original: "atram bilem"; the literal meaning of "melancholy."</note> to use this purgation twice every year—namely in spring and autumn—for fifteen or twenty consecutive days; specifically, the pills taken with the syrup and similar liquids. Those, however, who are slightly less subject to this affliction will find it sufficient if they take the first or the last pills throughout the whole year, once every week: in summer indeed with julep (as we said), but at other times with wine.

BOOK I.

### On liquid medicine. Chapter XXI.

One must remember that when the greatest danger of drying out is imminent, yet necessity forces a purging of the humors, it is worthwhile to pause the use of pills. Instead, when it is time to purge, one should use the syrup itself, or a similar decoction made in bugloss water <note>original: "aqua buglossæ"; bugloss or oxtongue was a herb highly prized for its ability to "gladden the heart" and moisten the body.</note>, and occasionally infuse into it one ounce, or at least half an ounce, of *diasenna*, or *diacatholicon*, or Persian *triphera*. <note>These are complex electuaries—medicinal pastes made with honey and herbs—used to gently purge the body of excess humors.</note> If the body is more robust, or the bowels are more constricted and hard, add one or two drachms of the electuary of *hamech*. <note>The Electuary of Hamech was a specific medieval remedy used to purge "burnt" or "adust" black bile.</note> Prepared cassia is also useful here, and manna is even more useful; however, these do not suit every type of melancholy, but especially that which is created by adustion. <note>original: "aduſtione"; a medical state where the humors were thought to be "scorched" by excessive heat, making them toxic and dry.</note> 

But if the melancholy is "natural" <note>Natural melancholy refers to the standard temperament, whereas adust melancholy refers to a pathological state caused by heat.</note>, these remedies are indeed suitable, especially if a double or triple portion of polypody <note>a type of fern</note> is added to the syrup, along with licorice, saffron, and raisins; likewise, two ounces of liquid honey of roses should be added to the medicine. We have stated in earlier sections how often the syrup should be taken, but the medicine must be taken with it for sixty days. <note>original: "ter viginti diebus"; literally "thrice twenty days".</note> 

Truly, if no melancholic humor is actually present, but only a melancholic "complexion"—that is, a cold and dry quality of the limbs—remember that it is not at all expedient to purge the bowels or let blood. Instead, do only the other things we have mentioned or will mention, especially whatever pertains to warming the body moderately and moistening it greatly, brightening the spirits as much as possible, and nourishing the limbs. But where the humor of black bile itself overflows, we do not only moisten the body and the humor, but we also loosen the bowels with the caution already mentioned, though never violently. Indeed, Plato in the *Timaeus* warns us that a long-lasting disease, such as melancholy, should not be provoked with excessively strong medicines or troublesome drugs.

---

### On bloodletting. Chapter XXII.

There are some who are too bold in letting blood, whom wise physicians greatly detest. For blood is the tempering agent of black bile, the fuel of the spirit, and the treasure of life. Only when an abundance of blood is indicated—either by excessive laughter, great boldness and confidence, or a ruddy color and swelling of the veins—should we let the blood of scholars. When the situation demands it, we should draw it from the "splenic vein" of the left arm <note>the *salvatella* vein, believed in Renaissance anatomy to be directly connected to the spleen.</note> with a wide incision: four ounces in the morning, and as many in the evening. 

Then, after a few days—at least seven, at most fourteen—one should irritate the *mariscae* <note>original: "mariſcas"; the hemorrhoidal veins. Drawing blood from the lower body was thought to divert harmful humors away from the brain.</note> through a rougher rubbing and by applying leeches (which they call "blood-suckers"), so that three or four ounces of blood may drip from there. Both of these actions seem appropriate only for the more robust; for the weaker, if necessity demands, one should only irritate the *mariscae* as we have taught. But neither...

One should not loosen the belly with medicines, nor is it permitted to let blood, unless you have first softened the bowels with fatty and mild clysters <note>A clyster is an enema, used here to hydrate and "slippery" the digestive tract before harsher treatments.</note>. And this becomes a general rule for the melancholic nature: one must take care, if necessary, that by the frequent use of such clysters, the lower belly is always kept lubricated and purged.

### On electuaries. Chapter XXIII.

Next come the electuaries <note>An electuary is a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup; it was designed to be licked or dissolved in the mouth.</note>, among which I certainly praise the one that Rhazes <note>A famous 9th-century Persian physician</note> called "the exhilarating one"; furthermore, those which Avicenna <note>The influential 11th-century Persian philosopher and physician</note> composes in his book *On the Powers of the Heart*. But I praise much more the one which Mesue <note>A 9th-century physician often cited in medieval pharmacy</note> writes as follows:

Take one pound of raw silk recently dyed a crimson color <note>original: "colore coccineo"; dyed silk was believed to have medicinal properties related to the heart and blood</note>; submerge it in one pound each of bugloss juice and rose water. After twenty-four hours, boil the whole mixture gently until the water turns red. Then remove the silk and squeeze it out thoroughly. Immediately pour in one hundred and fifty drachms <note>A drachm is a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> of the whitest sugar; boil it again until it thickens like honey. Then remove it from the fire, and while it is still warm, pour in six drachms of raw ambergris <note>A rare substance from the sperm whale, used as a fixative and heart tonic</note> that has been carefully chopped, and allow the ambergris to melt. Finally, add the following powder: take six drachms each of raw aloe wood and cinnamon; thirteen drachms of properly washed lapis lazuli; two drachms of "unions"—that is, white pearls; one drachm of true gold; and half a drachm of choice musk.

Two drachms, or perhaps one, are given with wine in the morning and evening, three or four hours before a meal. This recipe pleases me more than the others. Nevertheless, I also approve of Mesue’s "sweet musk" compound and his "composition of gems," provided they are taken with rose water. I would also wonderfully praise the one concocted by the great philosopher Pietro d’Abano <note>A 13th-century Italian physician and astrologer</note>, were it not that he himself feared that its excessive use caused too much dilation and exhaling of the spirits <note>In this medical tradition, "spirits" were the subtle substances that connected the soul to the body; too much "exhalation" could lead to weakness or fainting.</note>.

For this reason, I have devised two other extremely safe ones, which are most suitable for any time, age, or nature because of their balanced temperament, in which the useful is mixed with the sweet. These nourish as much as they soothe and strengthen; furthermore, they are as well-suited for stabilizing the spirit and the intellect as they are for sharpening and illuminating them.

Take four ounces of rose-sugar, two ounces of sugar boiled together with bugloss flowers, one ounce of candied citron peel, and two ounces of candied chebule <note>A type of myrobalan fruit used in Ayurvedic and medieval medicine</note>. Add one drachm of choice cinnamon; half a drachm each of sandalwood and red coral; likewise half a drachm each of chopped raw crimson silk, saffron, and pearls; one-third of a drachm each of gold and silver; and two grains each of ambergris and musk. Dissolve all of this together in the juice of a citron or a lemon boiled with sugar.

There follows another concoction that is somewhat more healthful and certainly much sweeter: take four ounces of sweet almonds and the same amount of pine nuts, which have been washed for a period of one <meta>catchword: day</meta>

How these are to be used, I have sufficiently explained above. 

If someone desires something simpler, suited to everyone, let them thoroughly crush an entirely ripe citron fruit and boil it with plenty of sugar and much rose juice. Once cooked, season it with a little cinnamon and saffron, or use "aromatic of roses" <note>original: "aromatico rosaceo"; a spiced rose cordial</note> tempered in this way: Take one ounce of aromatic of roses, and two ounces each of sugar of roses and sugar of bugloss <note>original: "diabuglosati"; bugloss is an herb believed to gladden the heart</note>; or similarly, mix in "diamuscum" <note>a musk-based tonic</note>. For although these two are not "simples" <note>A 'simple' is a medicinal herb used alone, rather than in a compound</note>, they are easily obtained; and if heat is feared, "diaprunis" <note>a plum-based laxative electuary</note> and sugar of violets may be added.

### On excessive sleeplessness. Chapter XXIV.

It often happens to melancholics, especially scholars <note>original: "literatis"; referring to those dedicated to letters and study</note>, that with the brain overly dried out, they are weakened by long periods of sleeplessness. Since nothing increases the evils of black bile <note>original: "atrum bilis"; the physical substance of melancholy</note> more than long wakefulness, such a great evil must be countered with all zeal. 

Therefore, let them eat lettuce after other foods along with a little bread and a tiny bit of saffron; let them sip pure wine after the lettuce, and not study by candlelight beyond an hour. When they go to sleep, let them take a concoction of this kind: two ounces of white poppy seeds, one ounce of lettuce seed, and a half-drachm each of amomum <note>an aromatic spice similar to cardamom</note> and saffron; add six ounces of sugar, dissolve, and boil it all together with poppy syrup. Let them eat two drachms of this, and at the same time taste a bit of poppy syrup or wine. 

You should smear their forehead and temples with oil of violets and water lily <note>original: "nenufare"</note>, adding camphor, as well as milk, almond oil, and violet oil. You will bring the scent of saffron, camphor, and the peels of sweet fruit to the nostrils, along with a little vinegar but plenty of rose water. You shall also spread the bed with the leaves of cool plants, and soothe the ears with heavy songs and sounds. You will often moisten the head with washes of this sort, namely...

### *On dullness of mind and forgetfulness.* Chapter XXII.

It truly happens sometimes to scholars—either because they read or write with their heads diligently bowed, or because they grow sluggish from too much idleness—that a certain viscous phlegm <term>pituita; one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture, thought to cause sluggishness</term>, together with an overly cold melancholy, occupies and weighs down the head, making them dull and forgetful. Therefore, the heads of these people must be unburdened by those remedies we have said elsewhere suit the phlegm. If those are not sufficient, turn to the "Indian" pills and *cocchiae* <note>pills used for purging the head</note>, and to the *hieralogodion* <note>a complex herbal electuary or purgative</note>. Furthermore, turn to the *hiera* <note>a sacred or divine medicine, usually an electuary</note> of colocynth, or that of Archigenes, or of Andromachus, or of Theodotion, or to the "Pills of the Jew," which Mesue <note>A 9th-century physician influential in the Middle Ages</note> describes in the chapter on headaches. 

But if the person's nature is colder due to age, and summer does not prevent it, use that "confection of anacardium" after purging, which Mesue calls the "confection of the wise" in his book of medicines; and again, that anacardine <note>derived from the marking nut (*Anacardium orientale*), believed to stimulate memory</note> mixture which they review in the chapter on forgetfulness according to the opinion of the son of Zacharias <note>referring to the Persian physician Rhazes</note>. Take one drachm <note>roughly 3.9 grams</note> early in the morning, but he who takes it must entirely abstain from anger, sexual intercourse, drunkenness, labor, and hot things on that day. These are indeed very powerful against dullness and forgetfulness. 

But if you prefer more familiar remedies, give ginger preserved in sugar, but mixed with a little frankincense, which greatly benefits the senses and memory, especially with these added: anacardine honey, honey of chebulic myrobalans, sweet flag, cyperus, amber, and musk. Beneficial also are *diambra*, *philarchoticon*, and *diacori* <note>various spiced electuaries intended to warm the brain and heart</note>. But these should be held in the mouth for a long time, and even infused into the nostrils and ears. The scent of frankincense, marjoram, fennel, nutmeg, and cloves also helps significantly. 

Remember, however, that *theriac* <term>a famous "universal" antidote and cure-all containing dozens of ingredients</term> should never be secondary to any remedy in these and similar cases, as we said from the beginning. Furthermore, for the dull and forgetful, anoint the temples and the neck with an ointment of this kind: Take one ounce of elderberry oil, two ounces of oil of ben <note>Moringa oil</note>, and half an ounce each of euphorbium and castoreum <note>a secretion from beaver glands used as a stimulant</note>. With this, you shall rub the arms, legs, and neck vigorously, and if necessary, apply cupping glasses <note>original: "cucurbitulas"; small vessels used to draw blood or humors to the surface</note> to the neck. Additionally, cover and warm the crown of the head with crushed marjoram, frankincense, and nutmeg.

<meta>This page concludes Book I. While the previous page provided physical remedies for the "dullness of mind" in scholars—such as purgatives and cooling milks—this final chapter shifts from the medical care of the body to the moral and religious cultivation of the soul, bridging the gap between medicine and theology.</meta>

BOOK I.

### *That we ought to care for the corporeal spirit, cultivate the incorporeal, and finally venerate the truth; the first is provided by medicine, the second by moral discipline, and the third by religion. Chapter XXVI.*

If men eager for the truth should care for the corporeal spirit <term>spiritus; in Renaissance medicine, a thin, vaporous substance that connects the physical body to the immaterial soul</term> with such medical diligence—lest, if entirely neglected, it becomes an obstacle or serves ineptly those seeking truth—then without a doubt it is much more fitting to cultivate the incorporeal spirit (that is, the intellect itself) through the principles of moral discipline. For it is by the intellect alone that truth, being incorporeal, is grasped. It is a sin to care only for the servant of the soul, which is the body, while neglecting the soul, which is the master and king of the body; especially since it is the opinion of the Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests and sages often cited by Ficino as predecessors to Plato</note> and of Plato that the whole body depends on the soul in such a way that unless the soul is healthy, the body cannot be healthy.

For this reason, Apollo, the author of medicine, judged Socrates to be the wisest, rather than Hippocrates, though the latter was born of Apollo's own lineage <note>Hippocrates was traditionally said to be a descendant of Asclepius, the son of Apollo</note>. Indeed, just as much as Hippocrates strove to heal the body, Socrates strove to heal the soul—although what they attempted, Christ alone accomplished. Therefore, if we are commanded by Socrates to cultivate our mind with the best morals so that we might more easily attain, with a serene mind, the light and variety sought by us through natural instinct, how much more is it right to worship divine truth itself through Holy religion? The mind was created for seeking and grasping this truth no differently than the eye was created for seeing the light of the Sun.

And (as our Plato says), just as sight perceives nothing visible anywhere except in the splendor of the highest visible thing—that is, the Sun itself—so the human intellect grasps nothing intelligible except in the light of the highest intelligible thing, which is God, who is always and everywhere present to us. I speak of that light <note>original: "quòd illuminat omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum"</note> "which illuminates every man coming into this world." I speak of the light of which David sings <note>original: "In lumine tuo videbimus lumen"</note>, "In your light we shall see light." Truly, just as the splendor of light is suddenly poured into cleansed eyes looking toward it, shining abundantly with the colors and shapes of things, so as soon as the mind is purged of all bodily disturbances through moral discipline and directed toward divine truth (that is, God himself) with a certain religious and most burning love, suddenly (as the divine Plato says) divine truth flows into the mind. It happily unfolds the true reasons of things contained within it, by which all things consist; and by as much light as it surrounds the mind, it simultaneously bathes the will with blessed joy.

->The End of the First Book.<-

# MARSILIO FICINO
## THE FLORENTINE
### PHYSICIAN,
### AND PHILOSOPHIER
#### MOST CELEBRATED,

##### An Epistolary Preface to Filippo Valori
##### on "On a Long Life."

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'M' depicting two figures in classical robes within an architectural space; one figure gestures towards a large armillary sphere or globe held by the other.</image-desc>

*Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends many greetings <note>original: "S. D." for "Salutem Dicit"</note> to Filippo Valori, the best and most noble citizen. Although our Plato lives by his own genius <term>genius; in the Renaissance sense, this refers both to a guiding divine spirit and the innate talent that grants a writer immortality</term> and will continue to live (as I believe) as long as the world itself shall live, my own genius nevertheless always impels me toward this: that after the worship of the Divine, I should favor the life of Plato above all else. You too, my dear Valori—my most intimate friend and a man most devoted to Platonic glory and learning—have long shared this aspiration with me. Therefore, the same long life I always desire for Plato, I desire also for the Medici <note>original: "medicibus." Ficino is making a pun here: he means both "physicians," who preserve life, and the "Medici" family, who were his patrons</note>, and a similar one for you, Valori. Wherefore I urge and beseech you, my Valori, that with the same great effort you always favor Platonic glory, you might at last read and keep these precepts of ours on prolonging life with equal diligence. By following these, and thus living a long life, you may be able to patronize the recently reborn <note>original: "refulgenti nuper," literally "recently shining forth," referring to the Renaissance revival of Greek philosophy in Florence</note> teachings of Plato for a longer time, together with the great-hearted Lorenzo de' Medici. Farewell.*

# BOOK TWO.

->*A long life is necessary for the perfection of knowledge, which diligence also provides. Chapter I.*<-

---

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring a landscape with classical architecture and figures within a square frame.</image-desc>

To achieve a perfect art and science, it is not so much a teachable intellect or a strong memory that leads us, but rather the clarity of prudent judgment. Yet judgment, because of the ambiguity born from a diverse range of conjectures, is so difficult that it must necessarily be confirmed by experiment. Experiment, too, is deceptive—both because of the difficulty of judgment itself, and because of the fleeting brevity of the opportune time for seizing the experiment. For these very reasons, we rightly conclude along with Hippocrates <note>original: "artem esse longam" – a reference to the famous first Aphorism of Hippocrates: "Life is short, the Art is long; opportunity is fleeting, experience is perilous, and judgment is difficult."</note> that the "Art is long," and that we cannot achieve its mastery except through the length of life. 

However, a long life is not only promised once by the Fates at our beginning; our own diligence also provides it. This is something that even Astrologers acknowledge when they discuss "elections" <term>elections; the branch of astrology concerned with choosing the most auspicious time to begin an undertaking</term> and "images" <term>images; astrological talismans or symbols used to capture planetary influences</term>, and which the diligent care and experience of physicians confirms. By this foresight, not only are naturally strong men most often preserved, but even the sickly sometimes achieve a long life. Thus, it is no wonder that a certain Herodicus <note>Herodicus of Selymbria was a 5th-century BC physician and gymnastics master mentioned by Plato and Aristotle; he was famously sickly but extended his life through strict diet and exercise.</note>, a student of letters and the weakest of all in his time (as Plato and Aristotle testify), fulfilled nearly his hundredth year through such foresight. Plutarch, moreover, relates that many who were otherwise of little physical strength achieved a long life through diligence alone. I will omit for now how many weak people I myself have known who, by the gift of prudence, have surpassed the years of the most robust. 

Therefore, it will be neither useless nor vain, following the book we composed on "Caring for the Health of Scholars" <margin>scholars</margin>, to provide additional precepts for those intellects eager <margin>for knowledge</margin> which lead toward a long life. These instructions are indeed <margin>not sluggish...</margin>

<header>ON A LONG LIFE</header>

...[with the wicked] and the lazy, for why should we desire such people to live long? They do not truly live; it would be as if we were nourishing drones rather than bees. Nor do we wish this to be spread among men dissolved by the lost lust for pleasures, who foolishly prefer a brief daily pleasure to a long one, nor revealed to the wicked and the unjust, whose life is the death of the good. Rather, we intend this only for men who are prudent and temperate, of skillful character, and men who will be profitable to the human race, whether in private or in public.

->Vital heat is nourished by moisture; where this is lacking, dissolution occurs, and where it is excessive, suffocation occurs. Chapter II.<-

Life indeed consists in natural heat, just as a light does. The food of this heat is an airy and fatty moisture, like oil <note>original: "humor aereus, atque pinguis quasi oleum" — Ficino refers to the "radical moisture," a concept in medieval medicine describing the innate fluid that acts as fuel for the body's internal fire.</note>. Therefore, if moisture of this kind should happen to fail, or if it should exceed entirely, or be contaminated, the heat is immediately weakened and, once weakened, is finally extinguished. If the heat is weakened and lost through a lack of moisture, death occurs by dissolution <term>dissolution; the "drying out" or dispersion of the body's vital heat</term>; if it is instead overwhelmed by an excess or vice of moisture, life perishes by suffocation. Indeed, suffocation occurs from an overflow or putrefaction of any humor <term>humor; one of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determine health</term>, especially when phlegm is either increasing or in some way putrefied, so that phlegm has not undeservedly been called "the seeker of life" <note>original: "pituita petens vitam" — a traditional medical saying suggesting that excess phlegm "seeks" to end life by quenching the vital flame.</note>. Therefore, the precepts most necessary for prolonging life avoid dissolution on one hand and suffocation and putrefaction on the other—equally, I say, by common reason. For if they happen to treat a man who is hotter or drier, and whose passages are open, the subtle humors and spirits are more prone to dissolution. But if they treat a body affected in the opposite way, they rather come to the aid of suffocation; they especially strive for one or the other if the place or time inclines toward either. But where the gifted and the studious are consulted, both precepts are almost equally necessary, and one labors similarly in both. For in these men, a sharp and hot intellect and the constant movement of the imagination seem to threaten dissolution, while the idleness of the body and indigestion seem to threaten suffocation; therefore, physicians never labor more intensely than in the treatment of such men. And although the entire discussion of the previous book contributes greatly to prolonging life, such a great matter seems to demand its own specific care, which I shall hereafter (as far as I am able) encompass in a few words.

->How heat must be tempered to moisture by a certain counsel of Minerva. Chapter III.<-

Furthermore, while we treat this fatty oil—necessary for this fiery vigor of ours—with "fat Minerva" <note>original: "pingui Minerva" — a Latin idiom meaning "with plain wit" or "coarse common sense." Ficino is playing on the word "fatty" (pinguis) used for both the body's oil and his own writing style.</note>, meanwhile the olive-bearing Minerva <note>Minerva, the goddess of wisdom, was credited with the gift of the olive tree (the source of oil).</note>, the origin of vital oil, born from the head of nourishing Jove, smiles because while we clearly see the quantity of her gift, we have not yet sufficiently seen its quality.

Laughing, then, she said to you: "I have given you not only enough oil to abundantly nourish the flame, but I also commanded that it be poured into the lamp pure and without dregs <note>original: "amurca" — the bitter, watery dregs of pressed olives; Ficino uses this to represent impurities in the body's fluids.</note>." So she spoke. We, however, wandering in our discourse, find ourselves interrupted: because "your word is a lamp to our feet" <note>A reference to Psalm 119:105, adapted here to mean the light of medical and philosophical truth.</note> has not yet been heard by us. From this lamp, then, let us learn that oil must be continually supplied to the flame, with such diligence that we neither overwhelm the light by a sudden flood of liquid, nor again withhold drink from the thirsty wick. But these two matters we think have been sufficiently treated in the previous sections; two others remain for us, one of which we seem to have touched upon lightly, and the other scarcely at all, meanwhile touching Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom, associated with the olive tree and thus the source of pure oil.</note> in such a way that she, who is never accustomed to laugh, might laugh at us.

What then? First, we shall consider that even a tiny flame is utterly devouring, and therefore that lamp shines longer in which the little flame is so tempered to the wick—that is, the lighting-match <term>lucinium; the wick or the part of the lamp that holds the flame</term>—that it does not drink the oil up, but merely sips it. And so we, in our entire diet, shall take care lest the flame ever grow too strong, especially in youth; for the innate fire is by its own nature voracious. It will be enough then to ward off the flooding moisture on one hand, and the penetrating cold on the other.

Next, we will reflect that the lamp is frequently extinguished when one has not dripped pure oil into it, but (if I may say so) oil full of dregs, from which shortly after "fungi" <note>the carbon crust or "snuff" that forms on a burning wick, dimming the light</note> grow out of the impurities and extinguish the light. Now indeed we have received nourishing oil from Pallas, namely that which is very airy, pure, and tenacious with a certain natural viscosity, and firm. Therefore, that which is supplied to replace what is gradually consumed must not only be equal to it, but similar; and for it to be similar, it must not only be airy and fatty, but entirely separated from the dregs—that is, from a certain sediment collected from earth and thicker water. To avoid this congestion and dregs, let us flee from such foods, and from idleness, indigestion <term>cruditatem; literally "rawness," referring to undigested food in the stomach</term>, and filth. Meanwhile, let us cultivate Minerva <note>Another name for Pallas Athena; she was famously born from the head of Zeus.</note> with such moderation that she may increase our head (from which she herself was born), but not diminish our nerves and stomach.

### *By what causes the natural moisture dries up, or foreign moisture overflows; and how necessary perfect digestion is for life. Chapter IV.* ###

These things quickly dry out the natural moisture: a more abundant flow of blood, a violent loosening of the bowels, long-term diarrhea, profuse sweating, pores opened too wide, sexual intercourse performed to the point of weakness, gasping thirst, agonizing hunger, and long vigils. The use of things both hot and dry, laborious movement of the mind and body, anxiety, anger, grief, air that is both drier and more burning (especially when heated by fire), and wind that is dry, violent, and long-lasting—all these increase moisture beyond measure <note>In Galenic medicine, while these factors dry the "natural" moisture, they often cause the body to produce an excess of "foreign" or "corrupt" moisture (like phlegm) as a side effect of inflammation or decay.</note>. Contrary to these, frequent drunkenness does both: for it dries by too much heat,

# ON LONG LIFE

...nature suffocates the drunkard with too much moisture; but nothing is more harmful to both the heat and the moisture than indigestion <note>original: "cruditas" — literally 'rawness,' referring to undigested food that has not been properly 'cooked' by the body's heat</note>. For when nourishment is not cooked <term>concoction; from the Latin "concoctio," the vital process of digestion viewed as a form of internal heat or cooking</term>, on one hand there is a lack of what should water the natural moisture, and on the other, a putrefied residue remains, which, by overflowing, overwhelms the natural heat. For this reason, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> says that the blood is corrupted whenever digestion itself is corrupted; and, following **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the Greek physician whose work formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries</note>, he calls digestion the "root of life."

Therefore, this rule of Galen's is the best, and almost the only one: to take care above all else for the digestion of food. For what appears to be the greatest precept—namely, to use healthy things—will be of no profit unless you digest them. Indeed, a harmful humor flows from these just as from their opposites if they flow into the limbs while still "raw." Furthermore, from foods that are less praised by the medical art, a less harmful nourishment is often received if they are more vigorously digested. Let us, therefore, most diligently avoid indigestion as a grave cause of both the dissolution and the suffocation of our vital spirit, by keeping to a quantity of food and drink that is suited to us. We should also manage this through the quality, simplicity, preparation, and grinding <note>meaning thorough chewing</note> of food, as well as through fasting to call back hunger, and (if necessary) even using an external warming poultice for the stomach, and certain astringent things taken internally after meals.

We must also be carefully on guard lest drink exceed the food, or the food become too liquid, or the nourishments be too vastly different from one another, or we add raw food to what is already raw in the stomach; for these things greatly hinder digestion. Moreover, we must be most diligently careful not to hinder digestion by engaging in sexual intercourse immediately after a meal, nor by frequent and unnecessary naps at midday, nor by staying awake through the night, nor by any untimely labor of the mind or body, or by any other means.

Indeed, I speak of digestion not only as the first stage, which occurs in the stomach, but also the second, which happens in the liver; the third, which happens in the veins; and finally the fourth, which is completed in the limbs <note>Ficino refers to the traditional four-stage model of digestion: 1. Stomach (chyle), 2. Liver (blood), 3. Vessels (distribution), 4. Tissues (assimilation)</note>. This last stage requires a long interval of time, and if it is hindered by anything, it fails to supply the fuel for our vital moisture. Therefore, just as we must aid digestion, it is also primarily necessary for life to assist in the purging of excrement, and it is necessary to sharply wipe away all filth.

Moderate movement of the body is as necessary as the continuous, tempered, and varied movements of the celestial bodies, the air, the fire, and the water—provided that the necessity of digestion and sleep is observed, and exhaustion and dissolution are avoided. Furthermore, we grow moldy and decay in the shade; we live when we are in the open air and in the light. This was a saying frequently on the lips of my father, **Ficino**, a distinguished physician. But to carry these things out successfully, it would be worthwhile to have accustomed the body from a tender age not so much to city affairs, but to certain rustic exercises, and even to occasionally varied types of nourishment and lifestyles. That wise man <note>referring again to his father</note> often used to warn me of this. For those who live with a certain excessive daintiness and refinement at every age often live less safely; but those who in youth...

# BOOK II.

...those who have accustomed themselves less [should], as adults at least, accustom themselves: attempting it, however, with more cautious steps.

->**Chapter V.**<-
**The blood and humor suited to life ought to be airy, temperate in quality, moderate in substance, and tenacious.**

All the Greeks, among the precepts most necessary for a long life, command that we be nourished by **euchimia**. We call **euchimia** <note>original: "euchimis," from the Greek *euchymia* (εὐχυμία), meaning "goodness of juices" or healthy humors</note> those healthy foods that bring good nourishment, that is, good blood. We call blood "good" when it is not cold, not dry, and not turbulent, but rather warm, moist, and clear. It should be warm with a heat that is not sharp, moist with a moisture that is not watery, and clear, yet not in the meantime extremely thin. 

Now, blood that is too hot both sharpens the natural heat and dries up the moisture; the moisture it introduces provides a heat that is easily dissolved and fleeting. Furthermore, blood that is too moist and more prone to being watery blunts the natural heat; it either dulls the natural moisture or drives it to melt under the heat, or it suffocates the heat with its wetness. In short, if any draft of natural moisture is drawn from watery blood, it both putrefies easily and quickly flows away and dissolves. From this it follows that those who eat softer fruits and herbs—unless they take them rarely and perhaps then only as medicine to soften the bowels—soon fill their veins entirely with a "raw" juice prone to putrefaction. To prevent this from happening, for the sake of nourishment, these foods are more safely either cooked or at least mixed with bread.

Indeed, blood should be neither fiery nor watery, but **airy** <note>original: "aerius" — corresponding to the element of Air, which is characterized as warm and moist, the ideal state for life</note>, not like thicker air, lest it be more prone to turning into water; nor like the most subtle air, lest it easily heat up into fire. Instead, it should maintain a moderate substance, in which the "middle air" has the most dominance, and the other elements are present only insofar as they are adapted to the rule of air. Its substance should not be extremely thin, lest it generate unstable moisture and a volatile spirit subject to dissolution. Nor should it be extremely thick; otherwise, it will barely serve the intellect <note>original: "ingenio"</note>, will hardly be transformed into natural moisture and spirit, will obstruct the pathways of the body, and will provide occasion for suffocation. Furthermore, the spirit which is finally created from such thick blood is itself unsuitable for life due to its density. It suffocates the natural heat just as thick smoke immediately compresses and extinguishes a flame—not to mention that it is so dark that it makes life mournful and worse than death. 

Above all (as it seems to me), for a long life, it is beneficial to have blood that is very airy in substance, not too thick, and which possesses within itself a certain sticky and tenacious humor, such as olive oil almost has in its refinement, or the moisture of an eel that is both fatty and thin, or oil extracted from turpentine by a certain sublimation. You, therefore, [should manage] foods and all other things which [produce] blood...

<meta>catchword: ...nem (referring to "sanguinem" or a similar continuation)</meta>

<summary>This page defines the ideal quality of blood for longevity, characterizing it as "airy" (warm and moist) and similar in consistency to refined olive oil. Ficino warns against "watery" blood from raw fruits and "thick" blood that stifles the vital spirits and the intellect.</summary>

<keywords>euchimia, blood quality, airy humor, natural heat, natural moisture, diet, olive oil, vital spirit, Greek medicine</keywords>

--- Page 361 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter V from Book II of Ficino's *Three Books on Life*. The text transitions from defining "good blood" (euchimia) to the practical methods of maintaining the proper thickness and quality of the blood to sustain the body’s "vital heat."</meta>

...diligently choose those things which, according to your strength, produce such a humor. For such blood and humor are the fuel for the **vital heat** <term>vital heat: the innate biological fire believed by Renaissance doctors to reside in the heart and drive all life processes</term>, just as oil is to a flame; and along with its refinement, it also possesses a certain firmness. For we have been instructed, for the sake of preserving youth, to use things that draw the blood toward the **precordia** <note>the region around the heart</note>, thickening it everywhere and nourishing the heart (as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> approves), while advising that watery and unstable blood must be avoided. 

However, one must account for the differences between individual bodies: for where the body is more dense, one must lean toward refining the blood; where the body is more porous or "rare," one must avoid thinning it further by using all available remedies for thickening. Where the body’s constitution is in the middle, we proceed more safely by a middle path. Yet, we should never attempt to uproot the body's natural constitution, otherwise we might uproot life itself. Furthermore, it is useful to remember that when we greatly fear a thinning of the blood, but the stomach is not particularly strong by nature, we must approach the thickening of the blood by smaller degrees. 

In a slender person, we strive to nourish them with thicker foods, and in the meantime, the stomach should be encouraged, sleep should be lengthened, and physical exercise increased according to their strength—while mental exertion should be decreased, as it very often harms many people. If the person cannot tolerate foods that are too viscous, hard, or very cold, we will finally achieve that firmness of the blood and humor through the use of **corals**, **sandalwood**, **roses**, **coriander**, **myrobalans** <note>astringent fruit used in ancient and medieval medicine</note>, **quinces**, and **diacydonion** <term>diacydonion: a medicinal quince jelly or confection used to aid digestion</term>, as well as **rose-sugar** and septic things—a firmness which we cannot safely achieve here with overly "gluey" substances.

Indeed, those who are unable to digest the viscous limbs of larger animals will be most conveniently nourished by **pine nuts** and **pistachios** with **licorice juice** and **starch**, adding **sweet almonds** and their oil, as well as **quince seeds** and **sesame oil**, together with the purest **sugar candy** and **rose water**. We shall grant them, furthermore, the extremities of chickens or kids, and **turtles**, and **snails**, and **testicles** <note>considered in the Renaissance to provide "vital essence" or "generative heat"</note>. We will give them wine that is not white, but red, styptic <note>astringent or mouth-puckering</note>, and somewhat bitter, tempering the wine with **iron-water** <note>water in which hot iron had been quenched, believed to strengthen the organs</note> or **mastic** <note>a resin from the mastic tree used for digestive health</note>. 

We shall also lightly soothe the skin with **oil of mastic** and **quinces**, and in the meantime, we will forbid those things that make the blood thin or boiling—unless perhaps we infuse a little **saffron** or **cinnamon** into the thicker meals so that they may be more easily digested, and once digested, be transferred through the narrow passages to the limbs. For it is difficult to move viscous or slightly firmer foods from a stomach that is not very strong all the way to the **third and fourth digestions** <term>third and fourth digestions: in Galenic medicine, the third digestion happens in the blood vessels and the fourth occurs within the tissues/limbs themselves</term> unless they are carried by such "vehicles." 

In addition, let them be stimulated by light **frictions** <note>massages</note>; when you perform these, do so with very soft hands, and remember to moisten the hands with a certain fragrant wine in which you have cooked **chamomile**, **myrtle**, and **roses**.

<header>BOOK VII <note>The original Latin header reads "Book VII," though in standard editions of Ficino's *Three Books on Life*, this text constitutes Book II, Chapter VI.</note></header>

### General rules for eating and drinking, and the quality of feasts. Chapter VI.

---

But for the present, let us set aside those bodies that are either very dense or very thin, and let us come to a common way of living, suited entirely to the common and middle-ground constitution of the body. Take care that by no means the **passages of the body** <term>passages: "meatus" in Latin, referring to the pores and internal channels through which humors and spirits flow</term> are either opened beyond measure or too greatly obstructed. For in the former case, there is a risk of dissolution and injury from external forces; in the latter, there is the danger of **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: the metabolic "spoiling" or decay of bodily fluids when they become stagnant or overly moist</term> and suffocation. While I do not restrain you with the tightest bridle of rules (which **Hippocrates** <note>Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BCE), the ancient Greek "Father of Medicine"</note> condemns), I nonetheless do not loosen the reins to the point of license. 

Take herbs and the more moist fruits sparingly; even more sparingly milk and fish, and both of these with honey; most sparingly of all, take mushrooms, and then only with aromatics and pear seeds. Similarly, drink pure water sparingly. Those things which are more moist or fatty should be seasoned with aromatics and sharp spices; otherwise, they introduce a foreign and putrid humor into the limbs. Furthermore, if they do provide some humor necessary to nature, they offer one that is very quickly subject to corruption—no differently than watery wine, which is easily disturbed and spoiled. From this comes rapid **graying of hair** <note>original: "canicies"</note>, paleness, and senile wrinkling. 

Even meat, if eaten every day—and especially if its weight approaches that of the bread eaten—brings on rapid putrefaction. For this reason **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 CE), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote "On Abstinence from Animal Food"</note>, relying on the authority of the ancient Pythagoreans, detested the eating of animals. Have we not heard that the long-lived men before the **Flood** <note>The Great Flood of Genesis; Renaissance thinkers believed people lived centuries longer in that era due to a more "pure" diet and environment</note> spared the animals? Although physicians do not so much forbid the use of meat as they do its abuse. 

In short, flee moist things as if they were liable to putrefaction, keeping in memory that the moist and the fat grow old more quickly and die, as **Hippocrates** says and as the matter itself declares. Conversely, take very dry things in moderation, or at least temper them with more liberal drinking; choose the middle path as the safest. Nevertheless, **Avicenna** prefers food that is a little dry over soft food for the sake of avoiding gray hair. Be most cautious regarding things that are too cold or too hot. Things that are hot and moist at the same time foster humor; in both qualities, however, let the excess be moderate. Everywhere, let the heat and moisture have something slightly "gluey" and **astringent** <term>astringent: "stipticum," meaning substances that contract tissues and help the humors "stick" to the organs to nourish them</term>, so that the humor distributed to the limbs may cling more firmly and last a long time under the influence of heat. 

Select wheat and select bread possess this quality above all; second is red and astringent wine that is not too sweet; third are pine nuts and things very similar to them in their balance and "stickiness"; fourth are meats that are simultaneously moist and tender, such as suckling pig and lamb. Nevertheless, the ancient physicians, especially **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), whose medical theories dominated European medicine for over a millennium</note>, strongly recommend pork and blood because of a certain similarity they share with our own bodies.

<header>ON LONG LIFE</header>

<note>original: "Optimę sunt igitur similibus corporibus..."</note> These foods, therefore, are best for similar bodies, such as those of rustics and the robust who exercise the body heavily—especially if the meat is kept for four days seasoned with cloves, prepared coriander, and salt. Perhaps even the blood is useful, provided it is cooked with sugar, thoroughly purified, and remains liquid. 

But to return to our list, those moister meats we mentioned are not recommended, nor are those that are simultaneously hard and dry, such as the meat of an older hare or ox. Rather, choose certain "middle" meats, such as young chickens, capons, peacocks, pheasants, partridges, and perhaps even young pigeons, especially the domestic variety. Such also are roe deer, young calves, yearling **wethers** <term>wether: a castrated ram, considered in period medicine to have more balanced "humors" than a bull or a ram</term>, as well as wild boars. I do not reject suckling kids or fresh cheese. 

I have indeed omitted small birds, for the frequent use of such delicate foods is suitable only for a stomach that cannot tolerate coarser things. One who is stronger, however, gains from these only a fleeting vapor or a thinness of the humors. Yet I do not omit the eggs of hens, provided the yolk is eaten together with the white. For the yolk alone is nourishment for the delicate; indeed, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook in the Renaissance.</note> proves that no nourishment is more beneficial for the loss of blood or the **dissolution of the cardiac spirit** <term>cardiac spirit: in Renaissance medicine, a subtle substance that carries life-force from the heart to the rest of the body</term> than the yolk of a hen’s egg, or that of a partridge or pheasant. 

Nor would it perhaps be out of place to feed geese with spelt or clean water, and after they are killed, to keep the meat for seven days seasoned with salt and coriander prepared in vinegar before you eat it. Stags may be eaten similarly if the stomach is very strong, for it is probable that certain long-lived animals contribute to a long life in the consumer—provided, however, that the meat of such young animals is eaten. Let other meats be taken in turn, sometimes roasted and sometimes boiled. 

Let the food be double the amount of the drink. Let the bread be twice and sixfold <note>original: "panis duplus & sex qualiter." Ficino is likely suggesting a weight or volume ratio of bread relative to other ingredients like eggs.</note> in proportion to eggs, triple to meats, and quadruple to fish, herbs, and moister fruits. Let the meal not begin with a drink, nor should you drink too much at once. Always let something **styptic** <term>styptic: an astringent substance that "constricts" the stomach tissues to prevent food from leaving before it is fully digested</term> follow the meal, taken without drink or with only a very small amount. 

Where the **complexion** <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual</term>, age, location, or season leans toward heat or dryness, you should also turn slightly toward their opposites. Where it leans toward cold or moisture, likewise turn toward the opposite; where there is balance, maintain that balance. 

Furthermore, exercise of the body should be increased and that of the mind decreased to the extent that we eat harder foods, which are perhaps sometimes necessary for the longevity of life. You should have two meals within nine hours of the day, both of them frugal, though the supper should be the more frugal of the two. There should be two physical exercises, performed roughly after the first digestion is complete and carried out until they almost produce a sweat. Nighttime sleep, because it is always necessary, is always good; but daytime sleep, unless it is absolutely necessary, is never good.

<header>BOOK II.</header>

### That one should not use foods that rot quickly; wine and wheat are to be chosen above others; putrefaction and dissolution must be avoided. Chapter VII.

Any animals that come into our care must be nourished with clean and select foods before we eat them; these, and all other things, should be chosen from higher and fragrant pastures. Among these rules, always keep in mind the one approved above all others by the philosopher **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated Catalan physician and alchemist whose works on hygiene and longevity were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>: that it is necessary to choose living creatures, herbs, fruits, grains, and wines from high and fragrant regions (as we have said). These areas should be cleared by temperate winds and cherished by the gentle rays of the sun, where no waters stagnate and the cultivated lands are not fattened with manure, but by their own native moisture—places where everything that grows remains uncorrupted for a long time. 

In such places only should one dwell, and on such things should one feed. One must not trust that we can obtain a lasting moisture, free from **putrefaction** <term>putrefaction: in the humorist system, this refers to the "rotting" of bodily fluids (humors) due to heat and stagnant moisture, leading to disease</term>, from foods that rot in a short time. Nor should we hope to live long and easily where the fruits of the earth do not keep for long, or where men are very rarely long-lived. 

Indeed, the peach demonstrates how great a difference there is in location and diet: in Persia it is a poison, but in Egypt it is a "friend to the heart." Likewise, **hellebore** <note>A plant used as a powerful (and dangerous) purgative in antiquity.</note> is taken without harm in Anticyra, but is a poison elsewhere. **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE).</note> chooses a dwelling that is high, facing the south and east, under thin air that is neither moist nor cold; and **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 427–347 BCE).</note> found long-lived people in the highest and most temperate regions. 

It is truly the worst practice to manure the fields or to fail to drain stagnant waters from the land, for everything grown there is subject to quick corruption. For this reason, I cannot help but disagree with those who criticize the wise **Hesiod** <note>An early Greek poet (c. 700 BCE) who wrote "Works and Days," a poem on farming and morality.</note> because he omitted manuring in his work on rural matters. That prudent man looked to health rather than fertility; he thought the field could be sufficiently enriched by the leaves of lupins and beans turned over at the right time. 

But if we are compelled to inhabit more humid and unclean regions, and to eat foods that will not last, we should maintain the diet that physicians have prescribed for **pestilential air** <note>Referring to the "miasma" or foul air believed to cause the plague.</note>, a subject I have treated sufficiently in my book against the plague. In short, we shall use sweet and somewhat warm scents, and we shall be purged often and lightly with properly prepared **aloe**. 

We say it is "properly prepared" if it has been washed with rose water or the juice of roses, or if it has been perfectly mixed with fresh, crushed roses, with **myrobalan** <term>myrobalan: a dried, plum-like fruit from India, used in Renaissance medicine to balance the humors and strengthen the stomach</term>, mastic, and perhaps more rose added later. This medicine is beyond controversy wonderful for preserving for a long time a "sound mind in a sound body" <note>original: "mentem sanam in corpore sano"</note>. Furthermore, we shall exercise the body and make use of a hearth at the appropriate time. We shall season our feasts with this powder: of **emblic** myrobalans <note>The emblic myrobalan (Amla) was specifically prized for its cooling properties and its ability to protect the "vital spirits."</note>...

...of these, let there be a fourth part of an ounce, with half an ounce of sandalwood, a full ounce of cinnamon, and an eighth of saffron. With this powder, and with other sharp substances used together, we may perhaps be able to inhibit the corruption that threatens us from putrid foods and decayed places. We should remember, however, that where many more people perish from **putrefaction** or suffocation than from **resolution** <term>resolution: the "melting" or thinning out of the body's vital moisture and heat, often caused by overexertion or extreme heat</term>, it is there that putrefaction and suffocation must be most strongly resisted. Where the opposite is true, one should instead use aromatic and somewhat austere <note>original: "austeris"; refers to sharp or astringent flavors that "bind" the humors</note> seasonings and similar scents, which prevent putrefaction at any time. 

Anointing oneself with oil wards off the injury of cold; using baths of water and oil prevents the resolution that threatens from hard labor or hot weather. Similarly, one should often rinse the mouth with water, hold **liquorice** juice or crystalline sugar in the mouth with plenty of rose water, and wash the hands and face with a little rose vinegar, using similar fragrances. Every seven hours, one should be refreshed with moderate food, resting both body and mind while avoiding heat. 

It is of the greatest importance what kind of wheat and wine we eat and drink steadily; these should be of such quality that they remain untainted for over a year, or preferably up to three years, if we are to hope for incorruptible nourishment from them. Wine—whether it be white or red—should be clear, pleasant, **styptic** <term>styptic: astringent or mouth-puckering; believed to help "tighten" the body's tissues</term>, fragrant, and of a kind that requires water, unless you happen to find a wine that is both light and durable, which is very rare. 

The philosopher **Isaac** <note>Isaac Israeli (c. 832–932), an influential Jewish physician whose "Book on Diet" was a standard medical textbook in medieval and Renaissance Europe.</note> says that the strongest wine is "winy" wine, cooked by the Sun and purified by the winds; he orders this to be tempered with pure spring water some time before we drink it, so that it may be more perfectly mixed. He warns us to flee from watery, weak, or bitter wine, as it quickly becomes acidic within the veins and limbs, or otherwise rots. Indeed, watery wine is subject to putrefaction, though if it is "cooked" while its substance is preserved, it might at least be useful—otherwise it is not praised, because it will not create corruptible humor, but its sharpness must be tempered with chosen water. 

Isaac says that the kind of wine we have approved is, in the opinion of the ancients, very similar to the "great **theriacs**" <term>theriac: a complex herbal compound used as a universal antidote and life-extender</term>. As we have said, when tempered, it warms a cold constitution of the body, cools a heated one, moistens a dry one, and dries out a moisture-heavy one. As **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the Greco-Roman physician whose humoral theories dominated medicine for over a thousand years.</note> says, it recreates the natural moisture, fosters the heat, and balances both. 

It is more necessary to mix such wine with water for young people, less so for the elderly, and for cold old men, not at all. For a cold and hard old age—as **Plato** says <note>Referring to Plato's *Laws*, where he suggests wine acts as a medicine to soften the "iron" rigidity of the elderly</note>—is warmed and softened by pure wine just as iron is by fire or a lupin bean by water. We have said that through wine, opposites are harmonized and disagreements are tempered. Know also that this can be achieved through liquorice, though more weakly, and also through rose oil, though applied externally. Let these things be familiar to you, and do not doubt that whatever is tempered in quality and powerful in virtue can balance all other things, just as cold [balances] other...

### *Diet, lifestyle, and medicine for the elderly. Chapter VIII.*

Those who have already completed their seventh seven-year period <note>The "climacteric" years; seven-year cycles were believed to mark major shifts in human development and health.</note> and are approaching their fiftieth year should reflect that Venus signifies the young, while Saturn signifies the old. Among astronomers, these two stars are known to be the greatest of enemies. Therefore, those of a Saturnine age <note>The elderly, who are governed by the cold and dry planet Saturn.</note> should flee from the works of Venus <note>original: "Rem Veneream"; refers here to sexual activity.</note>, which takes a great toll on life even for the young. For sex does not benefit those who are born, but only those yet to be born; even plants dry up immediately once their seed has been produced. Furthermore, the elderly should consider cold and night air to be deadly to them. They should maintain a diet from which they can hope for the most blood and the greatest amount of spirit <term>spirit: in Renaissance medicine, "spiritus" was a subtle vapor in the blood that connected the soul to the physical body</term>. This comes especially from the fresh yolks of eggs and from wine that is somewhat sweet and very fragrant. 

For these yolks specifically restore the blood of the heart, and wine especially refreshes the spirit. They should use the finest meats that are very easy to digest, and in short, follow a diet that increases both heat and moisture <note>Old age was viewed as a process of becoming "cold and dry," so health depended on "hot and moist" nourishment.</note>. They should constantly refresh their spirit with scents, especially that of wine. They must avoid sleeplessness, hunger, and thirst, as well as excessive labor of the body and mind, solitude, and sorrow. They should return to music if they have perhaps set it aside; it should never be interrupted. They should recall certain games and habits from their past childhood, insofar as it is proper. For it is very difficult—if I may say so—to rejuvenate the body unless you first become a child again in your mind. 

Indeed, at every age it is greatly conducive to life to retain something of childhood and to always seek out various delights. However, long and profuse laughter should be avoided, for it dilates the spirit too much toward the exterior. But let us return to the elderly: if they feel cold, they should seek aromatic fomentations <note>Warm, liquid-based medicinal applications or poultices.</note> that are both warm and moist. They should remember that "youthful fomentation" mentioned by Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text.</note>, which was indeed first practiced by David <note>A reference to the biblical King David, who was warmed in his old age by the young Shunammite woman, Abishag.</note>, though perhaps practiced too late. 

A wonderful fomentation for an old man is the marrow of still-fresh, warm bread, soaked in Malvasia wine with mint powder, applied to the stomach and often held up to be smelled. Indeed, such bread-marrow alone held the spirit of Democritus <note>A Greek philosopher who, according to legend, delayed his death for several days by smelling warm bread so he could witness a festival.</note> when he was about to expire, keeping his "fugitive" soul for as long as he wished. 

Furthermore, they should use light rubbing <note>original: "frictionibus"; therapeutic massage to stimulate the humors.</note> or occasional baths that draw nourishment to the extremities. Above all, they should make a habit of eating pine nuts—washed, of course—for ancient physicians approved of this as the most obvious nourishment for the elderly. For it is hot, moist, and fatty; it soothes all internal roughness and, at the same time (which is marvelous), while it increases natural moisture, it also dries up superfluous moisture and purges putrid humors. Some give one drachm <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce.</note> of these pine nuts to the elderly to be eaten daily after meals; I also recommend two drachms for the elderly on an empty sto...

It is certain that the elderly ought to make frequent use of the select juice of licorice. For they say that licorice is very similar to the heat and moisture of the human body, and furthermore, it assists with various diseases of the elderly. Almond milk and food made of starch should also be familiar fare, as well as sugar and raisins.
