Avicenna <note>original: "Auicenna"; a 11th-century Persian physician and philosopher</note> praises the greater and lesser trifera of myrobalans; again, he orders a confection of iron scales <note>original: "squama ferri"; iron filings were often used as a tonic</note>, and most especially he commands that one eat gold daily, and particularly Chebulic myrobalans <note>original: "chebulas"</note> properly preserved, to postpone the inconveniences of old age.

### *On the necessary natures of aromatics and cordials, and again regarding*

For this reason, some might think that the Tree of Life in Paradise was perhaps a myrobalan tree. ### BOOK II.

...provide the capacity for illumination through their aromatic virtue. But you must remember that aromatics are most beneficial to us for life—as we have indicated above—when they are equally moist and warm, possessing a certain aromatic vigor and a fatty smoothness suitable for growth. Such are, primarily, the roots of white behen <note>original: "beeniæ albæ"; likely referring to *Centaurea behen* or *Silene behen*, roots used in medieval medicine to strengthen the heart</note> as well as the red ones, especially when fresh. Alternatively, they are beneficial when they possess a dense substance and a strongly styptic <term>styptic: an astringent quality that contracts tissues or stops bleeding, often used here to "bind" the vital spirits to the body</term> property alongside a subtle, fragrant, and sharp virtue. This quality is seen primarily among the cold cordials <term>cordials: medicines or drinks intended to stimulate or support the heart</term> in myrobalans <note>original: "myrobalanis"; a dried fruit used to balance the humors</note> and amber, then in roses and rose juice, citrus seed, and thirdly in sandalwood, coriander, myrtle, and other similar things.

Among the warm cordials, however, this quality is found in zedoary <note>original: "zedoariæ"; a root related to turmeric and ginger</note>, aloeswood, citrus peel, cloves, nutmeg, mace, frankincense, mastic, and leopard's bane <note>original: "doronico"</note>; we also experience this in sage. They say that musk and ambergris <note>original: "ambram"; referring to ambergris, a rare substance from the sperm whale used in perfumes and medicine</note> also possess a styptic virtue. Ginger, however, on account of its particular moisture, especially when fresh and preserved, is often beneficial to the elderly; but this, and cloves, must be taken cautiously because of the vehemence of their heat. Zedoary must also be used cautiously, even though it is judged similar to theriac <note>a famous polypharmaceutical "universal cure"</note> and has a nature that is both styptic and fatty, making it most suitable for the elderly. Ambergris, because of its nearly tempered heat, is taken quite safely; because of its smoothness mixed with a styptic subtlety, it has a special prerogative for strengthening life in the limbs and the spirits. Indeed, if a water is made from it and the skin is washed, it restores the fourth digestion <term>fourth digestion: in Galenic medicine, the final stage of nutrition occurring within the tissues and organs themselves</term> and expels diseases resulting from its failure.

Truly aromatic substances that have a very subtle substance, such as cinnamon and saffron, should be mixed with cold and harder cordials. For if aromatics are only warm and subtle and are taken alone, they excite the natural heat too much and dissolve the humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health</term>. Nevertheless, they are necessary for digesting colder and moister meals, and for transporting the hard cordials to the precordia <note>original: "præcordia"; the region of the body around the heart and diaphragm</note>. For it should not escape your notice that the humor necessary for life itself has its primary seat in the heart, its arteries, and its veins. Isaac <note>likely Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher</note> teaches this clearly, and (as Avicenna <note>the famous Persian polymath and physician</note> proves) this humor is frequently irrigated and cherished by the natural humor of the other members. Therefore, one must take care lest the humor of any member should dry out by some accident, and much more so lest the humor of the heart's region be diminished.

And so that nutrients, or fomentations, and all cordials may be carried most widely through the narrow passages to the heart's region, include saffron among them. To ensure they stay there, however, employ myrobalans. But to achieve both, take musk and ambergris among the warm substances, and roses and myrtle among the cold. Remember that sweet fennel <note>original: "maratrum"</note> will be of benefit to the elderly. For it both spreads nourishment through the limbs and, by its power...

### *On gold, golden foods, and the restoration of the elderly. Chapter 10.*

Everyone approves of gold above all else, as it is the most temperate of all things and the safest from corruption. It is consecrated to the Sun because of its brilliance, and to Jupiter because of its temperance; therefore, it is able to wonderfully balance natural heat with moisture, preserve the humors from corruption, and bring a solar and jovial virtue to the spirits and limbs. However, they desire to make the very hard substance of gold more subtle <term>subtle: in alchemy and early medicine, this refers to making a substance "thinner" or more refined so it can penetrate the body's channels</term> and very easy to penetrate. For they know that heart-strengthening medicines <note>original: "cordialia"</note> most effectively restore the hidden power of the heart when the heart is least fatigued in attracting them—either because they have already been made very refined, or because they are administered alongside very refined substances. They think it would be best if "potable gold" <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary alchemical life-extending elixir</note> were made without any foreign mixture; but if that is not possible, they wish for it to be taken crushed and reduced into leaves.

You will have a nearly potable gold, so to speak, if you follow this: collect the flowers of borage, bugloss, and melissa (which we call lemon-balm <note>original: "citrariam"</note>). When the moon enters the sign of Leo, or Aries, or Sagittarius, and looks upon the Sun or Jupiter, dissolve these flowers with white sugar and rose water. For every ounce of this mixture, carefully insert three leaves of gold; take this while fasting with a certain "golden wine."

Likewise, take the water distilling from a capon <note>original: "capone"; a castrated rooster, considered more nourishing and temperate in medieval medicine</note> over a fire, or otherwise consumed, together with rose julep <term>julep: a sweet medicinal syrup</term> in which you have previously crushed some gold leaves. Furthermore, extinguish glowing gold in the clearest spring water; with that same water, crush leaves of gold; with the same, temper "golden wine"; and along with a drink of this kind, eat a fresh egg yolk. Indeed, you will easily preserve the humor in the whole "tree of the body" if you preserve it in the roots.

Take, therefore, the heart, liver, stomach, testicles, and brain of hens, chicks, and capons of this sort; cook them in a little water with a very small amount of salt. Once cooked, crush them—using all the meat and all the broth—and with sugar and a fresh egg yolk added, make a small cake seasoned with a little cinnamon and saffron, and gilded with gold. Eat this when hungry at least once every fourth day, and then eat it alone, though with clear wine added for your drink.

Then, first of all, this human tree must be irrigated with a human and youthful liquid so that it may turn green again. You shall therefore choose a girl who is healthy, beautiful, cheerful, and temperate...

...tempered, and while hungry, let him suck her milk <note>original: "lac eius sugito"; Ficino is referring to the milk of a young, healthy woman, a common Renaissance recommendation for the elderly</note> while the Moon is waxing, and immediately eat a small amount of sweet fennel <note>original: "maratri dulcis"</note> powder properly prepared with sugar. As for those whom senile wasting <note>original: "hectica senilis"; a chronic, consuming fever associated with old age and the drying out of "radical moisture"</note> consumes, diligent physicians strive to restore them with the liquid of human blood, which has been distilled by a sublime art over a fire. Why, therefore, should we not occasionally refresh those who are already almost finished by old age with this drink?

There is a certain common and ancient opinion that certain old hags—sorceresses who are called *striges* <note>original: "striges"; in folklore, these were screech-owl-like witches believed to suck the blood of infants</note> in the common tongue—suck the blood of infants so that they may become young again as much as possible. Why should our elderly, clearly destitute of all other help, not also suck the blood of a youth? Of a willing youth, I say, healthy, happy, and temperate, whose blood is indeed of the best quality but perhaps too abundant. They shall therefore suck, in the manner of leeches <note>original: "more hirudinum"</note>, one or two ounces from a barely opened vein in the left arm; then let them immediately take an equal amount of sugar and wine, and they should do this while hungry and thirsty during a waxing Moon. 

If raw blood is difficult to digest, let it be cooked first together with sugar, or let it be moderately distilled with sugar over hot water, and then drunk. To warm the stomach then with pig's blood is also a ready aid; let a sponge soaked in warm wine soak up that blood as it flows from the pig’s vein, and let it be applied warm to the stomach at once. 

Galen <note>original: "Galenus"; a prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> and Serapio <note>original: "Serapio"; likely referring to Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Christian Syrian physician</note> say that the bite of a rabid dog is cured by drinking dog's blood, though it did not please them to assign a reason for it. I, therefore, searching for a reason for two days, finally think that the poisonous saliva of the rabid dog, pressed into a person's injured foot, gradually ascends through the veins to the heart like a poison, unless something distracts it in the meantime. If, therefore, in the meantime he drinks the blood of another dog, that raw blood floats in the stomach for many hours, as he is eventually bound to expel it through the bowels as a foreign substance. Meanwhile, this canine blood diverts the canine saliva—which was grasping at the upper limbs—to the stomach before it can reach the heart. For there is a power in canine blood to attract the saliva of a dog, and in the saliva, in turn, a power to pursue similar blood. The poison, therefore, being removed from the heart and absorbed into the blood floating in the bowels, is led down through the lower parts along with the blood, and thus leaves the man unharmed. 

Why all this? First, so that I might reveal a supporting cause for such an occult <term>occult: hidden or secret; referring to natural forces that are not immediately visible</term> matter while discussing it; second, so that I may advise that blood can be drunk, and indeed healthily. And that there is a virtue in human blood which attracts human blood and mutually pursues it, lest perhaps you doubt that youthful blood drunk by an old man can be drawn to the veins and limbs, and there be of the greatest benefit.

### On Gold, Golden Foods, and the Recreation of the Elderly. Chapter X.

All people approve of gold above all things, as it is the most temperate of all matters and safest from corruption. It is consecrated to the Sun on account of its splendor, and to Jupiter on account of its temperance; therefore, it is able to wonderfully balance natural heat with moisture, preserve the humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that governed health</term> from corruption, and bestow solar and jovial power upon the spirits and limbs.

### Diet, habitation, and the company of the elderly. Chapter XII.

It is beneficial for those in their twilight years to remember that a weak nature must not be burdened by a heavy weight of nourishment, nor distracted by too great a variety of dishes; for even the youthful age becomes senile quickly through this vice. Therefore, let them divide their meals, and refresh their nature not so much with a great quantity of food as with frequent nourishment, though allowing an interval in between for digestion. For often, even after the stomach itself has cooked the food <note>original: "concoxerit"; the ancients viewed digestion as a process of "cooking" food through internal heat</note>, if the liver has not also, as it were, processed the nourishment, it distracts and fatigues nature. When this exhaustion is repeated too often, untimely old age flies toward us. In winter, let the elderly seek sunny spots like sheep; in summer, let them seek pleasant places and revisit streams like birds. Let them frequently dwell among green and sweetly fragrant plants; for these living, breathing things conspire to increase the human spirit <term>spirit: a subtle vapor in the body that links the soul to the physical members</term>. Indeed, let them take refuge in places commonly friendly to bees, and taste honey in winter; for honey is a food primarily friendly to the elderly, except where a burning of bile is feared <note>original: "bilis... incendium"; in the theory of the four humors, honey was considered "hot" and might aggravate a choleric or "bitter" temperament</note>. Very fresh cheese is a friend, as are dates, figs, raisins, capers, sweet pomegranates, jujubes, hyssop, scabious, and betony, but pistachios much more so.

Truly, pine nuts are the most helpful of all, as we have said, from which they will receive the greatest assistance if they keep them in slightly warm water for twelve hours before eating them; for in this way they will not harm the stomach. Furthermore, it is beneficial if, while using these, they also dwell among pine groves, olive groves, and vines, or at least receive the vapor and scent of the pine. Likewise, let them often rub the body with the gum and tears of the pine mixed with oil or wine. For it is probable that trees naturally endowed with a long life—especially if they remain green even in winter—will profit you toward a long life through their shade, vapor, new fruit, wood, and any timely use. We have spoken above concerning long-lived animals. Now indeed, it will perhaps lead to the same result if you live mostly among those who are healthy, similar in nature to your own healthy self, and friends—and perhaps even more so if they are a little younger. But whether and how the frequent company of the young can retard old age a little, the modest Socrates should be consulted <note>Ficino refers to the Platonic idea that the "vital spirit" of the young can refresh the elderly through proximity or conversation</note>.

### What aids the elderly receive from the planets to cherish all their members. Chapter XIIII.

But instead, you anxious old men, consult Apollo, who judged Socrates the wisest of the Greeks. Consult Jupiter moreover, and Venus. Phoebus <note>another name for Apollo, the sun god and god of medicine</note> himself, the discoverer of the medicinal art, will give you nutmeg to cherish your stomach; Jupiter with Phoebus will give you mastic <term>mastic: a resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree used for digestion</term> and mint; and Venus will give you coral. For cherishing the head, Phoebus gives peony, frankincense, and marjoram; and with Saturn he gives myrrh; Jupiter gives spikenard and mace; and finally, Venus gives sweet fennel and myrtle. For cherishing the heart, you shall receive from Phoebus citron, saffron, aloeswood, frankincense, amber, musk, a little leopard's bane <note>original: "doronicum"</note>, cloves, and citron peel.

### The conversation of old men under Venus through green meadows. Chapter XIV.

But from these heavier deities, I recall you old men for a little while through gardens and green meadows to nurturing Venus; I summon you all, not indeed to play with you, but to joke. She pours out this playful oracle for you—and for me, now an old man myself. "I, my children, if you do not know it, gave life to you through pleasure and motion; I, therefore, by a certain pleasure and motion (though not of the same kind as before) will preserve life for you. Liber <note>another name for Bacchus, the god of wine</note>, the planter of vines and propagator of life, will preserve it with that same freedom <note>Ficino plays on the name "Liber" and "libertate" (freedom)</note>. Liber himself always hates slaves, and the long life he promises through wine he fulfills only for the free. Formerly, when Saturn was reigning, a small amount of mint benefited both my life and my mind, and it pleases me daily; but for you, a larger amount of mint benefits the mind and life, while a diminished amount hurts. Gather laughter from my gardens, but neglect the fig. Indeed, when you pluck these violets, imagine that you are plucking lilies; and when you take up the lily, believe you are grasping the saffron."

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the therapeutic use of plants and planetary influences on health. While the previous page focused on specific recipes for different organs (liver, heart, spleen) using herbs associated with Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, this page shifts to a philosophical and physiological explanation of the "color green" and its restorative effects on the "spirit" and the sense of sight.</meta>

### ON THE LONG LIFE

Jupiter himself, having obtained Saffron from Phoebus <note>original: "Crocum à Phębo"; Saffron is traditionally associated with the Sun/Phoebus</note>, propagated it into the lily; looking up to Jupiter, I have transformed that lily into these violets which you see here. Finally, let the rose be your morning star <note>original: "lucifer"</note>, and the myrtle your evening star <note>original: "hesperus"</note>. After this oracle, he commands us to consider the nature of green things; insofar as they are green, they are not only alive but also youthful, overflowing with entirely healthy moisture and a certain vivid spirit. For this reason—through their scent, their appearance, their use, and frequent dwelling among them—a youthful spirit flows into us. Meanwhile, as we walk among these green things, we shall investigate the cause.

Why does the color green soothe the sight above all others and delight it in a healthy way? We shall eventually find that the nature of sight is luminous and a friend to light, yet it is volatile and easily scattered. Therefore, while it expands through light as if toward a friend, it is sometimes snatched away by an excessive surplus of light and dissolved by violent expansion. Conversely, it naturally flees from darkness as if from an enemy, and thus draws its rays back into a narrow space. But the sight desires to enjoy light in such a way that it is indeed amplified by this, its friend, yet not scattered in the process. Now, in any color where there is significantly more darkness or blackness than light, the ray of sight does not expand, and thus it is not delighted as it wishes. Where, in turn, there is significantly more brilliant color than black, the sight is spread too wide, distracted by a certain harmful pleasure.

For this reason, the color green, which tempers black with white more than any other, provides both: delighting and preserving the sight alike. Moreover, with its soft and still-tender quality—just as water resists the rays of the eyes without offense—it prevents the rays from being lost by wandering too far. For things that are both hard and rough break the rays in some way; things that are very thin <note>original: "rarissima"; referring to low-density or porous materials</note> open a path for dissolution; but things that have a certain solidity combined with a gentle smoothness, like mirror-like bodies, neither break the rays nor allow them to be scattered too far.

Finally, besides these benefits, things that are also tender and soft, like water and green things, entice the liquid rays of the eyes with their softness. After all, the ray of sight is something ignited within us naturally in a certain "water" of the eyes; it requires a tempered light in a somewhat resistant water. Thus, the eye rejoices in water, is delighted by mirrors similar to water, and is charmed by green things. In these green things, the light of the Sun surely dwells; they still possess a spring-like moisture and a subtle water full of a certain hidden light—from which it also happens that when the color green is thinned out, it dissolves into saffron-yellow. 

To what end is all this? So that we may understand that the frequent use of green things refreshes the animal spirit <term>animal spirit: in Renaissance medicine, this is the "spirit of the soul" (anima), a subtle vapor that carries out the functions of the brain, including sensation and movement</term>. Since the spirit of sight is in some way the most important part of the animal spirit, refreshing the sight also refreshes the animal spirit as a whole. And let us also remember: if the color green, because it is the middle and most tempered step among colors, benefits the animal spirit so much, then many...

...all the more, those things that are most balanced in their qualities will assist the natural and vital <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, the *spiritus* was a subtle, airy vapor that acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</note>, and will be greatly beneficial to our life. Nothing in the world is more balanced than the heavens; nothing in this body is more balanced than the human body; nothing in this body is more balanced than the spirit. Therefore, through balanced things, the life remaining in the spirit is restored, and the spirit is conformed to the celestial bodies through these balanced things. Finally, let us learn from the balance of greenness, which, by its illumination, equally gathers and expands the animal spirit, and therefore helps it most of all. 

When choosing, composing, and using heart-strengthening medicines, we should also mix aromatic, subtle, and sharp things—which tend to extend or even illuminate the spirit, as do **saffron** <note>original: "crocus"</note> and **cinnamon**—with aromatics that are always styptic and gathering, such as **myrobalans** <note>a plum-like medicinal fruit used for its astringent properties</note> and similar things, and vice-versa. Nor should we omit those things which, even without aromatic sharpness, accomplish both effects at once: they expand the spirit slightly, gather it significantly, and illuminate it greatly. We have spoken of these elsewhere: **gold**, **silver**, <term>spodion</term> <note>original: "spodion"; a medicinal powder made from the ashes of minerals or burnt ivory</note>, **coral**, <term>electrum</term> <note>original: "electrum"; this could refer to amber or a specific alloy of gold and silver</note>, **silk**, and **precious stones**. Among these gems, the **hyacinth** <note>a blue or yellow gemstone, often identified as sapphire or zircon</note>, even when held in the mouth, is highly approved for its Jovial <note>associated with the planet Jupiter</note> balance. Since these most beautiful and almost celestial things cannot be created under the earth without some supreme benefit from the heavens, it is probable that such things possess miraculous virtues from the sky. 

Indeed, a composition of this kind—which equally gathers the spirit while expanding and illuminating it—delights the spirit inwardly and restores it, just as greenness delights the eyes outwardly. It preserves the spirit, even in old men, in a certain natural greenness for a very long time, like the **laurel**, the **olive**, or the **pine**, which stay green even in winter. It does this all the more effectively because it works internally, and especially if such a composition glows with an aromatic scent and entices with its flavor. Indeed, just as the body, composed of the thicker parts of the humors, is reduced to a "fifth form" <note>the <term>quintessence</term>, or the purest, most stable state of matter</note>, so the spirit, constituted from the most subtle portions of those same humors, possesses a fifth form that is naturally most balanced, clear, and therefore celestial. And it must be preserved in this very form, so that it is indeed subtle and yet firm, as we have said—entirely clear, yet also in some way solid. Furthermore, it should be continually fostered with fragrant, firm, and clear things if we desire to preserve the life that flourishes in the spirit and to claim celestial gifts for ourselves. Thus far, having contemplated these things by the command of Venus, let us imagine we have heard Venus herself.

# ON LONG LIFE

...while he urges the mind, pregnant with its own seed, toward birth. You, therefore, mindful of the proverb **nothing in excess**, must restrain the driving urges <note>original: "libidinem" – here meaning an intense, procreative drive of either the body or the intellect</note> of both as they give birth, using the constant reins of prudence. This is necessary even though it harms those whom it weighs down with boredom, sluggishness, sorrow, cares, and superstition much more quickly and severely than those whom it elevates to the heights, far above the strength of the body and the ways of mortals.

By all means, keep (I advise you) what the just Jupiter taught Pythagoras and Plato: that human life is preserved in a certain equal proportion of the soul itself with the body, and that each is nourished by its own specific foods and exercises, and similarly increased. If anyone eventually makes one of the two much stronger than the other through their chosen education, they cause no small loss to life. Therefore, whoever chooses among the highly praised resources of physicians those which benefit the body and the mind at the same time, secures for themselves the greatest aid for life. 

Among their number, consider wine, mint, myrobalan <note>a plum-like fruit used in medieval medicine for balancing humors</note>, musk, ambergris <note>original: "ambram"</note>, fresh ginger, frankincense, aloes, hyacinth <note>referring to the jacinth gemstone, often ground or worn to protect health</note> and similar gemstones, or similar herbs, and those which are equally compounded by doctors for the benefit of both.

But having cut short these somewhat long-winded digressions, I too have approached here as a physician. If flavors taken from things that are no longer living, and likewise scents from spices already dry and devoid of life, are thought to contribute much to life, why do you doubt that scents from plants still clinging to their roots and living will accumulate the powers of life in a marvelous way? Finally, if vapors exhaling from merely vegetable life benefit your life greatly, how much do you think "airy" songs will benefit? These are songs which are harmonic to the truly airy spirit <note>The "spiritus" was thought to be a thin, vaporous substance that linked the physical body to the immaterial soul</note>, still warm with harmony, living songs for the living, perceived by the physical senses, and conceived by rational reason.

Therefore, I hand over to you this lyre fashioned by me, and with it, song—which is Phoebus <note>Apollo, the god of music and healing</note> himself—a consolation for your labors and a pledge of a long life. For just as things most temperate in quality and at the same time aromatic temper both the humors <note>original: "moris," likely a typo for "humores" or "dispositions"</note> among themselves and the natural spirit within itself, and as such odors temper the vital spirit, so in turn similar musical harmonies temper the "animal" (or soulful) spirit. While you tune the strings on the lyre and the sounds, and while you temper the tones in your voice, consider your own spirit to be tempered within in the same way.

And lest I be more stingy than Venus—who grows cold without Bacchus—receive this nectar from Father Liber <note>Bacchus/Dionysus, the god of wine</note> himself through me. Those among you who are especially cold at such times should take, every fourteenth day <note>original: "bis septimo quoque die"</note>, two ounces of Vernaccia <note>a strong white Italian wine</note> or sweet Malmsey <note>original: "maluatici"</note> wine with one ounce of bread, three hours before a meal. Once a day, take one drachm of "sublime water" <note>distilled alcohol or brandy</note> distilled from wine with half an ounce of rose julep <note>a sweet medicinal rose syrup</note>. With this liquid, you may also anoint the skin, and it can be used very conveniently for smelling; and after such nectar, I shall bring you ambrosia as well, received from above...

BOOK II. 153

...received from Jupiter, I bestow this medicine. Take four ounces of myrobalans <note>a plum-like fruit highly valued in medieval and Renaissance medicine for purging humors</note>, three of chebula <note>original: "chebularum" — the black or chebulic myrobalan</note> with rosewater, preserved sugar, an ounce of ginger in winter (but a half-ounce in summer); boil these three gently with the honey of emblics <note>original: "emblicarum" — the Indian gooseberry, another type of myrobalan</note>, and decorate it with seven leaves of gold. ### Confirmation of the things above, and that we ought to avoid constant contemplation and sexual intercourse. Chapter XVI.

Astrologers say that Venus and Saturn are enemies to one another; but since in the heavens—where all things are moved by love and where there is no defect—there can be no hatred, we interpret "enemies" as meaning they are diverse in their effects. Let us set aside other matters for the present; behold, Saturn has placed pleasure for us in the center <note>the internal or profound core</note>, while Venus has placed it in the circumference <note>the external or sensory periphery</note>. Since pleasure is a kind of food for the spirits, Venus and Saturn lie in wait from opposite sides for the flight of our spirit. She, through her pleasure, lures it toward external things; he, meanwhile, through his own, recalls it to the innermost parts. Thus, they pull the spirit apart if they move and scatter it at nearly the same time. 

For this reason, nothing is more destructive to a contemplative or a seeker of knowledge than the sexual act; conversely, nothing can be more foreign to one pursuing the latter than care and contemplation. Indeed, we count the natural philosopher and the religious person in the same rank, as well as anyone deeply preoccupied with their business and subject to heavy cares. From this it follows that if we wish to relieve or comfort someone who is either too occupied by Saturnian contemplation or weighed down by care, and we attempt to do so through sexual acts, games, and jokes—as if through distant remedies—we would strive in vain and even with loss. Conversely, if we wish to moderate someone lost in sexual work or loosened by games and jokes, we cannot easily correct them through Saturnian severity. 

The best discipline is to recall men leaning toward one extreme or the other back to the middle through certain studies and similar remedies of Phoebus <note>original: "Phoebi" — Apollo, representing the Sun, music, and harmony</note> and Jupiter, who are intermediate between Saturn and Venus. But so that we may finally become physicians: just as a flame is commonly extinguished in two violent ways, either blown out by winds or, conversely, as if smothered by ashes, so we either quickly dissipate the spirit through the sexual effect or gradually suffocate it through the Saturnian effect; we often squeeze it out by compressing it, and likewise dissolve it. The spirit, frequently flying to the outermost parts, leaves the innermost parts either empty or foreign to life; but toward the innermost...

## On the nourishment of the spirit, and the preservation of life through scents, aromatics, pure air, and music, especially if all these things are blended together.

### Chapter XVIII.

We read that in certain hot regions, which are filled everywhere with a great abundance of fragrance, many people of slender body and weak stomach are nourished, as it were, by scents alone. Perhaps this is because the very nature of the place reduces almost all the juices of herbs, grains, and fruits into scents, and then dissolves the humors of human bodies there into spirit. Since both of these—namely, scent and spirit—are a type of vapor, and "like is nourished by like," it is no wonder that a person of a spiritual nature <note>original: "spiritalis homo" — referring to a person whose "vital spirits" (the subtle fluids responsible for life and thought) are dominant or refined</note> receives a great deal of nourishment from scents. 

Indeed, nourishment through scents (or whatever kind of sustenance it may be) is especially necessary for the elderly and the thin, so that we might compensate in some way for a lack of more solid and substantial food. However, some people tend to doubt whether the spirit is truly nourished by scents. For my part, I believe that it is perhaps only nourished in this way: unless heavy foods are finally thinned into vapors through digestion, the spirit itself—which we have said is a vapor—receives no nourishment from them. Therefore, wine full of aroma immediately restores the spirit, whereas other things can barely refresh it after a long time. We call that vapor, into which cooked foods are eventually transformed, an "odor" because every scent is a type of vapor; and this vapor drawn inside from food, unless it pleases the spirit with a certain scent, hardly offers that spirit any nourishment. 

For this reason, we strongly approve of our <term>Avicenna<note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the primary medical textbook in Europe during the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note></term> when he says that the body is nourished by sweetness, but the spirit is nourished by—to use his words—a certain "aromaticity." Since the density of the body can only grow through a dense nature, such as is found in sweetness, the thinness of the spirit cannot be refreshed by anything other than a certain smoke and vapor in which that very aromaticity thrives. We define an "aromatic quality" as something fragrant, sharp, and in a way astringent <note>original: "stipticam" — a quality thought to help "bind" the spirits so they do not dissipate too easily</note>. Furthermore, since the liver provides nourishment to the body through the blood, it is greatly increased by sweetness; but the heart, because it both creates the spirit and produces nourishment for the spirit, rightly desires aromatics. It is...

# BOOK II.

...it is beneficial <note>original: "expedit" — the first syllable was at the end of the previous page</note>, however, for aromatics meant for the heart to be seasoned with sweetness, and for sweets meant for the liver to be mixed with aromatics, while in the meantime avoiding excessive sweetness. What more can be said? Galen himself, following Hippocrates, believes that the spirit is nourished not only by scent, but by air—air, I say, that is not simple, but rather suitably blended. 

If we place our trust in these men, we will judge that no choice of food, nor of anything else, is more necessary for life than the choice of air that is well-suited to us. For air—being very easily and constantly affected by the qualities of both the lower world and the heavens, and surrounded by an immense (so to speak) magnitude, and in perpetual motion, penetrating us from every side—miraculously transforms us into its own quality. This is especially true of the spirit, and specifically the <term>vital spirit</term> <note>In traditional medicine, the vital spirit was a refined substance produced in the heart that sustained life and heat throughout the body.</note> flourishing in the heart, into whose innermost chambers the air flows both steadily and suddenly. 

Thus, the air immediately affects the spirit according to how the air itself is affected; and through the vital spirit—which is both the substance and the origin of the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>The "animal spirit" (from the Latin *anima*, meaning "soul" or "breath") was a further refined vapor in the brain responsible for movement, sensation, and thought.</note>—it likewise affects the animal spirit. The quality of this spirit is of the greatest importance for gifted people who work extensively with this kind of spirit; therefore, the choice of pure, luminous air, scents, and music pertains to no one more than to them. 

For these three are judged to be the primary nourishments of the animal spirit: but choice air is the most powerful for life. Indeed, many born in the eighth month survive in Egypt, and some in the temperate regions of Greece, by the benefit of very healthy air—a fact that Aristotle relates and Avicenna confirms <note>Ancient medicine commonly held that infants born in the eighth month were too weak to survive; the author argues that exceptionally pure air can overcome this biological fragility.</note>. 

But truly, just as the body is composed of various parts and must be nourished by various foods (though not all at the same table), so too must the spirit, being similarly composed, be delighted and fostered by a certain variety of carefully chosen air. It must also be daily refreshed by a similar variety of chosen scents; for air and scent seem to be, as it were, a kind of spirit themselves. 

Now indeed, Alexander and Nicolaus the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>Followers of the philosophical school of Aristotle.</note>, together with Galen, conclude that the vital and animal spirits are nourished by both scent and air because both are mixed and of a similar nature. Both, when inhaled, penetrate into the <term>praecordia</term> <note>Literally the "regions before the heart," referring to the chest or the diaphragm.</note>, where they are "cooked" and tempered for life, and then diffused through the arteries. Once "cooked" there, the air again nourishes both spirits (as they say), but especially the animal spirit.

They also say that breathed air is beneficial not only for cooling internal heat, but also for nourishment; for even very cold animals breathe. They add that thicker air is suitable for the <term>natural spirit</term> <note>The natural spirit was believed to reside in the liver and govern digestion and growth; it was the most "physical" of the three types of spirit.</note> as it is more bodily in nature; but thin, pure, and clear air is better for the vital spirit, and most of all for the animal spirit. Nor should it seem strange...

# ON THE LONG LIFE

<meta>catchword: however</meta>

...it must be considered <note>original: "deri debet" — the full word is "consideri debet," with the first part on the previous page</note> that the spirit, being so refined, should be nourished by refined things, just as many small fish are nourished by the clearest water, and basil lives, grows, flowers, and smells sweet in similar water. I pass over which elements some say the chameleon and the salamander are nourished by. <note>In ancient lore, the chameleon was said to live on air and the salamander on fire.</note> Let us return to our own concerns; it certainly matters as much as possible what kind of air we breathe and what kind of scents we inhale. For the <term>spirit</term> <note>The "vital spirit" in Renaissance medicine—a subtle, vaporous substance that carries life through the arteries.</note> within us becomes like these; and to that extent the soul [anima] gives us life through vitality, as long as the spirit maintains a harmony that accords with the soul. 

Indeed, the spirit is the first thing in us to live, and the most, and it almost lives alone. Does not life, sensation, and motion often suddenly desert the limbs due to some sudden accident or event, when the spirit has retreated into the inner chambers of the heart? And often these return to the limbs immediately through massages and scents, as the spirit returns there—as if life exists in the spirit itself (a volatile thing) rather than in the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health.</note> or the limbs. Otherwise, because of the thick density of the limbs and humors, life would return to and depart from them much more slowly. 

Therefore, whoever desires to prolong life in the body, cultivate the spirit above all else. Increase it with nutrients that increase the blood—refined and clear blood, that is—nurture it with chosen air, nourish it daily with sweet scents, and delight it with sounds and songs. But in the meantime, beware of scents that are too hot, and flee from those too cold; choose temperate ones, tempering cold with hot, and dry with moist. Know that every scent, because it is the most subtle part of a body, possesses some heat; and choose scents from things that are themselves nourishing, such as from aromatic pears, peaches, and similar fruits, and even more so from the scent of warm bread, especially roasted meats, and most of all from wine. 

And just as a flavor that is wonderfully pleasing is the cause or occasion for abundant and rapid nourishment for the body, so you should consider scent to be for the spirit. I would like to remind you again of <term>Democritus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 460–370 BCE) famous for his atomic theory and long life.</note> who, when about to die, in order to comply with his friends' wishes, maintained his spirit for up to four days by smelling warm bread; he would have preserved his spirit even longer if he had wished. There are also some who say he did this with the scent of honey. I believe that if he did use honey, he poured honey dissolved in white wine over warm bread, for the scent of honey is not to be despised. 

For honey is the "flower of flowers"; it nourishes not a little by its very sweetness, and its quality preserves whole things from <term>putrefaction</term> <note>Decay or rotting.</note> for a long time. Therefore, if anyone knows how to eat this as food in such a way that it neither clogs the <term>passages</term> <note>original: "meatus" — the internal channels of the body.</note> with excessive sweetness nor increases the bile through its heat, he will have a sure aid for a longer life; at the very least, use this seasoning for cold and moist constitutions. But, to call you back to scents: whenever you fear excessive suffocation or compression of the spirits—which frequent grief and lethargy tend to cause—embrace surrounding scents. Where, however...

### The Medicine of the Magi for the Elderly. Chapter XIX.

The **Magi**, those observers of the stars, came to Christ, the leader of life, guided by a star; they offered a precious treasure of life: **gold**, **frankincense**, and **myrrh**. These were three gifts dedicated to the Lord of the stars on behalf of the three lords of the planets. They offered **Gold** for the temperament of **Jupiter**, the most balanced of all planets; **frankincense** for the **Sun** <note>original: "Phœbo" — Apollo or the Sun.</note> especially, blazing with both heat and fragrance; and finally **myrrh**, which firms and strengthens the body, for **Saturn**, the firmest of all planets. 

Come here then, all you elderly, to the wise Magi! They bring gifts to you that will also prolong life, just as they once honored the Author of Life. Come, I say, you old men who endure old age with difficulty; and come also you others, whom the dread of approaching old age disturbs; receive, I pray, these life-giving gifts with joy. Take two ounces of frankincense, one of myrrh, and half a drachm of gold beaten into leaves. Crush these three together and mix them into pills with a certain pure, golden wine. Prepare this at the opportune time, when **Diana** <note>The Moon.</note> enjoys the favorable aspect of the Sun or Jupiter. After this, take a small portion of such a great treasure at any dawn, and wash it down with a little pure wine, unless perhaps the summer has grown hot; then it is better to drink rose water. But if any among you fear heat at any time, let him add Chebulic or Emblic myrobalan equal to the combined weight of the frankincense, myrrh, and gold. This undoubtedly [protects] the natural moisture from...

...will protect from putrefaction, this will push away the dissolution of the humors further, and this will nourish, confirm, and strengthen the three spirits within you—the natural, the vital, and the animal <note>In Renaissance medicine, these three "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle substances that mediated between the soul and the body: the natural spirit (centered in the liver), the vital spirit (heart), and the animal spirit (brain).</note>. This will again refresh the senses, sharpen the intellect, and preserve the memory.

### *On the dangers to be avoided, which are imminent from every seven-year period of life. Chapter XX.*

Since astronomers have distributed the individual hours of the day to the planets in order, and similarly the seven days of the week, and have arranged the duties of the planets through the months in the fetus itself, why should we not also arrange the same through the years? Just as **Saturn** ruled the infant while it lay hidden in the womb in the first month, and the **Moon** in the last, so immediately upon birth, with the order now reversed, let the **Moon** lead in the first year, **Mercury** in the second (if you wish), **Venus** in the third, the **Sun** in the fourth, **Mars** in the fifth, **Jupiter** in the sixth, and **Saturn** in the seventh. Thereafter, let a similar order be repeated throughout life.

Therefore, in every seventh year of life, a very great change occurs in the body, and it is therefore most dangerous, since **Saturn** is generally a "stranger" <note>original: "peregrinus" — an astrological term for a planet that has no essential dignity in its current position, often making its influence unpredictable or weak.</note> to us, and the governance then returns from him, the highest of the planets, straight to the **Moon**, the lowest of the planets. The Greek astronomers call these "climacteric" <term>climacteric: from the Greek 'klimakter' (step of a ladder), referring to critical years in a person's life, usually multiples of 7 or 9</term> years; we call them "scalar," "gradary," or "decretory" <note>original: "scalares, vel gradarios, vel decretorios" — terms suggesting steps on a ladder or days of critical decision.</note>. Perhaps in diseases, the planets rule the very motion of the humor or of nature through the days in that same order, which is why every seventh day is called "judicial" <note>The "critical days" in medicine where the course of a disease was thought to be decided.</note> for the same reason, and also the fourth day because it holds the middle position in the seven-day period.

You, therefore, if you desire to prolong life to old age, uninterrupted by such steps, as often as you approach any seventh year, consult an astrologer diligently to learn from where danger may threaten you; then either go to a physician or summon your own prudence and temperance. For even **Ptolemy** <note>original: "Ptolemeus" — Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose works were foundational to Renaissance astrology.</note> confesses that the threats of the stars can be averted by these remedies. He even adds that the promises of the stars can be increased just as a cultivator of fields increases the strength of the earth.

**Pietro d'Abano** <note>original: "Petrus Aponensis"</note> proves with many arguments and the testimony of **Aristotle**, **Galen**, and **Ali** <note>original: "Aly" — Likely the Arabic physician Haly Abbas or Ali ibn Ridwan.</note> that the natural end of life is not determined exactly to the nail <note>original: "ad unguem" — a Latin idiom meaning "perfectly" or "exactly."</note> from the beginning, but can be moved further or nearer; he asserts this both from the influence of the stars and from the quality of the matter. He concludes from these authors and reasons that even a natural death can be delayed both with the "engines" of Astrology and the protections of physicians. Therefore, we do not labor rashly in these precepts, nor should it trouble you to inquire from physicians what your natural diet is, and from Astrologers which star favors your life and when it is well-disposed; and according to that **Moon**, arrange those things you have learned to be beneficial. Nor should you be ashamed to often listen to those who govern themselves not so much by fortune as by virtue...

<column-break/>

<summary>Ficino explains the theory of seven-year life cycles (climacterics) governed by the planets, arguing that medical and astrological intervention can delay natural death. He emphasizes that while the seventh year is dangerous due to Saturn's influence, human prudence and professional advice can mitigate these risks.</summary>

# ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE

...they seem to have achieved a prosperous old age. Furthermore, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose works formed the basis of Western astrology.</note> and other professors of astronomy promise a prosperous and long life by means of certain images <term>images: astrological talismans or amulets</term> made from specific stones and metals, fabricated under a certain star. Regarding these images, however, we are currently composing a commentary on Plotinus <note>A third-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired.</note>—mostly concerning the remaining celestial favor—and we believe this book should be subjoined to this work hereafter, just as we intended this present book to be written after the volume we composed on caring for the health of scholars. 

As for that celestial favor I just mentioned for the preservation of youth, we shall now seek it from **Phoebus** <note>The sun god, Apollo, representing light and order.</note> and **Bacchus** <note>Dionysus, the god of wine and vital heat.</note>, speaking as much as a poet is permitted to speak, and acting as much as a doctor is permitted to act.

> To **Phoebus** and to **Bacchus**, the Sun’s youth is eternal,
> For unshorn hair is becoming to both Gods.

**Phoebus** and **Bacchus** are always inseparable brothers; indeed, they are almost the same. **Phoebus** is the soul within the solar sphere; the sphere itself is **Bacchus**. Or rather, **Phoebus** is the entire circuit of the sphere, while **Bacchus** is that flaming circle within this circuit. Or better still: **Phoebus** is the nourishing light in this flaming globe, and **Bacchus** is the healing heat arising from that light. Therefore, they are always brothers and companions, almost always one and the same. 

And why not? If the Sun in the spring is indeed **Phoebus**, awakening the songs of birds with his own song and tempering the seasons with his lyre, then in autumn the same Sun exists as **Bacchus**, the author of wine. That "Father Liber" <note>An ancient Italian deity identified with Bacchus; the name means "The Free One."</note>, who loves the hills, brings us three things to preserve our youth: first, the sunny hills themselves; second, the sweetest wine from those hills; and third, a perpetual sense of security within that wine. **Phoebus**, the brother of **Bacchus**, bestows three things with equal kindness: first, the daily light; second, the sweet-smelling herbs that grow under the warmth of that light; and third, the lyre and perennial song found in the shade. By these weights and by these threads, **Clotho** <note>One of the three Fates (Parcae) of Greek mythology, responsible for spinning the thread of human life.</note> will no longer be stingy, but will draw out long threads of life for us.

Almost all poets sing of the three **Fates**; we too, though not poets, sing of three things. A prudent **moderation** <note>original: "parcitas" — Ficino is making a pun on the words "Parcae" (the Fates) and "parcitas" (moderation or frugality). He suggests that by practicing moderation, one masters the Fates.</note> in all diet begins a long life for us; a constant moderation in undergoing cares prolongs life; but a moderation that is negligent in enjoying the heavens kills life. **Pythagoras** <note>The ancient Greek philosopher who emphasized harmony, mathematics, and a disciplined lifestyle.</note> celebrates three "temperances" above all; we also celebrate three at present:

1. Maintain **temperance** in your emotions.
2. Maintain **temperance** in your entire diet.
3. Observe the **temperance** of the air.

For by this foresight, and with God’s breath, you will drive far away the imbalance of the humors, which is the cause of early old age and untimely death. That Author of life will breathe upon you, provided you desire a long life only on the condition that you live longer to serve the human race, and especially that you live for Him, by whose inspiration the entire world lives.

->F I N I S.<-

**Vocabulary:** Ptolemy, astronomy, Plotinus, Phoebus, Bacchus, Clotho, Fates, Pythagoras, temperance, old age.

### Preface to the Most Serene King of Pannonia. <note>original: "Pannoniæ Regi." Pannonia was a Roman province; Ficino uses the term to refer to the Kingdom of Hungary, ruled at the time by his patron, King Matthias Corvinus.</note>

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial M depicting two figures in an outdoor setting; one figure is seated on the left while another stands on the right.</image-desc>
MARSILIO Ficino the Florentine to the Most Serene King of Pannonia, ever unconquered. Most fortunate of all Kings, the ancient philosophers, having most diligently investigated the powers of the heavens and the natures of lower things, thought that a man is wise in vain who is not wise for his own sake. Therefore, they seem to have rightfully directed their entire investigation primarily toward obtaining a life for themselves from the heavens. They judged (as I believe) that both the elements and the things composed from them would be known to them in vain, and that the movements and influences of the heavens would be observed with too much rashness, unless these things, known and joined together at once, might eventually lead them toward life and happiness. Furthermore, such contemplation seems to have benefited them first in this present life: for Pythagoras, Democritus, and Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Greek Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker of the 1st century AD.</note>, and whoever else studied this most especially, achieved prosperous health and a long life through the use of the things they had learned. Moreover, it contributed to their future life, both through the propagation of their glory among posterity and through the enjoyment of eternity in the presence of God.

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Book Three of Ficino's work, where he introduces his treatise on astrological medicine to King Matthias Corvinus of Hungary. He argues that ancient philosophers studied the stars not for abstract knowledge, but to practically improve their health and longevity.</summary>

# PREFACE.

*If indeed they finally recognized the ruler of the whole world from its wondrous order, and loved him above all things once he was known. To you, however, your magnanimity, magnificence, and perpetual victory promise a glory that will remain through all future ages; divine clemency promises a blessed life with God in eternity to your distinguished piety and justice; and finally, I have been able to conjecture from certain signs that the fortunate stars have decreed for you a prosperous and sufficiently long life among mortals. But so that they may fulfill what they promise with the firmest faith, and moreover extend it with a more abundant increase, your own diligence and the care of physicians and astrologers can undoubtedly bring it to pass. Indeed, all the most learned astrologers and physicians admit that this can be achieved through science and prudence. Therefore, when I had recently composed a commentary among the books of Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the foundational philosopher of Neoplatonism. Ficino spent years translating and commenting on his "Enneads."</note> intended for the great Lorenzo de' Medici, specifically on the book of Plotinus dealing with the drawing of favor from the heavens, I decided to select that work from among my other commentaries (with the approval of Lorenzo himself) and to dedicate it especially to your majesty. I hope, indeed, that while I look out for your life and prosperity, I shall in the meantime look out for the life and splendor of our age and of the human race. And so that these writings of ours might more powerfully benefit the royal health and prosperity, I thought they should be sent by Valor <term>Valor: Refers to Niccolò Valori (1464–1526), a Florentine nobleman, diplomat, and close associate of Ficino who physically delivered the manuscript to the King.</term> himself. I pray, therefore, most merciful King, that you embrace our Valor, for your nature, virtue, and authority have such power <note>The original Latin "valet" means "to be strong" or "to have power."</note> that without you, Valor himself could not be well <note>original: "absque te nequeat vel Valor ipse valere." Ficino is making a sophisticated pun on the name of his messenger, Niccolò Valori, and the Latin verb "valere," which means both to be physically healthy and to have influence or power.</note>.*

->*July 10, 1489. Florence.*<-

# OF MARSILIO FICINO

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' featuring a seated figure in a robe, possibly a scholar or clerical figure, surrounded by stylized foliate patterns.</image-desc>

**GREETINGS**, ingenious guest; greetings again, whoever you are who hunger for health <note>original: "salutis". The Latin "salus" carries the dual meaning of physical health and spiritual salvation, both of which Ficino aims to provide.</note>, and who make your way toward our threshold. I pray you, eager guest, see first how hospitable I am: it was certainly the duty of one who enters to immediately offer a greeting to the household. I, however, anticipating your greeting, have already bidden you welcome from afar. I have very willingly received you as you enter—though still a stranger—and if you linger with me, I shall, if God breathes favor upon us, grant you the promised health.

You have therefore found a hospitality that is friendly indeed to all, and now full of love toward you. If by chance you carry anything with you contrary to love, if you have any hatred, I pray you lay it aside before you touch these life-giving medicines. For love and the pleasure of your parents gave you life; in turn, hatred and grief take life away. Therefore, for the man whom hateful grief vexes, no place is left anywhere for life-giving medicine. 

For this reason, I no longer address you merely as a guest, but as a friend. The workshop <note>original: "officina". In the Renaissance, this term referred to both a scholar's study and a pharmacist’s laboratory where medicines were prepared.</note> of your Marsilio is somewhat larger than can be confined within only these boundaries <note>original: "cancellis", literally lattices or railings; here meaning the physical limits of the page or specific chapter.</note> which you see here. For it is not circumscribed by this following book alone, but also by the two preceding ones. Indeed, the whole work, in short, is a certain medicine intended to assist your life according to its powers, so that your life may be healthy and long; and everywhere it strives for this through the work of physicians, aided by the heavens. 

Vast indeed are the antidotes, drugs, poultices, ointments, and remedies which this workshop of ours offers for the various temperaments and natures of men. If some of these should perhaps please you less, I grant you those others; do not, therefore, reject the whole. Finally, if you do not approve of the astronomical images— <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "astro-", referring to "astronomical images" or talismans, a controversial topic Ficino defends in the following pages.</note>
astro-

# PREFACE.

...astronomical <term>astronomical: in this period, "astronomy" and "astrology" were often used interchangeably, referring to the study of the stars' influence on Earth.</term> matters—otherwise discovered for the health of mortals—which I do not so much approve as recount. These, you may certainly set aside with my permission or even (if you wish) my advice. But at least do not neglect those medicines strengthened by some heavenly support, unless you happen to disregard life itself. 

For I have found through long and frequent experience that there is as much difference between medicines of this kind and others made without astrological selection <note>original: "delectu astrologico". This refers to the practice of "electional astrology"—choosing the specific time when planetary alignments are most favorable to harvest herbs or prepare a remedy.</note> as there is between pure wine and water. This is so much the case that even an infant born in Florence in the eighth month after conception—in the month of March, at night, when Saturn was retrograde <note>original: "Saturno retrogrado". A planet is "retrograde" when it appears to move backward in the sky. In Renaissance astrology, a retrograde Saturn was considered a particularly "malefic" or weakened influence, especially for a newborn.</note> and rising—a child half-dead, seemed through such diligence to have been restored to life rather than merely saved, by us or rather by God; and that child has now completed nearly three years in good health. 

Now, if I were to recount more stories of this same kind, I would speak the truth; I would assert them not boastfully (which is entirely foreign to a philosopher), but rather to encourage you. But we have addressed you enough, partly winning you over and partly encouraging you. Therefore, let us speak henceforth with Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD) was the foundational philosopher of Neoplatonism. Ficino's "Three Books on Life" is deeply influenced by Plotinus’s theories on how the soul relates to the physical world.</note>, and in this way we shall consult more carefully for your benefit.

In all things treated by me here or elsewhere, I wish only as much to be asserted as is approved by the Church.

ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS

# THE THIRD BOOK 
## OF MARSILIO FICINO, 
### THE FLORENTINE 
### PHYSICIAN, 
### AND MOST CELEBRATED PHILOSOPHER.

->On obtaining life from the heavens, composed by him among<-
->his commentaries on Plotinus.<-

*In what the power of attracting favor from the heavens consists, according to Plotinus: namely, that the soul of the world, and of the stars, and of the spirits <note>original: "daemonumque." In Ficino's Neoplatonic philosophy, "daemons" are not evil demons in the modern sense, but rather intermediary spirits or celestial beings that exist between humans and the divine.</note>, are easily attracted by forms adapted to bodies. Chapter I.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with foliate patterns.</image-desc>
If there were only these two things in the world—on one side Intellect <note>original: "intellectus." In this context, it refers to the pure, divine Mind or the realm of Platonic Ideas.</note>, and on the other Body—but the Soul were absent, then Intellect would not be drawn to the Body (for it is entirely motionless and lacks any impulse toward movement, being most distant from the body), nor would the Body be drawn toward Intellect (being ineffective and unfit for movement by itself, and far removed from Intellect). But if a Soul is placed between them, conforming to both, an attraction will easily occur from both sides and toward both. 

First, the Soul itself is led most easily of all things, since it is the "first mover" <term>first mover: the "primum mobile," or the source of all motion in the universe that is itself moved by its own internal nature.</term>, and is movable of its own accord and spontaneously. Furthermore, since it is (as I said) the intermediary of things, it contains all things within itself in its own way, and is closely related to both sides. Therefore, it is reconciled to all things—even to those things which are distant from one another—because of its relationship to them. For besides the fact that it conforms on one side to divine things and on the other to perishable things, and leans toward both by its disposition, it is meanwhile entirely present everywhere at once. 

Added to this is the fact that the World Soul possesses, by divine gift, at least as many "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: 'rationes seminales' are the generative seeds or formative principles within the World Soul that act as blueprints for every physical thing in the material world.</term> of things as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind...

<meta>catchword: na, (completing the word "divina" or "divine")</meta>

Ficino argues that the Soul contains the "seminal reasons" that allow celestial influences to be channeled into physical objects.</summary>

# PREFACE.

...astronomical remedies, otherwise discovered for the health of mortals—which I myself do not so much approve of as recount—these you may indeed set aside with my permission, and even (if you wish) with my advice. But at the very least, do not neglect medicines strengthened by a certain celestial aid, unless perhaps you have neglected life itself. For I have found through frequent and long experience that there is as much difference between medicines of this kind and others made without astrological selection <term>astrological selection: "delectu astrologico," the practice of choosing specific auspicious times (elections) based on the positions of the planets to perform medical treatments or create remedies.</term> as there is between pure wine and water. This was so evident that even an infant born in Florence in the eighth month from conception, in the month of March, at night with Saturn retrograde <note>original: "Saturno retrogrado." In astrology, a planet is retrograde when it appears to move backward in the sky; Saturn is traditionally associated with decay and death, and its retrograde state was considered particularly weakening for a newborn's vitality.</note> ascending and appearing half-dead, was seen by such diligence from us—or rather from God—to be restored to life rather than merely saved, and has now completed nearly three healthy years. 

Now indeed, if I were to relate more things of this same kind, I would speak the truth; and I would offer them not boastfully (which is entirely foreign to a philosopher) but rather as an encouragement. But truly, we have addressed you enough, partly winning you over and partly encouraging you; hereafter, therefore, let us speak with Plotinus <note>original: "cum Plotino loquamur." Plotinus was a 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism; Ficino's work is essentially an expanded commentary on Plotinus's ideas about how the soul relates to the physical world.</note>, thus finally consulting for you more diligently.

# THE THIRD BOOK 
## OF MARSILIO FICINO, 
### THE FLORENTINE 
### PHYSICIAN 
#### AND RENOWNED PHILOSOPHER,

->Composed by him on how to obtain life from the heavens, found among his commentaries on Plotinus.<-

->*In which is discussed, according to Plotinus, what the power is that attracts favor from the heavens—namely, that the soul of the world, and the souls of the stars and the spirits, are easily attracted by the suitable forms of bodies. Chapter I.*<-

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' featuring scrolling floral or foliage motifs.</image-desc>

If there were only these two things in the world—on one side Intellect, and on the other Body—but the Soul were absent, then the Intellect would not be drawn to the Body (for it is entirely immobile and lacks the impulse of motion, being most distantly removed from the Body), nor would the Body be drawn to the Intellect (since by itself it is ineffective, incapable of motion, and far removed from Intellect). But if a Soul is placed between them, one that is compatible with both, an attraction will easily occur from both sides and toward both things. 

First, the Soul itself is the most easily led of all things, because it is the "primary mover" <note>original: "primum mobile." In Neoplatonic philosophy, the Soul is the first thing in the hierarchy of existence that has the power to move itself, unlike the static Intellect above it or the passive Body below it.</note>, moving from within itself and of its own accord. Furthermore, since it is (as I have said) the intermediary of all things, it contains everything within itself in its own way, and is closely related to both sides. Therefore, it is reconciled to all things—even to those that are distant from one another—because they are not distant from the Soul itself. For besides the fact that on one side it is compatible with divine things, and on the other with fleeting <note>original: "caducis," referring to things that are perishable or subject to decay.</note> things, and leans toward both with its affection, it is meanwhile entirely present everywhere at once. 

Added to this is the fact that the World Soul possesses, by divine gift, at least as many "seminal reasons" <term>seminal reasons: "rationes feminales," or seed-like powers. These are active, formative principles within the World Soul that act as the blueprints for everything in the physical world, corresponding to the eternal Ideas in the Divine Mind.</term> of things as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind...

### ON THE LIFE OF THE HEAVENS. COMPOSED BY [MARSILIO FICINO]

...ns all the reasons, by which reasons she fashions just as many species in matter. Each species, through its own **seminal reason** <term>ratio seminalis: a "seed-like" formative power in the Soul that guides the growth and form of physical things</term>, properly corresponds to an **Idea**, and it can easily and often receive something from that source, since it was created from there by means of that reason. Therefore, if it should ever degenerate from its own form, it can be reformed again by this medium nearest to it, and through that medium, it can be easily reformed from above. 

And if you properly apply to a certain species of things, or to an individual of that species, many things that are scattered but conform to it, you will soon draw down a specific gift from the **Idea** into this material—now so opportunely prepared—by means of the **seminal reason** of the soul. For it is not the **Intellect** itself, properly speaking, that is drawn, but the **Soul**. 

Let no one, therefore, think that through certain materials of the world, certain divine powers <note>original: "numina." Ficino distinguishes between the transcendent God and these natural cosmic powers.</note> are drawn that are entirely segregated from matter; rather, they are **spirits** <note>original: "daemones." In Neoplatonism, these are intermediary beings or spiritual forces that inhabit the air and the heavens.</note> and the gifts of the animate world and of the living stars. Again, let no one wonder that the soul can be "enticed," as it were, by material forms, since she herself made those very baits—by which she is enticed—congruent to herself, and she always and willingly dwells within them. 

Nor is there anything found in the whole living world so deformed that it does not have a soul, or in which the gift of the soul is not present. Therefore, **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, whom Ficino believed was a source of "ancient theology" that prefigured Christianity.</note> called such congruities of forms to the reasons of the World Soul "divine lures," which **Synesius** <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher-bishop who wrote on the magical power of dreams and the sympathy of all things.</note> confirmed were magical allurements. Finally, let no one believe that all gifts whatever are drawn from the soul to a specific kind of matter at a certain time, but rather—according to the opportunity—only the gifts of the **seed** from which such a species sprouted, and of conforming seeds. 

Thus, if a man applies only human things, he does not claim for himself the specific gifts of fish or birds, but rather human and similar ones. He will receive those gifts which belong to such a star and to the **spirit** of that star, and he undergoes the specific influx of this spirit, just as wood prepared with sulfur is drawn to a flame present everywhere. He receives this influx not only through the rays of the star and the spirit, but also through the very **Soul of the world**, which is present everywhere; in her, the reason of every star and spirit flourishes—partly as a **seminal reason** for generating, and partly as an **exemplary reason** for knowing. 

For, according to the older **Platonists**, the Soul built figures in the heavens beyond the stars, and parts of those stars—so that those figures themselves are certain types—and she impressed properties upon all of them. In these stars, figures, parts, and properties, all the species of lower things are contained, along with their properties. In total, she established forty-eight figures: namely, twelve in the **zodiac**, and thirty-six outside of it. Likewise, in the zodiac there are thirty-six figures according to the number of **faces** <note>Also known as decans, these are 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiacal signs.</note>. Furthermore, there are three hundred and sixty there, according to the number of **degrees**; for in every degree there are many stars from which the images there are made. Similarly, images outside the zodiac are divided into many...

Indeed, figures of this kind each have their own continuity from the rays of their stars cast into one another with a certain peculiar property; from these most ordered forms depend the forms of lower things, which are clearly ordered from that source. 

But even those celestial forms, though they proceed as if disjointed from one another, come from the principles <note>original: "rationibus." These are the *logoi*, or rational formative powers, within the Soul.</note> of the soul joined together—and, in a way, changeable things proceeding from stable ones. But insofar as these do not comprehend themselves, they are referred back to the forms in the mind—whether that of a living being or something even more eminent—which do comprehend themselves. These, as manifolds, are reduced to the simplest **One** and the **Good**, just as celestial figures are reduced to the pole <note>The celestial pole, around which the entire heaven revolves.</note>.

But let us return to the soul. When, therefore, the soul generates the specific forms of lower things, she effects those powers through her own principles, with the support of the stars and celestial forms. However, the unique gifts of individuals—which are often as wonderful in some people as they usually are in entire species—she exhibits through similar **seminal reasons** <term>seminal reasons: the underlying archetypes or "seeds" within the World Soul that determine the physical development and unique traits of organisms</term>, not so much with the support of celestial forms and figures, but by the position of the stars, the state of their motions, and the aspects of the planets, both among themselves and toward the stars higher than the planets.

Our soul, indeed, beyond the specific powers of the limbs, brings forth everywhere in us a common virtue of life: especially through the **heart**, as if through the source of fire closest to the soul. Similarly, the **World Soul** <term>Anima Mundi: the "Soul of the World," a spiritual force that connects the physical cosmos to the divine mind</term>, flourishing everywhere, explains the virtue of common life everywhere, especially through the **Sun**. This is why some people place the soul—both in us and in the world—entirely in every limb, but most especially in the **heart** and the **Sun**.

Always remember: just as the power of our soul is applied to our limbs through the **spirit**, so the power of the World Soul is spread through all things by the **fifth essence** <term>quinta essentia: "quintessence," a subtle, celestial substance or ether that is purer than the four physical elements and acts as a bridge between spirit and matter</term>, which flourishes everywhere like a spirit within the worldly body under the World Soul. This power is most especially infused into those things that have drawn in the most of this kind of spirit.

Moreover, this fifth essence can be taken into ourselves more and more if one knows how to separate it when it is mixed with other elements, or at least to frequently use those things that abound in it—especially the purer ones, such as choice **wine**, **sugar**, **balsam**, and **gold**, precious stones, myrobalans <note>a type of medicinal fruit or plum highly valued in medieval and Renaissance pharmacy</note>, and things that smell most sweet and those that shine.
