->DE VITA COELI. COMP.<-
<meta>catchword: tæ (this catchword suggests the following word will begin with "tæ", likely "tæda" or "tædet")</meta>

...only <note>original: *taxat*, likely part of *dumtaxat* from the previous page</note>, such as the work of the fiery rays we clearly see, namely: to illuminate, to heat, to dry out, to penetrate, and to thin out. These effects are very well known to our senses, but these rays possess many more and more wonderful powers and effects; otherwise, the lower matter and our fleeting senses would be considered entirely equal to the divinity of the heaven. 

But who does not know that the <term>occult virtues</term> <note>Hidden properties of objects that cannot be explained by the four elements (hot, cold, wet, dry) alone</note> of things, which physicians call "specific properties," are not produced by elemental nature, but by the celestial? Thus, as they say, the rays can imprint hidden and wonderful powers—beyond those already known—upon images <note>In this context, "images" refers to astrological talismans or amulets</note>, just as they instill them into other objects. For they are not inanimate, like the rays of a lamp, but are living and sentient, flashing out like the eyes of living bodies; they bring with them marvelous gifts from the imaginations and minds of the celestial beings. 

They also exert a most powerful force through their strong affection, the most rapid motion of their bodies, and they act properly and most especially upon the **spirit** <note>The "spiritus" was thought to be a subtle vapor that linked the soul to the body</note>, which is very similar to the celestial rays. Moreover, they act even upon the hardest bodies: for all these things are very weak compared to the heaven. 

There are, however, different powers in different stars, and therefore their rays differ among themselves; besides, in the strikes of rays falling in different ways, diverse virtues are born. Finally, in the mutual meeting of rays—differing here or there, and now or at another time—diverse powers suddenly arise. This happens much more and more quickly than in the various mixtures of elements and elemental qualities, and even much more quickly than in the tones and numbers of a musician harmonizing in different ways. 

If you consider these things carefully, perhaps you will not doubt what they say: that powers are imprinted on images by a certain sudden casting of rays, and different powers from different casts. Is it then so fast? I pass over **fascinations** <note>original: *fascinationes*; the "evil eye" or the ability to influence others through a gaze</note> made by a sudden look, and the sharpest loves instantly kindled by the rays of the eyes—which are themselves a kind of fascination, as we prove in our book *On Love*. I omit how quickly a bloodshot eye infects a beholder, or how a menstruating woman looking into a mirror affects it. Is it not said that certain families among the Illyrians and Triballi kill men by an angry look? And that certain women in Scythia used to do the same? Both the <term>catoblepas</term> <note>A mythical beast whose gaze was fatal</note> and the <term>basilisks</term> <note>original: *reguli*; literally "little kings," the traditional name for the basilisk serpent</note> kill men by the casting of rays from their eyes. 

The marine <term>torpedo</term> <note>The electric ray fish</note> also suddenly numbs the hand by touch, even from a distance through a rod. Furthermore, the little *echinus* fish <note>Commonly identified with the remora or "suckerfish," which was legendary for its ability to stop ships in their tracks</note> is said to stop a large ship by touch alone. The <term>phalangia</term> <note>Venomous spiders, likely the tarantula of Apulia</note> in Apulia also change the spirit and mind with a sudden stupor by a certain hidden sting. What does a rabid dog do, even without a visible bite? What about a broom, and then what about the strawberry tree? Do they not provoke poison and madness by the lightest touch? 

Will you then deny that the celestial bodies—with the rays of their eyes, with which they look upon our things and touch them simultaneously—can immediately perform wonders? Even now, a pregnant woman marks a limb of the child to be born by a touch, [based on] the thing she desires...

<summary>Ficino argues that celestial rays are not just physical light but living, sentient forces that can instantly imprint "occult virtues" onto objects. He supports this by citing natural wonders like the basilisk's gaze and the numbing touch of the torpedo fish.</summary>

### BOOK III.

...noted. <note>original: *tæ nota*. Likely the end of a phrase like *propertæ nota*, "well known."</note> Or will you truly doubt that rays touching things in different ways produce different results? Consider when you gather the herb **hellebore**: whether you pull the leaf downward or upward, by this sudden touch, you cause the hellebore to draw the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine health and temperament.</note> either downward or upward. 

Does not the <term>celestial influence</term> <note>The "influxus" or flow of power from the stars into the material world.</note>—at the very beginning of any thing's generation—bestow miraculous gifts once the "cooking" and "digestion" of the matter is complete? This happens not so much over time, but in a single moment. Does not the favorable "face" of the heaven often cause countless frogs and similar creatures to leap forth from the sands in an instant? <note>This refers to the historical belief in "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to arise from inanimate matter through the heat of the sun and stars.</note> Such is the power of the heaven upon prepared materials, and such its speed. Finally, if fire has this quality—that it accomplishes in the shortest time what other things do over a long time, primarily because it is most like the heaven—who would doubt that the heaven completes great things as if in a moment, even in material that is less prepared, just as a greater flame is accustomed to do? 

Why then do you doubt, they ask, that the heaven acts almost similarly in the construction of an image? You will say (I think), just as I used to say, that the natural steps of alteration are missing here; this defect certainly diminishes the celestial gift, yet it does not seem to take it away entirely. For natural philosophers [physici] do not want an image to be fashioned from just any metal or stone, but from a specific one in which celestial nature long ago began to work naturally toward the very thing desired, and has almost now completed it—just as flame is latent in sulfur. 

The heaven finally perfects this power when this material is vigorously agitated by art under a certain similar celestial influence, and through that agitation it grows hot. Thus, art awakens the power begun there; and while the material is formed into a figure similar to its own celestial figure, it then exposes it entirely to its own "Idea" <note>In Platonic philosophy, the "Idea" is the perfect, spiritual archetype of a physical thing.</note> there, which the heaven then perfects with the same power it had begun. 

It is like presenting a flame to sulfur. Similarly, a certain power for snatching up straw is given by the heavens to **amber** <note>original: *succino*</note>; though this power is often weak, it becomes stronger through friction and heating, and suddenly it snatches the straw. Serapio <note>Likely Ibn Sarabi, a 12th-century physician whose work on "simples" (medicinal herbs and minerals) was widely read in the Renaissance.</note> writes that a similar power is given to the **albugedi stone** <note>A white stone mentioned in medieval lapidaries, possibly a type of chalcedony or quartz.</note>, which is similar to a jacinth, but it does not draw straw until the stone is rubbed with hair. 

Likewise, that Jovian stone, the **bezoar** <note>A stone-like mass found in the digestive tracts of animals, highly prized as an antidote to poison. Ficino calls it "Jovian" because he associates its protective qualities with the planet Jupiter.</note>—that is, "liberator from death"—which we described in the book against the plague, received power against poison from Jupiter from the beginning, but not so strong that it could pass the same power to other materials to be used. But indeed, as soon as it receives the figure of that upper power under the influence of the celestial **Scorpio**, it is thought to suddenly bring back a perfected power against scorpions, which it can then communicate to mastic or incense. 

The same reasoning must be held regarding the jacinth, topaz, emerald, and others: that the crafting of figures has efficacy only when the material agrees with the star and the effect from which the craftsman desires to receive it. And furthermore, where this material is already almost such from the start as you intend to make it through the figure. Therefore, they advise using no materials for images except those very ones which you know already possess almost this same power.

...bt what you desire. <note>original: *bere, quam cupis*. This completes the word *dubitare* (to doubt) from the previous page.</note> And so, they command us to most diligently investigate the powers of gemstones and metals. Meanwhile, remember that among gemstones, the **carbuncle** <note>A red gemstone, usually a garnet or ruby, believed in the Middle Ages to glow with its own light in the dark.</note> which flashes in the dark, and especially the **pantaura** <note>A legendary stone mentioned by ancient writers like Philostratus, said to attract other stones like a magnet and to contain the light of the sun.</note> are subject to the **Sun**; the **sapphire** to **Jupiter**; the **emerald** to **Venus** and **Mercury**; and to the **Moon** as well. Furthermore, they say that metals—besides gold and silver—have hardly any power for these purposes, and that the reasoning in these matters will be safer if you refer pure gold to the Sun and also to Jupiter—to the Sun because of its color, and to Jupiter because of its temperate composition. For nothing is more temperate <note>In the sense of "perfectly balanced" according to the four qualities of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note> than Jupiter and gold. 

Assign pure silver to the Moon, but also to Jupiter; and assign gold mixed with silver to Venus. Furthermore, an "image" <note>An astrological talisman or amulet.</note> will be more effective if its elemental power within its material matches the specific natural power ingrained in it, and if this, in turn, matches another specific power to be received from the heavens through its geometric figure. Finally, you will learn that lower figures and forms are conformed to celestial ones from the fact (as they say) that **Perseus**, holding the severed head of **Medusa**, has usually portended a future decapitation to some. They also do not doubt that, in a similar way, many things—including the Moon and other planets under certain signs—move specific limbs within our own bodies.

### ### How much power figures have in the heaven, and beneath the heaven. Cap. XVII.

But lest you perhaps distrust [this power] too much because of the "coldness" <note>Here, "coldness" refers to abstract mathematical or geometric forms which seem "cold" or lifeless compared to active qualities like heat.</note> of the forms, they will command you to remember that in this region beneath the Moon—the realm of the elements—elemental quality can do a great deal in any transformation tending toward an elemental result: namely heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. However, those qualities which are less elemental or material—specifically lights (that is, colors), and similarly numbers and figures—perhaps have less power for such physical changes, but they have (as they think) a very great value for receiving celestial gifts. 

For in the heaven, lights, numbers, and figures are almost the most powerful things of all, especially if there is no matter there, as most **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed the heavens were made of a "fifth element" (ether) distinct from the four earthly elements.</note> believe. For in that case, figures, numbers, and rays, since they are not supported by any other matter, seem to be almost substantial. And since, in the order of things, mathematical forms precede physical forms—being simpler and less "needy"—they deservedly claim for themselves the greatest authority in the higher ranks of the world (that is, the heavens). Thus, no less is accomplished there by number, figure, and light than is accomplished here by some elemental property. 

A sign of this authority is found even beneath the Moon: for very material qualities are common to many species of things, and when these are somewhat changed, the species itself is not always changed. But the figures and numbers of natural parts possess a property that is inseparable and peculiar to the species, as they were destined from heaven along with the species themselves. Indeed, they have the greatest connection with the **Ideas** <note>In the Platonic sense: the eternal, divine archetypes or "blueprints" of all things in the Divine Mind.</note> in the Mind, the queen of the world, and...

# BOOK III.

...stances, since they themselves, and the various types of numbers, are marked by the Ideas <note>In Platonic philosophy, Ideas (or Forms) are the eternal, non-physical archetypes or blueprints of all things in the material world.</note> specific to that realm, they surely derive their specific powers from there. Therefore, not only are the forms of natural things bound to certain shapes, but also their motions, generations, and changes are bound to certain numbers. And what shall I say about light? For it is either an act of intelligence or its image. Colors, moreover, are a kind of light; for this reason, when astrologers say that light—that is, color—along with shapes and numbers, can have the greatest power in preparing our physical materials for celestial influences, you should not (as they say) rashly deny it. You are well aware that musical harmonies, through their numbers and proportions, have a miraculous power to steady, move, and affect the spirit, <note>In Renaissance medicine, the "spirit" (*spiritus*) was a subtle, airy substance that acted as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul.</note> the soul, and the body. These proportions, established from numbers, are like shapes made from points and lines, but they are shapes in motion. Similarly, the celestial figures behave in their own motion toward action; for these figures, with their harmonic rays and their all-penetrating motions, daily affect the spirit in secret, just as powerful music is known to affect it openly. 

You know, besides, how easily the figure of a grieving person moves many to pity, and how much the figure of a lovely person immediately affects and stirs the eyes, the imagination, the spirit, and the humors. <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were thought to determine a person's temperament and health.</note> The celestial figure is no less vivid or effective. Does not the merciful and cheerful face of a prince in a city gladden everyone, while a fierce or sad one suddenly terrifies them? What, then, do you think the faces of the heavens—the masters of all earthly things—can do in comparison to these? Indeed, even those coming together to conceive offspring often imprint upon the children to be born long afterward the faces not only of how they themselves appear at that time, but even the faces they imagine. For the same reason, the faces of the heavens immediately stain earthly materials with their own marks; and if they sometimes seem to remain hidden there for a long time, they emerge later at their own proper times. 

The "faces" of the heaven are the celestial figures. You may call the figures there that are more stable "faces," <note>original: *facies*. In astrology, these are specific 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac signs.</note> while those that change more frequently you may call "countenances." <note>original: *vultus*. Ficino uses this to describe the more fluid, expressive "look" of the sky at a specific moment.</note> You can likewise call the "aspects" <note>The specific geometric angles (like 60 or 90 degrees) formed between planets that astrologers believe transmit influence.</note> formed by the daily motion of the stars "countenances" and "figures," for they are named hexagons, pentagons, and squares. <note>original: *hexagoni, pentagoni, tetragoni*. These refer to the sextile, quintile, and square aspects.</note> 

Someone might say: "Let it be as you wish; let celestial figures be most powerful for producing effects. But what has this to do with figures and images made by human artifice?" They <note>The ancient Neoplatonists and Hermetic philosophers.</note> will answer that their primary aim is not that our man-made figures should be most powerful in themselves, but that they should be most prepared to receive the actions and powers of the celestial figures, provided they are made at the opportune time under those ruling figures and are modeled exactly after them—for that figure demands this figure. When a certain lute is played, does not another one resound? <note>original: *cithara*. This refers to "sympathetic resonance," where a string vibrates without being touched because a nearby instrument is played at the same frequency.</note> This happens only if it has a similar shape, is placed within sight, and its strings are positioned and tuned in the same way. What else causes one lute to suddenly be affected by another, if not a certain position and a shared shape? The figure of a smooth mirror...

->ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE. COMPENDIUM.<-

...stances, concave, shining, and suited to the heavens, for this very reason receives such a gift from the heavens that it gathers the rays of Phoebus <note>original: "Phębi"; the sun god, often used by Ficino to refer to the Sun itself.</note> into itself in the greatest abundance, and suddenly burns any solid object placed at its focal point out of sight. Therefore, do not doubt, they will say, that a certain material for making an image—which is otherwise very congruent with the heavens—once given a shape similar to the heavens by art, both conceives the celestial gift within itself and then transmits it to someone nearby, or to the one wearing it. 

Not only shape, but also a "permeable" disposition, which they call transparent <note>original: "diaphanam"; referring to substances like glass or crystal that allow light to pass through.</note>, is something ineffective and passive by its own nature. However, since a permeable disposition in the heavens is the proper vessel for light, wherever this is found naturally under the heavens or is prepared in some way, the present celestial light is suddenly acquired and even preserved. Where, along with this, there is either fiery heat (as in a flame) or something simultaneously airy or watery and sticky—as in glow-worms <note>original: "noctilucis"</note>, night-shining creatures <note>original: "nocticernis"</note>, and carbuncles <note>original: "carbūculis"; gemstones like rubies or garnets anciently believed to emit their own light</note>, and perhaps in a certain way in camphor—consider for yourself what follows from this regarding images.

## *What kinds of celestial figures the ancients used to engrave on images, and concerning the use of images. Chapter XVIII.*

Someone might ask, however, which celestial figures they were most accustomed to engrave upon images: for there are forms there that are very conspicuous to the eyes, and have been depicted by many just as they appear, such as Aries (the Ram), Taurus (the Bull), and similar figures of the zodiac, as well as those prominent ones outside the zodiac. There are, besides, many forms there that are not so much visible as imaginable through the "faces" <note>In astrology, "faces" or decans are 10-degree sub-divisions of a zodiac sign, each associated with specific imagery.</note> of the signs, observed or at least devised by the Indians, Egyptians, and Chaldeans. For instance, in the first face of Virgo, a beautiful maiden sitting with two ears of corn in her hand and nursing a boy, and the rest, such as Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar (787–886 AD), a Persian astrologer whose work was a primary source for Renaissance magic.</note> and several others describe; finally, there are certain characters <note>Glyphs or magical symbols representing planetary or zodiacal forces.</note> of the signs and planets designated by the Egyptians. 

They wish, therefore, for all these things to be engraved on images, so that if someone expects a particular benefit from Mercury, he should place him in Virgo, or at least the Moon there in aspect with Mercury. And then he should make the image from tin <note>original: "stanno"; associated with Jupiter, though here used in a Mercurial context</note> or silver <note>original: "argento"; associated with the Moon</note>, upon which should be the whole sign of Virgo and its character, and the character of Mercury; and if you are going to use the first face of Virgo, you should also add the figure we mentioned as being observed in the first face, and similarly for the others. 

The most recent authors of images took their entire form to be round, in the likeness of the heavens; however, the more ancient ones—as we have read in a certain collection of the Arabs—preferred the figure of a cross above all others. They believed that bodies act through a power already diffused to the surface, and the first surface is described by a cross. For in this way, it primarily possesses length and width; and this is the first figure, and the straightest of all...

### BOOK III.

Thus, in the highest degree, it contains four right angles: for the effects of the heavens result primarily through the straightness of the rays and the angles. For the stars are then most greatly powerful when they occupy the four "angles" of the sky—or rather, the hinges <term>cardines; these are the four pivotal points of an astrological chart: the Ascendant, Descendant, Midheaven, and Imum Coeli</term>—namely, those of the east, the west, and the midheaven on both sides. When arranged in this way, they cast their rays into one another so as to form a cross. Therefore, the ancients used to say that the cross was a figure formed by the strength of the stars and a receptacle for that same strength; they believed it held the greatest power in talismans <note>original: "imaginibus"; Ficino uses this to mean medically or magically prepared objects</note> and could receive the powers and spirits of the planets. 

This opinion was either introduced or strongly confirmed by the Egyptians, among whose characters the cross was a distinguished sign signifying "the life to come" according to their custom; they even carved this figure onto the breast of Serapis <note>An important Greco-Egyptian deity representing both abundance and the afterlife</note>. I, however, believe that the excellence of the cross among the Egyptians before Christ was not so much a testimony to the gift of the stars as it was a prophecy of the power it would receive from Christ. I think that the astrologers who lived immediately after Christ—seeing the wonders performed by Christians through the cross, but being either ignorant or unwilling to attribute such things to Jesus—referred this power to the heavens. They ought to consider, however, that miracles are not performed by the cross itself without the name of Jesus. It is perhaps probable that the cross is suitable for talismans because it reflects the strength of the planets and all the stars. Yet it does not possess such immense power for this reason alone, though it may have some effect when joined with other necessary things, perhaps for the prosperous health of the body. But let us return to recounting the opinions of others, as we began. 

For longevity, the ancients used to make an image of Saturn on a *pheyrizech* stone—that is, a sapphire—during the hour of Saturn, while he was ascending and favorably positioned. The form was an old man sitting on a high throne (or on a dragon), his head covered with a dark linen cloth, lifting his hands above his head, and holding a scythe or a fish in his hand; he was dressed in dark clothing for a long and happy life. 

They made an image of Jupiter on a clear or white stone: a man sitting upon an eagle or a dragon, wearing a crown, during the hour of Jupiter while he was favorably ascending in his exaltation <term>exaltatio; a specific sign where a planet's influence is thought to be most potent</term>, dressed in a saffron-colored garment. 

Against fear, they manufactured images in the hour of Mars, with the first face <term>facie; a ten-degree division of a zodiac sign</term> of Scorpio ascending, depicting Mars armed and crowned. 

To cure diseases, they fashioned an image of the Sun in gold during the first hour of the Sun, with the face of Leo ascending with the Sun: a king on a throne in a saffron garment, with a crow and the form of the sun. 

For joy and physical strength, they made a maidenly image of Venus holding apples and flowers, dressed in saffron and white, during the first hour of Venus with the face of Libra, Pisces, or Taurus ascending with Venus. 

They made an image of Mercury for wit and memory in the first face of Gemini. Likewise, against fevers, Mercury was carved as a man holding a web <note>original: "tela"; this refers to weaving or a piece of cloth, symbolic of binding the illness</note> in his hand,

# ON THE CELESTIAL LIFE. A SUMMARY.

...holding <note>original: "tenens"; completing the word from the previous page</note>, in the hour of Mercury, while Mercury was rising, they would carve this image into marble and then impress it upon some substance to be taken by the sick; from this, they said every kind of fever was cured. They also made an image of the rising Moon in the first **face** <term>face; a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign, also known as a decan</term> of Cancer for the purpose of increase. The form of Mercury was a man sitting on a throne, wearing a cap and a crest, with the feet of an eagle, holding a rooster or fire in his left hand. 

Sometimes he was depicted as winged upon a peacock, holding a pen in his right hand, and wearing a multi-colored garment. The Moon was depicted as a beautiful girl with a horned head, riding upon a dragon or a bull, having snakes above her head and under her feet; this was used for curing stones <note>calculus; likely kidney or bladder stones</note> and pains of the genitals, and for staunching blood. They made this image in the hour of Saturn, when the third face of Aquarius was rising with Saturn. 

Likewise, they would strike the image of a Lion in gold—a stone rolling in the shape of the Sun beneath its feet—during the hours of the Sun when the first degree of the second face of Leo was rising; they believed this would be useful for expelling diseases. For diseases of the kidneys, one would make a similar image when the Sun, located in the "Heart of the Lion" <note>Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo</note>, occupied the midheaven. This practice was approved by Peter of Abano <note>Petrus Aponensis (1250–1316), a famous Italian physician and astrologer</note> and confirmed by experience, but on this condition: that Jupiter or Venus behold the midheaven, while the harmful planets fall away and are "unfortunate" <note>unfortunate; an astrological term meaning a planet is in a weak position or poorly aspected</note>. 

I heard from Mengo the Physician, a distinguished man, that an image of this kind—made when Jupiter was joined there with the Sun—freed Giovanni Marliani <note>Ioannes Marliani (1420–1483), a preeminent mathematician and physician in Milan</note>, a singular mathematician of our age, from the terror he used to feel during thunder. 

Furthermore, to strengthen health and avoid poisons, they would fashion an image out of silver in the hour of Venus, with the Moon occupying the "angles" <note>the four pivotal points of the chart: Ascendant, Midheaven, Descendant, and Imum Coeli</note> and looking favorably upon Venus, provided that the lord of the **sixth house** <term>sixth house; the section of an astrological chart traditionally governing health, illness, and daily labor</term> looks upon Venus or Jupiter with a trine aspect <note>an angle of 120 degrees, considered harmonious</note> or an opposition, and that Mercury is not unfortunate. They did these things in the last hour of the day of the Sun [Sunday], so that the lord of the hour held the tenth region of the sky. 

Peter of Abano says that a physician can cure the sick through an image, provided that in its making he ensures the angles of the ascendant, the midheaven, and the west are fortunate, along with the lord of the ascendant; by the same reasoning, the second house should be fortunate, but the sixth house and its lord should be unfortunate <note>By making the house of disease weak or "unfortunate," the physician sought to diminish the power of the illness</note>. He also says that health will be firmer and life longer than it was ordained from the beginning if an image is made after examining the birth chart, in which these things are placed fortunately: namely, the significator of that person's life, the givers of life, both the signs and their lords, especially the ascendant and its lord. 

Likewise, the midheaven, the place of the Sun, the **Part of Fortune**, and the lord of the conjunction or prevention <note>the new or full moon immediately preceding birth</note> occurring before birth should be well-placed; furthermore, the evil planets should fall away as unfortunate. He concludes that no astrologer doubts that such things contribute to the prolonging of life. It would be tedious to relate which faces of the signs the ancients observed, and which stations of the Moon they considered necessary in expressing these images. For in the station of the Moon from the seventeenth degree of Virgo to its end, they made images against diseases, and

# BOOK III.

...hatreds, and for a happy journey. In the station <note>original: "statione"; referring here to a Lunar Mansion, a segment of the sky the moon passes through daily</note> from the beginning of Capricorn to the twelfth degree, [they made images] against diseases, discords, and captivity. In the station from the twelfth degree of Capricorn to the twenty-fifth degree, against lethargy and prison. In the station from the fourth degree of Pisces to the seventeenth degree of the same, for curing diseases, for profit, for companionship, for increasing harvests; and in other matters they similarly devised other things, often with a vain curiosity. 

I have only reviewed those things that smack less of the Mage than of the Physician; for I suspect that even medicine of this sort is often vain. For other more legitimate preparations of medicines, however, I believe these mansions of the Moon should be selected. 

And also in Aries at the sixth degree, and again the nineteenth degree, 26 minutes; likewise in Gemini the tenth degree, 51 minutes; in Cancer the nineteenth degree, 26 minutes; in Libra the sixth degree, 34 minutes; in Capricorn the nineteenth degree, 26 minutes; in Aquarius the second degree, 17 minutes; and in the same sign the fifteenth degree, 8 minutes. 

Furthermore, Haly’s <note>Haly Abenragel, a 10th-century Arab astrologer whose work was central to Western astrological magic</note> opinion should be kept in mind: that any sign becomes "alive" as long as the Sun is in it, dominating the others, and its effect occurs above all others, so that you should direct the Moon there to receive the specific gift from it for medicines. To that place, I say—that is, to the sign, the **face** <term>face; a ten-degree subdivision of a zodiac sign, also known as a decan</term>, and especially the degree—so that if you seek the benefits of Jupiter, you should raise the Moon directed toward these or united with them, as long as the Sun illuminates such a place where the Jovian property flourishes; and similarly for the others. 

It would be curious to relate, and perhaps harmful, what images they fabricated—and how—to bring minds together or drive them apart, to bring about happiness or inflict calamity, whether upon one person, a household, or a city. I do not affirm that such things are possible; however, astrologers think they are possible and teach how, things which I do not dare to relate. 

Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, where he describes the life of his master Plotinus, confirms that such things can happen; he relates that Olympius the Mage and Egyptian astrologer attempted such things against Plotinus in Rome, while he tried to *star-strike* <term>syderare; from the Latin 'sidus' (star), meaning to blast or paralyze someone through a concentrated beam of celestial influence</term> Plotinus through images or similar means. But because of Plotinus’s lofty soul, these attempts were turned back upon their author. 

Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath who sought to reconcile science and religion</note>, professor of both astrology and theology, also says in the *Mirror* <note>The "Speculum Astronomiae," a famous medieval guide to which astrological books were safe for Christians to read</note>—where he says he distinguishes the licit from the illicit—that images properly constructed by astrologers acquire power and effect from the celestial figure. And immediately after, he relates their marvelous effects, such as Thabit ibn Qurra <note>original: "Thebith Benthorad"; a 9th-century Sabian mathematician and astronomer famous for his work on talismans</note>, Ptolemy, and other astrologers promise. And he describes images for bringing calamity or prosperity to someone, which I omit by design; and meanwhile he confirms that they can have an effect. Although, as a good man, he condemns the abuse of the art, and as a legitimate theologian, [he condemns] the prayers, fumigations—

# ON LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS. COMPENDIUM.

...and detests those things which certain impious men employ for [summoning] demons by the fabrication of images. Nor, however, does he reject the figures, letters, and words impressed upon images for this purpose alone: that they might receive some gift from a heavenly figure. That such things can indeed be obtained through images was confirmed by Peter of Abano <note>Petrus Aponensis (1250–1316), an Italian physician and astrologer who was often accused of magic</note>; indeed, he even asserted that some region or other was destroyed by that very image which Thabit <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century astronomer and mathematician from Harran</note> relates was crafted by the astrologer Phedica. 

But Thomas Aquinas, our leader in Theology, fears these things more and attributes less to images. For he thinks they acquire only as much power <note>original: "virtutis"</note> through heavenly figures as is conducive to those effects which the heavens commonly produce through herbs and other natural things. This is not so much because such a shape exists in that material, but because such a compound is already placed within a certain kind of artistic form that harmonizes with the heavens. He says these things in the third book of *Against the Gentiles* <note>original: "contra Gentiles"</note>, where he mocks characters and letters added to figures; however, he does not mock the figures themselves as much, unless they are added as signs to summon demons. 

In his book *On Fate* <note>original: "de Fato"</note>, he also says that the constellations give an order of being and of enduring not only to natural things but also to artificial ones; therefore, images may be crafted under certain constellations. But if anything miraculous should happen to us through them beyond the usual natural effects, he attributes this to demons, the deceivers of men, as is clearly evident in the book *Against the Gentiles*. This is especially seen in the short treatise *On the Occult Workings of Nature* <note>original: "de occultis naturæ operibus"</note>, where he seems to place little value on the images themselves, however they are made—and I too, as far as he has commanded, shall value them as nothing. 

To attribute certain wondrous effects of images to the deception of demons is not foreign to the Platonists. For even Iamblichus <note>a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and the soul's relationship to the divine</note> says that those who, having set aside the highest religion and holiness, rely solely on images and hope for divine gifts from them, are very often deceived in this matter by evil demons who appear under the pretext of being good spirits. 

However, he does not deny that certain natural benefits can result from images constructed according to the legitimate principles of astrology. Finally, I think it is safer to trust in medicines than in images. The reasons we have assigned concerning heavenly power on behalf of images may have more efficacy in medicines than in figures; for it is probable that if images have any power, they do not acquire it so much through the shape recently given to them, but possess it through the material itself, which is naturally affected in such a way. 

And if anything new is acquired while the image is being engraved, it is obtained not so much through the shape but through the heating that results from the striking and friction <note>original: "contusione"</note> of the material. This striking and heating, performed under a heavenly harmony similar to the harmony that once infused power into the material, excites and strengthens that very power—just as a breath of air fans a flame and makes manifest what was previously hidden. Just as the heat of fire...

...brings to light letters written in onion juice, which were previously hidden; and letters written on stone with goat fat—completely invisible—appear and stand out as if carved in relief if the stone is submerged in vinegar. Indeed, just as the touch of a broom <note>Ficino likely refers to the plant *Cytisus scoparius* or perhaps a broom made of specific wood believed to have sympathetic effects</note> or the strawberry tree awakens a dormant madness, perhaps some specific crushing and heating alone brings forth the power <term>virtus: the inherent celestial potency or "flavor" of a material</term> latent in the matter, provided it is done at the right moment. 

One should certainly use such celestial timing <note>original: "opportunitate"</note> in preparing medicines; or, if someone happens to want to work with metals and stones, it is better only to strike and heat them than to shape them into figures. For, besides the fact that I suspect such figures are useless, we must not recklessly admit even the shadow of idolatry. Likewise, one should not recklessly use stars—even beneficial ones—to expel diseases very similar to them, for these often increase the ailment. Just as harmful stars sometimes diminish diseases unlike themselves, as Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and geographer</note> and Haly <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer whose work was central to Medieval and Renaissance astrology</note> clearly teach.

### On Making the Figure of the Universe. Chapter XIX.

But why do we omit the universal image itself—that is, the image of the universe itself—from which we hope to receive benefit from the whole cosmos? A follower of those [ancient] practices will perhaps carve an archetypal form of the whole world, if he pleases, in bronze, which he then stamps at the opportune moment onto a gilded silver plate. 

But when specifically should he stamp it? When the Sun has reached the first minute of Aries <note>The sign of the Ram, marking the Spring Equinox and the start of the astrological year</note>. For from this point, astrologers look for the fortune of the world for at least the coming year, as if from the revolution of its own birthday. He will therefore stamp the figure of the whole world upon this very "birthday" of the world. 

Do you see how beautifully an argument for the world having been born once upon a time has occurred to us during this discussion? Since it is reborn every year, don't astrologers measure first where the Sun was in its sign, degree, and minute at a man's birth, and there lay the foundation for the whole chart? And in each subsequent year, as soon as the Sun enters that same minute, they consider the man as if reborn, and from that they predict the year's fortune. Just as they could not do this for a man unless he were, in a sense, reborn, and he could not be reborn unless he had once been born, so we may infer that the world was once created with the Sun positioned at the first minute of Aries. Since a certain fate of the "birthing world" revolves every year through that same position, he shall then fabricate the figure of the world. 

However, he must take care not to carve or stamp the figure on Saturday, the day of Saturn <note>original: "sabbato Saturni die"</note>; for on this day God, the maker of the world, is said to have rested from His work, which He had begun on the ideal day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note>. For as much as the Sun is suited for generation...

# ON THE LIFE OF THE HEAVENS. (CONTINUED)

Saturn was unsuitable, but he had perfected the work in Venus: signifying the beauty of the completed work. But I shall say nothing further regarding the proportions of the world’s structure, for our own **John Pico of Mirandola** <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a close associate of Ficino who wrote *Heptaplus*, a mystical commentary on the Seven Days of Creation</note> has recently expressed the divine mysteries of Moses regarding the genesis of the world in a divinely inspired way. Therefore, to return to our purpose, one should not carve his model of the world on the day or hour of Saturn, but rather on the day or hour of the Sun. He will imprint it on the "birthday" of the year <note>Likely meaning the Spring Equinox, when the Sun enters Aries</note>, especially if Jupiter and **Diana** <note>The Moon</note> are favorable at that time.

Furthermore, they believe it is best to apply colors to the craftsmanship in addition to the mere outlines. There are three universal and at the same time singular colors of the world: green, gold, and sapphire-blue, dedicated to the three Graces of heaven. Green is dedicated to both Venus and the Moon; it is a moist color for moist things, suited to growing things and to mothers. No one doubts that gold is the color of the Sun, and it is not foreign to Jupiter or Venus either. Finally, we dedicate sapphire-blue most of all to Jupiter, to whom the sapphire stone itself is said to be consecrated. 

Hence, **lapis lazuli**, being endowed with this color, has a special prerogative among physicians because of its **Jovian** <term>Jovian: possessing the qualities of the planet Jupiter, associated with health, justice, and balance</term> power against the **black bile** <note>Melancholy, which was believed to be caused by an excess of "black bile" governed by the planet Saturn</note> proceeding from Saturn. It is born with gold and is distinguished by golden flecks; thus, Jupiter is the companion of gold just as he is the companion of the Sun. The **Armenian stone** <note>original: "lapis armenus," likely azurite, a blue mineral often found near copper and malachite</note> has a similar power, possessing a color that is in some way similar to green. 

Therefore, they judge it advantageous, for the sake of receiving the gifts of the celestial Graces, to gaze very frequently upon these three colors. In the model of the world that you build, you should insert the sapphire-blue color into the spheres of the world. They also thought it worthwhile to add golden stars to the spheres in the likeness of heaven itself, and to clothe **Vesta** or **Ceres** (that is, the Earth) in a green garment. 

A follower of these teachings will either wear such a model or gaze upon it from the opposite side. It would be useful to look at a sphere endowed with its own motions, such as **Archimedes** once made, and recently one of our Florentines named **Lorenzo** <note>Lorenzo della Volpaia (1446–1512), a famous clockmaker and astronomer who built a renowned planetary clock for the Medici</note> has crafted; and one should not only look at it but also reflect upon it in the mind. 

Furthermore, in the innermost parts of his house, he will construct a bedroom built into a vaulted arch and decorated with such figures and colors, where he may spend most of his time awake or asleep. And when he leaves the house, he will not look at the spectacles of individual things with as much attention as he looks at the form and colors of the universe. 

But let those makers of images see to these things; you, however, shall fashion a more excellent image within yourself. For when you know that nothing is more orderly than heaven, and nothing more temperate can be imagined than Jupiter, you will hope to attain the benefits of heaven and Jupiter only if you present yourself as most orderly and temperate in your thoughts, affections, actions, and way of life. 

But since we have mentioned celestial temperance, it might perhaps be timely to remember that there is no excess of elemental quality in heaven (to speak in the **Peripatetic** <note>The school of philosophy following Aristotle; "Peripatetic" refers to his habit of walking while teaching</note> manner); otherwise, if it were so composed...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on the vital nature of the cosmos. ### BOOK III.

...if it were not so, it would have been dissolved over so many centuries already; or if it were a simple substance, it would have lost its great size, power, and motion. But indeed, it moderates all things just as it is itself most moderated, mixing diverse things into one. Furthermore, through this very **moderation** <term>temperantia: the perfect balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—which in Renaissance thought was the prerequisite for life and health</term> of its own, as well as the excellence of its form, it has earned its life from the divine. For we see composite things finally attain life only when a perfect mixing of qualities seems to have broken the previous opposition, as we see in plants. 

We see a more perfect life next in animals, insofar as there is in them a **mixture** <term>complexio: the combination of qualities in a living body</term> further removed from opposition than in plants. In humans, for the same reason, there is a life that is perfect and, in a way, already celestial. Indeed, the human mixture has already approached celestial moderation, especially in the **spirit** <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance that connects the physical body to the soul</term>, which—beyond the subtlety of its substance and the moderation of qualities by which it agrees with heaven—has also obtained celestial light. This spirit, moreover, where it is most of this nature, is most especially celestial, and has divinely obtained a celestial life above all others; and insofar as one makes and keeps oneself such in all their lifestyle and law of life, to that extent one receives singular gifts from the heavens.

When, however, we say there is no excess of elemental quality in heaven, we mean either that there is no such quality there at all, but rather the balanced powers that produce qualities, or if there are similar qualities there in some way, they have a temperament like that of air. And when we name certain things there as "cold" or "dry," we accept this in the **Platonic** sense: namely, that "cold" is the name for that which is the cause of the least heat, and "dry" for that which provides the least moisture to us. 

Thus the astrologer **Abraham** <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a renowned Jewish scholar whose astrological works were highly influential to Ficino</note> says that **Saturn** <note>The planet traditionally associated with melancholy, cold, and dryness</note> leaves our body, in a sense, cold and dry, because it brings less heat and moisture than the other planets. By the same logic, the meat of an ox or a hare is warm and moist in its own nature, yet to us it is "cold" and "dry" in its effect. 

From this logical path, receive these two **corollaries**: first, if bodies that are more tempered live more, then the heaven—being the most perfectly tempered—lives the most. Indeed, conversely, from the fact that the heaven is most exactly tempered, one can infer that it possesses within itself the most absolute life; thus, to the extent that other things approach its temperament and life, they are allotted a more excellent life. 

The second corollary is that life is a form perfect in itself, perfecting the body and providing the principle of motion—an internal principle, I say, of motion both driven from within and set free through every part from without. If, therefore, this is what life is, consider anyone **foolish** <note>original: "mentecaptum," literally "captured in mind" or insane</note> who does not recognize that such a form exists in the heaven, which is the most excellent body, always moving in a perfect circle, giving life to all things—and doing so more gradually to those things which have either naturally approached its likeness or daily expose themselves more aptly to its influences.

## **How much power images are thought to have upon the spirit, and the spirit upon them, and regarding the disposition of the user and the practitioner. Chapter XX.**

We have found that if anyone uses **hellebore** <term>elleborus: a potent medicinal plant used in antiquity and the Renaissance to purge the body of "black bile," often associated with madness and melancholy</term> correctly and can bear its potency, it changes the quality of the spirit and the nature of the body through an exquisite cleansing and its hidden properties; it even changes the movements of the soul to an extent, making one feel rejuvenated, as if they were almost born again. For this reason, it is said that **Medea** <note>A sorceress of Greek mythology known for her knowledge of herbs and rejuvenation</note> and the **Mages** <note>original: "Magi"</note> were accustomed to restoring youth with certain herbs—a youth which **myrobalans** <term>myrobalani: dried plum-like fruits used in traditional medicine, believed to preserve health and balance the humors</term> do not so much restore as they preserve. Astrologers believe that favorable images possess a similar power, through which they may, in a sense, change the nature and morals of the wearer and restore them for the better, so that the person emerges as if they were someone else entirely, or at the very least, they preserve prosperous health for a very long time.

Conversely, they believe that harmful images have the power of hellebore when used without skill—a power that is clearly poisonous and pestilential to the wearer. Furthermore, against another person toward whose calamity the images were fashioned and intended, they have the power of a concave brass mirror positioned in such a way that, by collecting and reflecting rays against the target, it burns them from up close or causes their vision to dim from afar. From this has arisen the history, or perhaps the opinion, that humans, beasts, and plants can be blasted by the stars and waste away through the "machines" of astrologers and the sorceries of Mages.

I myself, however, do not sufficiently understand how images could have any power over a distant object. I do suspect they have some power over the wearer, yet I do not think it is of the sort that many people imagine; I attribute this power to the properties of the **material** <note>The physical substance, such as a specific stone or metal</note> rather than the **figure** <note>The engraved shape or symbol</note>, and (as I have said) I prefer medicines to images by a long interval.

Nevertheless, the **Arabs** and **Egyptians** attribute so much to statues and images fashioned by astronomical and magical art that they believe the **spirits of the stars** <note>original: "spiritus stellarum"</note> are enclosed within them. By "spirits of the stars," some understand the marvelous celestial powers, while others understand actual **demons** <term>daemones: in Neoplatonic philosophy, these are intermediary spirits between gods and humans; they are not necessarily "evil" but are supernatural agents</term> who are the attendants of this or that star. Therefore, they think that spirits of the stars, whatever their nature may be, are inserted into statues and images, just as demons are sometimes known to occupy human bodies and speak through them, move them, and perform wonders through them; they believe the spirits of the stars do similar things through images. 

They believe that demons, who are inhabitants of the "worldly fire," insinuate themselves into our bodies through fiery humors, or through ignited spirits and similar emotions. Likewise, they think the spirits of the stars can be inserted into the appropriate materials of images through rays received at the right moment, and through **suffumigations** <term>incense or herbal smoke used in rituals to attract celestial influences</term>, lights, and powerful tones, and that these can perform wonders upon the wearer or those nearby. We, however, believe these things happen through demons—not so much because they are confined by a certain material, but because they delight in such **worship** <note>original: "cultu"</note>. But these matters are discussed more diligently elsewhere. The Arabs relate that our spirit, when it is rightly fashio[ned...]

->### LIBER III.<-

...[we fashion] images, if through imagination and emotion [the practitioner] is most attentive to the work, and is joined to the stars with the **world-spirit** <term>spiritus mundi: a subtle, ethereal substance that Ficino believed connected the physical world to the celestial heavens, acting as a bridge for planetary influences</term> itself and with the rays of the stars, through which the world-spirit acts. Thus joined, the practitioner himself is also a cause, so that from the world-spirit, through the rays, a certain spirit of a particular star—that is, a vivid power—is infused into the image, one that is most agreeable to the spirit of the person working at that time. Such work is also aided by **suffumigations** <term>suffumigationes: the practice of burning aromatic substances like incense to create a specific atmosphere or to attract planetary influences through scent and smoke</term> adapted to the stars, insofar as such fumigations affect the air, the rays, the maker's spirit, and the material of the image in exactly this way.

I indeed judge that certain odors are very similar in nature to the spirit and the air, and when they are lit, they are also consistent with the rays of the stars. If they are **solar** or **jovian** <note>Pertaining to the Sun or the planet Jupiter; Jovian influences were typically associated with health, growth, and justice</note>, they strongly affect the air and the spirit to receive the gifts of the Sun or Jupiter, which are then ruling opportunely under their rays. The spirit, thus affected and endowed, can—through a more vehement emotion—act not only upon its own body but upon a nearby one, especially one that is similar in nature but weaker, affecting it with a similar quality. 

However, I believe the harder material of an image can hardly receive anything at all from these odors or the practitioner’s imagination. Yet the spirit itself is so affected by the scent that one single thing is formed from both. This is clear from the fact that an odor no longer acts upon the sense of smell once it has acted enough; for the sense of smell, or any other sense, is not affected by itself or by something most similar to it. But more on this elsewhere.

Therefore, I believe that the intention of the imagination has power not so much in the *making* of images or medicines, but in their *application* and *use*. Thus, if someone wearing an image (as they say) that was correctly made, or certainly one who uses a medicine in a similar way, strongly desires help from it and believes and hopes most firmly without doubt, then a great heap of assistance will surely come from many sources. For when either the power of the image (if it has any) penetrates the flesh it touches—at least the natural power in its chosen material being warmed—or when the vigor of a medicine taken internally glides into the veins and marrow, it carries a **jovian** property with it. The spirit of the man is then transferred into a spirit of that Jovian effect—that is, through **love**. 

For the power of love is to transfer. **Faith** and undoubting **hope** then firmly establish the human spirit, already so moved, deep within that Jovian spirit and strengthen it. Now, if (as **Hippocrates** and **Galen** <note>The most authoritative physicians of Greek antiquity, whose works formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance medicine</note> teach) the love and faith of a sick person toward an inferior, external physician contribute greatly to health—indeed, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in European universities</note> says this confidence does more than the medicine itself—how much more should we think that emotion and faith contribute to celestial help? This is especially true when they are directed toward a celestial influence already implanted within us, acting inside and penetrating our very core. Now indeed, love itself and faith toward a celestial gift are often the cause of celestial assistance, and in turn love, and

*### On the power of words and song for capturing celestial benefits, and on the seven steps leading to the heavens. Chapter XXI.*

Furthermore, they believe that certain words pronounced with a sharper emotion have great power regarding images, specifically to direct their effect toward the goal intended by the emotion and the words. Thus, to reconcile two people in a most ardent love, they used to fashion an image under the Moon when it was joining with Venus in Pisces or Taurus. Meanwhile, they carefully observed many things regarding the stars and words, which I do not intend to recount here. For we are not teaching love potions <term>philtra: magical charms or potions intended to excite love or lust</term>, but medicines. It is more likely, however, that effects of this kind are accomplished either through Venereal daemons <note>original: *venereos dæmonas*; in Ficino's Neo-Platonic view, these are intermediary spirits associated with the planet Venus</note> who delight in these works and words, or through daemons who are simply deceivers. For they say that **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note> often discovered and exposed *lamias*—that is, certain fallacious and lustful daemons who simulate beautiful girls and entice handsome men. Just as a serpent might suck an elephant with its mouth, so do these spirits suck them out through the mouth and the womb alike, and utterly exhaust them. But let Apollonius himself see to these matters. 

However, **Origen** <note>An early Christian theologian</note> asserts in his work *Against Celsus* that there is a certain and great power in specific words, as do **Synesius** and **Al-Kindi** when they dispute concerning magic. Likewise, **Zoroaster** forbids "barbarous" words <term>barbara verba: foreign or ancient words (often Hebrew, Egyptian, or Chaldean) kept in their original form because their sounds were thought to hold inherent power</term> to be changed. **Iamblichus** says much the same. Likewise, the **Pythagoreans** were accustomed to performing certain wonders with words, songs, and sounds in the manner of **Phoebus** [Apollo] and **Orpheus**. This the ancient doctors of the **Hebrews** observed above all others, and all poets sing of the wonders performed through charms. Even the very serious **Cato**, in his work on agriculture, sometimes uses barbarous chants for curing the diseases of beasts. But it is better to set aside such chants; as for that harmony with which the young **David** redeemed **Saul** from madness—unless one commands that mystery to be referred to divinity—one might perhaps refer it to nature.

Since, according to the number of the seven planets, there are also seven steps through which attraction occurs from higher to lower things, voices hold the middle step and are dedicated to **Apollo**. 
1. The lowest step is held by the harder materials, such as stones and metals, which seem to represent the **Moon**. 
2. The second place in the ascent is held by those things composed of herbs, the fruits of trees, gums, and the members of animals; these correspond to **Mercury**, if we follow the Chaldean order of the heavens. 
3. The third consists of very fine powders and their vapors chosen from the aforementioned materials, as well as the simple scents of herbs, flowers, and ointments, all pertaining to **Venus**. 
4. The fourth consists of words, songs, and sounds, all of which are rightly dedicated to **Apollo**, the author of music above all others. 
5. The fifth consists of the vehement concepts of the imagination: forms, motions, and emotions, representing the power of **Mars**. 
6. The sixth belongs to the discourse of human reason...

discourses and deliberate consultations pertaining to **Jupiter**. The seventh step consists of more precise and simpler understandings, as if already separated from movement and joined to things divine; these are destined for **Saturn**, whom the Hebrews rightly call *Shabbath* <note>original: *Sebath*; referring to the Hebrew *Shabbat*, meaning "rest"</note> by the name of rest. Why all this? So that you may understand that just as from a specific composition of herbs and vapors prepared through art—both medical and astronomical—there results a certain common form, like a harmony of the stars endowed with gifts, so it is with music. From **tones** <term>tonis: here referring to musical pitches, intervals, or modes</term> first chosen according to the pattern of the stars, and then composed according to their mutual suitability, a certain common form is made, and within it a celestial power arises. 

It is indeed very difficult to judge which specific tones suit which stars, and likewise which compositions of tones agree especially with which constellations and aspects. But partly by our own diligence, and partly by a certain divine fortune, we can achieve this in no other way than **Andromachus** <note>Physician to the Emperor Nero and creator of the famous antidote 'theriac'</note> did, who was exhausted for a long time in composing **theriac** <term>theriaca: a complex herbal "all-heal" or antidote used from antiquity through the Renaissance</term> and finally, following his diligence, achieved the power of theriac through divine luck. **Galen** and **Avicenna** <note>The two most authoritative medical writers of the ancient and medieval worlds</note> confirm that this indeed happened by divine intervention; moreover, **Iamblichus** and **Apollonius of Tyana** bear witness that all medicine had its beginning in prophecies, and therefore they place **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the god of both the sun and medicine</note> the prophet in charge of medicine. 

We would bring forward three main rules for this, provided we first warn you not to think we are speaking here of worshiping the stars, but rather of imitating them and capturing them by imitation. Nor should you believe we are dealing with gifts that the stars give by choice, but rather by **natural influence** <term>influxu naturali: the "pouring in" of celestial energy, like heat or light, rather than a conscious decision by a deity</term>; to this manifold and hidden influence, we strive to accommodate ourselves in refined ways, just as we daily accommodate ourselves to receive the manifest light and heat of the Sun in a healthy manner. Indeed, to adapt oneself to the Sun's hidden gifts and wonders is the duty of the wise man alone; but let us now come to the rules for adapting song to the stars. 

**The first rule** is to seek out what powers and what effects any star, constellation, and aspect have within themselves—what they take away and what they bring—and to insert these into the meanings of our words: detesting what they take away and approving what they bring. 

**The second rule** is to consider which star rules most over which place or person, and then to observe what kind of tones and songs these regions and people commonly use, so that you may apply similar ones along with the meanings just mentioned to the words you intend to present to those same stars. 

**The third rule** is to observe the daily positions and aspects of the stars, and under these to explore what kinds of speeches, songs, movements, dances, morals, and acts most people are usually incited to, so that you may imitate such things as best you can in songs that will please a certain heaven and receive a similar influence. <meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s argument in Chapter XXI of Book III, *De Vita Coelitus Comparanda* (On Obtaining Life from the Heavens). Having just compared the composition of music to the composition of a medicinal "theriac," Ficino now explores why music is uniquely effective at capturing celestial power.</meta>

->ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS. COMPENDIUM.<-

But music is indeed the most powerful imitator of all things. For it imitates the intentions and affections of the mind, and it reflects words as well as gestures, movements of the body, the acts of men, and their moral characters. It imitates and performs everything so vehemently that it suddenly provokes both the singer and the listeners to imitate or perform those same things. By this same power, when it imitates celestial things, it wonderfully provokes our spirit to a celestial influx on one hand, and draws that influx to our spirit on the other. 

Furthermore, the very matter of a **harmony** <term>concentus: a "singing together" or musical concord</term> is much purer and more similar to the heavens than the matter used in medicine. For it consists of air—and this air is warm or tepid, still breathing, and in a way living; it is composed of its own specific "joints" and "limbs" <note>original: *articulis, artubuſque*; Ficino views musical phrases and intervals as the anatomical structure of the sound</note> just like a living animal. Not only does it carry movement and display emotion, but it even brings with it a meaning like a mind, so that it might be called a kind of "rational aerial animal." 

Therefore, if a harmony—full of **spirit** <term>spiritus: in Renaissance thought, a subtle fluid that connects the soul to the physical body</term> and sense—should happen to correspond to this or that star (both according to its meanings and its "joints," and the form resulting from those joints, as well as the emotion of the imagination), it transmits no less power into the singer, and from him into the nearest listener, than any other composition. It maintains this power as long as the song preserves its vigor and the spirit of the singer—especially if the singer himself is **Solar** <note>original: *phœbeus*; belonging to Phoebus Apollo, the god of the Sun and music</note> by nature, and possesses a vehement vital spirit of the heart, and moreover, an animal spirit. 

For just as the natural power and spirit, where it is most powerful, immediately softens and liquefies the hardest foods, and soon makes sweet things out of bitter ones, and also generates outside of itself a sprout by the production of seminal spirit—so the vital and animal power, where it is most effective, acts powerfully upon its own body through the conception and agitation of its own spirit in song. Then, by an outpouring, it immediately moves anyone nearby, affecting both its own spirit and that of others with a certain "sidereal property," according to what it conceives from its own form and from a chosen opportunity of time. 

For this reason, many Eastern and Southern people, especially the **Indians** <note>Ficino often cites "the Indians" as people possessing ancient, natural magic due to their proximity to the Sun</note>, are said to possess an admirable power in their words, as they are largely Solar. They possess a power—I do not mean a natural one, but a vital and animal one—that is perhaps the most powerful of all; the same is true of whoever in other regions are most "Solar." A song conceived with this power, opportunity, and intention is almost nothing else than another "spirit" just now conceived within you—a spirit made Solar, and acting both in you and in your neighbor, able to grant you Solar benefits. For if a vapor and a certain spirit emitted through the rays of the eyes (or otherwise) can sometimes fascinate, infect, or otherwise affect a neighbor, how much more can a spirit do so when it flows more abundantly from the imagination and the heart together—being more fervent and more powerful in its movement...

### BOOK III.

It should not be surprising that certain diseases of the soul and the body can sometimes be taken away or brought on in this manner—especially since a **musical spirit** <term>spiritus musicus: the "breath" of music which Ficino believes shares the same nature as the human spirit</term> properly touches and acts upon the **spirit** <term>spiritus: the subtle, vaporous substance connecting the physical body to the immortal soul</term> which is the medium between the body and soul, and it thoroughly affects both with its own disposition. You must concede that there is a wonderful power in a spirit that is singing and aroused, if you grant to the **Pythagoreans** and **Platonists** <note>Ficino heavily relied on these ancient Greek philosophers who believed the universe was structured according to mathematical and musical ratios</note> that the heaven is a spirit disposing all things by its motions and tones. 

Remember, indeed, that all music proceeds from **Apollo** <note>Apollo/Phoebus is the god of the Sun, healing, and music</note>, and that **Jupiter** is musical only insofar as he is in concord with Apollo. **Venus**, moreover, and **Mercury** derive their music from their proximity to Apollo. Furthermore, musical **harmonies** <term>concentus: musical concords or arrangements of sounds</term> pertain only to these four; the other three planets indeed have voices, but not songs.

Now, we attribute slow, deep, hoarse, and complaining voices to **Saturn**. To **Mars**, we attribute the opposite: fast, sharp, harsh, and threatening voices. To the **Moon**, we attribute those that are in the middle. We ascribe deep, intense, sweet harmonies—and those that are joyful with constancy—to Jupiter. Conversely, we attribute voluptuous songs, full of wantonness and softness, to Venus. Between these, we attribute middle harmonies to the **Sun** and Mercury. If they are venerable and simple, along with grace and sweetness, they are judged to be **Apollonian**. If they are somewhat more relaxed along with joy, yet are vigorous and multifaceted, they are judged to be **Mercurial**.

You will, therefore, reconcile each of these four to yourself by their own songs, especially if you apply sounds suited to the songs in such a way that when you have called out to them by singing and playing opportunely in their manner, they seem likely to respond immediately—either like an **Echo**, or like a string on a lute which trembles when another string tuned similarly is plucked. And, as **Plotinus** and **Iamblichus** <note>Neo-Platonic philosophers who wrote about the "sympathy" of all things in the universe</note> wish, this will happen as naturally from the heaven as a resonance or tremor comes from a lute, or as an Echo comes from an opposite wall.

Indeed, whenever through the frequent use of a Jovial, Mercurial, or Venereal harmony—made, evidently, while these planets are ruling—your spirit, by singing most attentively to this very thing and being shaped by the harmony, turns out to be Jovial, Mercurial, or Venereal. In the meantime, it becomes **Phoebean** (Solar), since the power of Phoebus himself, the leader of music, flourishes in every consonance; and in turn, from Phoebean song and sound, you yourself will become Phoebean, while claiming for yourself the power of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury. And again, from the spirit thus affected within, you similarly affect the soul and the body. 

Remember also that a speech aptly and opportunely composed, full of emotion and sense, and delivered with vehemence, has a power similar to songs. It is not expedient to relate how much power **Damis** and **Philostratus** <note>Ancient biographers of the miracle-worker Apollonius of Tyana</note> say certain Indian priests have in praying, nor with what words they affirm that **Apollonius** called up the ghost of **Achilles**. For we are not speaking now about worshiping divinities, but about a certain natural power of speech, song, and words.

That there is a Phoebean and middle power in sound is clear from the fact that those in **Apulia** <note>A region in Southern Italy</note> who are bitten by the **phalangium** <term>phalangio: the tarantula spider</term> all become dazed and lie half-dead until each one hears his own specific sound.

He concludes by noting that speech and specific sounds have natural powers to heal, as seen in the musical cure for tarantula bites.</summary>

### How we can adapt ourselves to the heavens in seven ways; for whom Saturn is harmful and for whom he is favorable; whom Jupiter defends from Saturn; and how the heaven acts upon the spirit, the body, and the soul. Chapter XXII.

Since the heaven is indeed composed according to a **harmonic ratio** <term>harmonica ratione: the mathematical proportions that govern both music and the structure of the universe</term> and moves harmonically, producing all things through harmonic motions and sounds, it is only right that through harmony alone not only humans, but all these lower things are prepared—according to their capacity—to receive celestial influences.

We distribute this harmony, which is capable of receiving higher things, through seven levels: 
1. through **images** <note>astrological talismans or visual symbols</note> (as some believe) harmonically constructed; 
2. through **medicines** tempered by their own kind of consonance; 
3. through **vapors and odors** prepared with a similar elegance; 
4. through **musical songs and sounds**, to whose order and power we wish the gestures of the body, dances, and rhythmic movements to be referred; 
5. through the concepts and elegant movements of the **imagination**; 
6. through the congruent discourses of **reason**; 
7. and through the tranquil contemplations of the **mind**. 

For just as we daily expose the body—through its own harmony, that is, through its position, posture, and shape—appropriately to the light and heat of the sun; so too must we prepare the **spirit** <term>spiritus: the subtle, airy substance that acts as a bridge between the physical body and the immortal soul</term> to receive the hidden powers of the stars. This is achieved through the spirit's own similar harmony, matched to images (as is thought) and certainly to medicines and odors harmonically composed. 

And finally, through the spirit thus prepared for the higher powers (as we have often said), we expose the soul and the body to them. I say the **soul** <term>anima: the immortal life-force</term> insofar as it is inclined by its affection toward the spirit and the body. Within the soul we now place the imagination, the reason, and the mind. Indeed, our **imagination** can be so disposed, composed, and conformed to **Mars** or the **Sun**—whether because of the quality and movement of the spirit, or through our own choice, or both—that it immediately becomes a proper vessel for the **Phoebean** <note>Solar</note> or **Martian** **influx** <note>the "pouring in" of celestial energy</note>. 

Likewise, **reason**—either through the imagination and spirit together, or through deliberation, or both—can prepare itself for **Jupiter** by a kind of imitation. Because of its own dignity and proximity, reason itself receives Jupiter and the gifts of Jupiter much more than the imagination or the spirit do, just as the imagination and spirit receive celestial things far more than any lower objects or materials. Finally, the **contemplative mind** <term>mens contemplatrix: the highest faculty of the soul, focused on divine truth</term>, insofar as it withdraws itself not only from the things we sense, but even from those we commonly imagine, and from [daily] habits...
