BOOK III

<meta>catchword: life</meta>

...we argue, if one withdraws from human affairs and, through affection and intention, calls their life back toward separated things <note>Non-material or divine realities</note>, they expose themselves in a certain way to Saturn. To such a person alone is Saturn favorable. For just as the Sun is indeed an enemy to nocturnal animals but a friend to diurnal ones, so Saturn is hostile to those who lead a common or public life, or to those who, while fleeing the company of the common crowd, do not yet let go of common desires. For Jupiter has been granted the common life, but Saturn has claimed for himself the separate and divine life. Thus, Saturn is in some way a friend to the minds of men that are truly segregated from earthly concerns, as if they were his own kin. For to those spirits inhabiting the sublime air, Saturn himself—to speak in the Platonic manner—stands in the place of Jupiter. Just as Jupiter is a helping father to men leading a common life, Saturn is hostile to none more than those who merely pretend to lead a contemplative life without actually practicing it. For Saturn does not recognize these as his own, nor does the temperament of Jupiter—acting as a balance to Saturn—aid those who flee the common laws, customs, and commerce of men. For Jupiter claimed these for himself (as they say) when Saturn was bound, while Saturn claimed the things that are set apart.

Wherefore those **lunar peoples** whom **Socrates** describes in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the immortality of the soul</note>, inhabiting the most eminent surface of the earth—higher than the clouds—living quite soberly, content with the fruits of the earth, and devoted to the study of secret wisdom and religion, they taste the happiness of Saturn. They lead a life so prosperous and long-lived that they are regarded not so much as mortal men, but as immortal **daemons** <term>daemones: in the classical sense, intermediate spirits or divine beings, not necessarily evil</term>. Many call these **Heroes**, the Golden Race enjoying a certain Saturnian age and kingdom. 

I think perhaps the **Arab Astrologers** intended this when they said that beyond the equinoctial line <note>the equator</note> to the south, there are certain most subtle inhabitants—spirits who seem neither to be born nor to die—and that Saturn and the **Dragon’s Tail** <term>cauda draconis: the South Node of the Moon, often associated with endings or spiritual release</term> have power there. Indeed, **Albumasar** <note>original: "Albumasar"; Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer</note> seems to confirm this in the *Book of Sadar*, saying that certain regions of India are subject to Saturn, and that the men there are very long-lived, passing away only at the most extreme old age. He assigns the reason: that Saturn does not harm his own household, but only outsiders. 

Do not neglect the power of Saturn; for the Arabs say he is the most powerful of all. They say the other planets take on the strength of those planets they approach, but all planets approach him rather than the reverse, and that planets joined to him act according to his nature. For he is the head of the widest sphere among the planets. Indeed, any planet is the head, heart, and eye of its own sphere. Likewise, Saturn is closest to the innumerable [fixed] stars and, being most similar to the **Prime Mover** <term>primo mobili: the outermost moving sphere in the Ptolemaic universe that drives all others</term>, he performs a long circuit. He is the highest of the planets, wherefore they call him "happy" <note>original: "foelicem"; meaning blessed or fortunate</note> whom Saturn favors. And although they mostly venerate him as one estranged from the common life of men, he can nonetheless be appeased even by the common...

# ON THE LIFE OF THE HEAVENS. COMPENDIUM.

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

...they think [Saturn is beneficial] to life, if ever he holds the greatest power and dignity in the **Ascendant** <note>The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note>, or if his **Jupiter** looks upon him favorably, or receives him excellently in his own boundaries. Otherwise, his influence, when received improperly—especially in gross, heavy matter—becomes like a poison, just as an egg becomes poisonous through rot or scorching. From this are born, or emerge, certain filthy, idle, sad, and envious people, exposed to unclean demons; you should flee far from their company. For the poison of Saturn lies hidden elsewhere in a dormant state, like sulfur far from a flame; but in living bodies it often blazes, and like lit sulfur, it does not only burn, but also fills and infects everything around with a noxious vapor. 

Against his influence—which is commonly foreign and somewhat discordant to men—**Jupiter** arms us, both by his natural quality and by his specific foods and medicines, and (as they believe) even by images, as well as by morals, business, studies, and things properly belonging to him. 

However, they escape the harmful influence of Saturn and undergo the propitious one, not only those who flee to **Jupiter**, but also those who devote themselves with their whole mind to divine contemplation, which is signified by Saturn himself. For in this way, the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient Babylonian astrologers and sages</note>, **Egyptians**, and **Platonists** believe the malice of **Fate** can be avoided. Since they do not want the celestial bodies to be empty, but divinely animated and, moreover, governed by divine minds, they surely believe that not only many things pertaining to the body and spirit proceed from there to men, but also many goods overflowing in some way into the soul—not from bodies into the soul, but from souls to souls. 

Moreover, they believe that these things, and more of this kind, flow down from minds superior to the heavens. Among these, if you wish to assign all the reasons why **Moses** commanded the rest of the **Sabbath** to the Hebrews, perhaps beyond the more sublime and secret allegory, you will find that the day of **Saturn** <note>Saturday</note> is unfit for civil and warlike actions, but fit for contemplations; and on that day, divine protection against dangers must be entreated. 

**Abraham**, **Samuel**, and many Hebrew astrologers confess that this protection can be obtained against the threats of **Mars** and **Saturn** through the elevation of the mind to God and through vows and sacrifices, confirming that Chaldean precept, namely: *If you raise your mind burning for a work of piety, you will also save your fragile body.* <note>original: "si mentem ad pietatis opus ardentem erexeris, corpus quoque caducum servabis."</note> 

It is also worthy of consideration what **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who specialized in theurgy, or divine rituals</note> says: that celestial and mundane deities have certain powers in themselves that are superior and some that are inferior. Through the latter, they bind us to the effects of fate; through the former, in turn, they release us from fate, as if they have keys (as **Orpheus** says) for opening and closing. Much more, therefore, does the divinity superior to the world redeem us from fatal necessity. Most worthy of investigation is also that Hebrew practice regarding the slaughtering of animals and things...

# BOOK III.

...and our [ills] to be dissipated by sacrifice <note>Ficino is continuing a thought from the previous page about whether physical sacrifices or offerings can ward off astrological misfortune</note>, and whether evils looming from the heavens can be deflected from us toward our possessions, we leave this for our Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a famous Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of judicial astrology</note> to explore. Finally, whenever we say that the gifts of the celestial beings descend to us, understand this: first, that the endowments of the celestial bodies come into our own bodies through our **spirit** <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" was a subtle vapor that connected the physical body to the soul</note> when it is properly prepared; second, that these same gifts also first flow through their rays into the spirit naturally, or however it is exposed to them; and third, that the goods of the celestial souls partly leap forth through rays into that same spirit and from there overflow into our own souls, and partly come from their souls, or from angels, into the souls of men who are exposed to them—exposed, I say, not so much by some natural law as by the **choice of free will** or by affection. In summary, consider those who—through their vows, studies, life, and character—imitate the beneficence, action, and order of the heavens, to be more like the higher beings and thus receive more ample gifts from them; but those men who are artfully unlike and discordant with the disposition of the heavens are wretched in secret, and finally turn out openly unhappy.

->*That you may live and act prosperously, first learn your natural character, your star, and your guardian spirit, and the place suitable for them; dwell here, and follow your natural profession.*<-

### Chapter XXIII.

Whoever is born of sound mind and master of himself is naturally ordained by heaven for some honorable work and way of life. Therefore, whoever desires to have the heavens favorable, let him first undertake this work and this way of life, and pursue it diligently. For heaven favors its own undertakings; indeed, you were made by nature for this thing above all others which you have done, spoken, imagined, desired, dreamed of, and imitated since your early years—that which you do more frequently and more easily, in which you make the greatest progress, in which you delight above all else, and which you leave behind unwillingly. This is truly that for which heaven and the ruler of heaven begot you; therefore, it will favor your undertakings and breathe life into your existence to the extent that you follow the signs of your parent [star]. This is especially true if that Platonic teaching is correct—in which all of antiquity agrees—that for every person born there is a certain **daemon** <note>original: "daemonem"; here meaning a protective spirit or guiding "genius," not an evil entity</note> who is the guardian of their life, assigned by their very star, who assists in that very duty for which the celestial powers appointed the person at birth. Whoever, therefore, having examined their natural character <note>original: "ingenium"</note> through the signs we have just mentioned, finds their natural work in this way, will have found at the same time their star and their guardian spirit. Following their guidance, he will act prosperously and live happily; otherwise, he will experience adverse fortune and feel heaven to be an enemy. There are, therefore, two types of unfortunate men above all others: one of those who, having professed nothing, do nothing; the other of those who take up a profession foreign to their natural character and contrary to their guardian spirit. The former are sluggish through laziness, while heaven, always active, nonetheless urges them to action; the latter, while they do things foreign to their celestial patrons, [toil] in vain...

<header>ON THE STEWARDSHIP OF CELESTIAL LIFE. COMP.</header>

...struggle when destitute of heavenly patrons. First, this is confirmed by the ancient proverb: "God helps those who act, but is hostile to the lazy"; and second, by a similar proverb: "Do nothing against the will of Minerva" <note>original: *invita Minerva*; a phrase meaning acting against one's own natural inclination or talent</note>. For this reason, I believe Jupiter is entreated in the Pythagorean verses <note>The *Golden Verses* of Pythagoras, a collection of moral exhortations</note> that he might either relieve the human race of so many evils himself, or at least show us what <term>daemon</term> <note>In this context, a *daemon* is a tutelary or guiding spirit assigned to a person, not an evil entity</note> we should use as our leader. 

Accordingly, it would be worthwhile to investigate which region your star and your spirit guide <note>original: *daemon*</note> have designated for you from the beginning to inhabit and cultivate; for there they breathe upon you more favorably. Indeed, that is the place where, upon first arriving, your spirit is somehow refreshed, where your senses remain more vigorous, where the constitution of your body is stronger, where most people favor you, and where your prayers succeed. Therefore, test these things, choose this region, and cultivate it happily; clearly you will depart from here unhappy unless you either intend to return or proceed toward similar places. 

But meanwhile, exercise yourself with frequent movements in this region, and trace certain circles in the likeness of the heavenly bodies; for having been born within such a movement and circuit, you will be preserved by similar things. Furthermore, as far as habitation is concerned, you will find it useful to remember that just as the countryside supplies the city with the food necessary for life, while the city consumes it, so life itself is greatly increased by frequent time in the country—provided you are not seized by boredom there—but it is worn away by both the leisure and the business of the city. 

Regarding both habitation and profession, that teaching of the Eastern <note>Ficino often refers to Persian or Arabic sources as "Oriental"</note> astrologers should not be ignored: namely, that by a change of name, profession, clothing, diet, or location, the celestial influence upon us is changed, sometimes for the better and sometimes for the worse. The Platonists judge that <term>daemons</term> are also either changed, or that we relate to the same one differently here and elsewhere; moreover, the astrologers agree with the Platonists that the guardian spirit of each individual can be twofold: one belonging specifically to his birth <note>original: *geniturae*</note>, and the other to his profession. And whenever a man's profession harmonizes with his nature, the same spirit—or certainly one very similar—is present for both, and from this our life will be more in harmony with itself and more tranquil. But if the profession disagrees with one's natural character <note>original: *ingenio*</note>, the spirit acquired by art is discordant with the natural <term>genius</term> <note>In the Roman sense, a *genius* is the personal spirit assigned to a person at birth</note>, and life becomes laborious and full of anxiety. 

For those who wish to discover what kind of spirit presides over each person from the very moment of generation, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher, c. 234–305 AD</note> seeks a rule from the planet that is the lord of the nativity <note>The "Lord of the Geniture" is the most powerful planet in a birth chart</note>. Julius Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Roman astrological writer</note> says that the lord of the nativity is either the planet which holds the most dignities <note>Astrological strengths or honors</note> there, or, according to a more solid opinion, rather that planet whose house the Moon is about to enter immediately after the sign it already occupies when the man is born. But he does not think the guardian spirit should be sought by that same rule; rather, following the opinion of the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astrologers</note>, it should be sought from the Sun or the Moon. Specifically, from the Sun to the Moon in a daytime birth, and conversely from the Moon to the Sun in a nighttime birth, so that the calculation between these intervals...

<header>BOOK III.</header>

...proceed downward by an equal distance from the degree of the ascendant, and observe at which boundary you stop; for they judge that the spirit guide <note>original: *dæmonem*</note> belongs to the same star whose boundary that is. In short, they are accustomed to weigh the course and fortune of one's life together from the lord of the birth-chart <note>original: *genituræ*</note> and the spirit guide; I have added "fortune," since some calculate the "Part of Fortune" <note>A mathematical point in the horoscope representing prosperity and well-being</note> by nearly the same method. The ancients hoped that their own spirit guide would descend to them from some "pivot" of the heavens—namely from the east, or the west, or the midheaven (both above and below)—or at least from the eleventh or fifth region <note>original: *plaga*; in astrology, these "regions" refer to the twelve Houses of the zodiac</note>. 

The eleventh region succeeds the midheaven above our heads and is nicknamed the "good spirit" <note>original: *bonus dæmon*</note>; it gazes upon the ascending degree from the east by a <term>sextile</term> <note>An astrological aspect where two points are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious</note> aspect. The fifth region succeeds the midheaven of the antipodes <note>The *Imum Coeli* or bottom of the sky</note> and is called "good fortune" <note>original: *bona fortuna*</note>; it looks toward the ascending degree by a <term>trine</term> <note>A highly favorable astrological aspect where two points are 120 degrees apart</note> aspect. In the third place, they hoped that if the spirit guide came from a "falling" region <note>A "cadent" house, usually considered weaker in influence</note>, it would at least come from the ninth or the third. For the ninth is called "God," while the third is called "Goddess"; the former gazes upon the ascending degree from a trine, and the latter from a sextile. They truly dreaded the "falling" twelfth and sixth regions, calling the one the "evil spirit" <note>original: *malum dæmonem*</note> and the other "bad fortune" <note>original: *malam fortunam*</note>. 

We, however, consider it useless to wish for things already past. Instead, we advise that those same regions which the ancients desired for their spirits and fortunes should be observed for the purpose of making the planets and stars effective for us. They should be located in the "angles" <note>The four most powerful houses: 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note>, or in the two "succeedent" houses I mentioned, or at least in the two "falling" houses named before. For it is not without reason that they say the Sun rejoices in the ninth, the Moon in the third, Jupiter in the eleventh, and Venus in the fifth; for these all gaze upon the ascending degree. 

But let us return to the purpose: whether we first investigate the instinct of nature and the spirit guide from that experience and diligence mentioned above, or from this art I have just reviewed, we shall judge anyone who professes no honorable duty to be unfortunate. For one who does not undertake an honorable work truly has no leader for their profession, and hardly any natural leader; for the duty of stars, spirit guides, and leading angels—disposed by divine power for our guardianship—is to act always, excellently, and most widely. Furthermore, as we said above, one is unfortunate if they take up a spirit guide <note>original: *dæmonem*</note> that is different from their own innate genius <note>original: *genio*</note> by choosing a profession contrary to their nature. 

Remember that, according to the dignity of professions, more worthy spirits—or if you prefer, <term>angels</term> <note>Ficino here bridges the gap between pagan "daemons" and Christian "angels"</note>—are received step by step; and in public governance, even more worthy ones. It is possible for a skill and a course of life to be adopted that is not contrary to one's guardian spirit <note>original: *genio*</note> or natural talent <note>original: *ingenio*</note>, nor far removed from it, even if you proceed toward more excellent things. Remember again to enter into friendship with those upon whom celestial graces breathe, which you will judge from the blessings of their soul, body, and fortune. For just as a scent comes from musk, so from a good man nothing but good [comes]...

<header>ON THE LIFE OF THE HEAVENS. COMPENDIUM.</header>

[Nothing] exhales into its neighbor, and often remains infused. However, a gathering of three fortunate people, or even two who wonderfully overflow into one another, would be a marvelous thing. Finally, remember to flee far from the unbridled, the shameless, the malignant, and the unhappy; for these are full of evil spirits <note>original: *dæmonum*</note> or are the instruments of malicious rays from the stars. Like lepers or those carrying the plague, they do harm not only by touch, but even by proximity and sight. Indeed, the very proximity of living bodies is considered a form of contact because of the effective exhalation of vapors driven outward by the heat of the spirit <note>Ficino refers to the *spiritus*, a subtle, vaporous substance in the body that links the soul and the physical form</note> as long as the emotion remains. The company of the wicked and the cruel will be especially pestilential, if it is true that after the vegetative life <note>The basic biological life-force</note> is infused in the month of Jupiter (that is, the second month of gestation), the sensitive soul <note>original: *sensualem animam*; the part of the soul responsible for senses and passions</note> is infused thereafter in the month of Mars (the third month), making it a slave to disturbances. Thus, those who are carried away by passion, being full of Mars, infect those nearby with a "martial" contagion. Conversely, frequent association and continuous dealings with the fortunate and the excellent, as we have said, are customarily of wonderful benefit. They say that Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker from the 1st century AD</note> discovered an old man in Ephesus under whose form a demon was hiding, who by his presence alone was contaminating the whole city with plague. How much the presence of Socrates alone benefited many is testified by Xenophon and Plato.

### *By what means scholars may recognize their natural character and follow a lifestyle agreeable to their spirit. Chapter XXIV.*

Since I am speaking to students of letters, I want each one who is captured by the love of literature to remember first that he is "Mercurial" <note>Influenced by the planet Mercury, the patron of communication and study</note>; furthermore, he is "Solar," insofar as Mercury itself is related to the Sun. This is a common condition for all such men. Specifically, however, beyond the Mercurial nature, whoever excels in the grace of eloquence, wit, dignity, and charm should recognize Apollo and Venus in himself. He who is more inclined toward laws, or toward natural and common philosophy, should not be unaware that he has Jupiter as his patron. But he who is instigated to investigate the most secret things with curious scrutiny should know that he is not Mercurial, but Saturnine <note>Influenced by Saturn, associated with deep, melancholy, and solitary intellectual labor</note>. Under Saturn’s sovereignty are all those who are diligent in any study even to the end, especially those who are negligent in other matters. 

Finally, if it is true—as many physicians and astronomers teach—that the soul endowed with intellect descends into the human conception in the month of the Sun (that is, the fourth month), then those who live primarily by the intellect are from the beginning, and daily become, especially "Solar." Therefore, the favor of these planets must be sought by such men; their medicines should be compounded under the inspiration <note>original: *spiraculo*</note> of these stars, and they should live in their regions. But to you, O learned worshipers of the Muses, I call you first to Apollo, the leader of the Muses. Therefore, whoever among you, most beloved brothers in the love of the Muses, are much stronger and more enduring in mind <note>original: *ingenio*</note> than in body, let them know that in their birth Phoebe <note>The Moon</note> indeed supplied very little matter, but a Phoebian <note>Solar</note>...

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s Book III of "De Vita Libri Tres" (Three Books on Life), specifically the section titled "Apologia," which defends his use of natural magic and astrology. The previous page discussed how the spirits of different people can influence one another. This page concludes a speech to his "brothers" (fellow scholars) about nourishing the "spiritus" and begins Chapter 25, addressing the religious concerns regarding astrology.</meta>

...[nature] has infused a great deal into the spirit. Indeed, daily the humors <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile, which determined health and temperament</note> and the nourishment in the body are for the most part resolved into spirit. Each of you, therefore, is almost entirely spirit—a spiritual person, so to speak, wearing the mask of this small earthly body. You fatigue the spirit before all else with constant labor, so that the spirit must be refreshed more assiduously than other parts of you; furthermore, in old age, when the spirit commonly becomes thicker, it must be restored to its proper subtlety. You know well that a thick body is nourished by the four thick elements; know then that the spiritual body is nourished by its own four thin elements. For this spirit, **wine** stands in for earth; the **scent** of wine takes the place of water; **song** and sound act as air; and **light** offers the fiery element. By these four things, then, the spirit is chiefly nourished: by wine, by its odor, by song, and by light.

But I do not know how, having first begun with Apollo <note>God of light, music, and healing</note>, we have now stumbled upon Bacchus <note>God of wine and divine ecstasy</note>; and rightly so, for we have come from light into heat, from ambrosia into nectar, and from the contemplation of truth into the burning love of truth. Phoebus [Apollo] and Bacchus are certainly brothers and inseparable companions. The former brings you two main things: light and the lyre; the latter likewise brings two: wine and the scent of wine to refresh the spirit. Through their daily use, the spirit itself finally becomes "Phoebean" <note>Radiant or inspired by Apollo</note> and "Liber" <note>original: *liber*; a pun on the name of Bacchus (Liber) and the word for "free"</note>. Therefore, you must prepare yourselves to receive the light of the Sun every day so that, as far as can be done while avoiding "distillation" <note>original: *destillatione*; a medical term for catarrh or the dripping of excess humors from the brain</note> and drying out, you may live as much as possible under the light, or at least in the sight of the light—whether from a distance or up close, whether sheltered or in the open—everywhere tempering the Sun's vital power for your use, and reflecting the Sun at night with fire, not forgetting the lyre and songs in the meantime. Always breathe, whether waking or sleeping, "living air"—air that is similarly alive with light—for you ought to have the pure gift of Bacchus produced through the benefit of Apollo. In the same proportion as you receive light, take wine in abundance, provided that neither distillation nor drying out (as I mentioned) nor drunkenness occurs. Rather, you should partly drink it to wash the mouth where the spirit is to be refreshed, partly wash your hands with it, and partly apply it to the nostrils and temples. We have spoken enough now, brothers, and we have drunk enough; therefore, farewell.

### *Astronomical diligence in procreating children, in preparing banquets, in buildings and habitation, and in clothing, and to what extent it is permitted to care for such things. Chapter XXV.*

But it is also pleasing for a moment to address the severe priest of religion. Tell me, then, what do you condemn in our practices, O Priest? "Whatever," you will say, "detracts from our free will, and whatever derogates from the worship of the one God." I not only join you in condemning such things, but I also greatly detest them. I know that you also curse—and I, moreover, shudder at—those who, when they wish to pray to God, look for that vast Jupiter in the middle of heaven...

### ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS. COMPENDIUM.

...those miserable as they are foolish take refuge under the **Dragon’s Head** <note>original: *draconis caput*; in astrology, this refers to the North Node of the moon, which was sometimes associated with draconic imagery and considered a point of increase or gain</note>, only to be devoured by that very dragon who once fell from heaven, dragging a third of the stars with him. But will you concede that it is acceptable to choose favorable hours for conducting contracts, marriages, conversations, journeys, and similar works? I see that you will not easily agree to these things, for I know not what you fear regarding **free will** <note>original: *arbitrio*</note>. Therefore, even if that great theologian **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on the compatibility of science, astrology, and faith</note> grants these things, and perhaps a certain reason dictates that through the <term>election</term> <note>The astrological practice of choosing a specific time to begin an undertaking to ensure a successful outcome</note> itself (which pertains to the will), celestial things are subjected to our prudence just as herbs are provided to the physician—nonetheless, for the present, I will trust you instead; and as difficult as you now find it to permit these things, I shall just as easily let them go. 

However, as I believe, you have for a long time permitted the observations of the **Moon**, and therefore of the other stars, for the sake of curing diseases and thus for preparing remedies. It is also conceded by you, and furthermore approved, that when the Moon is waxing and increased in light—and not otherwise afflicted by misfortune—one may scatter seeds in the fields and plant vines and olives. Why, therefore, should we not use the benefit of the Moon, of **Jupiter**, and of **Phoebus** [the Sun] for the "planting" (to speak plainly) of a human being? For indeed, we always use the service of **Venus** for these duties—or rather, I should have more correctly said "they" always use her, for to me Venus herself is **Diana** <note>Ficino suggests that while others use Venus for procreation/lust, he remains chaste like Diana, the virgin goddess of the hunt</note>. 

What likewise shall we say of sustenance? Shall it not be permitted and beneficial to produce wine in the autumn, and daily bread and feasts, under a happy star? And if we are unable to wait for the specific <term>aspects</term> <note>The geometric angles between planets, believed to change their influence</note> of the stars while preparing these things, it will at least be expedient to receive them when they are <term>ascending</term> <note>Rising over the eastern horizon</note> or otherwise in the <term>angles</term> <note>The most powerful positions in an astrological chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses</note>—namely the **Sun**, **Jupiter**, **Venus**, and the **Moon**. For in this way all things which we use, being happily affected by the heavens, will happily affect us. Thus far I see you will concede without controversy, unless perhaps you say that in this way our life would be nothing other than perpetual servitude. 

To this I would add: in vain do mortals serve the accumulation of money and honors (to which they are perpetually enslaved) unless, in the meantime, through <term>physical diligence</term> <note>original: *diligentia physica*; here meaning medical or natural care of the body</note> they accumulate more days for their lives. Therefore, let them either serve God alone—which indeed is the highest path—or if they are to serve cares besides, let them indulge in a life that is both strong and long, rather than in vain money and honors. In this, we are in agreement. 

But will they not also build houses rashly, or inhabit ill-fated ones, where a certain contagious calamity of the building infects the inhabitant almost as the poisonous vapor of a pestilence—preserved in a wall for even two years, or like a plague lurking in a garment—infects and destroys the unwary user long afterward? But since we have fallen here into the mention of clothes: will you, pious Father, forbid us to diligently watch for the **dart of Venus** <note>original: *spiculum Veneris*; likely a specific favorable astrological configuration of the planet Venus</note> when making or first putting on a garment? So that, the garment having been made "Venereal," as it were, it might firmly affect the body and spirit with a certain prosperous quality? Do not physicians forbid the skins of foxes but approve those of lambs? Not otherwise, perhaps, do the stars...

[The stars] affect clothes as if they are being born daily, rather than just once at their beginning. That clothes and other works of art receive a certain quality from the stars, **Thomas Aquinas** <note>A 13th-century Italian Dominican friar and immensely influential philosopher. Ficino often cites him to provide "orthodox" cover for his more controversial ideas</note> confirms in his book *On Fate* <note>original: *de Fato*; Ficino likely refers to Aquinas’s discussions on the influence of heavenly bodies found in the *Summa Theologiae* or his commentaries</note>; you, therefore, will affirm this as well. ### -> *How higher things are drawn down through lower things exposed to them, and especially worldly gifts through worldly materials. Chapter XXVI.* <-

But lest we wander too far from what we set out to do at the beginning while interpreting **Plotinus** <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism, whom Ficino translated and admired</note>, summarize it briefly as follows: The world was created by the "Good" itself (as **Plato** along with **Timaeus the Pythagorean** <note>Timaeus of Locri, the character in Plato’s dialogue who describes the creation of the universe</note> teaches) to be as excellent as it could possibly be. It is, therefore, not only corporeal, but also a participant in life and intelligence. For this reason, besides this body of the world which is familiarly manifest to our senses, there lies hidden in it a **spirit** <note>In Ficino’s medical-philosophical system, *spiritus* is a subtle vapor, the "glue" that connects the material body to the immaterial soul</note>, a body that exercises the capacity of our fading senses; within the spirit flourishes the **soul**; and within the soul shines the **intelligence**. 

And just as under the Moon air does not mix with earth except through water, nor fire with water except through air, so in the universe a certain **bait** or **kindling** for joining the soul to the body is that very thing which we call the "spirit." The soul, too, is a kind of kindling within the spirit and the body of the world for attaining intelligence by divine means—just as a certain extreme dryness in wood is prepared to receive the oil that will penetrate it, and the oil soaked into it is the fuel for the fire, or rather, specifically for the heat. The heat itself is the vehicle for light. And if this wood were of such a kind that it would shine in the presence of fire without being consumed—as we have sometimes seen—then by this example we would see whether a man, or something else under the Moon, through certain preparations (partly natural and partly sought through art), might be able to receive in an opportune way certain vital and perhaps even intellectual goods from above. 

Truly, what pertains to religion here we shall discuss elsewhere, when Plotinus brings these matters into the open. But as for what pertains to natural **influences** <note>original: *influxus*; the "flowing in" of celestial power from the stars into the material world</note>, of whatever kind they may be coming from above: know that they can only be prepared in us and in our materials through art when nature has suggested to us and our things the "kindling" for them, and when the heavens have conspired more opportunely toward them. Does not nature itself, the artisan of the fetus, when it has affected and shaped the little body in a certain way, immediately through this very preparation—as if by a certain bait—draw down the spirit from the universe? And through this spirit, as through kindling, does it not drink in life and soul? And finally, through a certain form and disposition of the soul...

<summary>Ficino explains the Neoplatonic hierarchy of the universe (Body, Spirit, Soul, Intellect) and argues that just as nature prepares a fetus to receive a soul, humans can use "natural kindling" to attract beneficial celestial influences.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s exploration of how the "World Soul" links all things. On the previous page, he used the authority of Thomas Aquinas to argue that even material objects like clothing can receive celestial influences, suggesting that natural magic is a legitimate branch of physical science rather than forbidden sorcery.</meta>

DE VITA COELI. COMP.

...[a] body living in this way is finally worthy to be gifted with the presence of mind by divine gift. Therefore, nature is great everywhere, as **Plotinus** <note>The 3rd-century founder of Neoplatonism</note> and **Synesius** <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop who wrote on dreams and the soul</note> say; specifically, she entices certain things with certain baits everywhere, no differently than the center of the earth draws heavy things, or the hollows of the Moon draw light things, or heat draws leaves, and moisture draws roots, and other things in a similar way. 

The **wise men of India** <note>Ficino likely refers to the Gymnosophists or Brahmins, regarded in the Renaissance as ancient keepers of natural secrets</note> testify that the world is bound to itself by this very attraction, saying that the world is a living creature <note>original: *animal*</note> that is everywhere both male and female at once, and through the mutual love of its members it unites with itself everywhere, and thus consists. Truly, the bond of its members exists through the mind implanted in it, which, "infused through the limbs, stirs the whole mass and mixes itself with the great body." <note>Ficino is quoting a famous passage from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (VI.726-7), often used to describe the World Soul</note> 

Hence **Orpheus** <note>The legendary poet and master of sacred songs</note> calls nature herself and the worldly **Jupiter** both male and female, so much so that the world is everywhere eager for the reward of its mutual marriage. That the masculine sex is everywhere mixed with the feminine is shown, on the one hand, by the order <note>original: *odor* (likely an OCR error for *ordo*), referring to the alternating gender of the Zodiac signs</note> of the signs, where the preceding sign is always masculine and the following is feminine in sequence; and on the other hand, by the trees and herbs, which possess both sexes just as animals do. 

Furthermore, fire stands in relation to air, and water to earth, as the male to the female; so it is no wonder that the members of the world and all its joints desire mutual marriage. The planets also bring this about, being partly male and partly female, especially **Mercury**, who is both male and female and the father of the **hermaphrodite** <note>In mythology, Hermaphroditus was the son of Hermes (Mercury) and Aphrodite (Venus); astrologically, Mercury is considered "common" or adaptable to either gender</note>. Observing this, agriculture prepares the field—acting as the female—for celestial gifts, and through certain graftings, it propagates the life of the plant and leads it to another, better species. 

The physician, the natural philosopher, and the surgeon perform similar things in our bodies, both to nourish us and to more fully align us with the nature of the universe. So too does the philosopher skilled in natural things and the stars—whom we are accustomed to call a **Mage** <note>original: *Magum*; Ficino defines a "Mage" not as a dark sorcerer, but as a "priest of nature" who understands the harmonies between heaven and earth</note>—who, by certain allurements, inserts celestial things into earthly ones at the right time, no differently than a diligent farmer grafts a fresh shoot onto an old trunk. 

**Ptolemy** <note>The premier ancient authority on astronomy and astrology</note> strongly approves of this, affirming that a wise man of this sort can assist the work of the stars just as the farmer assists the fertility of the earth. The Mage subjects earthly things to celestial ones, or rather, lower things to higher ones everywhere, like matching appropriate females to fertile males: like iron to be drawn by a magnet, like **camphor** <note>A volatile aromatic substance</note> to be scattered by boiling heat, like crystal to be illuminated by the sun, like sulfur and volatile liquids to be ignited by a flame, like an empty eggshell filled with dew to be raised by the sun, or indeed, like the egg itself to be warmed by the hen. 

Furthermore, just as some, by warming eggs even without animals, obtain life for them from the universe, and often prepare certain materials at the right time so that they procreate animals without eggs or visible seeds—as from **basil** <note>The text cuts off here; ancient lore suggested that basil, when crushed under a stone, could spontaneously generate scorpions</note>...

<meta>Catchword: Scorpio-</meta>

<summary>Ficino explains the "marriage" of all parts of the universe, arguing that the world is a single living organism with male and female principles. He justifies the role of the "Mage" as a natural scientist who, like a farmer grafting trees, uses these cosmic sympathies to draw down celestial influences into earthly matter.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marsilio Ficino’s discussion on how the World Soul acts as a bridge between the heavens and the earth. ### BOOK III.

[They produce] a scorpion, bees from an ox, and from sage a bird similar to a blackbird. <note>Ficino refers to spontaneous generation, a common ancient and medieval belief that life could arise from decaying matter or specific combinations of herbs under the right conditions.</note> Clearly, they apply life from the world to certain materials and at opportune times. So too that wise man, when he knows which materials—whether those partly begun by nature or perfected by art—if scattered and then gathered, can receive a certain celestial influx, he collects, prepares, and applies these materials most effectively when that [celestial influence] is ruling, and through them, he claims celestial things for himself. 

For wherever a certain material is exposed to the higher things, just as a mirror is to your face, or an opposing wall is to a voice, it suddenly receives an influence from above by the agent—namely, the most powerful one from the power and wondrous life present everywhere—and reports the virtue through that receptivity, no differently than a mirror represents an image from a face, and a wall reflects an echo from a voice. 

**Plotinus** <note>The 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> himself uses almost these very examples, where, imitating **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>original: *Mercurium*; refers to the legendary Egyptian sage and author of the Hermetica</note>, he says that ancient priests or magi used to receive something divine and wonderful in statues and through sensory sacrifices. But he wishes to clarify, along with **Hermes** <note>original: *Trismegisto*</note>, that through these material things, divine powers entirely separated from matter are not properly received, but only worldly ones, as I said from the beginning, and as **Synesius** <note>The 4th-century philosopher-bishop</note> approves. 

"Worldly things," I say—that is, a certain life or something vital from the **Soul of the World**, from the souls of the spheres and stars, or even a certain motion and a vital presence, as it were, from the <term>demons</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, *daemones* are mediating spirits, neither purely divine nor human, rather than "demons" in the modern evil sense</note>—or rather, sometimes the demons themselves are present in such materials. **Hermes** himself, whom Plotinus follows, says that aerial demons—not celestial ones, let alone higher ones—inhabit statues, which Hermes himself composes from herbs, trees, stones, and spices that have a natural divine power (as he says) within them. 

They add songs similar to celestial sounds, in which he says they [the demons] delight, and thus stay longer in the statues and benefit or harm men. He adds that the ancient **Egyptian** wise men, who were also priests, when they could not persuade the people by reason that there were gods—that is, certain spirits above men—devised this illicit magic by which they could draw demons into statues to prove that they were divine powers. 

But **Iamblichus** <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist who defended the use of ritual/theurgy</note> condemns the Egyptians because they did not only accept demons as certain steps to investigating higher gods, but adored them greatly. He prefers the **Chaldeans** <note>The ancient Babylonians, famous for their astrology</note>, who were not occupied with demons, to the Egyptians—I mean the Chaldean high priests of religion. For we suspect that the **Astrologers** of both the Chaldeans and the Egyptians attempted, in a certain way, to draw demons into molded statues through celestial harmony. 

Which the Hebrew astrologer **Samuel** <note>Likely Samuel ibn Abbas or a similar medieval source</note> seems to signify, relying on the authority of **David** <note>Referring to the biblical King David, whom Ficino here characterizes as an astrologer</note>, also an astrologer—namely, that the ancient makers of images made statues that pronounced the future. He records that a harmony of celestial things was adapted to these: to cast the metal into the form of a beautiful man on the day of **Mercury**, at the third hour (namely, the hour of **Saturn**). When Mercury joins Saturn in **Aquarius** in the ninth region of the sky, indicating prophecy...

->### ON THE LIFE OF THE HEAVENS. COMPENDIUM.<-
<meta>catchword: Apollo</meta>

...and the constellation of Gemini rises, signifying prophets (as they say). Mars is "burned" by the Sun <note>original: *comburitur*; in astrology, a planet is 'combust' or burned when it is so close to the Sun that its own influence is overwhelmed</note>, and does not look upon Mercury. Yet the Sun gazes at the place of that conjunction. Meanwhile, Venus occupies a certain angle; she is in the west and powerful. The Moon looks upon the degree of the ascendant from a trine aspect, as does Saturn—or so they say. 

However, I first think, following the opinion of **St. Thomas [Aquinas]**, that if they indeed made statues that speak, it was not the simple influence of the stars that formed the words there, but demons <term>dæmonas: in the Neoplatonic and Renaissance context, these are intermediary spirits, though Ficino here leans toward the more cautious Christian view of them as deceptive entities</term>. Furthermore, if it happened that they entered into such statues, I do not believe they were bound there by celestial influx, but rather they followed their worshippers voluntarily, intending to deceive. For a superior nature may sometimes be reconciled by an inferior one, but it cannot be constrained; and that arrangement of the stars described a moment ago perhaps cannot even occur. Although demons are not trapped in statues by astronomical calculations, they nevertheless appear where they are summoned through the worship offered to them. 

**Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> says they delivered oracles according to astronomical rules, and for that reason, they were frequently ambiguous—and rightly so, because **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist who defended the use of ritual and theurgy to reach the divine</note> proves that true and certain prophecy does not suit evil demons, nor human arts or nature, but arises from the divine breath in purified minds. But let us return to **Hermes** <note>original: *Mercurium*; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note>, or rather, to **Plotinus**. 

**Hermes** says that priests received a power from the nature of the world that was fitting, and they mixed it. Following him, **Plotinus** thinks this whole process can easily be achieved through the mediation of the **World Soul** <term>anima mundi: the spiritual force that connects the physical world to the divine realm</term>, insofar as it generates and moves the forms of natural things through certain **seminal reasons** <term>seminales rationes: the "seed-like" formative principles within the World Soul that dictate how matter takes shape</term> implanted in it by God. He also calls these "reasons" Gods, because they are never separated from the Ideas of the supreme Mind. 

Therefore, through such "reasons," the World Soul easily applies itself to the materials it formed from the beginning, whenever a magus or priest applies the forms of things—properly collected at opportune times—that specifically relate to this or that "reason." This works just as a **magnet** attracts iron, **rhubarb** <note>original: *reubarbarū*</note> draws out bile, **saffron** <note>original: *crocus*</note> aids the heart, **hemp-agrimony** <note>original: *eupatorium*</note> and **metallic ash** <note>original: *spodium*; a medicinal powder derived from minerals</note> aid the liver, and **lavender** <note>original: *spica*</note> and **musk** aid the brain. 

It is possible that sometimes, when these "reasons" are applied to material forms in this way, even more sublime gifts descend, insofar as the "reasons" in the World Soul are joined to the intellectual forms of that same Soul, and through them to the Ideas of the Divine Mind. **Iamblichus** also approves of this when he discusses sacrifices. We shall dispute this more conveniently elsewhere, where it will also appear how impure the superstition of the pagan people was. On the other hand, we shall see how pure the Evangelical piety was—something we have already largely addressed in our book *On the Christian Religion*.

He uses the concept of the World Soul and its "seminal reasons" to explain how material things are linked to divine ideas.</summary>

He addresses the potential controversy surrounding his work *De Vita Libri Tres* (Three Books on Life), defending his dual role as a priest and a scholar of medicine and astrology.</meta>

<page-num>194</page-num>
<header>BOOK III.</header>

### *A certain defense, in which he treats medicine, astrology, the life of the world, as well as the Magi <note>The Three Wise Men of the Bible, whom Ficino identifies as practitioners of a "holy" form of magic</note> who worshiped Christ immediately after his birth. Chapter XXVII.*

Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends three and fourfold greetings to his three dearest brothers in the study of truth: Pietro Nero, Guicciardini, and Soderini. I might perhaps have more correctly said "Tri-Peter" rather than "three Peters." For just as where there is one palm, the many fingers upon it do not make many hands, so your three bodies as friends seem to prevent nothing from your single will making one "Peter" <note>A play on the name Petrus, meaning "rock" in Latin and Greek, referencing the Biblical foundation of the Church</note>. Christ, the builder of that celestial fatherland, created such a great rock that this one rock was sufficient for founding the immense edifice of his Church. I too, by a certain divine fate, have obtained such great "Rocks" that three of them now support my own rather arduous building. Now, my friends, now—if you do not know it—that fortress of Pallas <note>The *arx Palladis*, a metaphor for wisdom and intellectual defense associated with the goddess Pallas Athena</note> seems necessary, by which we may ward off the cruel attack of impious giants from us. For this reason, I have decided to fortify the "Life" of my three books—which come to the aid of the public life—with your fortress first, constructed from three Peters.

You know (as I believe) that I have composed a book on life divided into three small volumes, of which the first is titled *On Healthy Life*, the second *On Long Life*, and the third *On Life from the Heavens* <note>original: *De vita coelitus comparanda*; often translated as "On Obtaining Life from the Heavens," this book deals specifically with astrological medicine</note>. Therefore, a title so sweet will entice as many as possible to taste it; but among such a great number, most will be ignorant (as I believe) and not a few will be malicious. One will say: "Is Marsilio not a priest?" And indeed he is. "Then what do priests have to do with medicine? What, again, is the commerce of priests with astrology?" Another will say: "What does a Christian have to do with magic <term>magia: Ficino distinguishes between "natural magic," which uses the properties of nature and the stars, and "demonic magic," which he rejects</term> or images?" Another, indeed unworthy of life, will envy a life drawn from heaven. Finally, all those so affected will be far too ungrateful for our benefit toward them. They will not be ashamed to be cruel against our charity, by which we consult the life and public prosperity to the best of our natural talent.

This labor, therefore, will be shared with you; but so that it may be somewhat lighter, since there are three of you against three enemies, take up the struggle in distribution. You shall not (for I know your character) refute an invective with an invective, but you will overcome the bitterness of another's gall with the wonderful sweetness of your honey, which is your natural kindness. In the beginning, most candidly respond to the first critics that the most ancient priests of old were likewise physicians and astronomers <note>original: *astronomos*; in Ficino's time, "astronomy" and "astrology" were often used interchangeably as the study of the stars</note>, as indeed the histories of the Chaldeans, Persians, and Egyptians testify. Furthermore, the duties of singular charity pertain to no one more than a pious priest, which truly shine most brightly in the greatest benefit of all. Indeed, the most excellent duty is undoubtedly that which is both most necessary and especially desired by everyone...

ON THE LIFE TO BE SOUGHT FROM THE HEAVENS. COMP. <note>Original: *DE VITA COELI. COMP.*, likely an abbreviation for "Comparison" or "Compendium"</note>

...to bring it about, namely, that men have a **sound mind in a sound body** <note>Latin: *mens sana in corpore sano*</note>. This we can only achieve if we join **medicine** to the **priesthood**. But since medicine without celestial favor is—as Hippocrates and Galen admit, and as we have experienced—more often useless and even harmful, certainly **Astronomy** <note>Ficino often uses "Astronomy" and "Astrology" interchangeably to mean the study of celestial influences</note> belongs to that same priestly charity to which we said medicine belongs. Sacred Scripture <note>Likely referring to Ecclesiasticus 38:1: "Honor the physician for the need thou hast of him: for the Most High hath created him."</note> commands that a physician of this kind be honored, because the Most High created him for the sake of necessity. And **Christ** himself, the giver of life, who commanded his disciples to heal the sick throughout the whole world, also commands **Priests** that if they cannot heal with words as the disciples once did, they should at least heal with herbs and stones. If these are not sufficient on their own, he will command them to brew these things with a certain opportune "breath of heaven" <note>Original: *afflatu cœli*, referring to the influx of planetary energies or "spirit"</note> and apply them to the sick. For he himself, by that same breath of heaven, stirs animals everywhere to seek their own medicine, so abundantly does he provide for the lives of all. Thus, by a divine celestial instinct, snakes heal their eyes with **fennel**, swallows with **celandine** <note>Original: *celidonia*, a plant traditionally associated with the sight of swallows</note>, and eagles, when troubled by birth, have divinely discovered the **eagle-stone** <note>Original: *ætitem lapidem*, a hollow geode believed to assist in childbirth</note> so that they might immediately lay their eggs with success.

<margin>+</margin>
Therefore God himself, who through the heavens prompts all animals to seek medicines, certainly permits Priests—not for profit, I say, but out of charity—to expel diseases through medicines strengthened by heaven. To these points you, in turn, will add more from your own sharp wit if it is helpful. Arise after this, you too, energetic **Guicciardini**, and respond to the curious minds that **magic** or **images** are not indeed *approved* by Marsilio, but are *recounted* while he interprets **Plotinus** <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher whose works Ficino translated and commented upon</note> himself—as my writings plainly declare if read with a fair mind. Nor is a single word asserted here about profane magic, which relies on the worship of demons, but mention is made of **natural magic**, which captures the benefits of the heavens through natural things for the prosperous health of our bodies. Surely this faculty should be granted to those using their wits legitimately, just as medicine and agriculture are rightly granted—and even more so, as it is a more perfect industry, joining heavenly things to earthly. From this workshop, the **Magi** <note>The Three Wise Men of the Bible</note> were the very first to worship Christ immediately after his birth. Why then do you dread the name "Magus," you fearful person? It is a name favored by the Gospel, which does not mean a sorcerer or a poisoner, but a wise man and a Priest. What does that first Magus, the worshiper of Christ, profess? If you wish to hear, he is like a **farmer**—indeed, he is a **cultivator of the world** <note>Original: *mundicola*</note>. Nor does he worship the world for this reason, just as a farmer does not worship the earth; but just as a farmer tempers his field to the air for the sake of human food, so that wise Priest tempers the lower things of the world to the higher things for the sake of human health. And just as a hen warms her eggs, so he seasonably submits earthly things to be nurtured by heaven. This he always does...

He distinguishes his "natural magic" from "profane magic," comparing the former to the work of a farmer who prepares the earth to receive the influence of the sun and air.</summary>

### BOOK III.

...by God himself, who both teaches by doing and persuades us to act, so that from the heavens the lowest things may be generated, moved, and governed. Finally, there are two kinds of magic. One belongs to those who, through a certain cult, win over demons to themselves; relying on their help, they often perform wonders. However, this kind was utterly exploded when the "prince of this world was cast out" <note>A reference to John 12:31, signifying the victory of Christ over demonic forces.</note>. 

The other kind of magic belongs to those who seasonably apply natural materials to natural causes, to be formed in a wonderful way. Of this skill, too, there are two types. One is "curious," while the other is "necessary." The former fabricates useless wonders for the sake of ostentation—as when the *Magi of the Persians* <note>original: *Persarum Magi*</note> took sage that had been rotted under dung while the *Sun* and *Moon* occupied the second face of *Leo* and held the same degree there. From this, they generated a bird similar to a blackbird with a serpent’s tail; when this bird was reduced to ash and poured into a lamp, the house immediately seemed full of serpents. This sort of thing, being vain and harmful to health, must be avoided at all costs. Yet, the "necessary" type must be maintained, which joins **medicine** together with **astrology**. 

But if anyone is so stubborn as to press the matter further, *Guicciardini* <note>Francesco Guicciardini (1483–1540), a famous historian and friend of Ficino.</note>, deal with him in this way: let him not read these writings of ours, nor understand them, nor remember them, nor use them—for such a man, if he is a man at all, is utterly unworthy of such a great benefit. There are many other arguments besides these that you, with your own wit, can bring forward against ungrateful ignorance. 

And what are you doing, our energetic *Soderini* <note>Piero Soderini (1450–1522), a statesman and supporter of Ficino.</note>? Will you tolerate certain superstitious and blind men—I know not who they will be—who see life clearly in the most lowly animals and the most common herbs, yet do not see it in the heavens or in the world? Now truly, if these little men grant life to the smallest particles of the world, what madness is this? What envy? To neither know nor wish the whole to be alive, in which "we live, and move, and have our being" <note>Latin: *in quo viuimus, & mouemur, & sumus*. A quote from Acts 17:28, where Paul quotes the Greek poet Aratus.</note>. 

Indeed, *Aratus* <note>A Greek didactic poet (c. 315–240 BCE) whose poem *Phaenomena* describes the stars.</note> sings of this, clearly signifying "Jupiter" as the common life of the worldly body. Somehow, quite opportunely, I seem to have stumbled upon these words of *Aratus*. I remember *Luke the Evangelist*, and I remember *Paul the Apostle* willingly using these words, in which those wise men do not shrink from the idea of the "life of the world" <note>Original: *mundi vitam*, often referred to as the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul.</note>. 

But a certain superstitious person might object to this, saying it is not easily proven from such words that *Paul* agrees the world has a soul, but only that it is subject to God, and that we live in this very God. So be it, then! Let us not use the name "soul" <note>Latin: *anima*</note> in reference to the world since it is displeasing; let the name of soul be considered profane. But will it not be permitted at least to speak of some kind of "life," which God himself, the architect of the world, mercifully breathed into this work of his that he finished so happily? Since He is not stingy toward even the most lowly living things, and daily provides life most abundantly through the heavens to as many things as are in it. 

Tell me, I pray, do you not see that oxen and donkeys—O you ox, O you donkey!—are alive because they were generated from living things by a certain touch? If, therefore, these things are seen to be alive because they come from themselves...

<summary>Ficino distinguishes between demonic magic and natural magic, arguing that the latter is a necessary fusion of medicine and astrology. He defends the concept of a "living world" (World Soul) by citing the Apostle Paul and Aratus against critics he views as willfully ignorant.</summary>

# ON OBTAINING LIFE FROM THE HEAVENS.

...would even generate things, would you not judge these heavens to be much more alive? That is, if you have any judgment or life in yourself. Heaven, as the husband of the Earth, does not touch her (as is the common opinion); the Earth does not copulate like a wife, but rather, Heaven surveys its wife from every side with the rays of its stars as if with eyes. By surveying her, it fertilizes her and procreates living things. Does it, therefore, while granting life even by its gaze, possess no life of its own? And because it gave life to the ostrich <note>original: *avi struthio*. Ficino refers to the ancient belief that ostriches hatch their eggs simply by staring at them intensely.</note> and a life-giving gaze, is it for this very reason much worse than the bird? 

Now that these points have been brought forward, unless you can persuade that superstitious, half-dead fellow—or rather, a man not living at all—I shall dismiss him from our midst. Furthermore, so that we may argue our cause with more patrons, add, Peter, that we should send our "Amphion," <note>Amphion was a mythological figure whose music was so sweet it moved stones; here, Ficino refers to the eloquence of Cristoforo Landino.</note> Cristoforo Landino, the orator and likewise the poet; our Amphion, with wonderful sweetness, quickly softens the stony hearts of our enemies. But you, Guicciardini, my dearest godfather, go now, go swiftly and summon the Herculean Poliziano. Just as Hercules used to call upon Iolaus whenever a more dangerous struggle was ahead, you now likewise call upon Hercules. You surely know how many barbarian monsters now devastating Latium <note>Italy</note> the Herculean Poliziano has attacked, torn apart, and slain—how fiercely he attacks them everywhere, how safely he defends us. This man, therefore, will immediately shatter with his club and consume with flames the hundred heads of the Hydra threatening our children. 

Come, my sweetest Soderini, rise and go greet the Phoebean Pico; I often call him my "Phoebean" <note>Referring to Apollo/Phoebus, the god of light, medicine, and prophecy.</note>, and he in turn calls me Dionysus and Liber <note>Both names for the god of wine and divine frenzy/inspiration.</note>. We are therefore brothers. Tell my Phoebus that a poisonous Python <note>The monstrous serpent slain by Apollo.</note> is even now emerging from the swamp against us; I beg and pray that he stretch his bow and immediately let fly his arrows. He will stretch it at once—I know what I am saying—and he will kill the whole poison with a single death. Farewell now happily, my most beloved brothers, worthy not only of happy health but of happiness itself; take care for the health and happiness of my "children" <note>Ficino frequently referred to his books as his children.</note> now coming into the light. September 15, 1489.

->That security and tranquility of mind are necessary for life. Chapter XXVIII.<-

Marsilio Ficino sends greetings to his most beloved brothers in the hunt for truth: Bernardo Canigiani, Giovanni Canacci, and Amerigo Corsini. Since we had established a certain "hunt" in these very first words, we perhaps rightly employed "hounds" and "runners" at once. Indeed, we have appropriately called those who practice philosophy "hunters," as they are always laboring in the breathless tracking of truth; but was it also appropriate to call them "hounds"? "Most appropriately," says Socrates in the *Republic*. For those practicing philosophy are either legitimate or spurious, and both are hounds. The former search out the truth itself with keen scent and, once found, hold it with their teeth...

# BOOK III.

...truly bark, bite, and tear in defense of their opinions. Indeed, dogs claim such a place for themselves among the philosophers that they not only inserted themselves into a sect, but even established their own sect at one time under the name "Cynic" <note>original: *cynicam*. From the Greek *kyon*, meaning dog; the Cynic philosophers, like Diogenes, were known for their biting wit and rejection of social norms.</note>. Furthermore, the Academy has its own dogs; therefore, I call upon you, wise dogs of the Academy, you swiftest runners. For you are three, and I pray that you now defend my three books, which are still quite tender and will (as I fear) immediately emerge among wolves. Run, I say, eagerly, for I now entrust to you desired tasks, not burdens. 

You know my Giorgio Benigno Salviati <note>Juraj Dragišić (c. 1445–1520), a Franciscan theologian and associate of the Medici circle. "Salviati" refers to his patron family.</note>, who long ago wisely attained that truth whose tracks you are now hunting and scouring everywhere, and who, like a greater Sun, illuminates his own brothers. If you hear any howling of wolves, report it to him; that most courageous Giorgio will easily put all the wolves to flight, he who once pierced the vast dragon <note>A reference to the Salviati family coat of arms, which features a dragon; Ficino also implies Salviati’s prowess in theological combat.</note>. He, therefore, will relieve me of anxiety and you of care at the same time.

For one of you is accustomed to say—and indeed quite often—that he experiences nothing more healthful for life than to "swallow down time" with great security; the others, meanwhile, immediately smile at the speaker. But come, tell me, Canace <note>Likely a nickname for one of the "Academic dogs," named after one of the hounds of Actaeon in classical mythology.</note>, what is this "devouring of time" you repeat so often? What do you mean by it? You will say it is not to "be," but rather to "drink"—not to chew or crush, but to engorge with a full throat. 

For time itself is a certain fluid nature (so to speak) and slippery. This is the condition of fluid things: if you confine them in a narrow space, you suddenly lose them; for when forced, they flow away and quickly escape. If you happen to squeeze water soaked into a sponge, you will press it out and immediately scatter it; if you hold it more loosely, you will retain much more—likewise with air, fire, and the ether. Hence, among the poets, those who strive to grasp the vast images of gods or spirits in their arms struggle in vain. The widest fluid things must be accepted quite broadly, and the most expansive things must be possessed most expansively. 

Certainly, a sense of "narrowness" <note>original: *angustia*. In Ficino's Latin, this implies both physical confinement and the mental distress of anxiety or pedantry.</note> weighs heavily upon us when we reduce the soul itself and its naturally expansive movement into a narrow space. Whoever weighs their studies and business with extreme precision, and always grinds them down into the smallest details, meanwhile—alas—miserably wears away their own life in secret. 

Therefore, Pythagoras <note>The ancient Greek philosopher; Ficino often quotes him as an authority on the soul's relationship to the cosmos.</note> seems to have rightly commanded: "Beware lest you ever be confined in a narrow space." Nothing is broader than the heavens; nothing is more full of life. In turn, the narrowest earth has the smallest amount of life in the world. Finally, if we live by the heavens and by time, the more broadly we absorb these, the longer and more fully we live. 

Live, therefore, joyful and far from narrowness, O friends! Live joyful! Your own Joy <note>original: *laetitia*.</note> created the heavens for you, which it declares through its own "laughter"—that is, through its expansion, motion, and splendor—as if exulting. Your joy will preserve the heavens for you; therefore, live joyfully every day in the present, for anxiety over present things snatches from you

### ON THE LIFE OF HEAVEN. CONCLUSION.

...twice the present, and snatches away the future; curiosity about things to come quickly drags you back into the past. Therefore, again and again, I pray: **live joyfully** <note>original: *vivite laeti*. This is a central tenet of Ficino’s "Medical Philosophy," which argues that a joyful spirit is necessary for physical health and attracting celestial influence.</note>, for the fates allow it, so long as you live free from care. But so that you may truly live well-cared for, do not take up even this one care: that you should ever worry with what great diligence you might escape care. For this one care, alas, burns the hearts of wretched mortals with every kind of anxiety. Therefore, **neglect diligence; instead, love negligence**, and even love that negligence negligently <note>Ficino employs a clever Latin wordplay here (*negligite diligentiam, negligentiam vero diligite*), advising his friends to stop over-thinking and over-preparing, which only causes more stress.</note>, as far as is permitted and proper for you, I say. These things I command you, friends, not so much as a **Priest**, but as a **physician** <note>original: *Sacerdos... medicus*. Ficino was both an ordained priest and a physician; he saw the care of the soul and the care of the body as a single, unified practice.</note>. For without this one thing—which is like the "life" of all medicines—all **medicines** applied to prolong life simply die.

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a circular medallion that depicts a seated male figure, likely Orpheus or Apollo, playing a stringed instrument (lyre or viol) in a landscape setting with a tree.</image-desc>

I have deemed it a worthwhile task, driven by a sense of patriotic devotion, to write down certain counsels against the disease of the plague. However, so that everyone might be able to grasp the understanding of this work and put the treatment into practice, I have decided to set aside all overly subtle or lengthy debates. For it will be enough that whatever I am about to present—even if more cannot be said within such a brief context of words—is both proven and handed down by sufficient reasoning and the authority and experience of many, both ancient and modern. This is especially true of the experience of our father Marsilio Ficino, foremost among physicians, who restored many infected by this stain <note>original: *labe*. This Latin term literally means a "slip," "stain," or "ruin," and was frequently used in medical texts to describe the "taint" of contagion or infection.</note> to their former health. Therefore, we implore God, the Best and Greatest, the giver of human life and the revealer of true and healthy medicines, that He might reveal to us effective remedies against the dangers of the plague, and that He might preserve His gift of life for us, to His own praise and glory.

## *BOOK FOUR.*

->What the plague is, and of what nature. Chapter I.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within an architectural frame.</image-desc>

THE PLAGUE is a certain poisonous vapor condensed in the air, an enemy to the vital spirit <note>The "vital spirit" (spiritus vitalis) was understood by Renaissance physicians as a subtle, air-like substance in the blood that carried life-force from the heart to the rest of the body.</note>: not because it is opposed to it through some elemental quality <note>Hot, cold, moist, or dry.</note>, but by a certain specific property. Just as theriac <note>original: *theriaca*. A famous and complex ancient medicinal paste used as an antidote for poison and a preventative for disease.</note> is indeed a friend [to the body], not because it is hot or cold, dry or moist, but because from its entire composition a certain form results which is suited to the form of the vital spirit: so also that pestilential vapor is an enemy to nature, not because it is hot, cold, moist, or dry, but because its proportion is, as it were, exactly the opposite of the proportion in which the vital spirit consists within the heart. And just as poisons are constantly born in the earth, so a poisonous vapor is frequently born in the air; yet it is not quite as powerful, because it is more scattered. Nor can it be established in pure air, as long as such air is similar to the spirit and to fire, which by the power of its own nature does not receive the mixture of another nature, which is why it undergoes no putrefaction <note>Decay or rot.</note>. Thus pure air, by receiving no mixture, can by no means putrefy; on the other hand, a poisonous vapor of this kind only attaches itself to the human body in which there are humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that governed health.</note> fit for fever, namely those disposed toward putrefaction and inflammation. Indeed, if the vital spirit is more powerful than the vapor itself, it drives it far away; but if it is weaker, it flees from it, as if from its own contrary work. For this reason, it is useful to correct, purge, and strengthen the air, the humors, and finally the heart. It must be noted (so that you may understand correctly) that when I say this is a poisonous vapor, you should not believe that it...

<summary>Ficino defines the plague as a poisonous vapor in the air that specifically attacks the "vital spirit" of the human heart. He explains that the disease takes hold when a person's bodily humors are already prone to decay, emphasizing the need to strengthen the heart and purify the air.</summary>

<keywords>plague definition, vital spirit, theriac, humors, putrefaction, poisonous vapor, Renaissance medicine, Marsilio Ficino</keywords>
