BOOK IV.

...would be such according to its form and its whole nature, because all things would be undying: but it is of such a quality that it very easily turns into the nature of poison. And it specifically becomes a poison when, through it, the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that pre-modern medicine believed determined health and temperament.</note> in the human body reach a certain degree of putrefaction <note>Decay or decomposition within the body.</note> and simultaneously boil over. This commonly happens on the third day, and sometimes sooner, especially in those who abound in superfluous humors, particularly blood and yellow bile <note>original: *cholera*.</note>. And when it takes on the nature of poison, it receives the quality of lime or arsenic <note>Substances known for their caustic, burning, and corrosive properties.</note>, the effect of which is to rot, corrode, and burn both inside and out. It is therefore extremely necessary that we resist these three effects, especially internally, with all the industry we can muster.

### The causes of the origin of the epidemic, and which bodies are most vulnerable to this evil. Chapter II.

This kind of vapor is created in the air during a more widespread plague due to certain malignant constellations, especially from the conjunction of Mars with Saturn in human signs <note>Zodiac signs depicted as human figures: Gemini, Virgo, Libra, and Aquarius.</note>, and from eclipses of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. Such is the case of the present plague in the year 1479; and such it was also in the year 1408, and this primarily harms mankind. It spreads in places that have an unfortunate Horoscope or Ascendant <note>In astrology, the sign of the zodiac rising in the east at a specific time.</note> due to the aforementioned positions of the stars. In more localized outbreaks, however, the aforementioned poison is born from winds and malignant vapors from pools and sewers, and likewise from earthquakes.

But whatever the cause, it always reigns most powerfully in thick air, and in marshy, misty, and foul air. When it extends into subtle <note>Thin or refined.</note> air, it penetrates and kills more swiftly; yet it reigns more quickly, frequently, and longer in thick, humid, and foul air. Several doctors assert that pestilential putrefaction exists first in subtle air and later in thicker air, but that it is much more durable in the thick. I do not know by what line of reasoning or on what basis I should agree with the first part, since experience shows the opposite. 

Furthermore, reason dictates to us that since only a mixed element can putrefy—and not a pure one—the less mixed it is (as subtle air is known to be), the less fit it is for putrefaction. It does not increase except through the constant influence of the plague-bearing stars. But just as thick, stagnant, and standing water is more easily putrefied, so thick and misty air receives putrefaction without difficulty. Raymond <note>Likely Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull), a philosopher whose works influenced Renaissance medicine and alchemy.</note> gives this rule: that if the plague is stirred up from below <note>From the earth or sewers.</note>, one must seek higher and thinner air; but if it arises from above <note>From the stars or atmosphere.</note>, one must first flee downward for two months...

<summary>This page describes how plague vapors turn bodily humors into corrosive poisons and identifies astrological conjunctions and foul environmental vapors as the primary causes of epidemics.</summary>

...towards a somewhat thick, cold, moist, and pure air, where infirmity is usually rare. For the following two months, move toward the middle region of the air, and then to a slightly higher one—namely dry, cold, and subtle—always fleeing the hot, moist, and cloudy air. In such air, humans are like fish in turbid waters. Pestilential air does to humans what foggy and putrid waters do to fish. But what is poison to humans is not necessarily so for other living creatures, due to the diversity of celestial signs and the species of animals. 

From this arises a question, and I do not know what to say of the opinion of those who assert that when pestilential poison begins in the air, the little birds that usually live on high descend to the depths and inhabit the plains. But when it arises in the earth, they say worms and serpents emerge from the depths of the earth, and little birds whose habit is to fly and live at the bottom seek the heights and go to the mountains. They further add that when the poison is ignited first in the air and then later in the earth, animals sometimes flee from high to low and then return to higher places again. Hence it is commonly said that vultures or kites <note>original: *miluos*</note> yield to pestilential air, and locations where such kites stay are not subject to pestiferous air. 

We have often heard that this contagion has passed from humans to pigs. Perhaps this could happen through some similarity not of spirit, but of flesh. In these most recently passed days, cats and dogs have once or twice carried the plague disease from one house to another, yet they themselves were in no way harmed by this contagion. And let no wonder seize you that sometimes a human or beast may receive the aforementioned vapor without any harm, yet still infect others. For glowing iron consumes tow <note>The coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp, used here as a highly flammable material.</note> and straw, yet the iron itself is not consumed. 

This arises from the disposition <term>disposition: the physical state, temperament, or readiness of a body to be affected by external causes like disease</term> of the receiving subject, in which, according to **Aristotle**, **Galen**, and **Avicenna** <note>The three primary authorities of medieval medicine: Aristotle the philosopher, Galen the Roman physician, and Avicenna the Persian polymath.</note>, the effect of a thing primarily consists. So it was that in these recent days, a two-year-old <note>original: *bimus*</note> boy in our countryside stayed for an entire day with an infected boy of about seven years; he often ate food chewed by the infected boy's mouth, yet he contracted no stain of the disease from him, though others further away were seized by it. 

Do not have too much confidence in your own disposition, thinking that you are of such health that you need not fear this contagion. Instead, observe this medical <note>original: *physicum*</note> rule: when matter is highly disposed, then the acting cause, however weak, quickly produces an effect. Just as a spark ignites tow and sulfur because of the suitability of the receiver. Conversely, a cause that is powerful enough acts even on matter that is not disposed. And although sulfur receives the action of fire more quickly than

...wood, and specifically dry wood, finely chopped, ignites more easily than other logs. Nevertheless, a burning furnace immediately seizes even larger and green wood into its flame, because the supreme power of the acting force quickly prepares and shapes it. Many times, a pestilential vapor of this kind is made most powerful by the strength of its own causes, and you cannot know exactly when this happens. And even if such a susceptibility is not present at one time, it may be in the future at another.

### In what way, and what temperaments the plague from contagion strikes most swiftly. Chapter III.

This poisonous vapor is often so subtle <note>In early medicine, "subtle" means thin or refined enough to penetrate the body easily.</note> that it cannot be discerned by sight. Sometimes it is dissolved, but it is easily regenerated from that point as long as the celestial influence that prepares the way remains. Even if it is small at the beginning, it expands from place to place with a swifter course and much more vigorously than ignited sulfur. It is far more opposed to the **vital spirit** <term>vital spirit: a refined vapor arising from the blood, believed to reside in the heart and sustain life</term> of the heart than sulfur is to the nose. 

A vapor of this kind is ignited by the infected air only in bodies already "disposed" or susceptible to it. But once it has been ignited, it spreads all around with miraculous speed and ease—much like burning sulfur—especially when it has been ignited in "subtle humors" and the thin air of summer; it then scatters and leaps from one body to another. 

It is ignited most powerfully where there is a greater similarity of nature, such as:
* In a body full of waste products <note>original: *recrementis*</note> with foul vapors inside and out.
* In foods and superfluous humors prone to inflammation and putrefaction.
* Where the matter is hot and moist, and the heart has been weakened by sexual intercourse <note>original: *coitu*; medical writers of this era often warned that sex depleted the body's vital heat and opened it to infection</note>.

It strikes similarly in a body exhausted by the passions of the soul, or one that is excessively hot, or accustomed to frequent baths <note>Baths were thought to open the pores, allowing plague vapors to enter more easily</note>, or those whose pores are too open or significantly blocked. This indeed was the opinion of **Galen** and **Avicenna** <note>The two most authoritative figures in medieval and Renaissance medicine</note>. 

Children and women are very susceptible to the plague because thin and soft matter is more easily transformed, they are full of humors prone to putrefaction, and their lives are often lived beyond measure and order. Just as a hot and thick wind disturbs and spoils wine, so this pestilential vapor infects and forces everything toward the heart: first the spirits, then the humors, which, once putrefied, begin to boil. 

This "boiling" is the fever itself, which is then scattered through the entire body. It boils or swells more than other fevers because the poisonous matter is so great that nature tries to expel it from the principal members as immediately as possible. This vapor can stain every humor, but primarily the **blood**, secondly **yellow bile**, thirdly **phlegm**, and fourthly **melancholy** (black bile). Hence it follows that those of a "sanguine" temperament are most subject to this danger, and slightly less so the...

**choleric** people, and then the **phlegmatic**; and less than the others, the **melancholic**, because their cold and dry humor <note>The four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile (choler), and black bile (melancholy)—were believed to dictate health and personality.</note> is slow to begin inflammation and putrefaction, and especially because they have narrow **passages** <term>passages: Latin "meatus," referring to the pores or internal channels through which fluids and "vapors" move</term> through which the poison must pass. For this reason, the elderly are less subject to this pestilential disease, although this year's plague did not leave even the seniors untouched. The reason for this was perhaps that, beyond the ancient unfavorable planetary aspects, **Saturn** was the retrograde lord of the year <note>In medical astrology, Saturn is associated with old age and coldness; its "retrograde" movement was seen as a period of disruption and misfortune.</note>. It is a wonder to say that although nearly the entire population fled from our city of **Florence**, every day about one hundred and forty people still departed this life.

### On the signs and indicators of the plague. Chapter IIII.

No one can easily or clearly show which signs indicate a fever is pestilential, because of the great diversity and deceptiveness of the symptoms. This is attested by the entire assembly of learned doctors, especially **Avenzoar** and **Rhazes** <note>Avenzoar (Ibn Zuhr) and Rhazes (Al-Razi) were highly influential medieval physicians whose works remained standard medical texts for centuries.</note>. For sometimes the urine will be clear because the humors do not reach the liver; the fever will appear moderate because the poison is not contained within a hot humor and therefore does not spread outward, and so the patient dies suddenly. Sometimes the patient will seem restored, because **Nature** <note>The author personifies "Nature" as the body’s innate healing force and defensive intelligence.</note> in the first attack drove the poison away from the heart; yet a little later the person will be deprived of breath, because Nature will not be strong enough for the second defensive attack. This happens because she was exhausted by the first conflict, and also because the poison has multiplied, or turned more malignant, or moved closer to the heart than before. 

Almost everyone seems to improve slightly at the beginning because their robust nature gathers all its strength against the enemy; however, in other less severe illnesses, such a sudden and massive effort is not required. Furthermore, the patient will seem to maintain the strength of their faculties because the poison is not as hostile to other organs as it is to the heart at the start; but when it attacks the heart itself, it kills instantly. 

Therefore, in these times, it is not at all appropriate to delay by over-examining the signs of the disease, for you will be deceived, and Nature will not wait for you unless you hurry to administer remedies. For this reason, when you see a fever present in these times, assume it is the plague—or that it soon will be—and administer the treatment for pestilential fever. This is especially true because as long as the poisonous influence of the air lasts, every superfluous humor is easily infected. Any illness whatsoever can easily turn into the plague, especially frantic and continuous fevers. Hence it usually happens that in this diseased time, no illness appears except the plague. If other various illnesses should appear, then the pestilence is receding and ceasing. There are several signs of pestilential fever, namely

It emphasizes the extreme difficulty of diagnosing the plague due to its deceptive symptoms and urges immediate treatment at the first sign of any fever.</summary>

<header>BOOK IV.</header>

namely, a continuous fever without any orderly or manifest decline, accompanied by great difficulty in breathing and a tightness in the chest, a sudden weakening of the pulse, and a heaviness of the entire body—especially the head. Other signs include delirium <note>Latin: *phrenesis*, a state of acute mental confusion or agitation believed to be caused by the fever's heat affecting the brain.</note>, anxieties, burning heat, thirst, and numerous bloody spots appearing in many places, with urine that is thick, turbid, and like that of beasts of burden <note>original: *iumentorum*; medical writers often compared human urine to that of cattle or horses to indicate a loss of "human" refinement in the body's filtration.</note>. Remember, however, that these signs can be deceptive. Note furthermore that any child suffering from an illness of worms at that time can be said to be infected by the pestilence, because the matter in their body is as primed for the plague as sulfur is for fire. Many unskilled doctors, in their eagerness to help, have been deceived by this. 

Beyond the murkiness of the air and the abundance of creatures born from rot, the primary signs of an approaching plague are a multitude of worms, outbreaks of smallpox and measles, and continuous or "enclosed" fevers. Other indicators include turbid urine, redness of the eyes, sores on the palate, delirium, and generally any fever in which the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to govern health.</note> frequently direct themselves toward the heart; this signifies that the human temperament is primed for the plague. 

Know also that when a pestilential vapor lingers in the air for a long time, it then infects the water and the fruits of the earth. For this reason, it is safer to boil your water, or perhaps to prepare "iron-water" <note>Latin: *aquam ferratam*, water in which hot iron has been quenched; it was believed to have strengthening and astringent properties.</note> and use it to dilute your wine. This is because wine is "fuming" <term>fuming: Latin "fumosum," referring to the potent vapors of alcohol that were thought to rise quickly to the head and open the body to infection</term> and, according to the opinion of **Avicenna** and **Rhazes**, pure wine is not suitable in these times. Furthermore, it is beneficial to correct other foods by adding pleasant-smelling ingredients and salty or acidic flavors, especially when the plague arises after an earthquake. It will also be of no small benefit to use dry goods grown in fragrant, high-altitude places, and to live in the mountains and hills.

### Prophylactic treatment through diet and lifestyle during a time of pestilence. Chapter V.

In a time of plague, one must abstain from things that cause inflammation or are too "opening" <note>Medicines or foods that were "aperitive" opened the pores, which doctors feared would allow the plague-tainted air to enter the body more easily.</note>, as they make the body more susceptible to receiving the poison. Specifically, one should beware of external heat from the sun, as well as heat from fires and heavy clothing. Internally, one should avoid salt, hot spices, and medicines, as well as herbs of intense heat. Avoid the frequent use of sharp or pungent things, except for onions, chicory, or radishes with vinegar, because these resist the poison. 

Likewise, avoid wine that is too "fuming," and avoid exercise after eating—especially in hot weather—and avoid sweating, as it alters the humors. When the air is infected, one should not expose oneself to it much, nor engage in excessive exercise under the open sky; by heating the body and opening the pores, one immediately takes in a great deal of the infected air. Finally, one must abstain from things that cause blockages <term>blockages: Latin "opilationem," a technical term for obstructions in the vessels or organs that prevented the healthy flow of humors</term> and putrefaction, because these provide the material for a pestilential fever. These include things that are sticky, cold, and damp, especially when something accidental or external—

...nor do they take on heat. Also avoid things that are viscous, hot, and humid, where the moisture predominates over the heat and is poorly "cooked" <note>original: *decoctum*; in Galenic medicine, digestion was viewed as a process of "cooking" food within the stomach using natural heat.</note>. To sum up: moisture is the mother of putrefaction. Furthermore, things that are difficult to preserve outside of our bodies will also not be easily preserved within us.

Therefore, fish should be avoided as much as possible. Among their kind, small little fish are less harmful, specifically those from clear, stony, and flowing rivers. These should be fried in oil with salt and dipped in stavesacre <note>A species of larkspur used in ancient and medieval medicine.</note>, or vinegar, or orange juice with salt and a bit of pepper or cinnamon. One must also avoid milk and all reheated foods. But if you wish to use milk, let it be the first thing eaten among other foods, in a moderate quantity, and with a little sugar. 

All fruits are to be avoided, except for:
* almonds
* sour cherries
* pears
* apricots <note>original: *chrysomelis*; literally "golden apples."</note>
* peaches
* quinces
* hazelnuts
* prunes and sloes
* medlars and cornelian cherries
* Appian apples, pomegranates, and hard-skinned apples.

Do not use other fruits at all, or do so only rarely, or very rarely. You can, however, use for a longer duration those fruits and herbs that are cold, dry, and acidic, or somewhat bitter. But when eating hot and humid fruits—such as figs, grapes, mulberries, or sweet cherries—make sure the portions are small, and immediately afterward eat an orange with salt.

Furthermore, if you use cold and humid things—such as melons, soft and tender fish, or fat plums—take a little fennel and an orange with salt shortly after, drinking a little good, fragrant wine on top. You must also avoid mushrooms and "humid" herbs, such as purslane and gourds, and indeed all moisture, as well as anything that is prone to rot. Beware also of fruits and things that are too sweet, and humid herbs. I permit you lettuce, provided it is mixed with mint or cinnamon. You can also "correct" the lettuce <note>In humorism, "correcting" an ingredient meant adding a spice or herb with opposite qualities to balance its effect on the body's humors.</note> with very fine clove-basil, which tends toward a reddish color and smells of cloves; for this is most pleasing to the heart.

I also allow you gourds and the herb which in the Tuscan tongue is called *Selbastrella* <note>Also known as Pimpinel or Burnet; it was highly regarded as a heart tonic and a defense against the plague.</note>. Again, take care that the opinion of Rhazes <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925 AD) was a famous Persian physician whose medical encyclopedias were fundamental to European medical education.</note> does not mislead you; he allows cold and humid vegetables and fruits during very hot weather. However, he lived in Egypt, where the dryness is extreme and where such fruits and vegetables are perfectly "ripened" <note>original: *decocta*; literally "cooked" or "digested" by the heat of the sun.</note> by nature. Be cautious, therefore, not to take such liberty in regions that are not similar to Egypt.

It must be noted further that sour, harsh, and sharp things are to be administered in a preventive as well as a curative regimen. This is because the greatest danger looms in the "hot and humid," and in the putrefaction that results from it—leading to the dissolving of the vital spirits and the approach of poison to the heart. Thus, things with the flavors mentioned above resist all these evils, because they cool, dry, preserve, strengthen, bind, and unite. However, I forbid rocket, carrots, <term>sapa</term> <note>A syrup made by boiling down grape juice; used as a sweetener.</note>, mustard, watermelons, melons, bean pods, fresh chickpeas, cucumbers, sweet and soft cherries, grapes, sweet figs, and mulberries. In food and drink, be more sparing than usual; let the food be somewhat more abundant than the drink. Yet I do not wish for you to endure excessive thirst or hunger. Take care not to let the stomach become unsettled, but preserve it with moderation in food and drink, with exercise, fasting, and appropriate evacuations. Abstain from sexual intercourse and excessive passions of the soul, unless perhaps you find yourself completely burdened by the abstinence from intercourse. Recall the saying of Avicenna in the third book of *On Nature*:

> that the excessive evacuation of seed through intercourse harms more than if forty times as much blood were lost.

Hippocrates said:

> intercourse is a kind of epileptic disease. <note>Ancient and medieval physicians often compared the physical intensity of orgasm to a minor seizure or "falling sickness."</note>

Beware of air that is very cloudy, thick, enclosed, and humid, and know that air which is not frequently moved and renewed—where neither the wind nor the sun penetrates or purges it—easily takes on a poisonous mixture and putrefaction, just like stagnant water. Separate yourself from the crowd of men, especially when you are fasting, and when heat has succeeded moisture, or moisture succeeded heat. Also avoid excessively hot air, because it opens the pores and weakens the body too much. Your dwelling should be spacious and dry, receiving dry air continually, and in the summertime, let it be refreshed from time to time. When you have become very hot, take care not to expose yourself immediately to cold or damp, to cloudy weather, or to hot and humid winds—especially in infected places or when coming from an infected place. Avoid every wind blowing from the aforementioned places, unless it is from a very great distance or has been broken by rains. However, the wind which cools, dries, and clears the air is healthy by its nature, if you receive it with moderation; it is the principal physician against this kind of [plague].

...with the **acidity of lemon** <note>original: "acetositate citri"</note>, and they should be taken with white wine, rose water, or rose vinegar. In other cases, however, follow the aforementioned composition. Moreover, ensure that the **aloe** <note>A bitter plant resin used as a purgative and preservative.</note> is bright, light, somewhat reddish, delicate, fragrant, easily broken, and oily, and it should become moist when you breathe upon it. Let the **myrrh** also be clear, and the **coral** delicate; for without **theriac** <term>theriac</term> <note>A complex medical concoction, often containing dozens of ingredients, used as a universal antidote since antiquity.</note> and the said pills, protection cannot be properly achieved. Therefore, above all others, use these two: namely, theriac on two different days, and at least three of the pills, because by drying out excess humidity, they preserve the body from putrefaction. They also strengthen the heart and constrict the passages, so that the poison may not have a path to the heart, and they drive it away from there.

It seems to me that the aloe in the aforementioned pills should not be washed when the weather is humid and cold, nor for those with a similar **complexion** <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, this refers to a person's "humoral temperament"—the balance of hot, cold, moist, and dry qualities in their body.</note>. But in other seasons and for other temperaments, one should take the composition of pills in powder form; it is better only when there is a need for haste. They can also be taken three or four hours before dinner, just as before lunch. You may also, once or twice a week—or more, if the pills should prove bothersome (though they are of no offense)—during the winter and humid weather, take in place of the pills a **dried fig** with half a **walnut**, a little **rue**, and a bit of salt, drinking a little rose water or rose vinegar afterward. If even this should bother you, use in its place—taking nothing else—a bit of toasted bread dipped in strong white wine, with an **orange** <note>original: "pomo anaranciæ"</note> soaked in rose vinegar and dipped in cinnamon. 

There are some who give these kinds of pills in the evening or morning, namely one at a time. Take half a <term>dram</term> <note>A unit of weight; an apothecary dram is about 3.9 grams.</note> of **aloeswood**, two <term>scruples</term> of **tormentil**, one scruple of **white dittany**, half a dram of **zedoary** <note>A root related to ginger and turmeric.</note>, one dram of **saffron**, half a dram of **barberry**, two scruples of **burnt hartshorn** <note>The antlers of a stag, charred and powdered, believed to have cooling and absorbent properties.</note>, one scruple of **red sandalwood**, and one dram each of **sorrel seeds**, **red coral**, and **Armenian bole** <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>A medicinal red clay from Armenia, highly prized for its supposed ability to resist poison and plague.</note>; two scruples of **camphor**, half a dram of the **gems** from which the "Electuary of Gems" is made, one dram of **pearls**, and half a dram of **hyacinths** <note>Usually referring to the gemstone (zircon or sapphire) rather than the flower.</note>. Prepare this with syrup of currants or lemons.

I, however, am accustomed to giving these kinds of pills at all times, even in hot weather. Take one scruple each of **zedoary**, **aloeswood**, **agrimony**, **saffron**, **round birthwort**, **white dittany**, **gentian**, **citrus peels**, and **citrus seeds**; one dram each of **prepared coriander**, **tormentil**, **red sandalwood**, **red coral**, **red roses**, **spodium** <note>Likely zinc oxide or burnt ivory ash.</note>, and **emblics** <note>Indian gooseberry, a fruit used in many ancient compound medicines.</note>; two drams of **sealed earth** <term>sealed earth</term> <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a famous medicinal clay stamped with an official seal to guarantee its purity and origin.</note>, and four drams of **Armenian bole**. Make these into pills with the acidity of lemon, which you should administer with white wine, white rose vinegar, and rose water. I place much faith in this composition of ours, taking it when nothing else is being taken...

I believe that using **juniper seed** with **myrtle seed** is very useful against this kind of poison.

**Raymond** <note>Referring to Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath, though many medical works were later attributed to him.</note> said that in his time **Saturn**, **Jupiter**, and **Mars** were joined in the nineteenth degree of **Aquarius** in March of the year 1348. This conjunction signaled horrible things, especially severe plagues occurring frequently over the space of forty-five years, because it occurred in a "fixed human sign" in the house of Saturn. Among these was that great plague of the year '48, when the physicians of **Paris**, **Avignon**, and **Piedmont** composed a new theriac tested by themselves, which preserved them with great success. **Arnold** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> wrote down the recipe, which Raymond, his disciple, recited in these words:

Take two and a half drachms of **juniper berries**; two drachms each of **cloves**, **mace**, **nutmeg**, **zedoary** <note>A root similar to ginger.</note>, and **ginger**; one and a half drachms each of **long and round birthwort**, **gentian root**, **tormentil**, **betony**, **dittany**, and **elecampane**; one drachm each of **sage**, **rue**, **balsamita seed**, **mint**, **peony**, and **hart’s pennyroyal**; and half a drachm each of **Roman leopard's bane**, **laurel berries**, **sorrel seed**, **citron seed**, **basil**, **mastic**, **frankincense**, **Armenian bole**, **sealed earth** <note>original: *terra sigillata*; a medicinal clay stamped with a seal to prove its authenticity.</note>, **spodium** <note>A technical term usually referring to burnt ivory or zinc oxide.</note>, **bone of a stag's heart** <note>A small, bone-like cartilage found in the hearts of older deer, once highly prized in medicine.</note>, **ivory shavings**, **unicorn horn** <note>Likely ground narwhal tusk, believed to be a powerful antidote.</note>, **pearls**, **sapphire**, **emerald**, **red coral**, **aloeswood**, **red sandalwood**, **hyacinth** <note>A gemstone, likely a reddish zircon.</note>, and **topaz**. 

Add half a drachm each of **rose sugar**, and the preserves of **borage**, **bugloss**, **water lily**, and **wood sorrel**; also half a drachm each of the pulp of **sour tamarind** and **theriac**. Add three pounds of **sugar** and make an **electuary** <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</note> or lozenges with **scabious water** and **rose water** with a little **camphor** and **quince wine**, adding forty **gold leaves**. 

Anyone who suffers from thirst outside of meal times should use simple **sorrel** with a little cold water, or **sour pomegranate wine** with **rose syrup** <note>original: *iuleb rosato*</note>, or **vinegar-wine**. You may also squeeze the juice of a **citron**, a **lemon**, or an **orange** and drink it with water and sugar. Likewise, use **juice of roses**, **rose sugar**, **cherry preserve**, **plum preserve**, or **quince preserve** dissolved with strained water.

This is because a composition of this kind, being better fermented, acquires a specific medicinal virtue beyond its basic humoral mixture; and also because by remaining in the stomach, it preserves, strengthens, and comforts more effectively, and spreads better through the more remote parts of the body—provided one drinks a little of some liquid substance afterward and practices much abstinence. Yet we do not wish for the pills to be very dry and hardened; indeed, if they are such, they should be remade.

It is appropriate for those of a **sanguine** <term>sanguine</term> <note>The "blood-heavy" temperament, thought to be most at risk of fevers and inflammatory plagues.</note> temperament to use **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>Bloodletting; the most common surgical intervention in medieval medicine to "evacuate" excess humors.</note> to draw out blood so that they may be preserved, provided no other flow of blood occurs from them...

...should have a sufficiency of blood. I understand those to be of a **sanguine** temperament <term>sanguine</term> <note>One of the four temperaments in humoral theory, characterized by an abundance of blood, believed to make a person cheerful, ruddy, and robust.</note> who are properly fleshy, red in color, hairy, and robust, with large veins, and who eat highly nutritious foods. For these, I say, let blood be drawn from the **right basilic vein** <note>original: *basilica dextra*; the basilic vein in the arm was a primary site for bloodletting.</note>, and then after a two-month interval, let another **bloodletting** <note>original: *minutio*</note> be performed from the left basilic vein. You should not exceed the weight of one pound in a single session. This should also be done during temperate seasons of the year, and while the Moon is in a good and fortunate alignment. Pure blood is reduced at sunrise, **choleric** blood at noon, **melancholic** at sunset, and **phlegmatic** in the middle of the night. 

Therefore, **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1316), a polymath whose works on alchemy and medicine were highly influential.</note> insists that, according to the order of **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians" whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> and following the four types of blood previously mentioned, those four specific hours should be observed during the extraction. These types are recognized: first by their specific signs, and then according to the four ages of life in which they dominate, following the aforementioned order. But where a great abundance of blood is not apparent, he insists that bloodletting should not be performed at all, neither for the sake of preservation nor for a cure. 

And when you wish to extract blood, ensure that an **enema** <note>original: *clystere*</note> is administered the day before, and some non-laxative medicine is given. I also think it should not be overlooked that where the blood leans heavily toward other humors, it should be evacuated as little as possible. Remember **Galen** and Avicenna: the more they practiced the art of healing, the more cautious they always became regarding **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>The surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood.</note>, because phlebotomy draws more from the natural spirit and the good blood than medicine itself does, and it allows less time to distinguish bad blood from good.

For infants and children, those things which are effective against worms are beneficial, as the danger of these is especially imminent at such times. Administer to them in a drink once a week one drachm of **dittany** <note>original: *dictami*</note> with a somewhat astringent wine, or with a wine made from a decoction of **wormwood**, **black cumin**, or **wormseed** <note>original: *seminis sancti*</note>. Likewise, let the stomach, navel, throat, and chest be anointed with oils and bitter herbs and the like; sometimes you will also administer **rhubarb pills**. 

Truly, because a very moist and very hot temperament is dangerous during a time of plague, there is a need for cooling, drying, and frequent evacuation, which should be done with moderation according to the opportunity. Carry this small satchel applied to the heart: 

Take two drachms of **red roses**, one drachm each of **red sandalwood**, **red coral**, and **spodium** <note>original: *spodij*; likely referring to ivory black or calcined minerals used as a cooling agent.</note>, and half a drachm each of **zedoary**, **aloeswood**, **cinnamon**, **cloves**, **citron peel**, and **saffron**. 

Be diligent that every superfluity is purged, and take care that the bowels do not remain constricted. Be slow to block the body's accustomed purgings, such as regular flows or discharges, **hemorrhoids**, **scabs**, natural and usual sweats, old open wounds through which humor flows without trouble, tears, the usual and ordinary bleeding from the nostrils, general dropsy, and the like; for these mentioned purgings render one safer from...

disease. I advise the governors of public affairs, according to the experience of **Hippocrates** <note>Hippocrates of Kos (c. 460 – c. 370 BC), often called the "Father of Medicine," whose works emphasized environmental causes of disease.</note>, that if they should prepare and order fires and fumigations made from juniper, myrtle, turpentine resin, and frankincense, both morning and evening, before the back doors of every building, house, and dwelling, the plague would be immediately expelled from that place. In place of juniper, laurel, sage, rosemary, and any fragrant herbs are effective. But **turpentine** <note>original: *terebinthina*; a resin harvested from certain trees, highly valued for its aromatic and medicinal properties.</note> is wonderful. Many of the learned say that fire will always be useful during a time of plague, for the reason that it dissolves every vapor. **Raymond** <note>Raymond Lull, previously mentioned on the prior page as an authority on alchemy and medicine.</note> says that strengthening remedies should be used only when the vapors appear thick and humid. In hot seasons, cold scents should surpass others; conversely, when the seasons are cold and humid, roses, sandalwood, myrtle, camphor, apple peels, and pomegranates temper the hot scents; similarly vinegar and little green herbs that are somewhat cold.

The **Magi of the Persians** <note>Ancient Persian priests or "wise men" often associated in Renaissance texts with astrological and talismanic magic.</note> advised their king for his defense against every poison and poisonous disease, that he should have carved into a **hematite stone** <note>original: *lapide hęmatite*; a reddish-black mineral believed to have protective qualities, particularly regarding blood.</note> a man standing on bended knees, surrounded by a serpent, holding the head of the serpent in his right hand and the tail in his left; he should then have this stone pressed and bound into a gold ring. Furthermore, in the setting behind the stone, he should place the root of **snakeroot** <note>original: *barbam serpentariæ*; likely referring to the root of *Dracunculus vulgaris* or a similar plant believed to ward off venomous creatures and disease.</note>, and he should wear this ring on his finger. **Averroes** <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a Spanish-Arabic polymath whose commentaries on medicine were foundational to European universities.</note> praises the scent of goat's urine.

I advise that you use remedies continuously when you are in an infected place or nearby, because contagion is frequent, and the continuously harmful infected air causes damage. I want you to pay careful attention to when the conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurs, and when the opposition occurs—that is, when it is the **full moon**. Likewise, note when the Moon is joined to **Saturn**, and even more so when it is joined to **Mars**. Likewise, note when it is in a **square aspect** <note>An astrological position where planets are 90 degrees apart, generally considered a time of tension or difficulty.</note> with the said planets. And note (as **Rhazes** <note>The Latinized name of Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician who wrote extensively on infectious diseases like smallpox and measles.</note> reports) that the poison of this type of pestilence is usually strongly moved at sunrise, at sunset, at noon, and at midnight, because the Sun causes a change in the air at these four times.

The plague reigns in Spring, more so in Summer, and most of all in Autumn. In Spring, the air is hot and humid, and the dominance of the **blood** <term>sanguine humor</term> increases. In Summer, **yellow bile** <term>cholera</term> <note>One of the four humors, associated with fire, heat, and dryness.</note> dominates; the hot air opens and penetrates the body much more, bodies are weakened and filled with corruptible things, which contribute moist matter to the heat of the air for putrefaction. If indeed this heat were accompanied by dryness both inside and out, it would do little harm, just as moisture joined to the coldness of both the air and the constitution does not hurt much. But it is very dangerous where heat is mixed with moisture, whether outside or inside. We have found by experience that a long drought in hot weather diminishes the plague; but in cold weather, it excites and brings it on. Finally, in autumn, the abundance of fruit increases, as does the weakness of bodies; the air is thin because the preceding summer is easily susceptible to vapors, which it does not dissolve due to the decrease in heat, then fog...

It should also be known that when the pores are heavily blocked, they compress the putrefying matter inside. ## *On the Method of Healing According to Medical Principles. Chapter VII.*

In a pestilential fever <note>A fever associated with the plague, believed to be caused by "putrefaction" of the humors.</note>, as long as the poison has not been purged, beware of administering—either internally or externally—simple **opening medicines** <term>aperitiuas: substances intended to "open" the body's channels or pores</term> for the chest area. This is because they provide a path for the poison to reach the heart and expose the vital spirits to being exhaled. Instead, so that inflammation and putrefaction may be prevented, immediately use things that are slightly cooling and very drying. For these strengthen the heart and close the paths leading toward it, preventing the poison from reaching it. 

For its part, the humor must be well purged, and the spirits should be frequently refreshed with nourishment. Continually administer those things which are effective against poison, for the heart naturally seeks such protection. But if you delay until the poison has arrived there, it might happen that the parts of the heart become greatly constricted; to try and open them again at that point might be more harmful or dangerous than beneficial. 

Therefore, as soon as anyone perceives a heaviness of the head and all the limbs together with an accompanying fever, see that you do not place trust in lying or ambiguous signs, nor delay until a **swelling** <note>original: *inflatio*; referring to the characteristic buboes or lymph node swellings of the plague.</note> or a **blister** <note>original: *bulla*; likely a plague carbuncle.</note> appears. But as these begin to emerge, as quickly as you can, immediately anoint the pulse points of the temples, hands, and feet, the nostrils, the back of the head, the throat, the chest, and the place around the blister and the **abscess** <term>apostema: a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term> (if it has appeared) with **Scorpion oil** and **theriac** <note>Theriac was a famous ancient "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh, used for centuries against plague.</note>. 

The true composition of the oil is this: Take eight ounces of fifty-year-old olive oil and add fifty scorpions. Let them boil together with the oil until they sink to the bottom. You should do this in the summer, and especially in the month of August. Keep it and use it: for it is a miracle against poisons. 

If the stomach is burdened with food, vomiting should be induced with ease using warm water, vinegar, and oil, or even with radish, even attempting to provoke it with a feather; and immediately afterward, administer an enema. You shall renew every day a decoction of mallows, "mother of violets," beets, barley, lettuce, chamomile, violet honey, red sugar, one egg yolk, one ounce of *diaphoenicon* <note>A medicinal paste made from dates, used as a purgative.</note> or cassia, two drams of laxative rose juice, and a sufficient amount of common salt and violet oil. 

Once this is done, you shall apply a **poultice** <term>epithema: a liquid medication applied to the body via a cloth</term> to the heart made of "cordial" substances <note>Medicines believed to specifically strengthen or "gladden" the heart.</note> that are primarily cool in nature. Take two drams each of the waters of roses, bugloss, sorrel, and water lily; and waters of me- <note>The text breaks off; the catchword suggests "melissæ" or lemon balm.</note>

### The Use of Cupping Glasses and the Method of Healing through Bloodletting. Chapter VIII.

Once these things have been done and duly administered as stated, if a **bubble** <note>A bubo, the characteristic swelling of the bubonic plague.</note> or sign has not yet appeared on the legs, immediately apply two **cupping glasses** <term>ventosas: glass cups used in bloodletting to create a vacuum and draw "corrupt humors" to the surface</term> to the buttocks, and likewise two to the back of the thighs. The ancients wished that **bloodletting** <term>phlebotomia: the surgical opening of a vein</term> should be performed after the removal of such cupping glasses. 

If the usual bubble or sign has not appeared, let blood be let from the **common vein** on the right side to prevent the poison from reaching the regions of the heart. Even if such a sign or bubble has appeared, blood must be drawn from that same side so that the poison does not extend and spread (as it always tends to do) through all the veins and parts of the body. 

If a sign appears around the ears or the neck, blood should be diminished from the **cephalic vein** <term>cephalica: the "head vein" in the arm, thought to drain the upper body</term> on the side where the sign is, near the thumb of the hand. If it appears under the armpits, the **hepatic vein** <term>hepatica: the "liver vein" in the arm, associated with the mid-body</term> in the arm of that side should be evacuated. If it appears in the groin, let the bloodletting be done from the **saphenous vein** <term>saphena: the large vein of the leg, associated with the lower body</term>, which is below the ankle of the same side. 

Finally, as a general rule, whenever such a sign appears from the beginning of the throat up to the head, let the cutting be from the cephalic vein on the side of the appearing sign. If it appears from that part down to the navel, whether in front or behind, let the bloodletting likewise be from the hepatic vein. If it is from the navel downward, the saphenous vein ought to be diminished in the manner described above. And the bloodletting...

### BOOK IV.

The blood should be let as quickly as possible, at least as soon as an **abscess** <note>Original: "apostema," a swelling or tumor, often referring to a plague bubo.</note> first begins to appear. You should have a significant amount of blood extracted boldly, unless the patient happens to have very little blood. After about two ounces have been drawn, stop for a moment so it can be judged whether the blood is "good" or not. If it appears bad, you may extract more copiously; if it appears good, more sparingly. In weak patients or those without an abundance of blood, an extraction of two ounces is sufficient. However, you must never do this during the time of a feverish chill.

While the **bloodletting** <term>minutio: literally a "diminishing," a common term for phlebotomy or bleeding a patient.</term> is being performed, the patient should taste or hold an orange in their mouth, or something sour, and vinegar should be applied to the nose, the forehead, and the pulses of the temples; for this is the standard procedure for phlebotomy. **Gentile da Foligno** <note>A famous 14th-century Italian physician known for his commentaries on Avicenna and his work during the Black Death.</note> highly praises the following method as a proven thing:

*   If the typical abscess appears near the shoulder blades, **cupping glasses** <note>Ventosæ: suction cups used to draw humors to the surface.</note> should be applied where the shoulder blades meet. The bloodletting should be done from the **median vein**, which is commonly called the "common" or "black" vein.
*   If it appears on the neck or head, the **cephalic vein** <note>The vein running along the thumb side of the arm.</note> should be bled near the thumbs of the hands.
*   If it appears under or on the right arm, the patient should be bled from the **lung vein** <note>Original: "vena pulmonis," a historical term for a specific vein in the hand, typically between the middle and ring fingers.</note> between the middle and ring finger of that same side.
*   If it is around the left arm or side, bleed from the **Salvatella vein** <note>A vein on the back of the hand near the pinky finger.</note> between the ring and little finger of the right hand.
*   If it is in the groin or on the left side, the bloodletting must be performed from the **Paralytic vein** between the hollow of the knee and the adjacent area on that same side.
*   If it appears in the right shin or foot, use the vein called the **"Women’s Vein."**

Spanish and Catalan doctors usually perform phlebotomy in two intervals, either after an enema has been administered or at least by the second day. For robust, full-blooded men of a good age, they proceed this way on the first day: first, they extract blood from the opposite side of the body because the **humor** <note>In Galenic medicine, the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that governed health.</note> is still in motion and has not yet become poisonous.

For example, if an abscess appears under the left arm, they immediately draw four or six ounces from the right hand, or three ounces from the left ankle. Then, after six or eight hours, once the patient is rested and quiet, they extract four, six, or three ounces from the left arm according to the pressure and strength of the **larger vein**, as that vein shows itself more ready for phlebotomy.

They do the opposite when an abscess appears in the groin: first they bleed the arm of the same side, and secondly the foot of that same side from the **Saphenous vein**. However, if the patient is not very robust and does not have an abundance of blood, yet still possesses a decent natural vigor and constancy of strength—or if it is already the end of the second or third day, when it is likely that the matter has already begun its course and motion and is now infected with poison—they evacuate two or four ounces from the side where the abscess is located, in a spot as close to the abscess as possible. If it appears behind the ears, they bleed from the cephalic vein of the same side. But if this vein cannot be easily found, let it be done in the

# EPIDEMIC ANTIDOTES

...the **median vein** <note>The "middle" vein of the arm, often used in bloodletting because it was thought to drain the whole body.</note> since it communicates with the entire body. But if that vein is not visible, let the blood be drawn from the same hand from the vein located between the thumb and the index finger. Likewise, they perform this from the middle of the second day through the following days; however, from the beginning until the middle of the second day, they should perform **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood, a primary medical treatment for centuries.</term> on the opposite side, and similarly from the first day to the middle of the second.

If an **abscess** <note>Original: "apostema," referring here to a plague bubo or swelling.</note> is under the arm, the blood must be evacuated from the vein of the same arm, either from the "common vein" or at least from the **hepatic vein** <note>Also known as the basilic vein, historically associated with the liver.</note>, or from the same hand between the middle finger and the finger next to it. If, during the aforementioned time, the sign itself appears in the **groin** <note>Original: "inguinib."</note>, you should cut the vein below the knee on the same side, or below the **ankle** <note>Original: "cauilla."</note> of the same foot. If the sign tends toward the **buttocks** <note>Original: "nates."</note>, draw blood from the thicker and more visible vein on the back of the foot on that same side. The method for these is that before the middle of the second day, they mostly begin to extract blood from the opposite side; but after that time, they mostly do the opposite.

Now, let us turn to our **universal rules** <note>Original: "canones nostros vniuersales."</note>. Because a disease of this kind is located either in the blood itself or in the humors mixed with the blood, it seems to me that blood should be drawn from everyone between the ages of fourteen and sixty. I consider it far better that the poison expire through the opening of a vein than for the patient to be greatly tormented by the later outflow of blood. 

Extract the blood in repeated turns with a six-hour interval between them. For robust bodies with a great abundance of blood, extract up to one **pound** <note>A "libra" or medical pound, roughly 12 ounces in contemporary apothecary weight.</note>. For those of moderate strength and moderate blood, draw up to eight ounces; for weaker patients with a steady pulse, four or three ounces, or even two or at least one. Where **yellow bile** <term>cholera: one of the four humors; an excess was thought to cause heat and irritability.</term> holds dominion, the extraction should not exceed two ounces. 

Many practitioners command that blood be drawn until the patient, previously strong, becomes weakened. This pleases me not at all, since it dissolves the **vital spirit** <note>Original: "spiritus," the life force believed to circulate through the body.</note>. Where the pulse wavers, nothing at all should be extracted. My greater concern, however, is that the abscess appears first; even afterward, **hemorrhoids** <note>Here referring to the drawing of blood or humors to the lower body to divert them from the heart.</note> should be provoked by friction made with rough materials and onion juice, along with cupping, **scarification** <term>scarification: making small, shallow cuts in the skin to draw blood or fluids to the surface.</term>, and leeches. Where blood is abundant, do the same after a second bloodletting. Where there is little blood, you should at least do this.

->### ANTIDOTES FOR EPIDEMICS<-

...[these remedies] benefit the heart and assist it in expelling the poison from itself; they dry out the humors prone to putrefaction and restrain the passages of the heart so that the poison itself does not reach it. Frequently, they also expel the poison by way of sweat. It has been found through experience that the earlier, ancient prescription we mentioned, as well as the last among the modern ones, are much more effective than all the others. 

There are some who, after inducing vomiting (if it be necessary) and also performing an enema <term>clystere: a liquid injection into the rectum used to clear the bowels or deliver medicine.</term> and anointing the body, first administer the powders and a compress <term>epithema: a topical application or poultice, often placed over the heart or liver.</term>. Only after its operation do they then drain blood. They do this when the patient has an abundance of blood, and perhaps in this they are not mistaken. But when the extraction of blood is not possible due to a lack of blood, they administer medicine instead of bloodletting <term>phlebotomiæ: the surgical practice of opening a vein to balance the body's humors.</term>, yet they give the powder first. 

After the sick person has sweated, or the proper time for sweating has passed, one must not wait for the "digestion" <note>original: "digestio"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to 'concoction,' the process where the body matures or 'cooks' harmful humors so they can be expelled.</note> of the humor, because there is no time or opportunity allowed for waiting for that digestion to occur. Indeed, when necessity is imminent (since necessity itself is not subject to the law), the usual distinctions of times and days should by no means be observed. Nor should one trust in any hope that nature will successfully evacuate the humor on its own, because nature's work is irregular due to the lack of "digestion" and the force of the poison; indeed, an oppressed nature works more than it ought, as best it can. 

Therefore, after a suitable time for sweating, you will either reduce the blood if it is abundant, or if it is not abundant, you will provide a purgative, though using substances that do not disturb the stomach. For vomiting produced with violence, by dilating the passages of the chest, causes the poison to run through to the heart and draws it to the brain. For this reason, those who administer goat's rue <note>original: "capraginem"; likely Galega officinalis, used as a medicinal herb but here cautioned against if it causes violent vomiting.</note> and similar things that are emetic and poisonous are in error. For nature can barely resist a single poison. 

Perhaps someone might object to us, asking why physicians are accustomed to induce vomiting in those who have been poisoned. I say that the condition of these poisons is not the same: for other poisons have more physical matter and are more suitable for being drawn out through vomiting, as they are located in the stomach; but this [plague] is a certain poisonous vapor in the regions of the chest. Therefore, let no medicine be used that can violently produce vomiting, though I would not at all condemn one that does so without violence; yet I would prefer that the diversion of humors be made through the lower parts <note>i.e., through the bowels via purgatives or enemas.</note>. 

Let the medicine you give be dissolved in white wine and water of scabious <note>original: "scabiosæ"; a plant traditionally used to treat "scabby" skin and sores.</note>, endive, roses, plantain, bugloss <note>original: "buglossæ"; a plant used to treat fevers and heart conditions.</note>, lemon balm <note>original: "melissæ"</note>, and rose vinegar, in which a decoction has been made of Damson plums, myrobalans <note>original: "myrobalanis"; a dried fruit from India used as a gentle laxative.</note>, and tamarinds. If, however, the disease invades someone with a full stomach, what then must be done according to the methods of the moderns? Ensure that after anointing with oil of scorpions <note>original: "oleo scorpionum"; an oil in which scorpions were steeped, believed to draw out venom by "like curing like."</note> and theriac, he vomits easily with warm water, vinegar, oil, and radish juice, even trying to provoke it with a long feather; then you will administer an enema, and afterwards a compress, and some of those powders.

<header>BOOK IV.</header>

Then, at a time when the patient is calmer and recovered, you should open a vein <term>venam seces: the surgical opening of a vein, also known as phlebotomy.</term> if they are of a sanguine temperament <note>original: "sanguineus"; according to the theory of the four humors, a person with an abundance of blood, often characterized as energetic and ruddy-faced.</note>. If not, administer medicine instead. If you extract more than four ounces of blood during the bloodletting, abstain from giving medicine until twelve hours have passed since the procedure. And even if you have performed the bloodletting, do not place your hope in that alone, especially in a body that is plethoric <term>plethorico: a state of having an excess of bodily fluids, particularly blood.</term>, sanguine, and robust. On the contrary, even in other patients from whom you have extracted little blood, medicine must still be administered at its proper time, according to the quality of the patient's complexion and their strength. Likewise, if you have given medicine first, do not be content with that alone; if the body is plethoric and the patient's strength allows it, you should also enjoin bloodletting at the proper time and in the proper manner.

You shall make this distinction when administering one or the other, where possible and appropriate: where blood is abundant, bloodletting should come first and be more copious; but where blood is not abundant, the medicine should come first and bloodletting should follow—though it should be moderate, namely for the sake of venting <note>original: "euentandi"; a medical term for allowing "vapors" to escape the body.</note> rather than reducing the total volume of blood. After the third day, no extraction of blood ought to be performed unless an extreme multitude of blood compels you to it. Whenever you administer medicine, bloodletting, or emetics <note>original: "vomituum"; treatments meant to induce vomiting.</note>, you must ensure that the poison does not return from the "sign" <note>original: "signo"; refers to the physical manifestation of the plague, such as a bubo or swelling.</note> to the internal organs due to the agitation of the treatment. If the sign is visible, make sure that during such a commotion you place cupping glasses <term>ventosas: glass cups used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw humors to the surface.</term> and leeches above and below the sign, and apply cold compresses <term>epithemata: topical medicinal applications, often liquid-soaked cloths.</term> over the heart.

Both before and after, you shall administer by mouth those things that defend against poison, namely theriac <term>theriacam: a complex herbal "universal" antidote highly prized in medieval and Renaissance medicine.</term>, Armenian bole <term>bolum armenum: a medicinal red clay from Armenia used as an astringent and antidote.</term>, emeralds, jacinths, topaz, or at least other kinds of gems, or corals mixed with the juice of anti-venomous herbs. When you perform a purging, give the medicine with a small amount of saffron <note>original: "croci"</note> in the aforementioned decoction.

The principal and safer medicine, according to the Persian physicians and Mesue <note>Mesue the Younger, a likely pseudonymous author of highly influential Arabic pharmaceutical texts.</note>, is one ounce of Persian Trifera <term>triferæ Persicæ: a complex Persian electuary, typically containing myrobalans and other fruits, used as a gentle purgative.</term> with two drams of the Electuary of Hamech <term>electuarij hamech: a strong purgative electuary containing senna, rhubarb, and black hellebore.</term>; or at the very least, half an ounce of the Persian Trifera and one or half a dram of the Electuary of Hamech. However, for particularly robust patients, one ounce is given with three drams of the Electuary of Hamech. The Persians administer this with cold water or the juice of nightshade or endive. I have heard of this frequently and have made a successful trial <note>original: "felix periculum feci"; a phrase meaning to successfully experiment or test a treatment.</note> of it in this present year.

Where the Persian Trifera and the Electuary of Hamech are unavailable, you shall administer *diasena* <note>a compound made primarily of senna.</note> in place of the Trifera, and *diamanna* <note>a compound made with manna, a sweet sap used as a mild laxative.</note>, as well as rose juice in place of the Electuary of Hamech in the manner described above. I have tested this and found this composition to be of great utility and safety:

Take half an ounce each of Persian Trifera and cassia pulp, and one dram of rhubarb, *diamanna*, or Electuary of Hamech. But where nature is strong and the bowels are bound <note>original: "venter stypticus"; constipated or resistant to purging.</note>, you shall give two drams of *diamanna* or Electuary of Hamech. Dissolve these with waters of bugloss and endive, and with the aforementioned decoctions and waters. As for myself, I steep the rhubarb in white wine and endive water with a little spikenard <note>original: "spicæ"; an aromatic essential oil from a Himalayan plant.</note> for one hour...

# EPIDEMIC ANTIDOTES

...which I give by mixing everything together in substance; quite often I even add one ounce <term>vncia: a unit of weight equal to about 28 grams.</term> of manna <note>A sweet, resinous sap from the flowering ash tree, used as a mild laxative.</note> afterward. Pills of fumitory <note>original: "fumo terræ"; a plant used in medieval medicine to "purify" the blood and treat skin conditions.</note> and "aggregative" pills <note>A standard compound medicine of the time, designed to "aggregate" and expel multiple humors at once.</note> in equal parts are also suitable. For robust patients, the dose is half a drachm <term>drachma: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams or 1/8 of an ounce.</term> in total, taken by drinking it down with white wine mixed with waters of endive, roses, or scabious. These aggregative pills alone are also useful at any time—especially when it is not the height of summer—in a dose of one drachm or half a drachm.

It must be noted that if the fever clings to thin and hot humors <note>In the "humoral theory" of the time, health was governed by four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. "Subtle" or thin humors were thought to move quickly and cause sharper, more violent symptoms.</note>, there will appear a vehement thirst, dryness of the throat, blackness of the tongue, sharp headache, "phrenesis" <note>A state of delirium or mental confusion caused by inflammation.</note>, or similar terrifying symptoms. If, however, the fever clings to thicker and less "furious" humors, the fever will appear sluggish and the aforementioned symptoms will be milder.

Observe these signs, and know that for any humor, "triphera" <note>A traditional herbal electuary or jam-like medicine.</note> with agaric is suitable, as are aggregative pills—either alone or with pills of fumitory. A laxative syrup, which we shall describe below, is also appropriate. If the matter is "furious" <note>Active or acutely inflamed.</note>, *diafene* <note>A laxative made from dates.</note> with electuary of hamech <note>A common purgative used to treat "melancholic" or thick humors.</note> or rose juice is also fitting. Likewise, cassia with rhubarb, or manna with "diamanna" in cold decoctions.

If the matter is thick, cold, and moist, two scruples <term>scrupulus: a small weight, about 1.3 grams.</term> of aggregative pills and one scruple of agaric pills are suitable for the more robust. For weaker patients, use one ounce of *diacatholicon* <note>A "universal" purgative compound.</note> with two drachms of *diasinicon*, or with one or a half-drachm of agaric troches <term>trohiscatis: medicinal lozenges or cakes.</term>. Likewise, one or a half-drachm of the "pills against the disease" mentioned above may be used; perhaps such pills are suitable for any humor. 

Note that agaric <note>A type of fungus (Larch Agaric) highly prized as a purgative for "cleansing" the organs.</note>, when well-prepared and made into troches, is extraordinary in this case for every humor and every limb. Therefore, when I am certain of its preparation, I use it in every medicine, giving two drachms, or one, or a half, according to the potency of the medicine and the "complexion" <note>The unique physical and temperament-based makeup of the individual patient.</note> of the person. If I were in doubt about its preparation, I would infuse it in oxymel of squill <note>A mixture of honey, vinegar, and sea onion (squill).</note> with rock salt, and afterward, having strained it, I would place it over the medicine without squeezing it out. 

It should also be noted that aggregative pills are specific to this use, but in their place for less robust patients, "pills without which" <note>original: "pillulæ sine quibus"; a famous recipe called "Pilulae sine quibus esse nolo" (Pills without which I do not wish to be), a general-purpose laxative.</note> should be administered. And know that it is better to give a liquid medicine than pills in this case. If it can be obtained, "diamanna" is better than rose juice and stronger. Indeed, the electuary of hamech is better than both—that is, better than diamanna and rose juice.

Finally, in every humor, this laxative syrup is wonderful in place of medicine, at a dose of at least one ounce, and at most two, taken with rose water and white wine: 
Take citron bark, caper roots, barberry, red sandalwood, and *spodium* <note>A medicinal powder, often oxide of zinc or burnt bone/ivory, used for its cooling properties.</note>, two drachms of each; clove-root <note>original: "caryophyllatę"; wood avens.</note>, lemon balm, bugloss, borage, and chicory, one handful of each; sorrel, horehound, and liverwort, one and a half handfuls of each; wild endive, two drachms; seeds of pumpkin, melon, watermelon, cucumber, and vio-

### BOOK IV.

...of asarabacca <note>original: "sarum" or "asarum"; a plant used to induce vomiting or as a purgative.</note> one handful; of thyme, dodder of thyme <note>original: "epithymi"; a parasitic vine often found on thyme, used to purge "black bile."</note>, larch agaric <note>A medicinal fungus used as a laxative.</note>, rhubarb, and senna; of polypody fern root <note>original: "polypodij"; used to treat respiratory and digestive issues.</note>, two <term>drachma: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams or 1/8 of an ounce.</term> drachms each; of the juices of wormwood, fumitory, dwarf elder, and plantain, six drachms each; of Chebulic myrobalans <note>An astringent fruit from India, highly prized in medieval pharmacy.</note>, one drachm; of Citrine myrobalans, half a drachm; of diagridium <note>A preparation of scammony (a harsh resin) juice thickened with quince.</note>, two drachms; and of white sugar, two pounds. Create a syrup with quince vinegar.

This syrup is called "Divine" by the doctors for its powers of preservation and healing, because it immediately cuts away the humors that are prone to rot, strengthens the principal organs, and drives poison outward. Many successful experiences with it have been observed. Among other doctors, Pietro da Tossignano <note>A famous 14th-century Italian physician known for his treatises on the plague.</note> and Gentile da Foligno <note>A prominent medical professor who died while treating plague victims in 1348.</note> commend it in a wonderful manner. It seems to me that it was made with the same intent as the "Persian Trifera" <note>A classic electuary (medicinal paste) of Eastern origin.</note>, but it is more laxative. It pleases me greatly for use in persons who are not extremely weak and who do not have excessively loose bowels. It should be taken once a week by both the healthy and the sick.

Note that after the operation of the medicine or bloodletting <term>phlebotomia: the surgical opening of a vein to balance the humors.</term>, if you have not administered medicine the following day, let one drachm of Theriac <note>The most famous "universal antidote" of the pre-modern world, containing dozens of ingredients including viper flesh and opium.</note> be drunk with one ounce of rose water and a small amount of rose vinegar. Do not fear the heat of the Theriac, for such a small portion can provide little heat. This is because an elemental quality—such as heat and the like—being very material in nature, does not do much unless there is a great deal of the substance.

Truly, its "specific virtue" <note>A concept where a drug works through its unique "occult" or divinely-given essence rather than its basic temperature (hot/cold).</note>—which is a celestial and almost spiritual gift—works greatly even with a small amount of substance, according to Galen <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated medicine for 1,500 years.</note>. Theriac, moreover, works against poison by this specific property. Beyond this, its heat scarcely reaches the "second degree" <note>In Galenic medicine, qualities like heat were measured in four degrees. The second degree was considered moderate.</note>; therefore, it is far more powerful at expelling poison than it is at heating the body. Likewise, a pestilential fever is much more poisonous than it is hot; thus, Theriac must be administered with rose water, and in other treatments one must take care that they tend toward a certain coldness, so that you may utilize this remedy.

Mithridatum <note>Another ancient complex antidote, similar to Theriac, named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note> can also be given in place of Theriac, but much more powerful experiences have been seen with Theriac. Therefore, Moses the Egyptian <note>The famous philosopher and physician Maimonides (1135–1204).</note> says it was related to him by a certain wise physician that while he was practicing his art in Antioch during a time of plague, he found by actual experience that all other remedies were weak. Only those who took Theriac upon his advice escaped safe and surviving; the others did not. And only those who used it after the onset of the disease were liberated; others exchanged their life for death. This confirms what Galen says in his book to Caesar regarding Theriac: that it is opposed to all poisons and will be powerful where others fail and are weak. This power it holds from a certain miraculous virtue.

There are also those who offer urine as a drink, or lye <note>original: "lixiuium"; a strong alkaline solution made from ashes.</note>; likewise the juice of white onions with vinegar—I know not what I should say about these. I warn you: do not have overconfidence in a purgation after you have performed it, even if the sick person feels better because of it; for when the patient seems to feel better...

->### ANTIDOTES FOR EPIDEMICS<-

It shall be given <note>original: "debitur," likely "dabitur"</note> on the third or fourth day after purging. If there is still a great superfluity of blood, extract a little blood and repeat the same medicinal purging. But if the blood does not greatly abound, at least repeat the powders and the medicine, lest the patient fall back into a worse state. Some provide euphorbium <note>A caustic resin from the spurge plant, used as a very strong purgative.</note> with mastic and gum elemi. Take five <term>drachma: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams.</term> drachms and one <term>scrupulum: a "scruple," roughly 1.3 grams.</term> scruple of euphorbium, two ounces of gum elemi, and one and a half ounces of mastic. Give one drachm to the robust, and one scruple to the weak, along with endive and scabious waters. It is indeed a dangerous medicine, and is not assigned to any but the strongest patients, and then only at the beginning of the illness. Some assert that gum elemi is the gum of the cedar tree. According to this case, a medicine that is not "weak" should be given—that is, one that produces a significant effect—because if the first medicine has not worked well, nature itself does not wait for a second. Yet, one should not purge with too much force, for by this the spirits <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" (spiritus) were the vital forces or vapors that animated the body.</note> are dissolved, and this evil consists more in a certain poisonous quality than in the quantity of the matter itself. Gentile da Foligno <note>A famous 14th-century physician who died while treating plague victims.</note> said he had experienced much with the aforementioned powder, and from the beginning he administered it thus: Take half a drachm of euphorbium and one drachm of mastic; of these he gave two scruples, and to those who were very plethoric <note>Having an excess of bodily fluids, especially blood.</note>, one drachm.

But to me, agaric <note>original: "agaricus"; the larch fungus, used as a gentle but effective laxative.</note> is much more pleasing, because as Democritus, Galen, and Avicenna say, it draws humor from all the limbs. Similarly, it possesses a virtue like that of theriac <note>A universal antidote or "cure-all" for poisons.</note>: it strengthens the heart against every poison and purges the heart of all venom. It principally purges thick humors, yet does not leave the thin ones untouched. It should be white, porous, round, and also easy to break, sweet, and light. It should also be of moderate bitterness and stypticity <note>The quality of being astringent or drawing tissue together.</note>, well-ground, and mixed with a third part of rock salt <note>original: "salis gemmae"; literally "gem salt," a high-quality crystalline salt.</note>. Thus it is corrected with the rock salt, strained honey of roses, oxymel of squill <note>A medicinal syrup made of honey, vinegar, and the sea onion (squill).</note>, and wine infused with ginger, and thus let it be prepared into troches <note>Small medicinal lozenges or cakes.</note>. For the weak, it is safer to give it mixed with other things than alone, and better in decoctions <note>Concentrated liquors made by boiling herbal materials.</note> than in its raw substance, for it frequently produces long-lasting vomiting and pains of the belly unless it is well chosen and prepared. But if it has been duly chosen and prepared, it is a holy and familiar medicine, according to Democritus and Mesue <note>A famous 9th-century Persian physician.</note>. For we have had successful experiences with this agaric (following the manner and order described).

But regarding euphorbium, we have found that it was sometimes a very good work, but more often the contrary. Universally, and in sum: be swift and frequent in evacuating, provided the proper manner and order are observed. Refresh the sick person frequently, because otherwise the spirits are greatly dissolved. Do not give only those things, whether foods or medicines, that merely soften <note>original: "mollicat"; likely referring to emollient or laxative effects.</note>, but mix with these things that are cooling, drying, and heart-strengthening, which also resist poison.
