->BOOK IV.<-

### On the feeding and regimen of the sick. Chapter X.

Food should be, according to Rhazes <note>A celebrated 9th-century Persian physician whose works were foundational to European medicine.</note> and Avicenna <note>A 11th-century polymath; the reference to the "fourth Canon" refers to the section of his *Canon of Medicine* dealing with systemic diseases like fevers.</note> in the fourth book of the Canon, frequent, moderate, light, boiled, and of much and moist nourishment, seasoned with acidic and cold things; namely with endive, sorrel, vinegar, verjuice <note>original: "agresta," the tart juice of unripe grapes</note>, pomegranates, oranges, lemons, sour cherries, and plums. Let the substance of the food be chicken, partridge, pheasant, consommé, distillations, and fresh eggs. I also do not forbid the meat of kids <note>young goats</note>. In short, let the patient be nourished with liquid and moist things of great nourishment. However, he should be nourished in such a way that nature can tolerate it, and so that the fevers do not increase; for in this case, much more than in others, there is need for more abundant food. Avicenna says in the fourth Canon that the filling of the veins through nourishment prevents the passage of the poisonous vapor of the air and of the humor, and that those who are fearlessly assisted by nourishment are more frequently set free <note>i.e., they recover from the illness</note>. Note that once a loosening clyster <note>an enema</note> has been administered, which we mentioned above, if another restoration is needed, let him take something by mouth; you shall produce a loosening either with an enema or a suppository, and from there, after four hours, you shall administer some nourishment of the kind we discussed just above.

Let the wine be white, thin, fragrant, and diluted with chalybeate water <note>original: "aqua ferrata," water in which hot iron has been quenched, believed to have strengthening properties</note>, or at least with fresh water in equal parts. Indeed, "golden water" would be better, in which glowing gold has been quenched; or the gold can also be quenched in wine. Do not allow him to suffer thirst, nor the mouth to be dried out, but continually make him gargle with well-diluted white wine. Let him hold moist, cool things in his mouth; let him drink frequently of citron acidity and rose julep <note>original: "iuleb rosato," a sweet medicinal syrup</note>, equal parts <note>original: "ana," a standard medical abbreviation for equal quantities</note> with pomegranate wine and water, or the juice of sorrel. 

Simple syrup of sorrel with chalybeate water is useful, as is the juice of citron, or lemons, or squeezed oranges; you shall give these with water and fine sugar, or perhaps better with barley water or chalybeate water. Likewise, rose sugar, or <term>diamarenatum: a medicinal confection made from sour cherries.</term> diamarenatum, or <term>diaprunis: a medicinal preserve made from plums.</term> diaprunis, and <term>diacydoniten: a jelly or syrup made from quinces.</term> diacydoniten dissolved in water, strained, and pressed; or roses, sour cherries, <term>myrobalanos: dried fruits of the myrobalan tree, used as a gentle purgative.</term> myrobalans, tamarinds, plums, quinces, and dried peaches—ground and infused in water, then strained, pressed, and presented with sugar and fresh water—are all useful. White vinegar with chalybeate water and sugar is suitable for the sick as well as for the healthy. Also beneficial is <term>oxysacchara: a medicinal syrup composed of vinegar and sugar.</term> oxysacchara compounded with white vinegar, the juice of sour pomegranates, and sugar. Also profitable is the juice of pomegranates of moderate flavor, or the juice or wine of sour things with a little sugar, and barley water with pomegranate wine. It is good to rub gold rings in water for so long that they are slightly worn down by the water. Likewise, it is good to boil water with gold and use it in food and drink.

->EPIDEMIC ANTIDOTES<-

According to Gentile <note>Gentile da Foligno (d. 1348), an influential Italian physician who died while treating plague victims.</note> it may perhaps be possible for gold to be reduced to a liquid form suitable for drinking, in this manner: Take one ounce of gold and two ounces of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>; mix them, and let them remain mixed together until the gold is dissolved. Then place it in an alembic <note>a chemical still used for distillation</note> over a slow fire, just enough so that the quicksilver exits the alembic. Afterward, take the gold from the bottom of the alembic and add forty-seven ounces of bugloss water <note>original: "aquarum buglossae"; bugloss was a common plant used in "cordials" to hearten the patient</note>, and place it in a glass alembic that is well-sealed. You shall continue the fire under it for three days and nights—I mean a well-proportioned fire. In the end, if you are skilled in the art, you will find the water not at all consumed, and the gold liquefied; this is "potable gold," the most heart-strengthening cordial <note>original: "aurum potabile cordialissimum"</note>, and it can be digested. Gold in any other form is of little use, because it can in no way be digested. 

You shall administer this on an empty stomach during the day from these syrups: namely, of citric acidity, of lemons, of chicory, and of fumitory <note>original: "fumo terrae," literally "smoke of the earth," a plant used to cleanse the blood</note>; half a drachm of each, with one ounce of lemon balm water and wood sorrel juice. Likewise, syrups of verjuice <note>original: "agresta," the tart juice of unripe grapes</note>, of currants, barberry jelly <note>original: "rob berberis"</note>, of quinces, of pomegranates of medium flavor, and of pomegranates with waters of endive and bugloss. Likewise, syrups of endive with endive waters, and citric acidity, with wood sorrel juice, and the wine of sour pomegranates. Likewise, the juice of lemons, or citron, or pressed oranges should be administered with water and sugar. 

It would not be displeasing if, in place of water, you administered a chicken broth, which is commonly called *Piperata* <note>a peppery or spiced broth</note>, or a partridge cooked with verjuice and endive, then strained, into which has been mixed some of the aforementioned juices, tempering the sour with the sweet, just as nature does in pomegranates of medium flavor. Also, sour pomegranates with wine and their own juice alone, or even with other juices—let all be well seasoned. Likewise, rose juice, myrobalans <note>a plum-like fruit used as a laxative</note>, tamarinds, rose-sugar, and sour cherry syrup <note>original: "diamarenatum"</note>, plum conserve, and quince confection, dissolved in water, strained, and pressed, are to be drunk with fresh water. Likewise, oxysaccharum <note>a medicinal syrup of vinegar and sugar</note> with rose julep and iron-water <note>original: "aqua ferrata," water in which hot iron had been quenched, believed to have strengthening properties</note>. Likewise, rose juice and citric acidity with pomegranate wine. 

Note: syrup of sorrel is useful in any syrup whatsoever. Where citric acidity is not available, squeeze lemons or oranges and temper them with sugar; where there is greater heat <note>i.e., a higher fever</note>, you shall give a greater quantity of acidic things; where there is less, a smaller quantity. And where acidic syrup is not available, you shall give vinegar, water, and sugar mixed together. White vinegar is better than red. 

Likewise, this excellent syrup: Take three ounces each of the purified juices of lemon balm, borage, and bugloss; one and a half ounces each of rose water and white vinegar; half an ounce of the acidity of citron and lemons; and one pound of white sugar. From this you shall provide two ounces to drink, with two and a half ounces of bugloss and wood sorrel waters. Use whichever of these pleases you; and at the same time, give two camphor lozenges. ### BOOK IV.

...[Some] of the wise physicians give this potion in place of a syrup: Take one pound of rose water, half a pound of fragrant white wine, and half an ounce of the best **Armenian bole** <note>original: "boli armeni"; a medicinal red clay thought to have astringent and antitoxic properties</note>, finely powdered and sifted. For one dose, administer two drachms; for it is a remedy both ancient and powerful. 

Practical experimenters use two things above all: namely, orange flower juice with wine in the case of a collapse and after a collapse <note>likely referring to fainting or a "falling sickness" associated with high fever</note>, and the seeds of **blessed thistle** <note>original: "cardonis benedicti"; a plant long used in herbal medicine to treat the plague</note> with wine, because these have been proven effective against the poison of mushrooms. 

The wise are also accustomed to give these: Take three ounces of scabious <note>a flowering plant whose name comes from "scabies," used here to draw out toxins</note> juice, one drachm of **sealed earth** <note>original: "terrae sigillatae"; a famous medicinal clay tablet from the island of Lemnos, stamped with a seal to guarantee its authenticity</note> with a little wine; likewise, two drachms of citron seeds with good wine. Also, amber and yellow amber with wine; likewise, one drachm of the "species of coagulants" with wine. 

These **coagulants** <note>original: "coagula"</note> are certain mucilages <note>sticky or gelatinous substances</note> found in specific bladders or sacs attached to the internal organs of young goats and hares. 

Likewise, the root of the **Palm of Christ** <note>original: "palmæ Christi"; a name for the castor oil plant, though here the root is used</note> with wine. These things, which (as we have related) the wise use, remove the poison from the heart. 

These preparations are suitable for preserving health and for curing. Place great trust in this, our own composition, which is simple, safe, and most effective: Take two drachms of Armenian bole, one drachm each of sealed earth and red corals, half a drachm each of citron peels, zedoary <note>a root similar to ginger</note>, and saffron; six ounces of rose sugar preserved with red roses, and ten ounces of citron acidity <note>citrus juice or extract</note>. Always administer this with white wine and rose water; sometimes a little rose vinegar should be mixed in. 

From these we can also make pills if, in place of the rose sugar, we take half an ounce of red roses with a sufficient amount of citron acidity. 

Some give these compositions: Take four ounces each of rose sugar, the three sandalwoods <note>red, white, and yellow sandalwood</note>, and tragacanth <note>original: "diadraganti"; a natural plant gum used as a binder</note>; ten gold leaves; and one drachm each of pearls, hyacinths <note>likely the gemstone zircon or a blue sapphire</note>, and the **bone from a stag’s heart** <note>original: "ossis de corde cerui"; a small piece of cartilage or bone found in the hearts of older deer, highly prized as a heart tonic</note>. 

Likewise, take one scruple of pearls; two drachms of sapphire, hyacinths, and emeralds; half a drachm each of sealed earth, "three-grains" <note>likely a specific pharmaceutical preparation</note>, and ground raw silk; one drachm of emeralds; as much **Hand of Christ with roses** <note>original: "manus Christi rosati"; a type of sugar candy or lozenge often containing ground pearls</note> as you please; and enough rose water in which gold rings or similar gold vessels have been rubbed. 

Likewise, one pound each of rose water and white sugar; half a drachm each of red and white sandalwood, red coral, and **spodumene** <note>original: "spodij"; here referring to the ash or metallic oxide residue used in cooling medicines</note>; one drachm of pearls; and one scruple each of hyacinths, emeralds, sapphire, and the bone from a stag’s heart. 

All aromatic substances are suitable for preserving health and curing, especially those pertaining to coldness and heat. And even if they are not suited for the heat of a fever, they are nonetheless effective against its poison—especially if they are tempered with cold ingredients, so that they tend toward a certain coldness. They should tend even more toward coldness when the heat of the season, the person’s constitution, or acute fevers persists.

->### ANTIDOTES FOR THE EPIDEMIC<-

Between **Armenian bole** <note>original: "bolum armenum"; a reddish medicinal clay from Armenia</note> and **sealed earth** <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a famous medicinal clay from Lemnos, stamped with an official seal to guarantee purity</note>, this is the distinction: although both are effective against poison and disease, the wise physicians nevertheless use "earth" more than "bole" for general poisons. However, in the case of a pestilential disease <note>the plague</note>, they do the opposite. On this point all agree: for other poisons, nothing is better than **sealed earth**, especially when administered with a small amount of **Armenian bole**, juniper berries, and diluted vinegar according to the method of **Galen** <note>a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note>. This is because it immediately constricts and closes the passages of the chest so that the poison cannot pass through them, and it expels the poison through vomiting. Similarly, for poison that can be drawn out through purgatives, it performs this task whether administered before or after the onset of illness, though it is safer to take it before.

Likewise, all agree that both for preserving oneself from the plague and for expelling it, **Armenian bole** surpasses all other simple medicines. It is best administered with white wine and rose water, following the order of **Galen**, **Serapio**, and **Avicenna** <note>referring to the great Greek, Arabic, and Persian medical authorities</note>, who say they have proven through experience during times of great pestilence that humors were easily preserved and healed with this remedy. For **Armenian bole** is red with a slight saffron tint, delicate, and easily broken; **sealed earth**, however, is somewhat reddish, slightly sour to the taste, dry, and a little viscous, yet not so sticky that it clings to the fingers.

Take note that sometimes the disease begins with an abundance of blood in the spit <note>hemoptysis, a common symptom of pneumonic plague</note>. In this case, **bole** should not be given, nor any other astringent <note>a substance that shrinks tissues or stops flow</note> for this poisonous blood. Rather, this flow should be assisted with pectoral <note>chest-relieving</note> remedies, and blood should be drawn from both **saphenous veins** <note>large veins in the leg</note>, depending on the quality of the patient's temperament. If the patient is very full-blooded, a later bloodletting should also be performed from the **median vein** <note>the middle vein of the arm</note>.

Nor should frictions <note>therapeutic rubbing or massage</note> on an empty stomach be neglected. See that a sponge soaked in rose water, rose vinegar, and fragrant wine is moved near the nose; with these liquids, you should also frequently wash all the pulse points and the face. Where there is a suspicion of future **phrensy** <note>original: "phrenesi"; a state of delirium or brain inflammation</note>, you should occasionally apply rose water with rose vinegar to the forehead. And unless you fear excessive sleepiness, add a little **camphor**. Take care that the sick person does not fall into too deep a sleep; for five or six hours a day and night are sufficient, since too much sleeping draws the poison inward. **Cupping glasses** <note>original: "ventosæ"; glass jars used to create suction on the skin</note> placed on the back, frictions, and bindings around the extremities help against both delirium and sleepiness. Likewise, a suppository made of hard soap with a little **rock salt** <note>original: "sal gemmæ"</note> is helpful. 

A moderate amount of sleep at the beginning of the disease is useful, but one should not stay awake so much that the spirits <note>the vital forces of the body</note> are exhausted. The chamber ought to be aired out by frequently opening and closing [the windows]; for this refreshes the air. However, it should be aired in such a way that the patient does not feel it or suffer any chill. Linen cloths moistened with vinegar should be hung along the sides of the bed. Sprinkle the walls and the floor of the room with vinegar mixed with water; let them be sprinkled here and there, and...

# BOOK IV.

In the corners and against the walls, place greenery: branches, vine shoots, reeds, willows, roses, small plants, leaves of citruls <note>likely watermelons or similar gourds</note>, and any other green things, little flowers, and fragrant fruits. You shall create a fumigation <note>a medicinal incense or smoke used to purify the air</note> using sandalwood, roses, myrtles, and camphor, turpentine, frankincense, citrus peels, pomegranate rinds, and common apples, adding a small amount of cloves and saffron. Nor do I wish to pass over in silence that when an unusual heat appears, along with strength in the stomach and freedom from intestinal pain, **Rhazes** <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> and **Johannitius** <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a famous 9th-century translator and physician</note> were accustomed to give cold, fresh water to drink only once, and in a large quantity. I, however, to act more safely, would give three pounds of fresh barley water with three ounces of sugar. And perhaps I would also give half a pound of cucumber juice well mixed with one ounce of sugar, followed by an ounce of orange or pomegranate juice and one drachm <note>a small unit of weight</note> of sugar.

A certain countryman of ours, a robust man, as soon as this disease attacked him, immersed himself in cold waters and stayed there for two hours; upon coming out, he was cured. Nevertheless, this is a most deceptive experiment. Perhaps it would be safer to sit in lukewarm water that does not reach the chest, since these parts should not be opened, nor should the humors be provoked toward them. In this case, some have even taken poisons—especially those of a cold nature, and perhaps even those of a warm nature—either before or after **theriac** <note>a famous polypharmaceutical "universal antidote"</note> or **sealed earth** with **Armenian bole**, and vinegar mixed with water, and similar things that act against poison. Among these people, a certain physician was cured. However, it seems to me a very dangerous matter.

### SYNOPSIS OF EPIDEMIC ANTIDOTES

...Armenian bole <note>original: *bolum armenum*, a medicinal red clay used as an astringent and antidote</note>; this is the difference between them: although both are effective against poison and disease, wise physicians nevertheless use "sealed earth" <note>original: *terra sigillata*, clay pressed into tablets and stamped with a seal to guarantee its origin and purity</note> more than the bole for other poisons. However, in cases of the pestilential disease <note>the plague</note>, they conversely prefer the Armenian bole. In this they all agree: that for other poisons, nothing is better than sealed earth, especially when administering it with a small amount of Armenian bole, juniper berries, and vinegar diluted according to the method of Galen. This is because it immediately constricts and closes the passages of the chest so that the poison cannot pass through them, and it expels the poison through vomiting. Likewise, for poison that can be drawn out through purgatives, it performs this function whether administered after or before the event, but it is safer before. Similarly, all agree that both for protecting oneself from the plague and for expelling it, Armenian bole surpasses all other simple medicines. This is especially true when it is administered with white wine and rose water according to the instructions of Galen, Serapion, and Avicenna <note>three of the most influential authorities in medieval and Renaissance medicine</note>. They claim to have experienced that during times of great pestilence, humors were easily preserved and healed with this remedy. For Armenian bole is red with a slight saffron tint, delicate, and easily broken; whereas sealed earth is somewhat reddish, slightly sour to the taste, dry, and somewhat viscous—yet not so sticky that it clings to the fingers.

Take note that sometimes the disease begins with an abundant spitting of blood. In this case, Armenian bole is not given, nor any other "strictive" <note>constricting or binding</note> medicine for this poisonous blood. Rather, this flow should be assisted with "pectoral" remedies <note>medicines for the chest and lungs</note>, and blood should be drawn from both saphenous veins <note>veins in the legs</note> to balance the quality of the temperament. If the patient is very "sanguine" <note>possessing an excess of blood, one of the four humors</note>, a bloodletting should also be performed afterward from the median vein <note>the middle vein of the arm</note>. Nor should one neglect rubbings performed on an empty stomach. 

See to it that the patient holds a sponge to their nose that has been soaked in rose water, rose vinegar, and fragrant wine; with these liquids, they should also frequently wash all their pulse points and their face. <center>ANTIDOTES FOR EPIDEMICS</center>

If a sign <note>likely referring to a plague bubo or swelling</note> appears, and the difficulty or shortage of time prevents the usual order of treatment, let <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: *phlebotomia*</note> and a purgation be performed. Once these are done, or at least the bloodletting, you shall prepare a <term>caustic application</term> <note>original: *ruptorium*, a substance used to irritate the skin and create a blister</note> and apply it to the same side of the body, at a distance of six fingers' width from the sign. There are those who do not trust the variability of timing, but instead, regardless of the usual order, they apply themselves to the remedies of the cure both before and after, as well as simultaneously, as best they can. The order followed by certain modern practitioners is such that, where nothing prevents it, the sick person is first purged with <term>enemas</term> <note>original: *clysteribus*</note>, powders, bloodletting, and medicine. Afterwards, however, the caustic applications must be applied as we have said (even **if no sign is appearing**). Indeed, it is safer to apply the caustics immediately (whether a sign appears or not) and the other things appropriate for this disease.

If the sign is visible, act as follows: If it appears around the ears, suddenly apply the caustic to the back of the neck on the same side as the sign. If it is under the arm, let the caustic be applied to the muscle of that same arm, or near the pulse, though not directly over it. If it is in the groin, place it near the ankle—that is, over the ankle bone of the same side. When it appears elsewhere, apply the caustic six fingers or two inches below the sign; however, let it never be placed, in any case, upon the chest. And if it should be in the throat, namely on the front part, let the caustic be placed at the back, specifically on the neck. But if it is in the back part of that same place, it should not be applied to the front, but rather below the site of the sign. You shall leave the caustic there until it has formed a blister, which you should then open and apply butter and cabbage leaves upon it; likewise a sponge soaked in this decoction:

Take a handful each of chamomile, <term>water dock</term> <note>original: *brictanicæ*</note>, sweet clover <note>original: *meliloti*</note>, and scabious. Let them boil in half a pound of water until half is consumed. Because this draws out the poison, keep renewing it frequently until the end of the treatment.

### Methods, Ways, and Conditions for Curing the Abscess. Chapter XIII.

This sign is called an **abscess** <term>original: *apostema*; a localized collection of pus or a swelling</term>. When it appears before the onset of fever, it indicates that the heart is strong and capable of expelling the poison; in such a case, the fever is merely a side effect of the abscess. It is the opposite when the abscess appears after the fever. This abscess is of two kinds: one is a **blister** <note>original: *bulla*</note>, known as **anthrax** or a **carbuncle**; the other is a **swelling** <note>original: *inflatio*</note>, known as a **bubo** or a **gland** <note>original: *glandula*</note>.

The blister usually emerges through the **emunctories** <term>original: *emunctoria*; historical medical term for the body's natural drainage points or lymph nodes</term>. The further it is from the vital organs, the less dangerous it is. A **black** one is the worst of all; **green** is the second worst; **bluish-grey** <note>original: *glauca*</note> is third; and **red** is fourth. Furthermore, the drier it is, the more dangerous it is.

The swelling usually appears in the emunctories—that is, the cleansing points of the vital organs—which are in three places: behind the ears, under the arms, and in the groin. The brain sends its poison down through the emunctories behind the ears and into the neck. The heart sends it under the arms. The liver sends it to or around the groin. For this reason, a swelling is worse than a blister, as it shows that much of the poison has flowed toward the vital organs. And the closer the swelling is to the heart, the more dangerous it is.

The cure for both the blister and the swelling is almost the same. There are those who, when the abscess appears before the fever and far from the heart, suddenly apply ligatures <note>tight bandages</note> between the site of the pain and the heart. They apply cold, dry things above the site to **repel** <note>original: *repercutiendi*; a treatment intended to drive "corrupt humors" away from the heart</note> the poison. However, directly upon the site of the pain, they place warm, moist, and **resolving** <note>original: *resolutivas*; substances meant to dissolve or break down the swelling</note> things. Others, as soon as the abscess begins to appear, apply **cupping glasses** <note>original: *ventosas*</note> both directly over it and to the side, as we have said, along with **caustics** <note>original: *ruptoria*</note>, administering this medicine immediately:

Take half a dram each of prepared black hellebore, senna, and cinnamon, and half a scruple of **diagridium** <term>original: *diagridij*; a preparation of scammony resin used as a potent laxative</term>. Let these be infused in four ounces of pomegranate wine and one ounce of sugar. It would be better if it sat in infusion for many hours; afterwards, strain and press it. This should be given to drink when the abscess appears, before the patient sleeps.

They prepare the **hellebore** <note>a toxic plant used in controlled doses as a powerful purgative</note> in this way: they cut it lengthwise into small pieces and place it inside a sweet apple. They wrap the apple in **tow** <note>original: *stuppis*; coarse flax or hemp fibers</note> previously soaked in rose water, and cook it under hot ashes. Once cooked, they throw away the apple and cook the hellebore again in another apple in the same manner as before; it is then kept separate from the apple. They give the hellebore to the most robust patients, mixed with the other ingredients in the manner and order described. To others, however, and those who are less robust, they give only...

## Rules and Methods for Applying Ruptories. Chapter XIV.

When it is not appropriate to draw blood with **cupping glasses** <term>original: *ventosis*; vessels used to create suction on the skin</term> or **leeches** <term>original: *sanguisugis*</term>, nor to burn a mark, **ruptories** <term>original: *ruptoria*; caustic substances applied to the skin to create a rupture or opening</term> should be applied either below the sign, or on both sides simultaneously, using the compositions I have mentioned and those I will describe in the following sections. You should apply the aforementioned treatments if the timing seems favorable after blood has been drawn and the patient has rested a little, or at least after the administration of medicine and its full effect. If a surgeon is not immediately available to perform the operation by hand, give the powder; if you do not have that, administer the medicine. If you have no medicine, apply the ruptories without delay above and outside the sign, with moderation and in the order we have described. If time is pressing and nothing has been done yet, administer the **purgation** <term>original: *purgationem*; the medicinal cleansing of the body's humors</term> and the ruptories at the same time. Never cease the administration of remedies, nor delay in the hope that you will do everything when the time is more convenient. 

Take care not to place things on the sign that are so cold and **styptic** <note>original: *stypticas*; substances that contract tissues to stop bleeding or secretions</note> that they drive the poison back inside. Use those things suitable for **drawing out** <note>original: *trahendum*</note> and **resolving** <note>original: *resoluendum*; dispersing or breaking down a swelling</note>, such as hot substances. These must sometimes be tempered if we use them alongside cold things to avoid excessive inflammation, yet not so cold that they **restrict** <note>original: *restringant*</note> the area. Do not fear the pain too much, for it draws the poison to the **abscess** <term>original: *apostema*</term>. However, I do not want you to tolerate excessive pain, as it would add strength to the poison, increase the fever, and exhaust the patient's nature too much. 

I do not want you to fully heal the site of the ruptory through medical art until three months have passed; when you finally do this, repeat the purgation. A certain **Florentine** fellow of ours cut open a **blister** <note>original: *bullam*</note> this spring. Because he was so liberated from the disease that he seemed no different from a healthy man, he closed the wound shortly thereafter. Yet, forty days later, he was infected by the disease again and died within two days; this happened largely because he had closed the wound without purgation. Know this: whoever dies after the seventh day, it happens more from poor care than from the nature of this disease. Know that after the poison flows to the abscess in such a way that the vital organs are relieved, if you do not draw it out well and continuously—rectifying and purging it—the internal poison of the abscess becomes more irritated, and the trapped vapor returns inside and kills. Therefore, continuously fortify the heart itself by narrowing its paths from the inside, and from the outside...

### Compound Ruptories and Certain Strong Plasters. Chapter XV.

There are many types of compound **ruptories** <term>original: *ruptoria*; caustic substances applied to the skin to create a rupture or opening</term>, which are strong in drawing poison to the outside. We shall describe many of them, so that you may conveniently use whichever aid is most appropriate for the situation. 

Take **figs** <term>original: *ficus*</term>, **orris root** <term>original: *ireos*</term>, and crushed wheat grains in equal parts; this ripens the swelling quickly and ruptures it. 
Also, leaven <note>yeast or fermented dough</note> with oil and salt. 
Also, **pitch** <term>original: *pix*; a sticky resin</term> with raisins and honey. 
Also, sparrow droppings with **hog's lard** <term>original: *axungia porci*</term>. 
Also, pulverized glass with **turpentine** <term>original: *terebinthina*</term>. 
Also, unless it were too loathsome, human excrement is very effective both before and after the rupture, by placing bread crumbs soaked in boiling oil on top. 
Also, oil boiled with ashes. 
Also, ten **Spanish flies** <term>original: *cantharides*; toxic beetles used in medicine to cause blistering</term>, with one ounce of raisins, one and a half ounces of leaven, and one ounce each of **scabious** <term>original: *scabiosa*; a flowering plant named for its use in treating skin ailments</term>, **hound's-tongue** <term>original: *cynoglossa*</term>, **great comfrey** <term>original: *consolidæ maioris*</term>, and **antidote** <term>original: *antipharmaci*</term>; let these be incorporated with oil of lilies. 
And if you wish to make it stronger, add salt, **pigeon-herb** <term>original: *columbinam herbam*; likely columbine or vervain</term>, and **rue** <term>original: *ruta*</term>, two **drachms** <term>original: *drachmas*; a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> each. 
Also, **watercress** <term>original: *nasturtium*</term> with oil and salt. 
Also, **orpiment** <term>original: *auripigmentum*; a toxic yellow mineral consisting of arsenic trisulfide</term> and pepper, two drachms each, with ten dried figs; make a plaster with as much honey as suffices. 

Also, **borax** <term>original: *baurach*</term>, **sal ammoniac** <term>original: *salis ammoniaci*; ammonium chloride</term>, scabious, antidote, garlic, and pepper in equal parts; make a plaster with the juice of scabious. 
Also, **galbanum** <term>original: *galbanum*; a bitter aromatic gum resin</term>, white lily roots, human excrement, and great comfrey crushed between two stones. 
Also, four ounces of leaven, one handful each of mustard, rue, scabious, and **wormwood** <term>original: *absintij*</term>, a third part of white lily roots, two drachms of **vitriol** <term>original: *vitrioli*; a sulfate mineral</term>, ten Spanish flies, one ounce of galbanum, three rancid nuts, and as much oil of white lilies as suffices; let the herbs and roots be cooked in the oil and made into a plaster, adding the other ingredients according to the art of the apothecary. 

Also, Spanish flies with soap oil. 
Also, four parts of **oak ash** <term>original: *cineris quercini*</term> (the kind that dyers use), and six parts of **lime** <term>original: *calcis*</term>; mix them, and when you use it, place the aforementioned plaster over it. But you shall make this newly mentioned plaster with oil of black olives, and it is stronger if the oil is boiled with the ashes. 
Also, equal parts of leaven, nettle, dried meat fat, **marshmallow root** <term>original: *barba maluauisci*</term>, and mallow. 

There are five herbs very suitable in this case, used both in all plasters and when taken internally, since they resist poison both inside and outside the body and are, as it were, tempered in their qualities: namely, **comfrey** <term>original: *consolida*</term>, **scabious** <term>original: *scabiosa*</term>, **agrimony** <term>original: *agrimonia*</term>, **water-dock** <term>original: *brictanica*</term>, and **birthwort** <term>original: *aristolochia*</term>.

### On Tempered Plasters. Chapter XVI.

**T**he aforementioned **ruptories** <term>original: *ruptoria*; caustic agents</term> and plasters are quite strong, both for breaking the skin and for quickly drawing out poison. However, they should not be used continuously, as they may cause excessive inflammation. Nevertheless, one might use them more often in cases where the **swelling** <term>original: *apostema*</term> is not a deep green, red, or black color. Furthermore, in cases where there is not much **corrosion** <note>The eating away or ulceration of the flesh.</note>, I shall provide certain more tempered and suitable remedies for when there is a fear of great inflammation.

Take two ounces of **marshmallow root** <term>original: *barbae malvavisci*</term>, one head of white lilies, and one and a half ounces each of flaxseed meal; let them boil in common water, and let them be crushed with leaven and **old lard** <term>original: *axungia veteri*</term>; apply it while warm. 

Also, take two handfuls of bran not entirely purged of flour, and let it be cooked in vinegar. 

Also, **pigeon dung** <term>original: *columbina*</term> with vinegar and rose oil. 

Also, barley flour with the juice of **brooklime** <term>original: *brictanica*</term> or **comfrey** <term>original: *consolida*</term>. 

Also, onions cooked with butter, adding afterward **dried figs** <term>original: *caricas*</term> and leaven; it can be sweetened with chamomile oil (if needed because of a harsh odor) by adding cooked apples, or marshmallow and mallow, and their **mucilages** <term>original: *nuccilagines*; the sticky, soothing extracts of the plants</term>. 

But if even greater soothing is needed, take cooked onions and cooked apples, namely with butter and chamomile oil. 

Also, take one handful each of mallow, marshmallow root, and **scabious** <term>original: *scabiosa*</term>; let the herbs boil in common water, with which the flour should be incorporated. Let the herbs be crushed and all seasoned together with one ounce of chicken fat, the same amount of chamomile oil, and half a drachm of saffron: for this is a most delicate plaster. 

Also, scabious, **dove’s foot** <term>original: *pes columbinus*; a type of geranium</term>, chicory, and **greater comfrey** <term>original: *consolida maior*</term>. 

Following these, a plaster of celery, brooklime, and **bitter vetch** <term>original: *orobus*</term> flour is suitable when mixed with the juices of the aforementioned herbs; according to some, it may also be mixed with **theriac** <note>A famous ancient "polypharmacy" antidote consisting of dozens of ingredients.</note>. 

Also, a plaster made of **opopanax** <term>original: *opopanax*; a gum resin</term> crushed with raisins. 

Also, **asafetida** <term>original: *assa*</term>, rue, and **nitre** <term>original: *nitrutum*</term> with honey. 

Sometimes it will be good to be anointed with theriac, with cooked onions and mallow placed on top. 

Some also place orange flowers and crushed leaves on top with lard and mallow. 

Regarding theriac itself, however, some argue that nothing should be placed over it, because it might drive the poison back inward.

Also, lentils mixed with bread and sifted bran.

## *On the manner of mitigating pain around the swelling itself. Chapter XVIII.*

The things treated in the previous chapter are confirmed for very black and corrosive blisters; but in others where there is not such great inflammation, be more moderate and more prepared to repel the heat and pain—partly arising from the disease, partly from the **ruptories** <term>original: *ruptoriis*; caustic agents used to break the skin</term>, or from the inflammation. 

If you wish to soothe it, place around the mark the crumb of warm, fresh bread taken first from the oven, soaked in sour wine or **plantain juice** <term>original: *succo plantaginis*</term>. Likewise, apply the aforementioned breadcrumb and also lentils in vinegar, and change it often; and so the plaster does not dry out, immediately place plantain leaves over it. When you remove the plaster, let the surface of the wound be washed with **astringent wine** <term>original: *vino pontico*</term> or sour wine; then apply barley flour with honey. 

However, I mean for these things to be placed not directly on, but *around* the wound, although according to **Peter of Tussignano** <note>A celebrated 14th-century physician from the University of Bologna known for his work on the plague.</note> and others who are both learned and experienced, these things we have mentioned do not repel much, but rather they drive out the heat, strengthen the site of the pain, and resolve it with a certain moderate warmth. Afterward, treat the remaining wound with those things which pertain to poisonous and corrosive wounds.

In order for the wound to form a proper crust <note>In this context, a "crust" refers to a scab or eschar.</note>, which you will later peel away after using the mentioned plaster, let it be anointed with butter and oil. However, do not remove the crust with any violence (for that would do much harm); wait until nature begins to do this on her own, and then assist her with the aforementioned remedies. Apply this cupping glass, for thus the poisonous blood must be drawn out from the depths, and it must be prevented from returning back inside.

### On the method of cleansing the wound. Chapter XX.

Once the abscess has ruptured and the matter of the venom has been extracted, tightening and cleansing medicines should be administered. Take barley flour with honey and a small amount of salt, and place cabbage leaves over it. Also take powdered **sarcocolla** <term>original: *sarcocollam*; a Persian tree resin used to "glue" wounds together</term> and an equal part of honey; if you wish it to be stronger, boil the honey first, and afterward add the sarcocolla. According to **Gentile da Foligno** and **Pietro da Tossignano** <note>Gentile (d. 1348) and Pietro (d. 1401) were famous Italian physicians whose works on the plague became standard medical textbooks</note>, this is a solemn and respected composition, as it cleanses every wound and every foul-smelling sore. I likewise recommend for this purpose the **diachylon** <term>original: *diaquilon*; a common medicinal plaster usually made of lead and plant mucilage</term> plaster.

### On the method of regenerating healthy flesh. Chapter XXII.

When the wound has been cleansed, to regenerate healthy flesh, take leaves of **basil** <note>original: *basiliconis*</note> that have been very well crushed. Also take equal parts of the yellow of **great centaury**, the herb **cinquefoil** <note>original: *pentaphyllon*</note>, and **great comfrey** <note>original: *consolidæ maioris*</note>; let them be distilled in Spring through an alembic, or make a juice from these herbs, and let them sit together until they are well mixed. Afterward, add a fifth part of **spirits** <term>original: *aquæ vitæ*; literally "water of life," referring to distilled alcohol or brandy</term> to them and save for use; for you will find this miraculous in regenerating flesh. Also useful for this is **asphodel root**, which is **burdock** <note>original: *lappa*</note>, cooked with the dregs of wine. Also a plaster made of fresh coriander with honey and raisins.

### On various ways of drawing blood from the mark. On the method of cauterizing by fire. Chapter XXIII.

All the care mentioned above regarding the mark <note>The "mark" or "sign" refers to the physical site of the plague boil</note>, which (as we have related before) is done with simple and compound **corrosives** <term>original: *ruptorijs*; substances intended to break or burn the skin</term>, would be made more praiseworthy, in the opinion of all the Italian Doctors, by the method we are about to describe, setting aside those corrosives and doing as follows: Place the **cauteries** <term>original: *cauteria*; tools used for searing the skin</term> at a distance from the mark as we have already said, and at the same time place a large cupping glass over the mark itself. Once it is removed, touch the spot in various places with a **razor** <term>original: *rasorio*</term>...

...and a small lancet, then put the cupping glass <term>original: *ventosam*; a glass vessel used to create a vacuum on the skin</term> back in place so that it may draw out the blood; when the blood ceases to be drawn, remove it. Next, apply three well-cleaned leeches <term>original: *sanguisugas*</term>, and once these are full and removed, cut open young roosters or pigeons <note>A common medieval practice; the warmth and "vital spirit" of the freshly killed animal were thought to draw out the plague's venom.</note> through the middle, and apply them one after another while still warm. Afterward, according to some authorities, the site should be joined with **theriac** <term>original: *theriaca*; a famous ancient "universal antidote" made of dozens of ingredients</term>, and then you should allow the patient to rest. 

In place of these methods, some practitioners pluck the area around the anus of a rooster and take about an ounce of somewhat dark, almost greenish soap, and half a **scruple** <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 1.3 grams.</note> of opium. They grind these well and, with very finely powdered white salt, they make a suppository for the rooster, and then place the bird's anus directly over the site. When this is finished, restore the patient's strength and afterward lightly cauterize him. I do not mean with wax or boiling oil—for these cause blockages—but with glowing gold, or silver, or iron. The instrument itself should have a round, flat surface at the tip in the shape of a large enough **farthing** <term>original: *quadrantis*; a small coin</term>, and in the middle of this flat surface, there should be a sharp edge or point in the shape of a diamond, though not too sharp. After the cauterization, rub it with butter and cover the place with a cabbage leaf, and let the patient rest. This is much more desirable than using **ruptories** <term>original: *ruptorijs*; caustic chemicals used to break the skin</term>, because it works faster, drives out the venom more effectively, and leaves the limb in a better condition. Afterward, use the dressings to be placed on and around the wound which we mentioned above to be administered after a ruptory, and in the same manner. 

Some who labor under the pestilential disease show no other sign than spots, like **measles** <term>original: *morbilli*; here referring to the dark red or purple spots, called petechiae, associated with the plague</term>, scattered across the skin of the body. Such patients should be wrapped in a warm scarlet cloth <note>The "color cure" was a popular medical theory; red cloth was believed to draw heat and blood to the surface to expel toxins.</note> and guarded from the cold. Let two large, warm sponges be applied to the back over the kidneys and to the chest; these should be soaked in a decoction of **melilot** <note>A type of sweet clover.</note>, chamomile, and lentils, then well wrung out, and applied while the stomach is empty. They should be changed often. You shall also give as a drink a decoction of dried figs, lentils, dyer’s grains, and saffron.

### *On the cure according to the custom of the Spaniards and Catalans. Chapter XXV.*

We have spoken in the preceding sections about the cure of this disease according to the intentions of the Greeks, the Latins, and also the Barbarians <note>In this context, "Barbarians" usually refers to Arabic medical authorities like Avicenna or Rhazes.</note>, and especially according to the use of the Italians. At present, we shall consider these medicines according to the custom of the Spaniards and also the Catalans. According to them, a **clyster** <term>original: *clystere*; an enema</term> is administered immediately; afterward, if the blood is too abundant, **phlebotomy** <term>original: *phlebotomia*; bloodletting</term> is performed. If not, medicine is administered according to the quality of the "offending humor" <note>Referring to the Four Humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Illness was seen as an imbalance of these fluids.</note>. From the beginning, they apply an **epithem** <term>original: *epithema*; a liquid poultice or medicated compress</term>. Then, after some evacuation has been made—at least with a clyster—they proceed to the treatment of the abscess <term>original: *apostematis*</term>. Also, according to their custom, nothing that inflames or burns should be placed over the abscess, because such things induce spasms and fever...

# EPIDEMIC ANTIDOTES

<note>original: *iii*; a signature mark used by printers to keep the pages in order.</note>
<meta>The text at the left margin is slightly cut off at the first line. Catchword: mark (signo).</meta>

...fevers ignite and make the poison <term>original: *venenum*; the toxic matter believed to cause the plague</term> more malignant, especially if the abscess <term>original: *apostema*; a swelling or boil</term> is located in the emunctories <term>original: *emunctoria*; the body's natural "cleansing" areas like the armpits, groin, and neck, where lymph nodes are located</term>. They also say that ripening agents <term>original: *maturantia*; medicines meant to bring a boil to a "head"</term> that are overly softening should not be applied at the beginning, because they "glue," block, and cause putrefaction; they cause the area to boil over and drive the poison inward. Nor should cold things be administered, they say, nor anything applied with a sponge or a cloth (because it dries things out), as this shuts the vapors inside and constricts the area.

However, using clean wool or oakum <note>original: *stuppa*; coarse fibers of flax or hemp used as a dressing.</note> (especially from hemp) is praiseworthy. The following decoction <note>A liquid medicine made by boiling medicinal plants.</note> is most familiar, particularly for those who are delicate by nature, and also for use on the emunctories: Take chamomile flowers, melilot <note>Sweet clover, often used as a soothing anti-inflammatory.</note>, and maidenhair fern <term>original: *capillos veneris*</term>; boil them in water, soak the wool or oakum, wring it out with your hands, and apply it while warm or slightly hot. Renew it every hour until the swelling resolves or opens. After it has opened and five days have passed, use ripening agents and those things which cleanse and regenerate the flesh.

To break the blisters <term>original: *bullis*</term>, one may safely apply crushed scabious <note>scabiosa: a plant traditionally used to treat skin eruptions and "scabs."</note>, either alone or with old, salted pig lard <term>original: *axungia porci*</term>. If the blister is green or black, but is not located in the emunctories, you should open it immediately in various parts with a lancet <term>original: *lanceola*</term> or a razor <term>original: *rasorio*</term>, so that the poison may exit quickly. Then wash the blister with salt water; so that clotted blood does not remain there, apply leeches <term>original: *sanguisugas*</term>. After it has been ruptured and purged of poison, and after five days have passed (as mentioned above), apply ripening, cleansing, and regenerating medicines.

Beyond these things (unless the patient is of a very tender age), a large cupping glass <term>original: *ventosa*</term> should be placed not directly over, but under the blister at a distance of six fingers. Afterward, an opening should be made with a lancet or razor, and the cupping glass reapplied to draw out blood—specifically two or three ounces, or even more, depending on the patient's condition and the strength of their vital spirit.

**Take heed** when a mark <term>original: *signo*; the physical manifestation of the plague, such as a bubo or spot</term> exists in the emunctories: do not apply cupping glasses directly to the mark itself, nor cut it, nor disturb it too much with frequent cupping. Doing so increases spasms, draws many "hot humors," and makes the poison worse; many perish by doing this. Rather, if a mark of this kind appears near the ears or in the throat, apply the cupping glass behind, under the vertebrae of the neck, or on the shoulder blades, but not directly on the mark. If it appears under the arms, apply the cupping glass on the same side, slanted toward the back. If it is in the groin, apply the cupping glass on the thigh, or behind under the buttocks.

In any of these cases, do as follows: Place the cupping glass six fingers away from the mark (as we have said), and by scarifying <note>Making small, shallow cuts in the skin to allow for bloodletting.</note>, draw blood with the cupping glasses or leeches. But on the mark itself, you shall place the aforementioned decoction to mildly soothe and resolve it. Along with the decoction, it would be good if you could apply some stone that draws out poison, either powdered or whole, such as an emerald <term>original: *smaragdus*</term>, a hyacinth <term>original: *hyacinthus*; likely a zircon or sapphire in this period</term>, or a topaz <term>original: *topazius*</term>. Nevertheless, according to some, we can also place over [the mark]...

Others add two ounces of coarse bread leaven—or more or less, depending on the need for drawing and bursting—which is more suitable for blisters than for swellings of the emunctories.

This herb causes an ulceration <note>a deliberate sore</note> in the emunctories <term>original: *emunctoriorum*; the body's natural drainage points like the armpits or groin</term> which draws the humors toward itself and away from the vital organs. Furthermore, he forbids these from ever being placed directly upon the sign; nor does he wish them to be applied unless the sign is outside of the emunctories, and even then, only before the third day and around the area, not directly on top. Armenian bole can also be administered after the seventh day once the wound has been purged of poison, by anointing the surrounding area. Thus, it is appropriate on the third day before the wound has become poisonous, and it is appropriate after the seventh day once the wound is cleared of poison. The surrounding area should be anointed with rose oil, rose vinegar, and rose water to protect the limb. 

Up to this point, we have recounted the opinions of the Spanish and Catalan doctors, along with the corrections of Arnald <note>Arnald of Villanova, a famous 13th-century physician</note> and Raymond, those singular physicians. It is a true matter—and Raymond is of this opinion—that a patient should not be purged through bloodletting, medicine, or vomiting when the aposteme <term>original: *apostema*; a large swelling or abscess</term> is completely full and poisonous. This is the case once the second day has passed, lest the poison be turned back inward by such a movement. 

This opinion, however, seems to require correction according to others; they argue that a patient should indeed be purged if necessary (following the aforementioned precautions) even after the second day. However, this must be done in such a way that while the patient is being purged, you apply cupping glasses <term>original: *ventosas*; heated glass jars used to create suction on the skin</term> and leeches <term>original: *sanguisugas*</term> both below and above the sign, and that the heart is defended internally and externally with "cold" cordials <note>medicines intended to cool and strengthen the heart</note>. This method is not entirely foreign to the intentions of the aforementioned Raymond.

They should carry burning torches in their hands, and well-lit coals smoking with pleasant odors; they should wash the whole body with warm vinegar twice a day—namely, in the morning and in the evening. One should change clothes frequently and renew the fumigations more often, especially using frankincense, turpentine, juniper, myrtle, sandalwood, roses, and camphor, or rosemary, laurel, and similar things. 

One should hold an orange in the hands, along with a bundle of rue, or greater germander <note>original: *querculæ maioris*; literally "little oak," a name often used for wall-germander</note>, and mint and lemon balm with myrtle and fresh flowers. One may also drink a small amount of this mixture and keep a sponge soaked in the same aforementioned mixture held to the nostrils, tied to a piece of ash wood <note>original: *ligno fraxini*</note>. For the ash tree has such power against poison that no venomous animal dares to approach its shadow, nor even its scent; indeed, such a creature would sooner give itself up to be burned by fire than remain close to this tree. One should frequently build fires and keep a hearth throughout the whole house, especially with wood and fragrant materials. 

Nor should anyone who has once been freed from this disease think that they cannot thereafter perish from it. For in the present year, this disease attacked one of our Florentines who, though he was perfectly cured a second time, could not escape death the third time. In that same year, in the month of September, I cured a certain poor woman of the plague; she was indeed healthy, like the others who had always remained safe. But when she spent time among the sick, after eighteen days she was infected again and died. 

In this matter, no one should trust in the fact that they are stronger or healthier than others, because the poison kills the strong just as it does the weak. In fact, this poison harms the sanguine <term>original: *sanguineos*; a personality or body type in the Four Humors theory, characterized by an abundance of blood, which was considered hot and moist</term> and the robust more than others, because the paths to their chests are open, and they have a very hot heart and much hot, moist blood. Therefore, the heat of the heart itself draws much of the destructive air through the open passages, and indeed draws it in suddenly before it can be tempered by the passage. Furthermore, the heat of the blood is very quickly ignited and inflamed. The moisture, into which the poison is converted, immediately undergoes putrefaction. Indeed, just as the more wine there is in a vessel, and the more potent it is, the more and more biting the vinegar becomes when it turns; so the potent poison becomes all the more abundant as the blood in the chest is hotter. Since the blood itself becomes the poison, it is very easily transformed into the same through even a small contact. For the parts, once touched, transform one another into poison. Nor...

# BOOK IV.

...lest it escape you, O you who carry out the care of the patient, that the closer you are to them—whether by kinship or by a similarity of temperament <term>original: *complexionis*; the specific balance of the four humors</term>, nature, or astrological constellation—the greater the danger of contagion you face. This is because there is a certain readiness in the quality of movement so that a transformation of like into like can be fulfilled, just as fire moves toward air, air toward water, and water toward earth. 

When two lutes <term>original: *citharæ*; stringed instruments like harps or lyres</term> or two fiddles are tuned to the same melody, then indeed the vibration and the sound of one resonates in the other. If you ask, however, by what paths the poison enters? I respond: through all the pores of the body, and especially those that are more open. It strikes more quickly when it enters through the nose, through the mouth, and through the pulses; it is much stronger if it finds the pathways open in those of warm, moist, and subtle humors. If it also originates from similar humors, and if the influence of Mars occurs in a different and contrary way, and under a Saturnine influx, it demonstrates itself more slowly. 

Often the poison remains in clothing for a long time, and on the skin where the pores are open, and in the veins near the heart. No one seems to be burdened by it then, because it is a very small and light vapor, nor does it have an opposition to the other parts as it does to the heart; but as soon as the slightest bit of it is brought into contact with the heart, it causes manifest, not hidden, harm. Similarly, the poison of a rabid dog, and others as well, reveal their injury even after a long period of time. 

Finally, I would have you know this: that the poison remains in persons for a space of two months. Walls, ironwork, and things constructed from wood, unless they are corrected with washings, fumigations, and fires, will perhaps retain their poisonous quality for a year or more. Woolen clothes and that sort, unless they are aired out, washed, and frequently fumigated, or placed by the fire, in the wind, or in the sun, remain infected for three years and beyond. 

You know indeed the musty smell of an orange <note>original: *arancij*</note> in a box where it has moldered, how it is preserved for many years. Similarly, the scent of musk remains for a long time in the cotton <note>original: *bombace*</note> where it was previously kept. Indeed, just as oil is to fire, so wool is the nourishment of this poison; and indeed, this wool nourishes the poison in such a way that it not only preserves it, but increases and strengthens it at the same time. One must not use the vessels of those who are infected for the preparation of food or drink, nor should anything that has adhered to them be touched. 

You must live joyfully, because happiness strengthens the vital spirit. Live temperately and soberly, for sobriety and temperance are of such value that by these means alone, during many and indeed severe plagues that occurred in Athens, the philosopher Socrates kept himself unharmed. Aristotle and Galen say that the disposition in pure bodies is such that they almost never feel the plague, or if they are infected, at least they do not perish. Behold, I now hand over to you two unique things to preserve yourself: Prepare an emerald <term>original: *smaragdum*</term> so that it can be drunk, and another to be touched or held in the mouth...

...and it should be hung from the neck. Its power against poisons is so great that, according to the testimony of Rhazes <note>original: "Rasi"; Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (854–925 AD), a Persian polymath and influential physician</note>, Avenzoar <note>Abu Marwan Abd al-Malik ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a famous Arab physician from Al-Andalus</note>, and Serapion <note>Likely Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syriac Christian physician</note>, vipers <note>original: "tyris"</note> and toads <note>original: "bubonibus"</note> immediately lose their sight just by looking at it. To the poor, I am accustomed to give wild radish <term>original: "raphanum syluestrem"</term>, a little at a time, so that it does not inflame the blood; for it has such great efficacy against poison that it causes a scorpion to burst upon contact. And Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> says that if its seed is crushed with vinegar and used to wash the hands, snakes cannot harm one by touch. The bezoar stone <term>original: "Lapis bezoar"; a mass found in the digestive tract of certain animals, highly prized in the Middle Ages as a universal antidote</term> (if anyone is able to obtain it) is powerful above all things against poisons. For although in the Persian language all things that have the property and virtue of expelling poison are commonly called "bezoar" by the ancients, yet according to Serapion and Rhazes, the name "bezoar" is principally given to a certain stone that resists all poisons—whether hot or cold diseases—and all poisonous ulcers by its own virtue. It is beneficial whether taken by mouth, held in the mouth, hung from the neck, or finally, applied externally in any manner whatsoever. It originates in Syria, India, and parts of the East, and it is diverse, appearing in three different colors. For some are gray and dark, some are gray, dark, and green, while another kind is white and somewhat pale gray, resembling the color of clear white wine. This last type is the best among the others—smooth, delicate, soft, without flavor, and shining like light. Its dose, when taken by mouth, is twelve grains. Rhazes and Serapion testify that they frequently discovered in their own times that this most precious stone, by its own inherent quality, surpassed all medicines—both simple and compound—as well as the compound theriacs <term>original: "theriacas"; complex medicinal pastes used as universal antidotes</term> in resisting poisons. Hahamed <note>An Arabic medical authority</note> says it should be set in a ring, and the image of a scorpion should be engraved upon the stone when the Moon is in Scorpio, while observing the sign as it ascends. When this is done, incense should be sealed with it when the Moon is in the sign of Scorpio. If, afterward, you give a proper amount of this pulverized incense in a drink to one who has been poisoned, it will be as effective against poisons as the stone itself. Abdallahamarach says that he saw this stone, which the son of Mamari is said to have purchased, giving the palace of Córdoba in exchange for the stone's weight <note>This anecdote emphasizes the stone's extreme value, worth an entire palace</note>. Serapion says that the same stone works wonders not only in humans, but also in certain other animals: first, that by touching a scorpion's stinger with this stone, it loses its power to sting. Furthermore, he asserts that when crushed and mixed with water and placed in a serpent's mouth, it kills it.

### BOOK IV. ###

(when you speak with him) stay back at least by a distance of six cubits <note>About nine feet; a cubit was roughly the length of a forearm</note>, and stay in the open air, or a well-ventilated place, and take care that the breath of the winds does not blow from him toward you. Let there be the sun, fire, fragrances, or the wind blowing toward him between you and him: for narrow places, and at the same time a crowd of people, are very dangerous. I also mention this: that the morbid contagion is multiplied by the enclosure of walls, and the touching and continuation of houses. Above all things, I advise that you flee quickly and far from those places where the plague is imminent, and return slowly <note>This is the famous medical advice "Cito, Longe, Tarde" (Flee quickly, go far, return slowly)</note>. I said quickly—that is, as soon as the signs of an approaching plague appear. These signs indeed are when the air of that place seems to be outside its natural state, leaning toward heat and humidity; when it appears foggy, with thick clouds, or dusty; when the winds are heavy and warm; and also when the waters and fields smoke and smell. Likewise, when the fish have a bad taste and smell. 

When many animals appear on the earth born from putrefaction <note>The author refers to "spontaneous generation," the discarded theory that small animals like insects or vermin were born directly from decaying matter</note>, along with an abundance of mushrooms and rotted herbs; when the fruits of the earth and animals are tasteless and do not keep well; and when wines become cloudy. When many animals, both of the land and the air, depart from that place; when unusual fevers arise—hidden, raging, continuous, and deceptive—with anxiety in the chest, with a collapse of the pulse, frenzy <term>phrenesis: an inflammation of the brain causing delirium</term>, turbulent urine, sores of the palate and intestines, redness of the eyes, worms, measles <term>morbilli: "little diseases," often referring to measles or other eruptive fevers</term>, many disturbances among women, rabid anger, quarrels, dire wars, monsters of nature, and wondrous signs, either of nature or from God, many of them unseen and rare. For these things which we have said are omens of an approaching plague. 

Then, therefore, flee before you become one of the twelve thousand marked ones <note>Original: "duodecim mille signatis"; likely an apocalyptic reference to those marked for death or those "sealed" in the Book of Revelation</note>. This [infection] can happen in two ways: namely, either because you will have already been caught by the contagion of the infected, or because you have already received the dismal quality of the infected air, so that gradually that air becomes familiar to you, so that neither nature resists the air, nor the air resists nature; but if you suddenly seek a different breeze, the first air will depart, and nature will resist it, and it will resist nature, from which comes the origin of the plague <note>The author believes that the body "adjusts" to bad air; a sudden change to clean air might then cause a violent internal reaction</note>. 

And I also advise you to flee far away, namely that you betake yourself to those places where neither things, nor persons, nor sounds, noises, or any rumors of the infected place can reach you. And thus be so remote that high mountains stand in between, by which the access of vapor is prevented, so that they cannot reach you by the blowing of the winds or the expansion of the air. Consider the disposition and site of the place to which you run, namely that it is not similar in any way to the pestilential air—such as in its heat, cold, humidity, dryness, clouds, rains, or winds. Finally, be established in such a place that winds, clouds, and rains cannot blow, expand, or move from there toward you. Nor let this escape you: that the horoscope or Ascendant <term>Ascendens: the sign of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time, believed to govern the health of a city</term> of any infected city or castle often extends the plague to all those places which, from the beginning, were [subject] to that city or castle...

# ANTIDOTES FOR EPIDEMICS #

...and hang it from the neck. Its power against poisons is so great that, according to the testimony of Rhazes, Avenzoar, and Serapion <note>Rasis (Rhazes), Avenzoar, and Serapion were highly influential medieval Islamic physicians whose works were translated into Latin and became standard medical textbooks in Europe</note>, the eyes of vipers and owls <note>original: "tyris, & bubonibus"</note> immediately fall out of their own accord just by the sight of it. For the poor, I am accustomed to give wild radish, but only a little at a time, so that it does not inflame the blood; for it has such great efficacy against poison that it causes a scorpion to burst from the mere touch of it. And Dioscorides <note>A famous 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> says that if one’s hands are washed with its seed crushed with vinegar, serpents can do no harm at all when touched. 

The Bezoar stone <term>Lapis bezoar: a mass found in the stomachs of certain animals (like goats), prized in the Middle Ages as a universal antidote</term> (if anyone is able to obtain one) is powerful above all things against poisons. For although in the Persian language that whole category of things whose property and virtue is to expel poison is usually called "bezoar" by the ancients, according to Serapion and Rhazes, a certain stone is principally called "bezoar" which, by its own virtue, resists all poisons—both hot and cold diseases—and all poisonous ulcers. It is beneficial whether it is taken by mouth, held in the mouth, hung from the neck, or finally applied externally in any manner whatsoever. It originates in Syria, in India, and in parts of the East, and is of various types and three different colors. For some are gray and dark, some are gray, dark, and green, while another is white and somewhat grayish—namely, similar to the color of clear white wine. This last one is the best among the others: smooth, delicate, soft, without taste, and shining like light. Its dose, when taken by mouth, is twelve grains <note>A grain was a very small unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams</note>. Rhazes and Serapion testify that they often found in their own times that this most precious stone, by its own quality, surpassed all medicines—both simple and compound—as well as compound theriacs <term>Theriaca: a complex "miracle" ointment or potion used against poison and plague</term> in resisting poisons. 

Hahamed says that it should be set in a ring, and an image of a scorpion should be engraved upon the stone when the moon is in Scorpio, while observing that sign as it rises. Once this is done, frankincense should be sealed with it when the moon is in the sign of Scorpio. If, afterward, you give a proper quantity of this powdered frankincense to a poisoned person in a drink, it will be as effective against poisons as the stone itself. Abdallahamarach <note>Likely a Latinization of an Arabic author's name</note> says he saw this stone, which he says the son of Mamar purchased, and that he gave a palace in Cordoba <note>A major city in Islamic Spain</note> in payment for the stone. Serapion says the same stone works wonders not only in humans, but also in certain other animals: first, that by touching a scorpion's stinger with this stone, it loses its power to sting. Furthermore, he asserts that when crushed and mixed with water and placed in a serpent's mouth, it kills it.

As for the condition of the air alone, one period of service <note>original: "angaria"; a term usually referring to a period of forced labor or a specific duty, here used to denote a set term of quarantine.</note> is sufficient; so that if everyone staying there has remained free from this disease for three months, it can be judged that the air is now purged. But be most cautious in approaching and touching those things which retain the poison longer than the air does. The projections of furnaces <note>original: "proinctus fornacium"; likely referring to the soot, bricks, or interior structures of ovens and fireplaces which were thought to trap heat and "poison."</note> in walls preserve the poisonous heat longer than wood does. However, these are purified (as we have often said) namely with fires, washings, ventilation, fumigations, scents, and the rest.

Humans are commonly purified in the space of fourteen days; houses, woodwork, and other things in twenty-one days. Fabrics, clothing, and such things in the space of twenty-eight days. During these times, keep separate vessels for drinking and eating, as well as all bedding <note>original: "lectisternia"; specifically the coverings or arrangements of a bed or couch.</note>; or at least, if you cannot manage the rest, purify the remaining linens with washings and fumigations. Horses, money, furniture, small bundles, and such things tend to preserve the poison for a long time unless you act with extreme caution; therefore, be vigilant, cautious, and prudent, and provide an orderly plan for everything.

# ON ASTROLOGY

### How a celestial theme might be constructed through the tables contained in ephemerides, omitting complex equations. <note>An "ephemeris" (plural "ephemerides") is a book of tables providing the daily positions of the sun, moon, and planets. "Equations" here refer to the complex mathematical adjustments usually required for high precision.</note>

To construct a celestial figure, three things are required: a certain time for which you seek the position of the heavens; the position of the Zodiac distributed through the twelve houses of heaven as it actually exists at that time; and thirdly, the placement of the planets in the zodiac just as they are at that same time.

A certain time is obtained in several ways: but it is more certain through an **Astrolabe**, a **quadrant**, a **sphere**, or another instrument of this kind. It is not so certain—for many reasons—through mobile clocks <note>Mechanical or portable watches were still relatively inaccurate in Gallucci’s time compared to astronomical observations.</note>, which men now use almost everywhere.

Furthermore, time is measured by the year, month, day, hour, minute, first, second, third, and so on up to ten <note>These "firsts" and "seconds" refer to the base-60 (sexagesimal) divisions of a degree or an hour.</note>.

Different people take the beginning of the daily measurement from different parts of the day: some from the setting of the Sun, others from midnight, others from the rising of the Sun, and others from noon, as Astrologers do.

However, so that the matter may be completed according to plan, once you have the hour with the <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupulis"; here meaning minutes or small fractions of an hour.</note> of your day, if they are present, you must carefully note what kind of hours you have, and those must be reduced to astrological hours—that is, post-meridian <note>Hours counted starting from noon (12:00 PM).</note> hours. Since for the sake of brevity we wish to use ephemerides for this task, and these tables are constructed for these specific hours, our time must be adjusted to match them.

This is done in the following way in Italy, where the hours begin from the setting of the Sun. When it is not possible to obtain the post-meridian time through an Astrolabe (for then there is no need to calculate what you already have, since the Astrolabe shows post-meridian time), it is done, I say, in this way, which I declare to you by this example: I wish to know, on the 10th day of September at the 8th hour of the preceding night—at which time I was writing these things in Venice—what hour it is after the noon of the preceding day. For the ninth day, which begins from noon, had not yet passed. First, I look in the ephemeris for the year, then the month, and finally the ninth day. On that day, it must be seen in which place of the zodiac the Sun is located, which the first column under the title **☉** <note>The symbol for the Sun.</note> will show you. It is at 16 degrees, 34 minutes, and 25 seconds of **♍** <note>The symbol for Virgo.</note>. Without error, it should be said in this place to be at 17 degrees of Virgo. 

With this degree, I enter the tables of the length of days, which begin in the ephemerides of Magini <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617) was a famous astronomer and mathematician whose tables were standard tools for astrologers.</note> on page 53. There, I seek this degree of the Sun in the table for the latitude of Venice, at 45 degrees (for such is the latitude of this city); and this same process must be followed for other cities using their own specific tables. It is necessary for you to seek this degree in that table, but it must be noted that a double order of degrees is present there: namely, ascending and descending. The ascending corresponds to signs in the lower part of the table, and the descending to signs placed in the upper part. Therefore, once the degree of the Sun and the sign in which it resides are found, the common angle will give you the arc, or the "semi-diurnal" <note>The "semi-diurnal arc" is half the time the sun spends above the horizon on a given day.</note> value, of 6 Hours and 21 Minutes. This represents the time from the noon of the 9th day until the setting of the Sun, at which time...

...is the beginning of our hours, which I said are 8.
